Ghana News.title: Trump to welcome investors at gala for his plunging meme coin
Ghana News.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump is applauded at the White House Crypto Summit

US President Donald Trump will headline his third meme coin gala on ‌Sunday night at his country club outside Washington, DC, for top token holders, whose tokens were once worth about $75 each but are now valued at less than $1.

Less than 20 months after the first $TRUMP token gala set off a frenzy among 220 wealthy crypto holders vying for spots at the dinner with ​the president, interest has waned for the latest affair at the Trump National club in Sterling, Virginia.

Organisers said 185 ​crypto wallets qualified for the dinner, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed only ⁠130 wallets when the contest concluded on November 16. Together, those listed wallets held only $8.6 million — a shadow of the $148 million listed for the first dinner in May 2025, when a time-weighted holding of $18.5 million took the top spot.

According to the contest's website, the top 29 winners—those with the highest time-weighted holdings during the contest scoring period from September 30 to November 16—will join a VIP reception with the president and receive a gift bag with Trump swag. The top four also get an 18-karat, Trump-branded gold watch.

Trump and his family have monetized ​his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures during his foray into politics.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly ​listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday's dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, ‌according to ⁠an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

Democratic leaders in the House and the Senate, where the party won a resounding victory in the midterm elections, have vowed to investigate what they say are unprecedented conflicts of interest posed by the Trump family’s business dealings during Trump’s presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that ​would ban such activities.

The Trump ​Meme Coin project and the ⁠White House did not respond to requests for comment, although the Trump administration has long said the president's business interests are clean.

"Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — ​in conflicts of interest," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters earlier this year. "President Trump proudly made ​the United States ⁠the crypto capital of the world through executive actions."

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5 billion, according to a Reuters analysis.

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635 million, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3 billion through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth ​crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about $430 million.

Ghana News.title: Fela never recovered from his mother’s death – Femi Kuti
Ghana News.content:
Afrobeat legend Femi Kuti has said that his late father, Afrobeat pioneer Fela Anikulapo-Kuti, never fully recovered from the death of his mother, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, before his own demise.

Speaking in a recent interview with OkayAfrica, Kuti said Fela lost "everything" after his mother's death due to government persecution.

The multiple Grammy-nominated musician recalled that Fela was unjustly imprisoned by the Buhari military regime and was only later released by Buhari's successor, Ibrahim Babangida, but he became poor and was living with 150 people in a three-bedroom apartment.

He explained that Fela only bounced back financially after he began touring abroad with his band.

He said, "Fela was very rich and famous, but the government did everything to break him. He declared his compound a 'danger zone' and brutally attacked it.

"He fled to Ghana, and when he returned to Nigeria, the Buhari regime unjustly jailed him.

"The new head of state, Babangida, released him from prison, but he came out poor. He was accommodating 150 people in a three-bedroom apartment.

"He only bounced back financially after he began touring abroad with his band.

“I don’t think Fela ever recovered from his mother’s loss.”

Kuti said he believes Fela would have found solace in the recognition he is currently getting from award bodies such as the Grammy, the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and others if he were alive today, even though he wasn't a fan of awards during his lifetime.

Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti died on April 13, 1978, from injuries sustained during a February 18, 1977 military raid on Fela’s Kalakuta Republic compound in Lagos.

Fela released his song 'Coffin for Head of State' as a protest over his mother's unjust death.

Ghana News.title: FIP Bronze S2 Accra: Ghana takes major step in Padel development with historic tournament
Ghana News.content:
Ghana made history on Sunday as the first International Padel Federation Bronze tournament in the country successfully concluded at the S2 Sport Club in Spintex, Accra.

The FIP Bronze S2 Accra, which offered world ranking points and entry into the professional circuit, ran for a week and crowned champions in both the men’s and women’s categories.

Spain’s Adrian Lopez and Guillem Santiago claimed the men’s title after beating Egypt’s George Wakim and Morocco’s Mohamed Alami in straight sets.

The Spanish pair won 6-4, 6-1 following a tougher semi-final earlier in the day.

Santiago says he is already looking forward to returning to Ghana for the next edition.

“Great tournament. Great crowd. Great organisation. It’s our first time here, and we enjoyed it a lot. I hope we will come back next year.”

In the women’s category, Spain’s Cayetana Sanchez Vera and Greece’s Christina Ntanou also won the title with a straight-sets victory over France’s Cimille Siriex and the Netherlands’ Tess de Vocht.

They won 6-3, 6-4 after cruising to a 6-1, 6-1 semi-final victory.

The victory also marked a personal milestone for Vera and Ntanou, who claimed their first international medals in Ghana.

For Professional Padel Association of Ghana president Jean Noel Said, the tournament has already made a significant impact on the growth of the sport in the country.

“It means improvement, growth and development because we started padel in Ghana four years ago, and today we're hosting the first FIP Bronze tournament in the country. I think it shows that the community is growing and that there's an interest in the sport in Ghana.

“We want to give the youth an opportunity to see what the pros are doing, how they're performing and how they're playing. I think it's a great opportunity for them. The kids really enjoyed it. They were interacting with the pros, asking questions and playing with them, so I think it was a great move.”

His vice-president, Nour Seklaoui, added: “Two years ago, when the federation was formed, nobody thought we would get here that quickly. Part of our mission and vision was to achieve this, and we can see now that the sky is the limit. If we're able to host an FIP Bronze tournament in just two years, you never know when we will host Silver and then Gold tournaments. This is a great achievement for Ghana.”

The tournament ended on a celebratory note, with the medal ceremony turning into a birthday celebration for Said and Moroccan player Mohamed Alami.

Ghana News.title: FIFA to confirm UK as host for 2035 Women’s World Cup
Ghana News.content:
Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup

FIFA is set to confirm on Monday that the United Kingdom will host the first football World Cup since 1966.

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are the only bidders to jointly stage the 2035 Women's World Cup.

A delegation will attend FIFA's Zurich headquarters, with national associations holding a specially arranged virtual meeting to vote on ratifying the co-hosts.

The tournament would involve 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid proposes 19 venues: 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

FIFA's evaluation of the bid, published earlier this month, rated it 4.3 out of five. However, it rated its contractual framework 'medium risk', and the document claimed that "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

This is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by FIFA for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

Fifa's bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium is one of 19 stadiums included in the 2035 bid

England hosted the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland are also joint hosts of the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it will still be considered in its current form.

Three more stadiums could be added, Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground, which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "Wales has been a football nation for 150 years and we have never hosted anything on this scale. World Cup football played here, in front of Welsh children, would change what this game looks like in Wales: in the clubs, in the schools, and in the number of girls who grow up seeing a pathway into it."

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not fund the redevelopment of Casement Park in time for the tournament, but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

The Irish Football Association's chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country. Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that."

The Scottish Football Association proposed Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow as the Scottish venues, with chief executive Ian Maxwell saying hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."

The special meeting of FIFA's Congress is also set to approve the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

Ghana News.title: Capital per worker in Ghana slows to 1.0% per year, job quality lags – GSS
Ghana News.content:
Government Statistician, Dr Alhassan Iddrisu,

Capital per worker in Ghana slows to 1.0% per year, job quality lags - GSS

The Ghana Statistical Service has revealed in its 2026 Productivity, Employment and Growth Report that the growth in capital per worker has slowed to 1.0% per year since 2020.

During the same period, productivity growth has also slowed.

In the report, the GSS said productivity gains are uneven across sectors.

Accordingly, information and communication recorded the fastest productivity growth, and electricity and gas the fastest employment growth, but both employ relatively few people.

However, agriculture remains the largest employer and has the lowest output per worker, at GH₵8,859 in 2025.

Manufacturing has held steady at about 10% of Gross Domestic Product, while its employment grew by about 5.0% to 6.0% a year.

The report further revealed that more people are working, but job quality has lagged.

Employment rose from 11.1 million in 2021 to 13.3 million in 2025. Yet unemployment stands at 12.8%, and at 32.4% among young people aged 15 to 24 in the labour force.

Close to one in five people aged 15 to 35 is NEET, at 17.9%.

About 86% of workers are in informal employment (quarter 3 2025 only), 72.0% are in vulnerable employment (72.2% in quarter 3 2025), and 11.6% work fewer hours than they would like.

Earnings below output per worker

Also, earnings are below output per worker.

In 2025, the average worker produced GH₵15,197 in value added and earned GH₵9,388. In industry, output per worker was GH₵30,588 and earnings were GH₵15,822. Average earnings remain below their level before the pandemic.

The report added that earnings are below output per worker. In 2025, the average worker produced GH₵15,197 in value added and earned GH₵9,388.

In industry, output per worker was GH₵30,588 and earnings were GH₵15,822. Average earnings remain below their level before the pandemic.

What this means for policy

The GSS said the evidence points to five priorities.

First, productivity should be measured and reported as a national goal, since it is the main link between growth and higher incomes.

Second, raising productivity where most people already work, in agriculture, trade, informal services and manufacturing, has the widest reach.

Third, investment needs to recover and to be used better: growth driven by adding capital and labour has limits, and the next phase depends more on using existing resources well, through technology, skills, management and a more efficient allocation of resources.

Fourth, young people's skills need to be matched to available jobs, given high unemployment among secondary school leavers.

Fifth, productivity gains should be linked to earnings and decent work through wage-setting mechanisms and social dialogue, since that determines whether growth improves living standards.

The second edition of the Productivity, Employment and Growth Report answered both questions for Ghana over 35 years, from 1991 to 2025.

It combined the national accounts with four censuses and surveys, and followed methods set by the International Labour Organization and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Indonesian police remove 24 body bags from factory fire site
World.content:
Authorities in Java are searching for dozens of missing workers as they continue to battle remaining hotspots.

Indonesian authorities are set to resume the search for missing workers on Monday after police removed 24 body bags from a factory in Java gutted by a fire.

Firefighters continued to battle remaining hotspots on Sunday after the blaze broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, Serang regency, West Java province.

A search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight but would resume Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told local broadcaster Metro TV on Sunday.

Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory’s parent company, PT United Family Food, said at a news conference that about 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift, with 65 of them believed to have been in the affected area when the fire broke out.

In a statement that followed, the factory said 24 of the 65 workers had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained ‌missing, and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed.

At a news conference on Sunday, Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had made it impossible to identify the recovered victims visually. She said they would collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks.

The number of dead was not immediately clear. Police said that one body bag could contain parts ⁠of more than one person.



Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated. Parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official added.

Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the factory, which borders the capital, Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.

Indonesia has suffered several deadly fires in recent years.

A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

World.title: US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’
World.content:
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Trump’s comments were ‘entirely appropriate’ in the context of the summit.

Share US intelligence chief defends Trump’s comments calling Putin his ‘friend’ on social media

United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has faced pressure to justify President Donald Trump’s claims that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin is a “friend”.

In an appearance on the ABC News show This Week, journalist Jonathan Karl pressed Clayton on Trump’s recent remarks.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked.

Clayton responded by calling Trump’s meeting “historic” and his remarks “appropriate”, but the intelligence chief also clarified that the US has not taken Russia’s side when it comes to the country’s invasion of Ukraine.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said.

The scrutiny follows a first-ever confirmed meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.

The three world leaders had a roundtable on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in Shenzhen, China.

Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly praised Putin. In August 2025, Trump hosted the Russian leader in Alaska for Putin’s first visit to the US in nearly a decade.

Upon reuniting with Putin at the Shenzhen conference, Trump offered him a warm, light-hearted greeting.

“Who is he?” Trump joked, first pointing to Putin, then striding across the room to shake his hand. “He’s my friend.”

Trump has since doubled down on his remarks, posting several images of their meeting on social media, one of which bore the caption, “My Friend”.



When a reporter asked whether Russia was a “friend to America” in a news briefing on Friday, Trump brushed aside the question.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, proceeding to explain that he and Putin had grown close during an investigation into whether Russia had interfered in his favour during the 2016 US presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it,” Trump explained.

The US State Department has long been critical of Russia over allegations of human rights abuses, including the torture and imprisonment of political dissidents.

Washington has also supported Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing billions in security assistance and weaponry.

Under Trump, however, that support has cooled, with the US president openly criticising his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for failing to cut a deal with Russia.

Such remarks have divided Republicans, with critics like outgoing US Representative Don Bacon accusing Trump of “playing footsie” with Putin.

“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and China,” Bacon said last week. “We stood for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values. President Trump has been terrible on this, right here.”

But in his television appearances on Sunday, Clayton defended Trump’s remarks, describing the president’s statements of friendship as “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.

He also praised Trump for uniting some of the world’s biggest powers for a conversation about nuclear proliferation.

“It should be assuring that you have the three world nuclear powers getting together and saying: We’re not going to go in that direction,” Clayton told This Week.

While the trilateral meeting concluded with a statement about “reducing nuclear risks”, critics point out no firm commitments were made.

Also on Sunday, in an appearance on CNN, Clayton reiterated his support for Trump’s remarks.

“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.

World.title: ‘Extremely concerning’: Inside a US Army plan to detonate Iowa lead stores
World.content:
The US Army plans to invoke emergency powers to detonate 4 tonnes of lead azide in an Iowa town, despite a court-ordered stay.

The United States Army intends to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide at a military base in Iowa, defying a federal appeals court’s order suspending its permit to do so.

In a fact sheet this weekend, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said that two controlled explosions were scheduled for around noon (06:00 GMT) on Monday.

That announcement follows statements from the Department of Justice, arguing that Tuesday was the cut-off date to carry out a planned detonation.

Lead azide is a key explosive used in military ammunition. The Iowa stockpile has reportedly grown unstable, and Justice Department lawyers have warned that sub-freezing temperatures could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.

“The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” their court filing said.

But critics have questioned the army’s rationale for pushing ahead with the planned detonation, despite the court order to pause it.

“Anyone can claim an emergency at any point and do whatever they want. I don’t think people can or should accept that,” said Thien Chau, a lawyer with the legal group Earthjustice, which represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.

Chau told Al Jazeera that not enough has been done to mitigate the risk from the explosions, which are expected to release a cloud of lead into the air.

Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure, and the dense metal can cause birth defects, brain damage and infertility.



“Anyone who hears that the army plans to explode nearly 10,000 pounds [4,500kg] of [this chemical] would recognise that that is not normal,” Chau said.

“That is extraordinary, and that is not something that you just take lightly.”

An 11th-hour legal battle

The impending explosions come after a tense legal battle between the US government and environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council.

The groups have questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13. The EPA authorised the Army to move forward with the explosions, originally scheduled for November 20.

The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).

They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.

The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted a pause on Friday. But in a Saturday court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the Army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.

“The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay,” the Justice Department said in its filing.

But Earthjustice has argued that such a manoeuvre would sidestep the court’s authority.

Government lawyers have “laid the groundwork for a possible detonation without a permit, which would effectively bypass judicial process and review”, lawyer Rachel Rintelmann wrote in a Friday filing.

A crisis ‘of the Army’s own making’

The controversy centres on a deteriorating stockpile of explosives stored for more than two decades at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.

The stockpile contains roughly 9,700 pounds (4.4 tonnes) of lead azide across 68 barrels, with lead accounting for approximately 6,900 pounds (about 3.1 tonnes) of its chemical mass.

The explosives had been kept in a mixture of water and ethanol to ensure their stability. But in March, military technicians at the facility discovered that the system was breaking down.

According to a court declaration, an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form.

That recrystallisation puts the lead azide at risk of exploding on its own, as a result of temperature charges or even friction. So many crystals had formed that it was no longer safe to even open the barrels, according to the expert.



But on Sunday, Earthjustice released a statement questioning how this problem was allowed to develop in the first place.

“This emergency is of the Army’s own making,” the statement said. “The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. ”

The US Army has said the barrels are set to be detonated in place at the Iowa facility.

But it claims to have explored other options as well. According to the Army’s environmental assessment, it has previously considered two alternatives: chemically neutralising the explosives, or transporting them to an on-site detonation facility.

It rejected both ideas due to concerns that handling or transporting the explosives could trigger an accidental detonation.

Burying the drums, meanwhile, risked subjecting the shock-sensitive material to jolts that could similarly cause an unintended explosion.

What should residents do before and after the explosions?

But the health risks of even a planned explosion have put residents and environmental groups on edge.

On November 15, the Army released two plume maps outlining the potential spread of lead contamination across a swath of eastern Iowa, though projections hinge on real-time wind conditions.

The first map traces what could happen if a lead-bearing plume drifts northward, with a potential airborne trajectory over communities like Burlington, Muscatine, Davenport, Iowa City and Cedar Rapids.

The second map presents a more tenacious problem: surface exposure.

As the plume tracks north, heavier lead-bearing particles are expected to coat the landscape, landing on outdoor furniture, cars, soil and crops.

Residents in the projected plume path were advised to shelter indoors with their pets, shut windows, and limit exposure to outdoor air during a precautionary period, pending the Army’s all-clear.

Those living near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were also instructed to leave their homes for six hours to avoid ground vibrations that could crack or shatter nearby windows.

In the plume’s aftermath, the Army said residents would need to hose down outdoor surfaces, vehicles, and play equipment in an effort to flush away any lead dust deposited during the detonation.

But experts have expressed doubt about how practical the safety guidance is.

At a news briefing, University of Iowa professor David Cwiertny, the director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, warned that long-term monitoring would be necessary to track the lead’s distribution.

“We know that, unlike a porch or patio table, you cannot simply wipe down farm fields, gardens or topsoil because those surfaces are hard to clean,” Cwiertny said.

“We will ultimately need to rely on actual field samples after the event to measure how much lead settles there and understand what it means for our land, those crops and the quality of the environment.”

The Army has yet to issue revised instructions or specify new evacuation hours following the delayed detonation.



Earthjustice lawyers like Chau say the lack of communication is part of the problem.

“The way they’ve gone about notifying people and claiming that they’re going to clean things up when they don’t even know the extent of impact, that is extremely concerning,” Chau told Al Jazeera.

Weather concerns?

US Representative Eric Sorensen, the only meteorologist serving in Congress, said the Army should be looking at a window of opportunity that presents the least potential for off-site exposure.

In a video posted on Thursday, Sorensen said, “The most optimum conditions for controlled detonation would be when we have an inversion of clouds, warm air over cool, with light winds.”

He warned that the National Weather Service’s forecast does not offer those favourable conditions over the coming week, and he questioned why the detonations were only announced when cold weather was imminent.

Other questions remain about whether the Army has exhausted every practicable means of containing the lead’s spread.

Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, told Al Jazeera that it should be up to the Army to provide credible estimates of airborne lead concentrations, ground-level deposition and exposure levels before taking action.

“The burden should be on them to demonstrate that this is the least harmful option, not merely the fastest way to eliminate an immediate danger,” Lanphear told Al Jazeera.

World.title: Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
World.content:
Polish confirmation comes after Copenhagen reveals alleged Russian plot to kill US-Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil.

Share Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice on social media

Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.

The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.

Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.

On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”

It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.

Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.

Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.

Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.

Two Danish men appeared ⁠in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.

Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.



Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.

Support for Ukraine

Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.

Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.

Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.

Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.

Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.

“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.

Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia has denied those accusations.
