The presidential hopefuls arrived Sunday at the historic Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., where they were photographed strutting across a red carpet, posing for pictures and standing atop the hotel's beds before their big day on the South Lawn.

THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION

The U.S. Department of Agriculture celebrated their arrival on X, announcing a "SPECIAL DELIVERY TO WASHINGTON, D.C.!" and describing the birds as "two VERY special guests" receiving the presidential treatment.

Photographs shared by the USDA, credited to the White House and National Turkey Federation, showed the plump white birds making their grand entrance before an audience of hotel guests and photographers. One turkey was even pictured riding through the hotel's ornate hallways inside a travel crate perched on a brass luggage cart.

The pair appeared equally comfortable with the accommodations, with one bird spreading its feathers atop a neatly made bed while its companion stood nearby.

But before the turkeys meet the commander in chief, Americans have been invited to settle a pressing matter of national importance: What should they be called?

SOCIAL MEDIA USERS ARE EATING HUGE AMOUNTS OF CARROTS AND SHRIMP FOR A NATURAL TAN

The White House launched an online contest offering three possible combinations: "Commander & Chief," "Freedom & Feathers," and "Honey & Ham."

Voting on the names closed Sunday at 5 p.m. ET, with the winning pair expected to be announced before a second round of voting opens Monday at 8 a.m. That final vote will determine which turkey receives the official ceremonial pardon.

The birds, raised by American turkey farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell at Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, have already received their own playful presidential biographies.

Both hatched July 15, but their tastes apparently differ. According to the White House, one enjoys Golden Delicious apples and scenic country drives, while the other prefers Dr Pepper and dreams of vacationing in Aggieland.

The pair was selected from a larger flock based on appearance and temperament, according to West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey's office. Their preparations included getting accustomed to crowds, camera lights and noise.

And for Americans who cannot get enough turkey-related excitement, the White House has unveiled "Gobble Getaway," an online game challenging players to help a turkey dodge a chef armed with a net and roasting pan while making its way across the South Lawn to the pardon podium.

The annual Thanksgiving tradition dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first presented a holiday bird to President Harry Truman.

FOX NEWS MEDIA KICKS OFF HOLIDAY SEASON WITH SEVENTH ANNUAL ALL-AMERICAN CHRISTMAS TREE LIGHTING

President John F. Kennedy spared a gift turkey in 1963, while President George H.W. Bush established the formal presidential turkey pardon in 1989.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in this year's ceremony on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2 p.m. ET on the White House South Lawn.

Although the public gets to vote on which turkey receives the ceremonial pardon, both birds are traditionally spared the Thanksgiving dinner table.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For now, the pair can enjoy their luxury accommodations and newfound celebrity status, knowing their next stop is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue rather than the oven.

World.title: John Malkovich recalls losing 'pretty much everything' to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

John Malkovich recalled once losing his entire fortune to disgraced financier Bernie Madoff.

Malkovich, 72, told "60 Minutes" that he had recently returned from directing a play in Mexico City when he found out about Madoff's Ponzi scheme.

"I got home from that and I saw this photograph of Bernie Madoff in handcuffs, and I thought, 'Oh, well that could prove interesting,'" Malkovich said. "I went in and said to my wife, you know, 'I'm just going to go around the corner, buy a pack of cigarettes.'"

FRAUD MASTERMIND BEHIND MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR PONZI SCHEME THAT VICTIMIZED TRAVIS KELCE IS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT

He added, "I said, 'We have a little problem. Bernie Madoff just got arrested.'"

Malkovich, a previous smoker, hadn't indulged in nicotine "for a while" when he left the house that day, he said.

"That was pretty much everything I'd ever made," he admitted before coming to terms with his situation. "You know, you look to blame, you're going to do this and that, and then you realize, 'Look, why don't you shut up?'"

FORMER DISNEY STAR ERIK VON DETTEN SUED FOR ELDER ABUSE AFTER COUPLE POURED $2.1M RETIREMENT SAVINGS INTO GOLD

"Whatever you lost, most people who were ever born will never have a 10th of that, no matter what they do. No matter what they do. Get on with your life and that's it."

Madoff died in April 2021 while serving a 150-year sentence at the federal medical care center in Butner, North Carolina, where his attorney said he was being treated for terminal kidney failure.

A decades-long force on Wall Street, Madoff shocked the world when he pleaded guilty in 2009 to running a vast Ponzi scheme that prosecutors said swindled thousands out of their life savings. The scheme began in the early 1970s, and by the time Madoff was arrested in December 2008, had defrauded as many as 37,000 people in 136 countries out of up to $65 billion.

His victims included the famous – director Steven Spielberg, actor Kevin Bacon and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel – as well as ordinary investors.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Madoff said he started the fraud, in which he appeared to deliver steady returns to clients, but was actually using money from new investors to pay off existing shareholders, in the 1990s because he felt "compelled" to give investors solid returns despite the recession and weak stock market. Prosecutors contend he started defrauding investors much earlier.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"When I began the Ponzi scheme, I believed it would end shortly and I would be able to extricate myself and my clients," Madoff told the judge at his plea hearing. "However, this proved difficult, and ultimately impossible, and as the years went by, I realized that my arrest and this day would inevitably come."

Prior to his downfall, Madoff was viewed as a self-made and respected figure among financial professionals as the head of the seemingly successful Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities firm. He also served as the chairman of the Nasdaq Stock Market in 1990, 1991 and 1993.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

In addition to being sentenced to the maximum 150 years in prison, Madoff and his family took a major financial hit: A judge issued a $171 billion forfeiture order in June 2009 requiring the disgraced financier to give up his interests in all property, including real estate, investments, cars and boats. Under the arrangement, the government also obtained his wife's interest in all property, including $80 million that she claimed belonged to her, leaving Ruth Madoff with $2.5 million in assets.

The decline and fall of Madoff also took a toll on his family. The oldest of his two sons, Mark Madoff, died by suicide on the second anniversary of his father's arrest in 2010. His other son, Andrew, died from cancer at age 48 in 2014.

World.title: Man convicted for role in Tessa Majors' 2019 NYC killing released on parole

One of the three then-teenagers convicted in connection with the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors in New York City has now been released on conditional parole supervision, according to the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision.

Luchiano Lewis, now 21, was released on Oct. 14 under conditional release and placed under community supervision after serving fewer than seven years behind bars for his role in the robbery and killing in Manhattan's Morningside Park in December 2019, state correction records show.

Lewis, who was released from the Franklin Correctional Facility, had been sentenced to nine years to life after pleading guilty in 2021 to second-degree murder and first-degree robbery in connection with Majors' killing.

MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE

Under New York State law, Lewis' conditional release did not require him to go before the State Board of Parole because eligible inmates can qualify for conditional release after serving two-thirds of their minimum sentence, subject to applicable requirements and good-time allowances.

Majors, who was 18 when she was killed, was attacked on Dec. 11, 2019, near a staircase in Morningside Park.

Prosecutors said a group of teens confronted Majors in an attempted robbery, during which she was stabbed multiple times. She was eventually able to climb a set of stairs and reach the street before collapsing. She was taken to a hospital, where she died from her injuries.

JUDGE SENTENCES LILY PETERS' KILLER 4 YEARS AFTER 10-YEAR-OLD FOUND DEAD IN WOODS

After the crime, then-14-year-old Lewis and another 14-year-old were both tried as adults for the attack. Prosecutors said Lewis held Majors in a headlock while the other 14-year-old stabbed her multiple times.

While Lewis was not holding the knife in the attack, prosecutors said he played a key role in the robbery that killed Majors.

At Lewis' sentencing, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Robert Mandelbaum said the killing "tore at the fabric of the entire city."

"The defendant was and is extremely young. He has his whole life ahead of him, but Tessa Majors does not," he added.

Majors' parents described the lasting impact of the loss of their child during Lewis' sentencing, remembering her as a talented student, musician and writer whose future was tragically ended too soon.

The two other teenagers convicted in connection with the killing — Rashaun Weaver, who was 14 at the time of the crime, and Zyairr Davis, who was 13 at the time — remain behind bars. Weaver was sentenced to 14 years to life in prison for murder and robbery, while Davis pleaded guilty to robbery and was sentenced to 18 months in juvenile detention. Davis completed his juvenile sentence but is now being held on an unrelated attempted murder case.

One of those three is really moronic.

Days after telling reporters he was going to retire from his signature backflip celebration, Skattebo apparently decided to ignore everything he said (good advice for all of us, actually) and performed one of his semi-plyometric flights near the end of the Giants game on Sunday.

"When energy calls for it, it calls for it," Skattebo boldly explained to reporters after the game. "My teammates, I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team and play this game with my heart and soul. So when that happens, it's second nature.

"It's hard to hold back."

You want to know the dumb part about this explanation? Neither energy, nor the team were calling for Skattebo to perform a backflip at the moment he did.

The Giants had clinched their 23-18 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars with two minutes to play when Skattebo delivered a 5-yard run. The game was effectively over.

But that's when Skattebo forgot everything he said about not risking an injury the way he watched Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson did on Nov. 15 – which was by leaving his feet to perform a celebration.

DAN CAMPBELL WON'T STOP PLAYERS FROM CELEBRATING EVEN AFTER STAR AIDAN HUTCHINSON WAS INJURED CELEBRATING

Hutchinson, by the way, last week promised he's done going airborne.

So, Skattebo did his unretired backflip when the game was decided. And wouldn't it have been utterly embarrassing if he'd done that backflip upon clinching a victory, injured himself needlessly, and been unable to play in the coming weeks?

Skattebo had coach John Harbaugh previously convinced he had gained some wisdom after the coach read the player's quotes about his backflip last Friday.

Harbaugh actually said in a press conference he was thinking of discussing the matter with Skattebo, but decided it wasn't necessary because the running back seemed to understand the celebration might not be in his or the team's best interest.

But, nope.

Skattebo in the air, feet above his head, relying on his feet and ankles to hold up during the landing and hoping his knees don't buckle.

So, a conversation with Harbaugh is likely incoming.

Skattebo is obviously valuable to the Giants. It's the reason they're not thrilled with these backflips in the first place.

A Purdue University professor and her two teenage daughters were killed in an apparent murder-suicide last week after the father reportedly opened fire on his family before turning the gun on himself, according to Indiana authorities.

Preliminary autopsy results identified the mother as Julie Tkach, 53, of West Lafayette, who died from multiple gunshot wounds, with her death ruled a homicide, the Tippecanoe County Coroner’s Office said Friday. Julie was a clinical assistant professor in Purdue University's Department of Hospitality and Tourism Management, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The father, Thomas Tkach, 51, died by suicide from a gunshot wound to the head, officials said. West Lafayette Police said the family members were found inside their West Lafayette-area home Wednesday evening, Nov. 18, after officers responded to a 911 call shortly after 8:30 p.m. The coroner's office was subsequently notified of multiple deaths at roughly 1:50 a.m. Thursday.

World.title: Democrats win the largest House majority since 1992
World.content:
Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats.

It’s the largest House majority that any party has held this century, according to the Office of the House Historian, and four races are yet to be called. It’s also the largest Democratic majority since 1992, when the party also won 258 seats.

The second-largest House majority for Democrats this century came in 2008, when the party won 257 seats.

The party cemented control of the chamber not only by winning competitive races in battleground districts, but also by winning in deeply Republican areas that voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins just two years ago.

In 2024, Trump won Foxx’s district by almost 18 percentage points, per an NBC News Decision Desk analysis.

Now, Hubbard is projected to win North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District by a fraction of a percentage point following a recount that Foxx requested after Election Day.

Earlier Sunday, Foxx called Hubbard to concede, according to a source familiar with the call.

In a post on X, Hubbard wrote: “Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process. Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.”

Foxx isn’t the only North Carolina Republican who lost in what was considered to be a solidly GOP seat heading into Election Day. Democrats flipped seven Republican seats in North Carolina, the most of any state in the nation.

In the state’s 9th Congressional District, Democratic Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda II defeated GOP Rep. Richard Hudson, who this year chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee. Elsewhere in the state, Democratic Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson defeated GOP Rep. Addison McDowell.

Trump won Hudson’s district by 16 percentage points in 2024 and McDowell’s district by 17 percentage points that year.

World.title: Trump hosts exclusive dinner for investors in his declining meme coin
World.content:
President Donald Trump will reward top investors in his declining meme coin with an exclusive dinner Sunday night as Democrats focus future congressional probes on the president’s business dealings, including his crypto ventures.

The event comes as the president’s meme coin, known as $TRUMP on crypto exchanges, has declined dramatically in worth since its launch just days before his second inauguration in January 2025. The coin’s value peaked at $74 per coin but now trades below $1.

Democrats, gearing up to take control of Congress in the new year, have signaled that the president and his family’s crypto ventures will be a target of oversight investigations.

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., and eight other Democratic senators sent a letter to the White House last month demanding answers about Sunday’s meme coin dinner.

“This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” the senators wrote.

“President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering while costs for the American people continue to climb,” they added.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, were among the letter’s signatories. Both senators have been sent letters from the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, warning them against investigating Trump and his associates.

The president’s net worth has increased by nearly $3 billion since he returned to office in 2025. More than $1 billion of that has been from cryptocurrencies tied to his family’s businesses, while many who invested in those cryptocurrencies experienced steep losses on their investments.

Sunday’s dinner will take place at his golf club outside Washington.

The White House referred questions on the event to the company that operates and sells the meme coin, Fight Fight Fight LLC. While the dinner is not listed on the president’s public schedule for Sunday, the president often holds off-the-record social gatherings at his properties on the weekends.

The “Most Exclusive Dinner in the World,” as it’s described on the dinner’s website, will feature a number of celebrities, including celebrity businessman Kevin O’Leary, professional boxer Floyd Mayweather and former NBA player Tristan Thompson.

The top 185 holders of the president’s coin will earn a seat at the dinner, with the top 29 gaining access to a “special VIP reception.” VIP guests will also receive Trump-themed goody bags, and the top four holders with at least 1 million $TRUMP coins are promised 18-karat gold Trump watches. Attendees, however, will not be granted a private meet-and-greet with the president, per the website.

The watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reacted to the dinner on social media on Sunday, writing, “Trump’s memecoin dinner today, where likely unvetted $TRUMP memecoin customers will gain special access to Trump, is EXACTLY the reason why we have to ban presidential profiteering.”

It’s not the first time the president has hosted a dinner for his meme coin investors. In 2025, the top 220 investors of the coin were invited to dine with Trump at his Sterling, Virginia, golf club.

World.title: COP31 climate talks break down after angry dispute over fossil fuels
World.content:
International climate talks in Turkey broke down Sunday after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement that had cut all references to fossil fuels.

Negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya fell apart two days after the United Nations’ COP31 conference was meant to end, after delegates from 196 countries and the European Union struggled to agree on new pledges for climate action and how to deliver on previous promises.

COP31 President Murat Kurum said Sunday that there would be no new climate agreement draft after a fourth draft was rejected.

“There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” said Kurum, who is host nation Turkey’s environment minister. “​We will not ​be carrying out ​work on a new ⁠text in an environment ⁠where there ​is no consensus.”

He later added that he had wanted a a “much stronger outcome” from the summit.

Chris Bowen, COP31’s president of negotiations, told reporters that there were “unbridgeable red lines” in the discussions.

“The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory,” the Australian minister said. “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time,” Bowen added.

The latest draft agreement, released on Sunday, had set out proposed measures for countries to accelerate climate action, but the 12-page document drew immediate criticism over its failure to mention a move away from fossil fuels, a key demand of the E.U. and other nations.

Irish minister Darragh O’Brien, representing the E.U. in Antalya, said the bloc “strongly objects” to the deal, which he called “greenwashing.”

“These decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change,” O’Brien said. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels.”

Panama also rejected the deal, saying it didn’t go far enough, as did the Marshall Islands, a low-lying Pacific nation that faces an existential threat from sea-level rise.

Kate Hughes, the spokesperson for the United Kingdom delegation, called the draft text the “lowest common denominator.”

All countries had to agree on the text for it to pass. The talks were the longest in COP history, surpassing the delay in negotiations at COP25 in Madrid.

The summit began on Nov 9. A first draft was circulated a week later and mentioned “fossil fuel” or “fossil fuels” six times. But a second draft, published Thursday, had removed all references, to the anger of many countries.

The conference officially ended on Friday without an agreement. Members have continued talks in a bid to find a resolution, but a fourth draft released Sunday still contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia and India have pushed back on including any reference to the words in the text, amid concerns that phasing out fossil fuels, central to their economies, could pose a financial risk.

The United States, one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases, is officially absent from the conference, having withdrawn from a series of international climate commitments under President Donald Trump.

The latest draft started by “recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety,” a reference to COP28 in the UAE, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away” from fossil fuels in energy systems.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said the world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

“We love the petroleum guys,” he told a press conference on Wednesday. “We can’t live without them, and they are so smart, they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa called COP31 the “worst ever.”

“The collapse of climate talks at COP31 in Antalya needs to be a wake-up call for the world,” he wrote in a statement. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.”

“But this setback does not change the facts,” he posted on X. “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

The latest draft also acknowledged that the goal set by the 2015 Paris Agreement of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius is going to be missed.

As warming goes beyond 1.5 C, the impacts of climate change, including extreme heat and other weather events, are expected to ramp up significantly.

As the talks break down, Kurum could choose to convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year’s conference, hosted by Ethiopia.

Talks last failed at COP6 at The Hague in the Netherlands in 2000.

World.title: Army plans to carry out detonation at Iowa plant on Wednesday
World.content:
The U.S. Army says it plans to move forward with the detonation of several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced," the military said in a post on social media Sunday night.

The Army had earlier said in a court filing that it planned to carry out the detonation by Tuesday.

The detonation is being planned despite a federal court order that paused it indefinitely, which the Army said it does not need to follow because of the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

In federal court records filed late Saturday, the Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.

On Friday, a federal court suspended the U.S. Army's plan to detonate the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.

The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.

The military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said.

A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In its filing on Saturday, the government had warned that it must conduct the controlled explosion by Tuesday because the temperature is expected to drop below 30 degrees in the next several days. It says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop. It did not immediately explain if the forecast or other factors had changed to make a move to Wednesday safer.

"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. "The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion."

In response to the Army's filing, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed a motion Sunday seeking to supplement their emergency request to block the planned detonation.

The filing includes three expert and local government declarations challenging the Army's assessment of the risk of delaying the detonation, as well as concerns about public notice and potential health and environmental impacts.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration, saying "this emergency is of the Army's own making."

"The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.

Iowa's new Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek said in a statement Sunday that he is "concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army's planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army."

"I also believe we need a full investigation into why this stockpile of lead azide, which has been at IAAAP for decades, was allowed to degrade into this critical state, why safer methods of disposal were not pursued, what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at the IAAAP and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again," he said. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning."

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

World.title: Tom Jackson, former Broncos star and sports broadcaster, dies at 75
World.content:
Former football star and famed broadcaster Tom Jackson has died, his family and ESPN announced Sunday.

Jackson rose to prominence as a Denver Broncos player and went on to build a career as a beloved NFL analyst for ESPN, becoming a mainstay of the network's Sunday football programs for three decades, including its "Sunday NFL Countdown" show. He was 75.

Jimmy Pitaro, the chairman of ESPN, praised Jackson in a statement released by the network after his death. In it, Pitaro called Jackson "one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN's history," who "brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans."

"Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make NFL Primetime an iconic part of our football weekends," Pitaro said. "Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him. His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure."

Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wish that his death not be announced until the start of the network's "Sunday NFL Countdown" show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman.

"Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom's was frequent and unmistakable," Berman said at the start of the show. "Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too."

Former NFL player Randy Gradishar, right, and his presenter form Denver Broncos teammate Tom Jackson pose with his bust during an induction ceremony at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, in Canton, Ohio, Saturday, Aug. 3, 2024. AP Photo/David Dermer, File

Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was the inspirational leader of Denver's first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team's second Super Bowl appearance. He was a two-time Associated Press All-Pro and three-time Pro Bowler.

Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on "Sunday NFL Countdown" and "NFL Primetime."

Before the internet and NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, "NFL Primetime" was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interplay between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other's sentences.

"I can remember coming from games and waiting in a rush to get home, to watch 'Primetime' because all I wanted to know was, what were you and Tom Jackson gonna say about one, the team?" ESPN analyst and Hall of Fame wide receiver Randy Moss said to Berman.

Jackson briefly returned to ESPN in 2019 and reunited with Berman to do an online version of "NFL Primetime." He was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

Tom Jackson preparing for a workout with the Denver Broncos on Jan. 22, 1987, in Irvine, California. AP Photo/Ed Andrieski, File

"In my lifetime there was Howard Cosell doing 'Monday Night Football' halftime highlights and then there were Boomer and TJ doing 'Sunday NFL Countdown.' I am not here as a colleague but as one of million who watched, learned from and idolized the two of you," ESPN host Mike Greenberg said during Sunday's show.

ESPN's studio crew wore orange ties in honor of Jackson during the three-hour show.

Berman said Jackson was the last of seven people interviewed for the studio analyst job and that the last person rarely gets the job. But Jackson nailed the interview.

ESPN's NFL studio in Bristol, Connecticut, is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. It is the only named studio on ESPN's campus.

"The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history," the Broncos said in a statement.

"An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos' first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country."

Jackson is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and daughters Taylor and Morgan.

World.title: U.N. climate summit ends without deal after contentious fossil fuel debate
World.content:
COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.

The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement that Sunday he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome of the summit.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," he said. "But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."

The United States sent no representatives to the climate conference for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. That accord set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a target that has anchored every U.N. climate summit since and that the world is now poised to overshoot.

Talks reached an impasse Sunday, as the European Union opposed a draft agreement that failed to mention fossil fuels and which, its delegates argued, placated countries that export them.

"We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuel, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU in Antalya. "And we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

The EU joined a group of smaller nations facing heightened threats of climate extremes and challenged oil producers, like Saudi Arabia, that staunchly rejected their views. The finale came after days of tense discussions over some of the core topics at issue during the summit, including whether to establish new rules and goals around transitioning away from coal, oil and natural gas in favor of renewable energy.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkey's environmental minister, said in televised comments from Antalya on Sunday that a draft had not been adopted due to a lack of consensus. The conference rules require unanimous agreement to reach a deal, so even a single nation's dissent can derail the process.

"We have always emphasized that this process is one that respects the will of the parties. We did everything we could," Kurum said. "In the end, we did not impose this text on anyone. We did not pressure anyone with a take-it-or-leave-it approach. There are parties in the hall that oppose this text, and we see that there is no agreement on it. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted."

Australia's climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, who shared the COP31 presidency with Kurum as Turkey and Australia jointly hosted this year's summit, said Sunday that talks broke down because of "unbridgeable red lines" and added that "the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory," reported CBS partner BBC News.

On Friday, the scheduled final day of the conference, a coalition led by France and Panama and including countries from Europe, Africa, Latin America and the Pacific rejected the latest draft agreement as too weak, according to the U.N. The group demanded explicit language on fossil fuels and stronger commitments on climate finance.

"We cannot continue to be held hostage by petroleum producers," said Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, at a news conference last week. He also vowed that Panama would formally object to any deal omitting issues related to fossil fuels.

People protest on the scheduled final day of the COP31 climate conference on Nov. 20, 2026 in Antalya, Turkey. Chris McGrath / Getty Images

An initial draft of negotiators' agreement had called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels," a recurring goal at these summits, and urged an end to inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. It also resolved to bring warming back below 1.5 degrees as early as possible this century. But that language was gone days later, reflecting deep divisions over timelines and financing.

Later drafts still did not contain language about fossil fuels, although they did include proposed targets to capture billions of tons of carbon dioxide annually from the atmosphere by 2035, using technology that critics have said distracts from the need to cut fossil fuel use. They also called for electricity to supply more than a third of the world's energy by the same deadline, alongside goals around renewable energy and energy efficiency.

Negotiators had expressed "deep concern" in drafted text over global warming, which at its peak is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees. They also reaffirmed the need "for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions," warning that every increment of additional warming will increase the frequency and intensity of climate-related loss and damage. If current international climate plans were fully implemented, they noted, the world would be on track for just over 2.5 degrees of warming, down from projections of more than 4 degrees before the Paris accord.

The COP31 summit unfolded in a year marked by deadly disasters, record heat, destructive wildfires, tumultuous surf and other anomalies, which meteorologists have largely tied to a powerful El Niño. Scientists say its effects are amplified by climate change.

Speaking in Antalya last week, Guterres urged governments to move away from fossil fuels, triple adaptation funding by 2035 and tax fossil fuel companies' windfall profits to help vulnerable nations recover from disasters. "Polluters must pay," he said. At a press conference two days later, he linked the climate crisis to deeper social and political instability.

"You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it," Guterres said. "You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause the crisis suffer first and worst."

Some environmental advocates felt the conference proposals didn't go far enough to meet the needs of communities that are already facing real consequences of the climate crisis.

Ellen Dorsey, named this month to the TIME100 climate list, told CBS News after leaving Antalya over the weekend that she hadn't expected substantial action from COP31, despite clear signs of urgency.

"The time for simply talking about phasing out fossil fuels is over. Governments need to act," Dorsey told CBS News. "That means no fossil fuel expansion, an end to fossil fuel subsidies, and an equitable phaseout that protects workers and communities."

Dorsey said fossil fuel lobbying has grown over the past decade, as has the presence of industry interests in national delegations at U.N. climate talks, including this one. Still, she sees promise in efforts pushing back, from grassroots movements to the Santa Marta process, a coalition using diplomacy to drive a transition away from coal, oil and gas.

"Momentum is building beyond the negotiations," said Dorsey, who called this "a historic inflection point" for climate policy. "The opportunity for real systemic change is here."

World.title: ICE officers arrest 2 passengers boarding flight in Seattle
World.content:
Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, federal officials said, causing what Alaska Airlines called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Videos of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and she has a work permit.

Alaska Airlines said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

An Alaska Airlines spokesperson told CBS News on Sunday that the flight, scheduled to depart at 8:45 a.m., left the airport at 11:03 a.m. after some crew members asked to leave.

"Immediately following the incident, some inflight crew members requested to be replaced. As we learned more about what occurred, we ultimately brought in an entirely new crew," the airline spokesperson said in a statement.

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday evening, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, said that ICE officers "conducted a targeted enforcement operation" on a Mexican national identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza who had "overstayed his visa."

During the arrest, a second passenger "hurled hot coffee" at the officers, the DHS spokesperson said in the statement. That second passenger, identified by DHS as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, is a Mexican national who had also been determined to have overstayed her visa, the spokesperson said.

Mejia was also subsequently arrested and will face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer, DHS said.

A DHS source told CBS News the two people arrested are a father and daughter.

Mendoza and Mejia remained in ICE custody in Washington, immigration attorney Olia Catala told CBS News on Sunday night, saying she was visiting her clients at the Northwest Processing Center in Tacoma.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith of Washington said in an earlier statement that "masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. Videos showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. ICE sources told CBS News in July that the uptick in arrests stems from increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration.

On Thursday, a Princeton University student and Chinese national was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson said in a statement. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said in a social media post that she was "disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac," adding that her office was "working to gather more information on the situation."

DHS numbers obtained by CBS News last week found that ICE arrested 491,000 people in FY 2026, a record, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, also a record. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

In a "60 Minutes" interview earlier this month following the heavy losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections, President Trump appeared to acknowledge that his administration's immigration crackdown may have contributed to his party's poor showing.

"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

Of his deportation policies, the president said: "I think it was too tough. A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough."

World.title: Delta Air Lines hit with delays after baggage network system issue
World.content:
A systemwide network issue affecting Delta Air Lines' baggage system that forced teams to manually process bags, resulting in nationwide delays during a busy holiday travel weekend, has been fixed, the airline said Sunday.

The airline said in a statement that the automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, several hours after it forced a temporary ground delay program to be issued at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport — Delta Air Lines' mega hub — to manage traffic backups caused by the system outage. The ground delay, which has been lifted, impacted only Delta's flights.

"Delta apologizes to customers for the delay in their travels today," the airline said. "Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary. For customers facing a canceled flight and don't wish to travel, refunds are being given."

Delta warned that while teams are focused on completing the 500 Delta and Delta Connection flights scheduled for Sunday, cancellations would be a last resort if all other options have been exhausted.

As of Sunday evening, Delta Air Lines had canceled 202 flights, or 4% of the day's total, departing from the U.S., which is higher than average for the airline. Only 50% of its flights were arriving on time Sunday, which is also highly unusual for the airline, which usually operates above the 80% mark each month.

According to FlightAware, Delta Air Lines currently has more than 1,900 delayed flights, as of 6:00 p.m. EST. The airline said about 70% of these delays are connected to the automation.

"The remaining are attributable to inclement weather and ensuring ATC programs in NYC and the U.S. Northeast," the airline said.

United Airlines had a similar issue last Monday that forced the airline to hold departures for about 90 minutes.

AAA projects nearly 6 million people will take domestic flights for Thanksgiving this week.

World.title: Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.
World.content:
Do not feed the animals. Vets explain why hats, coins and shoes can be deadly.

toggle caption i John Minchillo/AP

The death of Fiona, a beloved hippopotamus who captured hearts, has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.

Fiona, 9 years old, died Thursday after ingesting a hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat at the Cincinnati Zoo. The zoo said that the hat was lodged in the hippo's small intestine and surgery was not possible.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a statement .

While deaths are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall, and sometimes are tossed, into animal enclosures.

Sponsor Message

In 2024, 70 U.S. coins were successfully removed from an alligator at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium. And in 2025, a Komodo dragon ate a shoe that was thrown into its habitat at the Memphis Zoo. The shoe was removed and the dragon survived.

Dr. Gabriella Flacke, an associate veterinarian at Zoo Miami, said the zoo's staff have retrieved items such as cellphones from alligators.

"We've had to remove those items both endoscopically, which is basically putting a camera through the mouth and down into the stomach to grab and retrieve those items, or we've in a few cases had to do surgery where they were larger items that couldn't be removed that way," Flacke told NPR.

toggle caption i John Minchillo/AP

Recovering items from an alligator is easier than a hippo, she said. Unlike the alligator, which has a digestive system with one stomach divided into two parts, hippos have a multichambered stomach. This can make retrieving objects, such as the small hat that Fiona ingested, difficult, according to Dr. Jen Quammen, president of the American Veterinary Medical Association.

"It's not necessarily always the shape or size of the object, but it's maybe the twists and turns, metaphorically and physiologically, that things have to go through," Quammen told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Be aware that the animals have specialized dietary needs and requirements that caretakers provide them, Flacke said. She also asked visitors to follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.

"Anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head if you're leaning over and looking at something," she said. "If your child has a toy in its hand and you're walking around, it could just decide to throw the toy, whether it's thinking about that or not."

It's not just dangerous for zoo animals

Both Quammen and Flacke said people should not only be mindful of items that can harm animals at the zoo, but also what could hurt animals in the wild or pets at home.

Animals explore the world by putting things in their mouths, making them naturally curious about items that can be dangerous, Quammen said.

toggle caption i Frank Augstein/AP

To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.

"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen

To help prevent an animal from ingesting something dangerous, one should dispose of their trash and properly store items such as human medicines in a place where an animal cannot reach it.

"Don't feed an animal without permission and that includes our pets at home, but also wildlife," added Quammen

World.title: What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse
World.content:
What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse

After two weeks of negotiations, international climate talks fail to reach an agreement. NPR's Rachel Waldholz was in Turkey for the conference.

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended today after negotiations fell apart. NPR's Rachel Waldholz has been at the conference and sent us this report.

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: I'm here in the Antalya Expo Center, which, for the past two weeks, has been packed with some 70,000 people who came to the COP31 climate conference. Now it's almost completely empty. In fact, they're disassembling parts of the venue around me. The climate talks ran two days past their scheduled end. By the time the gavel fell, many negotiators had already left to catch their flights home. Australia climate chief Chris Bowen led the negotiations.

CHRIS BOWEN: I haven't slept for the last three nights, been negotiating all the way through, but more importantly, people on delegations came at it and gave it everything they had.

WALDHOLZ: Delegates came to Antalya with long wish lists, from electrifying more of the global economy to money for developing countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change. Looming over it all is that this is the first summit to squarely face the reality that the planet will miss a key target of the Paris Climate Agreement, reaching warming of 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above pre-Industrial levels. The U.N. says limiting that overshoot requires cutting the use of fossil fuels nearly in half in the next 10 to 15 years. Many countries wanted an agreement explicitly calling for a transition away from coal, oil and natural gas. But big oil-producing countries, like Saudi Arabia, blocked any mention of fossil fuels. Ultimately, the European Union decided no deal was better than the deal on the table. Darragh O'Brien is Ireland's environment minister.

DARRAGH O'BRIEN: We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.

WALDHOLZ: Many negotiators left the expo center dragging their suitcases on the way to the airport. They'll pick up negotiations next year at the next climate summit in Ethiopia. I'm Rachel Waldholz in Antalya, Turkey.

World.title: Philly festival-goers say pickles are a real big dill
World.content:
Philly festival-goers say pickles are a real big dill

Influencer and pickle enthusiast Dan Pancoast gives a first hand account of the festivities at the "The Big Dill" festival in Philadelphia.

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

We are now going to turn to pickles, a food that has seemed to follow me my whole life. When I was growing up, I used to watch my mom and grandma pickle cucumbers in the front yard. When I lived in China, every meal started with pao tsai, pickled vegetables. Then I moved to Germany and stumbled upon entire festivals devoted to the pickle. So I've been to places where people rave about pickles, but I've never been to a pickle rave. But we caught up with someone who has.

DAN PANCOAST: They had handed out, like, glow bracelets and glow necklaces, and everyone was just dancing and having a good time.

SCHMITZ: That is Dan Pancoast. Recently, he went to The Big Dill Pickle Festival, where they had a pickle rave. And...

PANCOAST: They have a brine chug. They give you a solo cup full of pickle brine. That was, like, the first thing that I put in my stomach today.

SCHMITZ: Pancoast is a content creator who lives in Pennsylvania, and he loves pickles.

PANCOAST: My tattoo is basically a dill pickle with a sombrero on, wearing sunglasses.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: It is National Pickle Day in Philadelphia, everybody.

(CHEERING)

PANCOAST: I walked up to the venue, and there was a good bit of people outside...

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: Who's ready for the parade of pickles?

PANCOAST: ...Probably a couple hundred people wearing pickle hats, pickle shirts, sweatshirts, costumes.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: So the Grand Gherkin is here to help lead us.

PANCOAST: Now they're doing the world record parade. People dressed as pickles (laughter). It's quite amazing, honestly.

UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: To clear the space for the count.

SCHMITZ: Pancoast said the festival exceeded his expectations. It was a sort of picklepalooza (ph).

PANCOAST: And no matter what kind of pickles you love, what style, what you like your pickles on, don't like your pickles on, how you eat them, everyone can just be here. There's no real - anything else to think about. You can't really overthink it (laughter).

SCHMITZ: That was Dan Pancoast. The Big Dill Festival did, in fact, break the record for people dressed like pickles - 1,597 pickled people.
