World.title: Will Canadian workers refuse to handle Israeli goods? Why unions increasingly say they should
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions and workers are preparing for potential battles with their employers.

The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC), which represents more than three million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be "hot cargo" and calling for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel. The CLC also resolved to cut ties with the Histadrut, Israel's largest trade union organization.

The move followed similar resolutions passed by numerous local and provincial labour groups over the past year, including the Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador labour federations.

Next week, the B.C. Federation of Labour will vote on a resolution that would "support affiliate locals and unions in refusing to engage with" Israeli goods and specifically ask the B.C. government to stop importing and selling Israeli wines.

A BCFL spokesperson said in an email that the union does not comment on resolutions before delegates have had a chance to debate them.

The movement to isolate Israel with economic pressure is growing as its deadly strikes on Gaza continue after a ceasefire deal was signed more than a year ago. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, while Israeli officials say five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

"I think the vast majority of union activists have come to see that this is a situation where people of conscience, and workers of conscience, need to do what they can to oppose Israeli crimes and our complicity in them," said Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee that pushed for the resolutions across Canada.

A report by the UN 's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian ‌Territory including East Jerusalem and Israel stated last month that Israel has continued to commit genocide since the ceasefire. Israel dismissed the charge as part of a "misinformation campaign."

Israel is facing accusations of genocide before the International Court of Justice, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is wanted on an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza.

Union says Palestinian workers made request

Levangie, a member of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers Atlantic in Halifax, says the Canadian government is not doing enough to stop the flow of weapons to Israel, or the import of products manufactured in illegal settlements in Palestinian territories, so it "falls on Canadian workers" to ensure they are complying with their obligations under international law.

Levangie visited the West Bank as part of a union delegation in September and October, where he met with Palestinian groups, including trade unions, who have asked unions in the West to take on this work.

"We're honouring a request that was made by Palestinian workers," he said.

"In that way, it's very similar to the South African context of the 80s and 90s, where South African trade unions, South African civil society organizations, were asking for us to isolate apartheid South Africa until the freedom struggle was won."

Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee, says workers want to comply with international law. (Submitted by Kevin Levangie)

Canadian dockworkers, postal workers and retail workers joined international campaigns declaring South African goods as hot cargo in the 1980s to pressure the country's government into ending apartheid.

Canadian workers also took hot cargo actions to protest Argentina's human rights abuses and suppression of trade unions in 1979 and joined a trade union boycott of Indonesia in 1999 to protest the country's military occupation of East Timor.

Canadian unions have not acted on the CLC resolution, though workers in other countries have taken action.

Italian workers staged a day-long general strike last month, blocking roads, causing rail delays and cancellations and disrupting airports to protest Israel intercepting an aid flotilla that was carrying food to Gaza.

Canada's unions did not participate in a global day of strike on Oct. 30, which saw efforts to disrupt weapons transfers to Israel as part of a broader anti-war protest at 113 ports across 22 countries.

Critic says Israel singled out

The CLC's resolution has created tension within the labour movement, according to Kim Kazur, labour consultant and adviser with the Canadian Jewish Labour Committee advocacy group.

A retired Ontario Public Service Employees Union member, Kazur says she feels unions are unfairly singling out Israel on the world stage and the resolutions are a way to "hide behind" what she views as "Jew hate."

Kazur says unions should "stay in our lanes" and not contribute to "divisive political ideology," adding workers could end up putting themselves at risk of being fired.

"The idea of a union encouraging its members to do some type of disobedience is not OK," she said.

Levangie denied accusations of hate and noted Labour for Palestine regularly collaborates with advocacy group Independent Jewish Voices in its organizing work.

"We in Labour for Palestine are strongly opposed to antisemitism and all other forms of hate," he said.

Advocates say they want to end Canada's involvement in manufacturing F-35 parts that could end up on Israeli jets. (Amir Cohen/Reuters)

Workers could face discipline

Levangie acknowledges a concern about discipline or retaliation by employers if workers refuse to handle certain goods — from components of F-35 fighter jets that are manufactured in Canada, to oranges shipped from Israel to Canadian grocery stores — but says the declaration of hot cargo is the labour movement's "greatest power."

The tactic is often used in the context of labour disputes, says Andrew Stevens, an associate professor at the University of Regina's school of business.

The BCFL issued a hot cargo edict on Nov. 2 — in solidarity with striking Trigon employees with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 523 — ordering workers not to handle Trigon coal and petroleum products.

Moving to concrete action can be complicated, however, especially on a heated political issue.

"If an individual worker engages in this, I think people are going to see it as insubordination, which means that they could be subject to discipline up to and including termination of employment," Stevens said.

If two or more workers deliberately refuse orders to unload goods or procure services, he says that would be deemed an illegal strike.

WATCH | CBC investigates allegations against Israel: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

Stevens says workers will need strong support from their unions and labour organizations if they plan to carry out the CLC's resolution on the ground.

"Its strength is really going to be premised on the support from the unions themselves," he said.

CBC News has reached out to the CLC for comment but has not heard back.

World.title: Satellites are constantly photographing Earth. A Waterloo student has compiled the pictures into one spot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Satellites are constantly photographing Earth, and a new website designed by a University of Waterloo student is making these photos more accessible to the general public.

Armaan Gupta is a computer science student. As a project one weekend, he decided to make a website, Watched.Earth, when he found out some of his friends were unaware that satellites are perpetually taking pictures of Earth.

When a user clicks on the website they are greeted with an interactive globe. Users can type in an address and will be taken to that place on Earth. The website shows how many satellites passed by over the past seven days, and any publicly available satellite photos. There is also a "surprise me" option, which takes users to a random place on Earth.

A time-lapse feature shows photos from the past 10 years of a specific area. Gupta says the time-lapse feature helps highlight the scale of destruction in war-torn areas.

WATCH | UW student creates website that shows time-lapse satellite images: UW student creates website that shows time-lapse satellite images | Duration 1:20 Armaan Gupta is a computer science student at the University of Waterloo. He recently created and launched the website Watched.Earth that shows publicly available satellite photos from anywhere on Earth, along with a 10-year timelapse of any location.

Gupta says seeing the progression of destruction in a war-torn area, such as Gaza, Ukraine or South Sudan can be eye-opening for people around the world.

"We always hear about these kinds of things, but it's never really brought to our attention the scale of the destruction. Like, I can't remember the last time it was made like so easily to see exactly how the shape of a particular war zone country has changed throughout the years," Gupta said.

Watched.Earth shows how many satellites passed over an area within the last seven days, along with the recent publicly available photos taken by these satellites. (Watched.Earth)

Although all the photos on Gupta's website are publicly available, he says compiling the photos from websites like NASA and other space agencies into one place makes them more accessible.

"I think that we should make it more accessible to the public that ... like 6,000 satellites are taking images of you every few hours. And so I think that kind of information should be accessible to everyone," said Gupta.

Not for professional analysis

Although the website is helpful for raising awareness about countries experiencing war, or just a spot for a curious person to go, the resolution of the photos are not clear enough for professional analysis, according to one expert.

Nathaniel Raymond is the executive director of the Humanitarian Research Lab at the Yale School of Public Health.

His team investigates war crimes and mass atrocities by analyzing satellite imagery, primarily from Google Earth and other high-resolution data sources.

Raymond says Watched.Earth allows the general public to access low-resolution imagery from one interface and "allows them to interact with it in a general way, but not to the degree you would if you were analyzing it to detect change."

He says when using Watched.Earth, it can be difficult to make out alleyways between buildings or distinguish between structures.

However, the imagery that his team uses has a very high resolution that allows them to tell the difference between models of cars.

"In the case of Sudan, we can see dead bodies on the ground," he said.

Despite the low resolution of most of the images on the website, Raymond says it is useful as an awareness-raising tool for the general public.

"It is important that platforms like this exist to allow members of the public to begin to gain familiarity with what can and cannot be seen at different resolutions, and to begin to understand how in conflict areas, damage happens over time at scale," he said.

A photo of Gaza on the left taken by a satellite Dec. 8, 2015, as shown on Watched.Earth's time-lapse feature. The photo on the right shows the same view of Gaza taken on Nov. 10, 2026. (Watched.Earth)

Gupta says he's received a lot of feedback from users asking for higher resolution photos. He says he's currently in the process of communicating with more satellite organizations to try and gain access to their data.

According to Raymond, higher resolution imagery is often highly access controlled, and isn't updated as regularly as lower resolution satellites.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: Cuba and the Unbearable Habit of Waiting for Miracles
World.content:
Life Happening. I refuse to accept that resignation is our only destiny. / 14ymedio

Perhaps my grandparents were right: Not even the US Americans can fix this. We’ll have to fix it ourselves.

By Yunior Garcia Aguilera (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – My grandparents used to repeat two sayings that seemed to sum up all the wisdom of our national pessimism. The first was: “Not even the US Americans can fix this.” The second: “Hope was green, and a goat ate it.” I grew up hearing them without imagining that, several decades later, they would still describe the mood of Cubans with such accuracy.

In Cuba, everything seems to be in free fall except the regime. The economy is sinking, buildings are crumbling, hospitals are collapsing, public services are disappearing, and the country is emptying out. But those in power remain firmly in place, clinging to their privileges, floating as though they had discovered the secret of political weightlessness.

For years, we have repeated that the dictatorship is about to hit rock bottom. Yet the bottom keeps moving farther away. Perhaps because, as the regime falls, it is society that absorbs the blows. The government has managed to survive the failure of absolutely everything it promised to save.

The capture of Nicolas Maduro in January unleashed a new wave of expectations. Many Cubans believed our turn had finally come. Trump fueled those hopes with warnings about the regime’s future and statements suggesting that an outcome was near. But the months passed, and the US strategy focused solely on intensifying economic and energy pressure.

And the negotiations, enthusiastically announced by some and downplayed by others, also seemed like the chronicle of a failure foretold.

Now Trump speaks of resolving the Cuban problem before the end of his term in January 2029. Freedom is once again postponed, like a public works project with no reliable completion date.

Perhaps we should update that cartoon of the ripe fruit that John Quincy Adams imagined falling toward the United States. Two centuries later, the fruit is bruised, indebted, depopulated, and in need of a billion-million-dollar investment to become edible again. It hardly seems like a delicacy Washington is in any great hurry to acquire.

But it would be unfair to place all our frustrations on the United States. We must also look in the mirror.

I left Cuba in November 2021, following the repression against my family and me. I was not willing to spend more than twenty years in prison for attempting to organize a peaceful march. Some compatriots called me a coward. Nor do I intend to portray myself as a hero. I know my fears, my limitations, and my contradictions.

Yet I have seen how opposition activists who did endure years in Castro’s prisons end up being subjected to the same public lynching on social media by people who supposedly share their democratic aspirations.

Those who leave are called cowards. Those who stay are expected to deliver results. Those who are imprisoned are constantly put on a scale to check whether they have really lost weight. Those who are released are scrutinized for some blemish that might discredit their sacrifice. We demand perfect heroes, without fear, without mistakes, without families to protect, and preferably with an unlimited capacity to endure torture.

There is no shortage of Facebook prosecutors. What is missing are citizens willing to assume even a small portion of the risks they demand of others.

And yet, inside Cuba, there are people who continue to resist. Anna Bensi, Alina Barbara Lopez, Yoani Sanchez, Camila Acosta, and many others who defy repression with admirable perseverance. They receive solidarity, especially from religious circles and activists, but that support rarely reaches the same scale in the streets as it does on the internet.

I do not intend to judge those who are afraid. That would be unforgivable hypocrisy. Fear is legitimate. Repression is real. But we need to recognize that no viral post can replace civic organization, and a million insults will not bring down a dictatorship.

Is there still hope? Yes, although it does not come wrapped in Trump’s promises or depend on finding another martyr willing to sacrifice themselves for everyone else.

Hope begins when we stop demanding impossible heroes and learn to protect the imperfect human beings who still dare to stand up. When we manage to disagree without destroying one another, offer support without imposing conditions, and turn outrage into meaningful solidarity.

The July 11, 2021, protests demonstrated that there is one thing the regime fears more than anything else: losing control of the streets. That is why the greatest strength of an organized civil society lies not only in its ability to denounce abuses, but also in its capacity to bring people together, sustain relationships, and mobilize.

The protests against power outages express needs that are as urgent as they are legitimate. But if scattered discontent finds a nationwide, sustained expression capable of moving beyond immediate demands, those in power will have to confront a reality they cannot resolve simply by restoring electricity to a circuit.

The true bottom of a political crisis is not measured by the depth of the economic disaster, but by the limits that organized citizens are capable of imposing on their rulers.

I do not know when this downward spiral will end. I distrust those who insist that freedom is always just around the corner. But I also refuse to accept that resignation is our only destiny.

Perhaps my grandparents were right: Not even the US Americans can fix this. We’ll have to fix it ourselves.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: The War of the Entire Cuban People
World.content:
Cuban president Miguel Diaz Canel in a meeting with top military officials.

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – Cuba has spent nearly 70 years preparing for a military war with the United States, but the truth is that, after the 1960s, that possibility became increasingly remote.

The current US administration has said on more than one occasion that it does not rule out that option, but the reality is that adding yet another armed conflict to the financial burden borne by United States taxpayers would be extremely complicated, to mention only the economic aspect.

Beyond that—which remains a hypothetical scenario—what is actually happening in Cuba is that fear of war is being used to serve the interests of the dictatorship. At the same time, the regime wants Cubans to believe it could withstand a military confrontation, when we all know that would be impossible.

This week, President Miguel Di’z-Canel met with the country’s top military leadership to reiterate the decision to repel any aggression (it would be the height of absurdity if they surrendered at the first opportunity). But far from projecting an image of strength, he looked exhausted.

His words conveyed anything but determination, confidence, courage, or leadership. What we saw was someone badly in need of sleep, someone weakened. Someone repeating the same old rhetoric while seeming almost to beg the United States not to go so far as to invade and to let them live in peace, as he claims the rest of the world advocates—even if that means he can continue enjoying his privileges while the vast majority of Cubans endure hardship.

What we witnessed at the beginning of this year with the capture of Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela demonstrated the enormous military disparity between a superpower and a Third World nation, a gap that would be even greater in a confrontation between Cuba and the United States.

Perhaps the dictatorship’s only advantage in such a scenario would be its extensive infiltration of US government institutions with spies, an effort that has been underway for decades and has proven highly effective. But even if military secrets could not be adequately protected, everything would ultimately be decided on the battlefield. And there, it would be the classic fight between a lion and a monkey—with the monkey tied to a post.

The tyranny’s position is clear: it seeks to impress those who still believe in it and intimidate everyone else, attempting to prevent these threats from triggering another social uprising, which would actually be the perfect formula for change.

To that end, every so often they display their obsolete weapons, which must give US military intelligence a good laugh, while here only the ignorant could believe they would withstand an assault.

Since Fidel Castro’s time, the island’s strategy has been based on establishing pockets of resistance throughout the country, under what was officially called the “War of the Entire People.”

But there is one enormous difference between the Fidel Castro era and today, and it is the key to understanding how different the situation would be now: the vast majority of Cubans do not support their leaders.

I know there are no reliable statistics to substantiate this. That would require the referendum we have been demanding for years, which the dictatorship refuses to hold. But it is what I see every day: countless people tired of being used in this political confrontation while watching their own dreams, and those of their children and grandchildren, continually postponed, just as the dreams of their parents and grandparents were buried.

There is a weariness that makes no noise, that is not proclaimed in public squares or featured in headlines. Instead, it settles on the shoulders of someone returning home late, in the hands of someone counting coins before making a purchase, in the eyes of someone who has learned not to promise their children too much. It is the exhaustion of feeling used.

For years, far too many people have been called upon to defend flags that offered them no shelter, slogans that put no food on their tables, promises that evaporated as soon as the march ended or the ballot boxes closed. They were asked for patience, sacrifice, and loyalty. They were told of a bright future, an imminent victory, a higher cause. And they gave their days, their enthusiasm, even their resentments, while watching the present slip through their fingers.

They had been promised that education would open doors, that honest work would allow them to build a home, that perseverance would be rewarded. But many of those doors remain closed. Owning a home has become a distant aspiration. Young people pack their bags not out of a thirst for adventure, but because they feel that staying means giving up. Parents watch silently as their children inherit not only a surname and a history, but also frustrations and the obligation to start over somewhere else.

That is why the frustration keeps growing. Not necessarily because people have abandoned their ideals, but because they are beginning to distinguish between ideas and those who exploit them. They no longer want to be a crowd, fuel for someone else’s cause, or an argument to be used. They do not want their suffering invoked in speeches by people who live far removed from its consequences. They do not want to keep sacrificing the present in exchange for a future that is always postponed.

The truth is that the real “War of the Entire People” is the struggle for survival. What people want is something simpler and, for that very reason, more profound: to live.

To live without having to justify their children’s hunger. To work without feeling that every effort disappears into a labyrinth. To grow old knowing that their grandchildren will have more opportunities than they did, not fewer. To reclaim the right to dream without asking permission, without waiting for another promise, without turning every hope into an act of faith.

Perhaps the time has come to listen to that exhaustion. Because when a society stops believing in those who summon it to action, it does not always abandon its dreams. Sometimes, at long last, it begins to demand that they be fulfilled. And that is the real terror sweeping through the corridors of the Central Committee.

Read more from Cuba here at Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba’s Benchmark Hospital That Lost Its Greatness
World.content:
Photo of the exterior of the Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital, taken from the hospital’s archives.

By Kamil Kenders

HAVANA TIMES – Some buildings are part of a city’s landscape, while others are also part of its memory. Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital belongs to both categories.

Its tower, visible from different points along Havana’s Malecon, was for many years an image associated with the development of Cuban medicine. For thousands of people, that building represented something more than a hospital: it offered the possibility of receiving specialized care, obtaining a diagnosis for a complicated condition, or undergoing treatment that was not available at just any other institution in the country.

Inaugurated on December 3, 1982, Hermanos Ameijeiras was conceived as a national referral center. Its facilities, equipment, specialists, and the diversity of services it offered placed it among Cuba’s most prestigious hospitals.

Highly complex medical procedures, research, and professional training programs were carried out there. For decades, its name inspired confidence. For many Cubans, being referred to Ameijeiras meant reaching one of the best possible places to receive medical care. But the years have passed, and that image of excellence seems to have become trapped in memory.

Today, speaking of Hermanos Ameijeiras also means speaking of shortages, deterioration, limited services, and difficulties that ultimately affect both patients and their families.

The reality behind its doors is far removed from the institution that was once a source of pride. It is not simply a matter of the physical deterioration of certain areas. It goes much deeper. The scarcity of material resources, lack of supplies, difficulties keeping equipment operational, and loss of medical professionals have gradually weakened the capacity of an institution that needs precisely the opposite: resources, technology, and specialized personnel.

Many healthcare professionals have emigrated in search of better living and working conditions. Those who remain in the country try to practice their profession under increasingly difficult circumstances. And those who continue caring for patients must confront a reality in which they do not always have what they need to do their jobs. Because a doctor may possess all the knowledge in the world, but without the necessary medications, reagents, instruments, or equipment, their ability to provide adequate care is inevitably limited.

According to accounts I have heard, difficulties performing certain clinical tests because of a lack of reagents have become another obstacle for patients at this hospital. Sometimes, even when a patient manages to obtain an appointment or see a specialist, completing the necessary diagnostic tests remains an unresolved problem.

A CT scan can be crucial in determining how a disease is progressing. An MRI can provide essential information for establishing a diagnosis. These are not optional machines or luxuries reserved for those who can afford them. They are fundamental tools of modern medicine. Yet breakdowns and a lack of resources to maintain and repair this equipment have ended up compromising essential services.

In July 2026, Associated Press published a report on the state of healthcare in Cuba that specifically included Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital. A patient with a history of cancer had been waiting seven months for a CT scan because the hospital’s machine was broken. Her story was a painful illustration of what it means to lack access to technology that can be decisive for a person’s life.

But some situations do not need to appear in a news report to reveal just how far the deterioration has gone. Not long ago, I witnessed a scene that I still find difficult to forget.

One of the hospital corridors. The cart with two blue tanks is used to transport water to the upper floors.

Family members accompanying hospitalized patients had to go down to the hospital basement to fetch water because the supply was not adequately reaching the upper floors. While patients remained hospitalized, their relatives had to take responsibility for obtaining something as basic as water. I am not talking about a bottle of drinking water out of personal preference or some additional comfort. I am talking about a basic necessity in any healthcare institution, especially in a place where there are sick people, some with mobility difficulties and others completely dependent on those caring for them.

I stopped to think about what it means for a family to have a loved one hospitalized and, on top of worrying about their health, have to go down to the basement to fetch water. How many other things must these family members manage on their own? How many needs end up becoming family responsibilities because the hospital cannot guarantee even the most basic conditions?

It is difficult not to feel disappointed. Because one can understand that a country is going through economic difficulties, that there are supply problems, or that certain resources are hard to obtain. But it is also impossible not to wonder how an institution of such importance has come to depend on such makeshift solutions for basic aspects of its operation.

And what is most troubling is that we are not talking about a small municipal hospital, a secondary facility, or a center that never had substantial resources. We are talking about Hermanos Ameijeiras.

That hospital which was once a national benchmark, which received patients from across the country, and which for years concentrated some of Cuba’s most specialized medical services.

I think about those who arrive there seeking answers about a serious illness. About those waiting for a diagnostic test that cannot be performed because the equipment is broken. About those who need laboratory tests and discover there are no reagents. About the family members who walk the corridors, climb up and down stairs, and end up taking care of needs that the institution itself should guarantee.

I also think about the doctors and other healthcare workers who remain there, trying to keep what still functions going, often under conditions that do not match the enormous responsibility resting on their shoulders.

Because the deterioration of a hospital is not measured solely by its walls, elevators, or facilities. It is measured, above all, by what it can no longer offer those who need its services.

And perhaps that is the saddest part of this story: the hospital’s name still carries the prestige of what it once was, but the everyday reality of many patients no longer seems to live up to that reputation.

The building is still standing. Its tower continues to dominate part of Havana’s skyline. It still bears the name “Hermanos Ameijeiras” and preserves the memory of an era when it represented the most advanced achievements of Cuban medicine.

But a hospital cannot live off its history. It cannot make diagnoses with memories of its former specialists, perform CT scans with broken equipment, or guarantee medical care by relying solely on the prestige of its name.

A hospital needs doctors, nurses, technicians, medications, reagents, water, electricity, and functioning technology. Above all, it needs to be able to care for its patients.

Hermanos Ameijeiras is still there. But I fear that, for many Cubans, its greatness is beginning to belong to the past. And that is much more than the deterioration of a building.

Read more from the diary of Kamil Kenders here on Havana Times.

World.title: Police Inaction Accelerates the Depopulation of Rural Cuba
World.content:
Photograph taken on April 1, 2025, of a farmer on his property in Cárdenas, Cuba. Julio, a 71-year-old Cuban farmer, decided to sell all his cows last year, fed up with vandals who would steal them at night to then sell the meat on the black market. File photo: EFE/ Ernesto Mastrascusa

By Amado Viera

HAVANA TIMES – It was not until late August, after a gang of cattle rustlers kidnapped a family on their farm, that the police in Guantanamo took notice of the wave of violence sweeping through the countryside of this eastern Cuban province. It took two weeks and an extensive operation to capture the 13 members of the gang responsible for the crime, some of whom resisted arrest with weapons.

Their behavior was predictable after months of growing accustomed to terrorizing vast rural areas of the province. At least a dozen families had been forced to abandon their farms for fear of violence.

The mass kidnapping in Palmarito del Guaso attracted attention because among the victims was a 10-year-old girl who was held captive along with her family while the thieves looted the farm. The outrage sparked by this abuse forced the police to launch an active search for the criminals. In the weeks that followed, the Palmarito gang and other criminals were captured in operations carried out throughout the province and neighboring Santiago de Cuba.

But shortly afterward, robberies and assaults were once again reported in the same areas. “There are mountainous areas of Guantanamo where people hardly plant crops or raise animals anymore because there are so many loafers waiting for a chance to steal whatever they can,” explained Yonimiller Horrutiniel, a Guantanamo native from the municipality of Niceto Perez.

The situation he describes is not limited to eastern Cuba. Nearly 500 kilometers to the west, in Camagüey province, the owners of the farm where he works decided to sell the property to “avoid trouble.”

That was the expression the owner used when he informed Yonimiller of his decision. Since the beginning of the year, thieves had stolen seven head of cattle and a myriad of other, less valuable belongings. But the incident that marked the point of no return was the theft of a horse to which the owner was particularly attached. The victim himself tracked down the animal and notified the authorities so they could arrest the thieves. But by the time they did so—a week later—the criminals had already slaughtered the horse.

Cities Come First

The farm where Yonimiller worked is located in Siete Palmas, a rural community southwest of the city of Camagüey. Because of its distance from the provincial capital, the community had its own police post for decades.

These neighborhood police posts form the foundation of Cuba’s public security system. Staffed by an officer and several agents, their responsibilities include compiling what is known as the “criminal potential” registry, a list of residents with criminal records or behavior suggesting a propensity to commit crimes. Traditionally, they have been an effective tool for preventing crime and identifying perpetrators.

Years ago, as part of a process of closing local police posts, the one in Siete Palmas was dismantled and converted into housing. To compensate, the police sent patrols through the community and surrounding areas for a time, but these visits gradually became less frequent. By the time the fuel crisis reached its peak this year, such patrols had long since become a thing of the past.

“We’d also have to see how they would manage to get here, considering the terrible condition of the roads. Modern patrol cars are only good for driving around town,” said Emilio Acevedo, a resident of the area.

When planning new purchases of police vehicles, the Ministry of the Interior has for years favored sedan models from brands such as Geely, Peugeot, and Hyundai, which are well suited to cities but impractical in rural areas. This reveals its priorities regarding public order: maintaining it in urban centers is considered more important than doing so in the countryside. To understand why, one need only ask where most anti-government protests have taken place in recent years.

More Crime Despite Harsh Sentences

In 2025, more than 90% of those tried in Cuban courts for stealing and slaughtering cattle and other large livestock were sentenced to prison. A report on the subject by the People’s Supreme Court adds that another 7.5% of defendants received fines, while barely 3% were found not guilty.

Such a high conviction rate is virtually unparalleled in contemporary legal systems. Nor is the severity of the sentences: according to the Ministry of Justice’s own statistics, judges’ decisions tend to be characterized by their “exemplary nature,” meaning that they impose the harshest penalties provided for in the Penal Code.

Despite the government’s punitive approach, reports of livestock theft and slaughter have continued to multiply. These cases represent only the “tip of the iceberg,” since “there are other crimes that aren’t even reported,” Felix Duarte Ortega, president of the National Association of Small Farmers (ANAP), pointed out a few months ago.

At an assembly of the organization held in the western province of Mayabeque, participants told him that many farmers find it burdensome to travel into town to report everything that happens on their farms. As a solution, the leader recommended “forming more farmers’ patrols.”

These groups attempt to make up for the absence of police in rural areas. Provinces such as Santiago de Cuba and Camagüey stand out for the number of farmers’ patrol units they have organized to confront cattle rustlers.

In September, ANAP’s leadership in Camagüey announced that it already had 25 such groups, with approximately 330 members in total. At first glance, that might seem like an impressive number, but in reality it falls far short of the province’s security needs. Covering 15,000 square kilometers, Camagüey is increasingly feeling the absence of the police, to the point that many farmers are beginning to wonder what purpose reporting a crime even serves.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.
