World.title: Argentina's lawyer in Hamburg: if Sea Lion goes ahead, "those rights are lost forever"
World.content:
Argentina's lawyer in Hamburg: if Sea Lion goes ahead, “those rights are lost forever”

22nd Sunday, November 2026 - 13:10 UTC Full article

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, part of Argentina's legal team, during the hearings before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg.

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, one of the lawyers representing Argentina before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, has argued that if the United Kingdom begins extracting oil at the Sea Lion project north of the Falklands, Argentina's rights over those resources “are lost forever”. The tribunal will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina's request to suspend the project.

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, one of the lawyers representing Argentina before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, has argued that if the United Kingdom begins extracting oil at the Sea Lion project north of the Falklands, Argentina's rights over those resources “are lost forever”. The tribunal will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina's request to suspend the project.

“States have the right to decide when, how and under what conditions they will exploit non-renewable resources,” Kohen said in an interview with Infobae. “Drilling and oil extraction cause an irreversible physical change to the continental shelf and its non-renewable resources. Once produced, there is no going back.”

Kohen, a native of Rosario based in Geneva, a professor of international law and secretary-general of the Institut de Droit International, previously represented Argentina before the same tribunal in 2012, when it unanimously ordered Ghana to release the frigate Libertad, held at the request of a creditor fund. In this case he is part of the team led by Argentina's agent, Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal.

According to the jurist, the United Kingdom centred its defence on sovereignty over the islands so that the tribunal would conclude it lacks jurisdiction, since it can only rule on matters under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Argentina, he said, limited itself to seeking to preserve its rights over the disputed continental shelf “while the dispute remains unresolved”.

At the November 10 and 11 hearings, the British delegation, led by Attorney General Ellie Reeves, argued that the tribunal has no jurisdiction over sovereignty issues and that suspending Sea Lion would “kill” it, with “devastating” consequences for the islanders. British lawyers estimated the loss for Rockhopper at about US$1 billion, and the chief executive of its Israeli partner, Navitas, warned in writing that even the briefest suspension would be “terminal” for the project. “Economic damage can be compensated; the modification of the continental shelf is irreversible,” Kohen replied.

The jurist also challenged the 2013 referendum invoked by Reeves as an expression of the islanders' self-determination, which he had described during the hearing as a “self-satisfaction referendum”. “It was a referendum that was neither organised nor supervised by the United Nations,” he said. In that vote, 99.8% of voters backed the islands remaining a British Overseas Territory. The United Kingdom maintains that the islanders have the right to decide their future and to develop their natural resources.

For Kohen, whatever the outcome, the case has already forced London “to justify itself before an international tribunal”. “The only way Argentina had to stop the United Kingdom from moving ahead with hydrocarbon exploitation was to turn to international jurisdiction,” he said.

World.title: Falklands: Public Accounts Committee to scrutinize several contracts and projects
World.content:
Falklands: Public Accounts Committee to scrutinize several contracts and projects

22nd Sunday, November 2026 - 13:09 UTC Full article

The contracts under scrutiny include the FIGAS hangar and the contract with construction firm RSK.

The Falkland Islands Public Accounts Committee (PAC) announced this week, as part of its remit, its routine 2026/27 programme of oversight and scrutiny of a number of government projects and contracts.

The Falkland Islands Public Accounts Committee (PAC) announced this week, as part of its remit, its routine 2026/27 programme of oversight and scrutiny of a number of government projects and contracts.

Over the next two months the programme covers two construction projects and three government contracts: the FIGAS hangar, FIGAS being the Islands government's air service; the contract with construction firm RSK; the lease contract for five cranes; the project for the installation of a new port; and the contract with Ramboll, the firm that advises and assists in planning the Islands' various infrastructure development projects.

The PAC's role is to provide external oversight of budget execution and of the legality of disbursements under current regulations.

The cases to be examined were selected by PAC staff, and the committee will also set the terms of reference for each before assigning them to an individual or team.

The PAC invites members of the public to contact that individual or team to assist with the scrutiny of the various cases if they believe they hold relevant information, which can be done in confidence. Those interested in joining as reviewers are likewise invited to contact the PAC.

PAC Executive Secretary Bernie Goodwin said the “function of the PAC is to ensure that the disbursements made by the Islands government are carried out properly, also drawing on the experience and skills of all members of the community.”

He added: “There are great benefits in including every possible area of information, not only within Government itself. We also hope to hear the views of any member of the public who feels able to contact or write to us, whether in confidence or publicly.”

The PAC can be reached on 22905 and at pacsecretary@horizon.co.fk

World.title: Danstar to follow international maritime law: will seek clearance only for Punta Arenas departure and Stanley arrival
World.content:
Danstar to follow international maritime law: will seek clearance only for Punta Arenas departure and Stanley arrival

22nd Sunday, November 2026 - 13:07 UTC Full article

The flyer announcing the arrival of the SSL Chile representatives.

Pablo Pacheco, owner and general manager of the shipping company Easter Island Logistics, told the Chilean press that the cargo vessel Danstar “will strictly follow international maritime law” on its inaugural voyage between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, scheduled for December, which has prompted reports in Argentine media about an alleged request to cross Argentine waters.

Pablo Pacheco, owner and general manager of the shipping company Easter Island Logistics, told the Chilean press that the cargo vessel Danstar “will strictly follow international maritime law” on its inaugural voyage between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, scheduled for December, which has prompted reports in Argentine media about an alleged request to cross Argentine waters.

“We are only going to request clearance for departure from Punta Arenas and arrival at Stanley,” Pacheco said, stressing that “this procedure is the one that corresponds under international regulations and the bilateral treaties in force.”

The Danstar, which sails under the Chilean flag and is currently undergoing technical maintenance at the ASMAR shipyards in Punta Arenas, is scheduled to begin commercial operations around mid-December 2026.

On this route — roughly 900 kilometres and two and a half days' sailing — the company will reactivate a direct maritime connection between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, suspended for more than a decade.

The shipping line also reiterated that the cargo carried is for exclusively civilian and humanitarian purposes, consisting of perishable foodstuffs, fruit, vegetables, liquefied gas and construction materials to supply the archipelago's residents, distancing itself entirely from any logistical operation linked to the hydrocarbons industry in the area.

In the Islands, meanwhile, the Falkland Islands Development Corporation, which reports to the Islands government and has conducted all the negotiations for restoring the commercial link with southern Chile, announced that it welcomed Jaime and Javier of Sea Shipping Line (SSL) this Saturday. They will remain in the Islands for a week, until November 28.

“The team will be available to provide support on supply matters and on loading and dispatch arrangements for the new Punta Arenas/Stanley supply line operated by Naviera Easter Island,” the Development Corporation said in a statement.

As part of their visit, Jaime and Javier will give a presentation on SSL Chile's services, covering who they are and what they offer, with an opportunity to meet them and put questions to them.

The presentation takes place on Monday November 23, from 4.30pm to 6.30pm, in the Events Room at the Harbour Lights cinema. Traders, business owners and the general public are invited to attend.

For further information, contact communications@fidc.co.fk

Sea Shipping Line (SSL) contact details: Jaime Alvarez: jaime.alvarez@seashipping.cl, +56 9 5640 1615. Javier Figueroa: jf@seashipping.cl, +56 9 7807 4100.

World.title: Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised in Brasília with abdominal pain
World.content:
Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised in Brasília with abdominal pain

21st Saturday, November 2026 - 06:25 UTC Full article

Jair Bolsonaro surrounded by security officers.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to hospital in Brasília on Friday after suffering abdominal pain and distension, according to a statement from the medical centre where he remains. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, under house arrest on health grounds.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to hospital in Brasília on Friday after suffering abdominal pain and distension, according to a statement from the medical centre where he remains. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, under house arrest on health grounds.

Doctors carried out a series of tests to determine the cause of his symptoms, the hospital said. News of his admission was first given on X by his son Carlos Bolsonaro, elected senator in October's elections, who spoke of “intense abdominal pain”.

Bolsonaro, who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022, was convicted by the Supreme Federal Court in September 2025 and has been serving his sentence since that year. He was granted house arrest at his home in Brasília on humanitarian grounds. Since 2018, when he was stabbed in the abdomen at a campaign event, he has undergone several surgeries and been hospitalised on numerous occasions.

His eldest son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, lost the October 25 presidential run-off to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, did not concede defeat and left Brazil via the Argentine border bound for the United States. From 2027, four members of the Bolsonaro family will hold seats in Brazil's Congress.

World.title: Trump threatens to penalise tech companies that build data centres outside the US
World.content:
Trump threatens to penalise tech companies that build data centres outside the US

21st Saturday, November 2026 - 06:22 UTC Full article

Donald Trump waves as he boards Air Force One.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to penalise American technology companies that build data centres abroad, through tariffs or other levies, although he did not explain what goal he was pursuing or how he would enforce the measure, and acknowledged he had not even presented the idea to his team.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to penalise American technology companies that build data centres abroad, through tariffs or other levies, although he did not explain what goal he was pursuing or how he would enforce the measure, and acknowledged he had not even presented the idea to his team.

“We are not going to allow companies to build data centres in other countries,” Trump said at a White House press conference, where he promised “tremendous punishments” for companies that try. Such a measure would likely face opposition from the companies affected and from Congress, which Democrats will control from January.

The threat comes amid heightened Washington scrutiny of data centres in third countries. The Commerce Department last week announced measures to prevent countries deemed a risk, such as China, from accessing Nvidia's most advanced chips through remote use of data centres located in other countries. The investigation centres on Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought billions of dollars' worth of chips from Nvidia and whose former executive, Alice Huang, is suspected by Washington of spying for China.

The case led to the resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive, after it emerged that he had an extramarital relationship with her. Trump again called for his return to the helm of the company, something Nvidia has said it is not considering. Huang may have made “bad decisions”, the president said, but “he is a brilliant man. We have to protect our brilliant men, and Jensen is one of them.”

Trump was speaking to review his Thursday meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. At his bilateral meeting with Xi, the two countries agreed to hold consultations to establish safeguards and warning mechanisms for possible problems in the development of the most advanced artificial intelligence models.

The president insisted that data centres are key to winning the artificial intelligence race and pledged to “fight hard” for them, despite growing opposition among Americans. According to El País, in this month's midterm elections voters approved 40 of the 41 measures put to referendums in various states to ban or restrict their construction.

World.title: UK and EU sign their biggest deal since Brexit in Brussels
World.content:
UK and EU sign their biggest deal since Brexit in Brussels

20th Friday, November 2026 - 19:42 UTC Full article

The flags of the United Kingdom and the European Union at the European Commission headquarters in Brussels.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa signed three agreements in Brussels on Friday on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility, the largest package agreed between the two sides since Britain left the European Union, a decade after the Brexit referendum.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa signed three agreements in Brussels on Friday on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility, the largest package agreed between the two sides since Britain left the European Union, a decade after the Brexit referendum.

“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe,” said Burnham, who called the agreement “landmark”. Von der Leyen described it as “a turning point” in relations. In a joint statement, both sides committed to building an “ambitious and dynamic” relationship, according to AP. It is the second summit between the two sides since Brexit; the first, held in London in May 2025, opened the negotiations that concluded on Friday.

The first agreement creates a common sanitary and phytosanitary area that will scrap checks on trade in animal and plant products, including goods moving between Great Britain, Northern Ireland and the EU. The British government puts its impact at £5.1 billion a year, about US$6.7 billion, although it will not apply before March 1, 2028, as the UK must pass legislation to align dynamically with EU rules. The second links the two sides' emissions trading systems, exempting British companies from the EU's carbon border levy from 2028. The third creates a scheme allowing 100,000 young people from each side to live in the other's territory for up to three years to work, study or travel. Burnham pitched the package as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people”.

Open questions remain, however. According to a member-state document obtained by AFP, the 27 are making ratification conditional on the UK lowering university fees paid by European students, currently higher than those paid by Britons; two diplomats cited by the press point to a compromise. Nor was British access to the EU's industrial programme resolved, which Brussels makes conditional on London aligning its trade policy, including tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The British government acknowledged that “talks will continue in some areas”.

Burnham, in power since July, announced he will open a discussion with European partners on “options for the long-term relationship,” ranging from maintaining the status quo to a customs union or membership, and did not rule out his party including re-entry in its next election manifesto. The next general election is due in 2029.

The opposition reacted sharply. “Naive Andy Burnham has gone to Brussels and run into the hard reality I have been warning about for decades. Flexibility is a fantasy,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage wrote on X. The Conservatives accused the prime minister of “betrayal” of Brexit.

World.title: Buenos Aires marks King Charles's birthday with a reconciliation message amid bilateral tension
World.content:
Buenos Aires marks King Charles's birthday with a reconciliation message amid bilateral tension

20th Friday, November 2026 - 14:21 UTC Full article

Guests and the Northlands school pupils' choir at the British ambassador's residence in Buenos Aires, during the reception marking King Charles's birthday.

The British Embassy in Buenos Aires celebrated King Charles III's 78th birthday on Thursday with a reception at which Ambassador David Cairns defended the strength of ties with Argentina despite “not-so-good days” and announced that in 2027 the 45th anniversary of the Falklands War will be marked together with veterans and families of the fallen from both countries.

The British Embassy in Buenos Aires celebrated King Charles III's 78th birthday on Thursday with a reception at which Ambassador David Cairns defended the strength of ties with Argentina despite “not-so-good days” and announced that in 2027 the 45th anniversary of the Falklands War will be marked together with veterans and families of the fallen from both countries.

“In international relations, as in personal relationships, there can be good days and not-so-good days,” Cairns told some 800 guests from politics, the judiciary, business, diplomacy and culture gathered at the ambassador's residence. “I am the 56th British ambassador to Argentina, and as such I will continue working to strengthen the ties between our two countries. I am convinced we will enjoy more good days than not-so-good days.”

As an example of that strength, the ambassador recalled last year's celebrations of the bicentenary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and announced that next year the 45th anniversary of the “South Atlantic conflict” will be marked “with respect and sensitivity, working together with veterans and the families of the fallen in both countries to promote reconciliation and friendship”. Cairns also highlighted values associated with the monarch, such as diversity, inclusion and care for nature: “Countries are stronger when their societies are diverse and open.”

The celebration, held as a garden party, included the British and Argentine national anthems performed by the pupils' choir of Northlands school, performances by the Orquesta de los Barrios, a programme for young musicians from disadvantaged backgrounds, and a mural by artist Costhanzo featuring British and Argentine icons. The event was sponsored by British and Argentine companies, including Pan American Energy, BP and Standard Chartered.

The reception took place two days after Javier Milei's government rejected Princess Anne's visit to the islands as a “provocation”, and nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rules on Argentina's request to halt the Sea Lion oil project.

World.title: Brazil's Central Bank sells US$1 billion to curb the dollar's rise
World.content:
Brazil's Central Bank sells US$1 billion to curb the dollar's rise

20th Friday, November 2026 - 04:27 UTC Full article

A person walks past the Central Bank of Brazil headquarters in Brasília.

Brazil's Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its international reserves on Thursday in an attempt to curb the rise of the US currency, which approached 5.93 reais, amid financial market distrust of the fiscal adjustment proposed by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government. The move brought initial relief, but the dollar rose again in the afternoon.

Brazil's Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its international reserves on Thursday in an attempt to curb the rise of the US currency, which approached 5.93 reais, amid financial market distrust of the fiscal adjustment proposed by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government. The move brought initial relief, but the dollar rose again in the afternoon.

The intervention follows several days of falls on the São Paulo stock exchange and a sharp depreciation of the real, which makes imports more expensive, especially fuel, and puts pressure on inflation. Investors doubt the government's ability to control spending and stabilise public debt, which exceeds 92% of gross domestic product.

The spending containment plan, already approved by the Senate, will be voted on next week in the Chamber of Deputies. The government estimated savings of between 50 billion and 60 billion reais in 2027, between US$8.4 billion and US$10.1 billion, although the figure may change due to amendments made in Congress. One of its pillars caps growth in public spending above inflation at 2% a year, down from the current 2.5%. Part of the market considers the plan insufficient.

The adjustment has drawn criticism from the Brazilian left, particularly from sectors to the left of the Workers' Party, who fear cuts to health and education. Lula said on Thursday that “some comrades” had not understood the proposal and pledged that, as long as he is president, “there will be no reduction in the rights the Brazilian people have won”. He told the market that he too wants fiscal control, but criticised the moves of recent days: “What is really happening is that there are people trying to make money from speculation, from rumours.”

Lula, re-elected on October 25, has not announced who will be his economy minister for the term that begins on January 5, another source of uncertainty. The current minister, Dario Durigan, expressed concern about the pace of the economy in 2027, although he ruled out a recession. According to the Central Bank's latest survey of analysts, published on November 16, growth will slow from 2.3% in 2025 to 1.7% this year and 1% in 2027. The benchmark Selic interest rate stands at 13.75% a year, after the Central Bank halted a cycle of five consecutive cuts in November.

World.title: The history of Mexico’s corridos and the controversy over censorship
World.content:
Talking about music and the effect it has on humans is complex. Music shapes brains and communities: it forges neural connections, helps regulate emotion and offers a language for belonging.

The corrido — Mexico’s narrative ballad — embodies all those powers. It has been a walking newspaper, a moral pamphlet, a protest song, and, increasingly, a contested cultural weapon.

So why does the Mexican state practice a veiled censorship of this genre today, and what does the corrido tell us about modern Mexico?

Jugglers and corridos

To find the corrido’s origin, we must look to medieval jugglers. Before newspapers and radio, itinerant narrators moved from town to town, recounting events and epics with a vihuela, a precursor to the guitar.

That practice evolved into the Spanish romancero of the 15th and 16th centuries: eight-syllable verses delivering current events in a direct, emotional tone. Some scholars trace a specific Andalusian strain — marked by a “correntío” or accelerated rhythm — as a key progenitor.

Arriving in New Spain, the romancero did not remain pure. It fused with Indigenous oral forms and Afrodescendant rhythms, folding pre-Hispanic narrative techniques into a hybrid vernacular that became uniquely Mexican. In Northern Mexico, a further infusion came from German, Swiss and Austro-Hungarian immigrants who introduced polkas, mazurkas, redovas, the violin and the accordion.

The guitar, bajo sexto, accordion, and polka and waltz-derived meters together formed the musical DNA that allowed Spanish-inflected corridos to evolve into the Northern Mexican styles now among the genre’s most recognizable variants.

The 19th-century corridos

Under Porfirio Díaz, European refinement was idealized. As a result, the corrido became a popular countervoice. In a mostly illiterate society, corridos functioned as both information and entertainment — often carrying clear moral lessons. They narrated land disputes, banditry, and local injustices in compact, episodic verses that crystallized communal memory.

The “Corrido of Heraclio Bernal” (circa 1870–1880) exemplifies this. Bernal — cast as a bandit and a kind of proto-Robin Hood who opposed Díaz’s order — was immortalized in song as a brave, authentic figure unafraid of death.

Contemporary corridos were pamphlets set to music: instruments of social critique and folk memory.

Revolutionary corridos (1910–1920)

During the Mexican Revolution, the corrido flourished. Thousands of ballads recounted the deeds and deaths of Emiliano Zapata, Pancho Villa, Francisco I. Madero, Venustiano Carranza and countless local actors. Corridos appeared in newspapers and on loose broadsheets advertised as “new corridos,” and for many they were a primary source of news.

But the songs did more than report events: they authorized new imaginaries. Much as muralists refigured the nation — elevating peasants and laborers into civic icons — the corrido became the musical narrative of rural life, a sonic repository of popular values.

“La Adelita,” “Valentina,” the “Corrido de la Toma de Zacatecas,” and an adapted “La Cucaracha” (used to lampoon President Victoriano Huerta) entered a shared cultural lexicon that helped legitimate postrevolutionary ideologies.

1930 to 1960

El Pablote - Francisco El Charro Avitia - Primer Corrido de Narcotrafico "Narcocorrido" 2da version

Watch this video on YouTube

After the Revolution, Mexico experienced a profound transformation in its political, social and demographic landscape. Urban centers — especially Mexico City — began to attract large numbers of newcomers lured by promises of modernity and a better future, fueling rapid city growth and social change.

At the same time, rural Mexico acquired a romantic-epic image, with inhabitants stereotyped as “rough, direct, uncivilized, but kind-hearted.” This dual narrative — that of proud countryside and modern city — would shape Mexico’s cultural landscape for decades.

In both music and cinema, rural people were portrayed as humble yet proud, embodying virtues that contrasted with urban sophistication but also contributed to a shared national identity. To legitimize this collective vision, the Mexican state deployed culture as a tool of consolidation: Literature, cinema, theater and especially radio were used to craft and disseminate a unified image of Mexico.

Corridos, alongside genres such as huapango, banda, sones and rancheras, transitioned from local, fiery oral traditions into part of a broader, state-backed cultural repertoire — an effort to forge a common cultural fabric across regional boundaries.

This period also marks the emergence of the first narcocorridos, even as they continued to contain cautionary messages. The earliest recorded narcocorrido, “El Pablote” (1931), tells of Pablo González, known as “The Morphine King,” and functions primarily as a warning, emphasizing the tragic, often deadly consequences of criminal life rather than glorifying the outlaw.

Unlike the narcocorridos of later years, which would celebrate criminal figures and their deeds, these early songs served to dissuade people from following such dangerous paths. As radio and cinema standardized and disseminated these songs, local variations and rough edges of regional narratives were smoothed, turning them into a national storytelling tradition — yet still rooted in the social realities of marginalized communities.

1960 to 1980

By the late 1950s, many regarded the corrido as folklore in decline — a nostalgic but dated taste of Mexican peasantry gone by. Themes shifted toward migration, identity and the reality of drug trafficking.

The late 1980s brought a pivotal rupture in the figure of Chalino Sánchez. His unpolished delivery and raw narrative aesthetic cut through studio gloss; he popularized the practice of composing commissioned corridos for criminal figures and, crucially, normalized a celebratory tone toward illicit actors. That normalization carried risks — several singers and composers of the time paid with their lives.

Infamously, Sánchez is said to have been handed a note before performing his final song, informing him that he would be executed at the conclusion of his concert. A video of him receiving and reading the note, before launching into a spirited final performance, has become an important part of Mexican folklore. Regardless of the contents of the note, Sánchez was shot and killed immediately after leaving the stage.

2008 and the ‘altered corrido’

President Felipe Calderón’s militarized offensive against cartels in the late 2000s altered the cultural ecology. Corridos evolved from chronicling social life to entering criminal ecosystems.

New singers — sometimes commissioned by cartels, sometimes seeking notoriety — produced explicit songs that described organizational structures, operations and personalities. In some regions, corridos functioned as targeted messages among rival groups or as status instruments within criminal networks.

Chalino Sánchez - Alma Enamorada (En Vivo) Video Oficial con Letras

Watch this video on YouTube

Mainstream radio and public venues — conscious of safety and reputation — began to restrict such songs. The state framed these restrictions as public safety measures: Songs that normalize criminality can arguably promote recruitment or confer legitimacy on violent actors.

Yet the evidence for direct causality is weak. Cultural products shape imaginaries but do not by themselves produce armed actors. What bans often achieve is displacement: corridos migrate to pirate radio, local stations and online platforms where they can become more clandestine and, in some cases, operational.

New media and corridos

Digital platforms have proven more permissive than traditional broadcasters. Streaming, social networks and video sites have decentralized control, allowing subgenres to proliferate and cross borders. Corridos tumbados — a hybrid of trap, hip-hop cadence, autotune and corrido storytelling — illustrates the genre’s current elasticity. It speaks to urban youth experiences of identity, marginalization and aspiration.

The growth of this genre, and major singers such as Natanael Cano, Junior H, Fuerza Regida and Peso Pluma, reflects Mexico’s continuing appetite for corridos — more specifically, narcocorridos.

Peso Pluma’s appearance on “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” in 2024 represented the moment at which the genre became mainstream among not only Northern Mexicans but also younger Mexican-Americans on the other side of the border.

Made in Mexico: Corridos

Watch this video on YouTube

Beyond the obvious parallels to urban music genres in the United States, their success underscores a deeper truth: In a country of nearly 130 million, stark economic inequality (INEGI figures show only about 1.2 percent in the upper class while 56.6 percent fall into lower brackets) makes narratives of rapid ascent and alternative forms of capital especially resonant.

Do corridos cause violence?

The government’s justification for restricting corrido broadcasts is straightforward: Songs that glorify crime can normalize and celebrate violence. Cultural expressions do shape worldviews. But violence has multiple and deeper causes — poverty, impunity, institutional weakness and the lucrative rewards of illegal markets. To treat songs as primary causal agents is naive.

Moreover, suppression can backfire. Making content forbidden can enhance its allure and shift it into darker channels where it accrues different kinds of power.

Luis R Conriquez, Neton Vega - Si No Quieres No [Video Oficial]

Watch this video on YouTube

Why are narcorridos being censored?

The state’s veiled censorship is partly symbolic. Controlling the airwaves is a visible way to contest narratives that valorize criminal actors. But censorship addresses a symptom, not the structural conditions that make criminal economies attractive.

A more effective public strategy would combine cultural measures — support for alternative narratives, protection for artists and journalists, media literacy — with robust action on inequality, corruption and impunity.

The continuing importance of the corrido

The corrido endures because it is a living archive. It records who people were, whom they admired, whom they feared and whom they aspired to become. Attempts to erase the genre will not silence the stories; they will only change their modes of circulation and, perhaps, their social meanings. If policymakers seek to blunt the corrosive effects of glamorization, they must address both symbolic and structural realities. Otherwise, the corrido will continue to sing Mexico’s contradictions — unaltered in form, but perhaps louder in the shadows.

The corrido’s long road — from medieval jugglers to global streams — reminds us that music is both history and argument. It is a conversation about memory, identity and legitimacy. Censoring verses is a poor substitute for fixing the conditions that give those verses their force.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico’s tourism sector rushes to ensure cultural heritage remains compatible with 32-ounce margaritas
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

GUADALAJARA, Jalisco — Following new government data showing that 36.3% of foreign visitors now travel to Mexico primarily for its culture rather than its beaches, tourism officials confirmed Tuesday that the hospitality sector is working quickly to make millennia of heritage compatible with a 32-ounce blended margarita.

The figures, announced during the opening ceremony of the inaugural ITB Americas trade show in Guadalajara, revealed that cultural tourism now more than doubles the 15% to 16% share of visitors seeking traditional coastal vacations. To meet the shifting demand, hotel operators and tour planners across the country have unveiled a new “Conscious Cuervo” initiative designed to pair pre-Hispanic history, contemporary art and regional gastronomy with an uninterrupted supply of salted-rim cocktails.

“Travelers today want a deep, meaningful connection to Mexico’s living traditions, provided it is accompanied by crushed ice and a tiny paper parasol,” said Rodrigo Villalobos, a hospitality consultant attending the Guadalajara conference. “Our data shows that visitors are thrilled to explore a 16th-century convent or a neighborhood artisan market, as long as there is a frozen margarita waiting at the exit.”

Under the updated guidelines, several museums and archaeological zones are piloting “interpretive refreshment stations,” where audio guides automatically pause every 15 minutes to direct guests toward the nearest mixology cart. Meanwhile, culinary operators in Oaxaca and Mexico City reported high satisfaction scores after introducing “heritage flights,” allowing visitors to sample three distinct varieties of ancestral mezcal alongside a pitcher of strawberry margaritas large enough to require two hands.

Tourism analysts noted that the trend reflects a broader global shift in which travelers increasingly view cultural enrichment as an essential vacation component, ranking just ahead of pool access and slightly behind happy hour.

“I came to Mexico specifically for the architecture and the history, and learning about the Zapotec civilization while holding a yard-long plastic cup really brought the ruins to life,” said a visitor from Chicago before boarding a tour bus to a local weaving cooperative. “Honestly, it is nice to engage with the real country without having to give up blended tequila.”

World.title: The two shipwrecked Spaniards who changed the history of Yucatán
World.content:
On Feb. 18, 1519, Hernán Cortés departed from Cuba on the great adventure that would end with the destruction of the Mexica Empire. By March, his small fleet sailed along the Yucatán coast, shores still uncharted by any Spaniard.

While on the island of Cozumel, he heard of a “bearded man” who lived some distance away. Excited that this sounded like a fellow Spaniard, he found villagers willing to take a message to this mysterious person.

Although the original letter has been lost, it was copied at the time, and we can be reasonably confident of its content:

“Noble sirs: Those of the island have assured me that there are in the country five or six men with beards and resembling us in all things. They are unable to give or tell me other indications, but from these I conjecture and hold certain that you are Spaniards. I and these gentlemen who go with me to settle and discover these lands urge that within six days from receiving this you come to us, without making further delay or excuse. If you shall come we will make due acknowledgment, and reward the good offices which this armada shall receive from you. I send a brigantine that you may come in it, and two boats for safety.”

A strange encounter off Cozumel

Unsure if the messengers would return, if the man they spoke of was still alive, or if he had even existed, Cortés continued his journey.

By chance, a leaking ship forced his return to Cozumel, and while repairs were underway, native canoes arrived from the mainland. Bernal Díaz del Castillo left a firsthand account of this encounter in his book, “The True History of the Conquest of New Spain.”

The canoes were greeted by a group of conquistadores out hunting, and one of their new arrivals stepped forward to greet them. The visitor was not immediately recognized as Spanish, for, as Díaz del Castillo writes, “they could not distinguish him from an Indian as he was naturally brown and he had his hair shorn like an Indian slave, and carried a paddle on his shoulder, he wore one old sandal and the other was tied to his belt, he had on a ragged old coat, and a worse loincloth with which he covered his nakedness.”

The man identified himself by shouting “God and Holy Mary and Seville!” in Spanish, and was immediately brought to Cortés.

The story of Gerónimo de Aguilar

Here, he introduced himself as Gerónimo de Aguilar.

Back in 1511, he had been aboard the Spanish caravel Santa María de la Barca, which had sunk in a storm while sailing from Darién to Santo Domingo. A dozen or so people had escaped the sinking vessel by clambering into a small boat. Without a sail, and with only minimal food and water, they drifted for 13 days on the open sea. The survivors had finally been washed ashore along the Yucatán coast, where they were captured by a Maya chief identified as Waymil.

Aguilar described how some of the survivors were immediately sacrificed and eaten by their captors, while he and a few others were caged “to be fattened” for the next festival.

This part of the story is doubtful, for while Maya society certainly made human sacrifices, there is no evidence of cannibalism. Similarly, no details are offered as to how Aguilar, along with a fellow prisoner, Gonzalo Guerrero, escaped from captivity. The most likely explanation is that they were passed on from their initial captors as a gift to a greater chieftain.

Two paths in captivity

The two survivors were separated and forced into slavery. Gerónimo de Aguilar was a religious man who refused all temptations to take a Maya wife, and he impressed Cortés by producing a worn prayer book that he had protected all those years. He saw Cortés as his long-awaited savior and happily joined the expedition as guide and translator.

Aguilar explained that his late arrival in Cozumel was due to trying to contact Gonzalo Guerrero. However, Guerrero, who lived some distance away, had declined to join him as he was “married and had three sons, and that his face was tattooed and his ears and lower lip were pierced.”

Aguilar served Cortés well and, after the conquest, settled in Mexico City, where he was granted land and slaves. He died in the city in 1531. He should not, it must be noted, be confused with Francisco de Aguilar, who later wrote “Brief Record of the Conquest of New Spain,” in which he also gave a passing mention of Cortés encountering a marooned Spaniard while on Cozumel.

A new attempt at conquest

A decade after Cortés had subdued the Mexica, the Maya remained stubbornly independent, but eventually Spain once again set her eyes on this world of dry scrub and thorny forests.

With this, our story switches from Hernán Cortés to Francisco de Montejo.

At this point, Montejo was in his 50s and had spent much of his adult life in the Americas. He had sailed with Cortés, for which he had been rewarded with mines and haciendas. Having been granted a charter by Charles V to “explore, conquer and colonize the islands of Cozumel and the Yucatán,” he reached Cozumel in September 1527. From there the party crossed the channel to the mainland, where they established a small settlement.

The Yucatán, however, would not be an easy conquest, and sickness, the lack of water and natives on the defensive saw the colony collapse. This was the start of a protracted struggle that would bring the Spaniards numerous setbacks, and it would be 170 years before the last independent Maya state finally fell.

The renegade Spaniard

When Montejo heard of a renegade Spaniard living with the Maya, he correctly assumed this was Gonzalo Guerrero, with whom Aguilar had been shipwrecked 16 years earlier.

While Gerónimo de Aguilar had been a priest, Guerrero was a soldier with experience from Spain’s numerous wars against the Moors and in Italy. Unlike the pious Aguilar, Guerrero had been more willing to make the best of his situation.

After 16 years with the Maya people, he was not only still alive but had used his military experience to reach a position of authority in his adopted home.

Frustrated at their lack of progress, and anxious to seek local expertise, Montejo sent Guerrero a letter reminding him of his Christian faith, and offering his friendship and a complete pardon if he would join them. Guerrero replied by writing on the back of the letter that he could not leave his lord because he was enslaved, “even though I am married and have a wife and children. I remember God, and you, Sir, and the Spaniards have a good friend in me.”

Historical accounts and condemnation

The use of the word “slave” has been questioned, as Guerrero seems to have achieved a high military rank, but there is no reason he could not have gained promotion while remaining the property of his lord.

For an account of this part of the story, we rely on the writings of Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés. After spending much of his life in the Americas, Oviedo returned to Spain, where he wrote “La Natural Historia de las Indias” in 1526 and “Historia General de las Indias,” which was published in 1535.

Oviedo was an eyewitness to much of what he recorded and is considered a “good” historian for conducting careful interviews with other veterans of the American campaigns. Where the facts can be checked, his work appears accurate, with none of the wandering into fantasy that marks many other travel accounts of this age.

Where Oviedo is at fault is not in his recounting of events, but in offering judgment on other people’s actions. He was obsessed with Guerrero’s physical transformation and his adoption of Maya culture, writing, “This Gonzalo, the sailor, had already been converted into an Indian and was much worse than an Indian. He was married to an Indian woman. His ears and tongue were disfigured by sacrifice, and his body decorated and painted like that of an Indian; and he had a wife and children.”

A warrior’s final battle and legacy

Oviedo attributes Guerrero’s reluctance to join his fellow Spaniards to shame about his appearance and what he had become. He does not consider that the man might have had genuine affection toward his wife and children.

Oviedo also felt the need to explain how a “primitive” people such as those of the Yucatán could have proved so resistant to Spanish arms. The answer, he felt, could only be that they had help, and the villain was obviously that lost soul Gonzalo Guerrero. Oviedo credited Guerrero with coordinating Maya resistance to Montejo in 1528 and being behind the ambush of Alonso de Dávila’s forces in 1531.

On Aug. 14, 1536, Andrés de Cereceda, governor of troublesome provinces in modern Honduras, wrote to Spain, informing the king that a party of 50 war canoes had arrived to support the uprising of the local people. They had paddled up the Ulúa River to Ticamaya, where there had been a fierce battle. During the fighting, a heavily tattooed white man had been killed by a shot from an arquebus. This was almost certainly Gonzalo Guerrero.

Oviedo wrote of Guerrero as a traitor, but that viewpoint has changed over the years. Today Guerrero is celebrated as a freedom fighter and father of the mestizo population. He has been the hero of historical novels, most notably Eugenio Aguirre’s bestseller “Gonzalo Guerrero,” and there is an impressive bronze statue of him and his family in the Yucatán resort town of Akumal. Whether a hero of the Maya or a traitor to the Spanish, he certainly appears to have been a brave and honorable man.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: ‘He woke us up’: The man who changed the map of Mexico (Part I)
World.content:
In my family, we called him Super Carlos. Together with the Wixárika people and his team of dedicated attorneys, he changed the map of Mexico.

Carlos Chávez Reyes, who died in October at the age of 72, was a pioneer in Mexico’s Indigenous rights movement. Working alongside the leadership of the Wixárika — the Indigenous group also known as the Huichols — and a team of attorneys, researchers and technicians, he led the recovery of 65,000 hectares of stolen land, according to his son Cristian — and trained a generation, Indigenous and not, to carry on the work. The effort also recovered land in the disputed borderlands between Jalisco and Nayarit — territory lost to ranchers backed by the government in Tepic, which prompted the Nayarit governor to declare Chávez persona non grata and suggest he was Subcomandante Marcos.

“Carlos Chávez educated us. He woke us up when we were terrified — when we had no knowledge, no wisdom to defend ourselves,” said Maurilio Haiwiye Ramírez, general coordinator of the Wixárika Regional Council. When Carlos arrived, he added, “there was no one who could speak on our behalf.”

Chávez was one of a generation who chose to drop out of the system and look to Nature — and, increasingly, to those who lived closest to it — for answers.

As UC-Berkeley geographer Diana Negrín tells it, Carlos belonged to a first generation of “huicholeros de corazón” (“Huichol supporters of the heart”) who came to the sierra as collaborators rather than researchers or bureaucrats. Among them were Rocío Echevarría and Diana Negrín’s own parents, Juan and Yvonne.

The late 1970s were a hinge for the Wixárika communities. “The first roads had been built, and the logging companies were coming in with a vengeance,” explained Diana.

In 1977, at the age of 23, Chávez met Eulalia González Ávalos, his beloved Lala; together the two had five sons, each of whom carries on his legacy. Tunuary and Cristian, his twin sons, have gone on to earn degrees in environmental science, deepening and broadening the territorial defense that their father began.

Carlos and Lala launched a natural medicine project in the countryside outside of Guadalajara, exploring the healing properties of plants and treating people for miles around. His search for plant medicines led him to the Wixárika, and to the mara’akate (shamans).

Rocío Echeverria, a registered nurse who ran the health center in San Andrés Cohamiata for six years before founding Casa Huichol, remembers those days fondly, having logged many miles with Carlos.

“Those were crazy, crazy times,” she recalled. In their first journeys, the highways to Wixárika territories had not yet been built, so reaching the communities meant a plane and then days on foot. There they accompanied the people to other dimensions, sitting around Tatewari, Grandfather Fire, through long nights of music, dance, sacrifice and vision.

They walked with local medicine men and women through the Western Sierra Madre, learning the Wixárika pharmacopeia. But the most important medicine did not grow in the Sierra Madre. Hikuri, the Wixárika word for peyote, is gathered in their annual pilgrimages to Wirikuta, one of the five most sacred sites in their millennial cosmology.

In those journeys, Carlos and Rocío observed the terrible poverty of the people, a bare subsistence that left them vulnerable to hunger and common illnesses that could quickly turn deadly with the lack of care. And as Carlos himself told the story to this reporter on a long-ago journey to the Sierra in his trusty grey Toyota pickup truck, the people told him repeatedly that what they really needed was their land — the best land, taken by neighboring ranchers to harvest timber, graze cattle and, in the worst cases, grow marijuana and poppies for the cartels.

They needed an advocate, not an herbalist. In his travels, he met Juan Negrín, another pioneering figure who came to the same conclusions. Juan, roughly a decade older, had already built the organizations through which Chávez learned institutional work, and the two joined forces. In 1990, he helped found the Asociación Jalisciense de Apoyo a Grupos Indígenas (AJAGI), which would become the legal and technical backbone of the Wixárika land struggle for the next three decades.

Paul Liffman, an anthropologist who served as an expert witness in a number of AJAGI’s land cases over two decades, remembers Carlos describing the realization himself. He had begun believing healing came through medicine. “But then he understood that for people to be healthy, they first had to eat well. And to eat well, they needed maize. And to have maize, they needed land.” The illness and the landlessness were the same problem.

Under a blanket in the back of a pickup

The danger was not abstract. Yvonne Negrín, Juan’s widow, learned that a $25,000 bounty had been placed on her husband’s life. “Every time my husband went to the sierras, I didn’t know if he would come back.”

A decade later, as the Wixárika community of Bancos de San Hipólito in Durango planned an amparo against illegal logging, Maurilio Haiwiye Ramírez was hiding Chávez under a blanket in the back of a pickup so the ranchers who controlled the road through San Juan Peyotán would not see him.

“We hid him because we didn’t want the mestizos who were against us to know,” Ramírez said. Meetings were held at night for the same reason: “So no one could find out.”

The danger was not abstract to me, either. In the winter of 2010, as I rode with Carlos through the night toward Bancos de San Hipólito, he told me plainly that the road ahead ran through territory controlled by narcos, and that if I wanted to get out and run now, he would understand.

He said it wryly, the way a man says something he has said before, to other passengers, on other nights. “Vamonos,” I said. He put the truck in gear and drove.

Five little boys and a washboard

What held was Lala. Yvonne Negrín remembers driving past the couple’s place in the countryside and seeing her at a washbasin, “scrubbing diapers on a washboard for five little boys,” the clothesline so full she never forgot it. Tunuary described parents who never let their children see the strain — not when Lala was ill, not when Carlos was. “They decided to resolve it themselves, so that we could grow up without having to resolve their affairs.”

The children kept codes and false names; Carlos saved each of them in his phone under someone else’s name, and the habit outlasted the danger. What healed the family, Tunuary said, was Wirikuta. He dropped out of school at 15 and asked his mother to let him go to the desert. She put him on a train.

A seat at the Zapatista table

In 1996, when the Zapatista army and the Mexican government sat down in Chiapas to negotiate the terms of constitutional recognition for Indigenous rights, Carlos Chávez and the lawyer Ángeles Arcos, of AJAGI, were named advisors to the dialogue tables held in San Andrés Sakamchén de los Pobres. The Zapatista uprising two years earlier — an armed rebellion in the south of the country that captured the attention of Mexico and the international community and placed Indigenous rights at the center of the national agenda — had turned the negotiation into a national event, and the list of advisors was published in the national press.

“Without a doubt, the Indigenous movement was never the same after the Zapatista uprising,” Arcos said. “It put the question of constitutional recognition of the collective rights of the pueblos at the center of the federal agenda.”

What the Wixáritari brought to those tables were territorial claims argued under AJAGI’s most powerful weapon: Convention 169, the International Labour Organization treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples’ rights, which Mexico had ratified in 1990. What they took away was something less tangible: the Wixárika delegations traveled to Chiapas and spent time with the Zapatistas, and Arcos remembers it as a period of mutual enrichment.

“The Wixáritari occupied a very important place in the demands the Indigenous movement put to the Mexican government,” she said. “Their territorial struggle was iconic, and the EZ (Zapatistas) also showed them new forms of struggle.”

‘He didn’t want to be indispensable’

What made Chávez effective was not only conviction but method. Agustín del Castillo, who has covered agrarian conflicts for top Guadalajara media outlets for 38 years, argues that his contribution was strategic rather than moral. “He gave the struggle a component of intelligence, of a sense of strategy,” del Castillo said. “Many can fight. Fighting with intelligence, with strategy — that’s the merit I attribute to Carlos.”

What distinguished Chávez, del Castillo said, was that he deliberately made himself unnecessary.

“He didn’t want to be indispensable. He wanted the communities to take their own destiny in hand.” By the time of Wirikuta, del Castillo said, “I no longer saw him in the leading role he had in the ’90s. I saw him as an accompanist” — and that, he insists, was the triumph of the model rather than its failure.

What Liffman remembers is a seemingly fearless man who was “as much a moral as an intellectual example” — and he doubts the communities would have trusted him otherwise.

The communities describe something more concrete. Ramón González López, a community member from Tuxpan de Bolaños, remembers the workshops on Convention 169 and the agrarian law. “That was what opened our eyes,” he said. “We realized we had many rights — and many obligations, too.”

The money was modest and came from far away. Outi Hakkarainen, a Finnish researcher who met Chávez in 1995 while studying civil society in Jalisco, spent two decades channeling funding to AJAGI — much of it from a student union at the University of Turku.

“Our money was not much,” she said, “but it was essential for this work,” because it could be directed at what most donors avoided: litigation over land tenure.

She was candid that the finances were chaotic. “We understood that his way of working was chaotic too, but we couldn’t change it.” What she never doubted was that the funds went where they were meant to.

Lalo Guzmán, who worked alongside Chávez for years in the Wirikuta Defense Front and has defended the desert for decades, rejects the accusations that have circulated about the money. He is a witness, he said, that the family never enriched itself — that everything Carlos raised went into the struggle, sometimes at the cost of his own household.

“That will sound bad to others,” Guzmán said. “To me it speaks well of him.”

Quetzal Prado, a lawyer who joined AJAGI in December 2012, described an organization built around a division of labor: a technical team, a legal team, and Chávez holding the political and strategic vision.

“You present him with a problem and he was very good at understanding the whole broad picture of it — not just the present moment, but how we can project it into the future.” She recalled leaving meetings and having Chávez decode them afterward: “No, this person told us such-and-such, because what he actually means is this.”

Raymundo Vázquez Sánchez, an agrarian lawyer from San Sebastián Teponahuaxtlán, described the years before AJAGI as stalled. Petitions went nowhere, and the community had no legal footing.

What Carlos left behind, he said, was a generation that could argue its own case.

Next week, Part II: ‘They don’t see with their eyes’ — Carlos Chávez’s last 15 years, from the fight for Wirikuta to the fire that sustained him.

Tracy L. Barnett is an independent journalist and founder of The Esperanza Project. She worked with Carlos Chávez on the Wirikuta Defense Front’s communications team for two years, and loved him and his family like her own. She counts him, as do countless others, as a mentor and a guide.

World.title: From the archive: A comprehensive guide to Mexican hangover cures
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in December 2024 — explores the distinctive approaches taken by Mexicans when it comes to curing a hangover.

If you’ve been in Mexico for any amount of time, you’ve no doubt noticed something: Mexicans do not shy away from drinking.

When I first arrived, this was a shock to me, though I knew “in theory” to expect it.

My own family leaned puritanical when it came to any mind-altering substances; drinking, even a little, was never not considered deviant. There was hardly ever alcohol on the table, and once when I found cigarettes in my mom’s purse, I almost fainted, pearls tightly clutched.

Fast forward to the beginning of my first year in Mexico. I remember staring open-mouthed as the study abroad program director ordered a beer with his lunch. What?! As far as I knew, one beer could get you fall-down drunk and into all sorts of trouble.

Learning to drink, the Mexican way

Ah, such innocent times. As the year wore on, I loosened up a bit. I started having a little beer at parties, not knowing any better when it came to quality. I loved a good paloma on a night out. I was into wine for a while too when living in Querétaro, where nearby Tequisquiapan was an up-and-coming producer. And straight tequila and mezcal, I’ve loved from the first sips.

But as all of us who are old enough know, learning to “hold our liquor” takes time and practice. After sleeping a few times with one foot on the ground to keep the room from spinning or rushing to the bathroom when our bodies have had enough, most people are incredibly motivated to prevent the sick feelings that come after too much and that can last hours to days.

It speaks to the tastiness and inhibition-shedding qualities of alcohol that we don’t just give it up after a nasty experience, doesn’t it?

Instead, we try to game the system of our body’s response. Is this the part where I need to say that Mexico News Daily does not condone drinking excessively? Well, we don’t, I guess.

Anyway. Because most Mexicans really like to drink and do not have the kinds of puritanical views of it that some to the north do, hangover cures are an important aspect of cultural knowledge.

And besides, they can even be an extension of the fun!

So without further ado, let’s take a look at some of Mexico’s favorite remedies.

First, plan ahead

Before you start out on your imbibing, plan what you’re going to drink. If it’s a fancy affair, have some fancy drinks. “Entre más fino, menos cruda,” one friend told me (the fancier it is, the less of a hangover it will cause).

The exception to this, apparently, is red wine, no matter how fancy it is. Most of my friends here have told me that it’s a surefire way to wind up with a hangover the next day.

Mezcal, on the other hand, has a reputation for not causing hangovers at all. I have a feeling that I don’t actually believe that, but honestly I can’t remember, so take from it what you will.

Not mixing the type of alcohol you have in one sitting is also considered a good strategy. If it’s beer, stick to beer; if it’s tequila, stick to tequila. You get the idea.

And finally, drinking lots of water is a good idea all the time, but especially if you’re drinking lots of other stuff as well. I don’t drink a lot personally, but if I have more than one of something, I’ll make sure to have a big glass of water in the middle. So far, it’s proven a good strategy.

Shoot, I got carried away and didn’t prepare at all

Well, my friends, you’re not alone. Luckily, plenty of other people have been in your shoes and shared their hard-won lessons. Especially luckily, most of them involve food!

Let’s have a look at the traditional cures:

A michelada

Now, if you ask me, curing a hangover with even a little alcohol is not a good idea. But it’s not just beer, and Mexicans really have a lot of faith in it. From this article on the famous michelada: “Apart from the flavor, we argue that Clamato contains electrolytes that can rehydrate us, vitamin C from the lime juice that can strengthen our immune system, antioxidants from the tomato that can help maintain our youthfulness, and the capsaicin from the chili that can help keep us alert. While these claims haven’t been scientifically proven, we feel that our health improves every time we drink it.”

I mean, I guess, but I’d still personally classify it as one of the grossest drinks I’ve tried. Bleh.

Suero

Now this, I can get a bit more behind. “Suero” can mean a lot of things, but it’s basically electrolytes. This could be in the form of Gatorade or Powerade, but it could also be a simple marinero: mineral water with salt and lime. That’s something I drink anyway because I like it, so I’m going to go ahead and count some free health points for myself.

Alka-Seltzer Boost

I haven’t personally tried this one, but I have a friend who swears by it. When you’re feeling like death, though, anything’s worth a try!

Hearty, spicy food

Through the power of corn and chiles, you will come back to life! And if you don’t, you’ll at least get some good, sturdy food in your stomach. Chilaquiles are an incredibly popular choice, as is a nice, spicy pozole.

Seafood is also a popular choice, especially if you choose a nice shrimp cocktail, which actually has some of the same ingredients as a michelada. Maybe they’re on to something!

In the end, the best cure might actually be the memory of a past experience. But in case you get caught up and forget, we’ve got your back!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum in China, Rodríguez at the mic and a kingpin behind bars
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent most of the week in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. That left Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez running the mañaneras from Monday on. The Minnesota Vikings, meanwhile, were pumping thin air into a chamber in the Midwest to prepare for Sunday night’s kickoff in Mexico City.

It was a relatively calm week at home while the president was abroad. That changed Friday night, when Mexican special forces captured an alleged drug kingpin on the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted list, sparking violence in Sinaloa.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Nov. 16? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum touches down in Shenzhen

Sheinbaum left Mexico City’s airport at 11 p.m. on Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana. She then boarded China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen. It was another commercial flight, in keeping with the austerity symbolism started by her predecessor. She arrived at 11:30 a.m. Monday local time and went straight to the Tequila Coyote’s restaurant to meet Mexicans living in China, whom she called “extraordinary.” The economy-class journey also struck a chord online: Bloomberg reported that a hashtag about her arrival was seen 10 million times on Weibo.

Sheinbaum pitches Plan México at APEC

In a 13-minute speech at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday, Sheinbaum told more than 2,000 business and political representatives that Mexico “guarantees conditions for investment.” She said the government and private companies expect to invest US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030. She also described the plan as having a “humanist vision.”

Mexico News Daily noted that foreign direct investment hit a record of almost $35 billion in the first half of 2026, though growth was only 2.1%. Insecurity, USMCA uncertainty and the recent judicial reform are seen as deterrents. On Thursday, she gave a four-minute address at the Leaders’ Meeting, calling this “a decisive moment for humanity.” Mexico will host APEC in 2028.

Meetings with Xi, Carney, Trump and more

Sheinbaum told Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday that her visit marks “a new era” in bilateral ties, focused on science, technology, clean energy and health. Neither side’s readout mentioned Mexico’s new tariffs on Chinese goods. She also revealed she had asked Xi for a panda for Chapultepec Zoo.

She also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that day, and both reaffirmed support for renewing the USMCA. Carney said bilateral trade is up 18% this year.

On Wednesday came the one many were watching: a roughly 20-minute meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, her first formal in-person talks with him. Sheinbaum said trade negotiations are “very far along” but gave no timeline for a deal. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said 56 technical meetings have been held. Trump’s recent tariff threat over the migrant caravan went unmentioned, and the two agreed to meet again at next month’s G20 summit at Mar-a-Lago.

She also met leaders from Vietnam, Australia, Singapore and Peru, plus the IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva. At her closing press conference, Sheinbaum called the trip “very productive and very successful” but said Mexico has no plans for a free trade agreement with China.

Rodríguez takes the mañanera podium

With the president away, Interior Minister Rodríguez led this week’s morning press conferences. On Monday, the mañanera featured World Bank data showing that Mexico’s monetary poverty rate fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025, with 17.3 million fewer people in poverty projected by the end of 2026. Officials also touted a CB Global Data poll putting Sheinbaum’s approval at 69.8%, the highest in Latin America.

Sheinbaum joined Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday’s mañanera by video link, and on Thursday, Rodríguez praised her boss’s “composure” and “firmness, without confrontation or subservience.”

Mexico ranks fourth in APEC tech exports

An APEC report showed that Mexico ranks fourth among APEC economies in the share of exports that are medium- and high-tech goods, at 70.6%. Only Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea rank higher. Mexico sits ahead of China (61.6%), the United States (46.5%) and Canada (31.7%). APEC projects regional growth of 3.4% this year and 3.1% in 2027.

Revolution Day parade

Hours after landing from China, Sheinbaum presided over the parade marking the 116th anniversary of the Mexican Revolution. She invoked the 1917 Constitution and defended democratic freedoms. She also accused political opponents and foreign interests of trying to weaken her administration and delegitimize the 2027 midterms. Pageant floats and military contingents then rolled through the Zócalo and down Paseo de la Reforma.

What’s going on with the peso?

The peso sank past 19 per dollar on Thursday, hitting 19.04, its weakest level in 17 months. Bloomberg tied the move to Banxico’s dovish stance, after a 25-basis-point cut to 6.25%, and expectations of another Fed hike in December. That would narrow the interest-rate gap that supports the carry trade. The peso is down about 5.5% this year.

The November MND Peso Index™ offers some context. It found the peso 4.2% undervalued at 18.67 per dollar, versus a 0.7% undervaluation in October. The swing was driven almost entirely by depreciation.

Mexico and US lose measles-free status

The Pan American Health Organization revoked the measles-free status of Mexico, the United States and Bolivia after 12 months of continuous transmission. Canada lost its status a year earlier. Mexico has recorded 20,601 cases over 2025 and 2026, but only 14 are currently active, down from a February peak of 1,314. The government aims to end the outbreak in the second half of 2027 and regain recognition in 2028.

Migrant caravan trudges north

A caravan of about 1,500 migrants left Tapachula last Tuesday, and Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if it isn’t stopped. By Tuesday, it had shrunk to 781 people in Mapastepec, Chiapas, as migration officials urged people to go home. On Thursday, Rodríguez responded to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s remarks by saying Mexico “will continue detaining” people involved in smuggling.

Former Iguala mayor sentenced

José Luis Abarca, Iguala’s mayor during the 2014 Ayotzinapa tragedy, was sentenced to 60 years on Nov. 10 by a federal judge in Tamaulipas. He and 25 co-defendants, including the police chief, were convicted of six counts of aggravated homicide and attempted murder. Those charges stem from the attack on a bus carrying the Los Avispones soccer team. Abarca is already serving 20- and 92-year sentences. His lawyer argued police control had been ceded to then-Gov. Ángel Aguirre.

‘El Chapo Isidro’ captured in Sinaloa

Friday night’s big news came from Sinaloa. Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” and two other leaders of his organization.

The FBI lists Meza Flores on its Top 10 Most Wanted list and had offered up to US $5 million for information leading to his arrest. Agents came under fire from gunmen using explosives during the raid in Guasave, according to the Defense Ministry. Violence erupted afterward, with civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game and vehicles burning on a highway near Los Mochis. The Mexican government said U.S. intelligence helped, giving few details. The three were flown to Mexico City.

Looking ahead

The aftermath in Sinaloa is the story to watch, as violence following the capture may not end quickly. On trade, Sheinbaum and Trump are due to meet again at the G20 in Florida next month. Sheinbaum has said talks are “very far along,” but no deal date has been set, and the U.S. has still not agreed to any tariff reductions for Mexican automobiles, steel or aluminum. Financial markets, meanwhile, will be watching the Fed’s December meeting and Banxico’s decision on Dec. 17 for clues about whether the peso’s slide continues. Back at the Estadio Azteca, the Vikings and 49ers will find out Sunday whether their different altitude strategies paid off.

Mexico News Daily

This story contains summaries of original Mexico News Daily articles. The summaries were generated by Claude, then revised and fact-checked by a Mexico News Daily staff editor.

World.title: Mexican Journalist Humberto Padgett Dies
World.content:
Brief · Mexico

Humberto Padgett León, a Mexican investigative journalist and author, died on Sunday 22 November after more than a year of fighting tongue cancer. His wife, Mariel Ibarra Falcón, announced the death on Instagram the same day.

Ibarra Falcón wrote that he died at home, calm and surrounded by the people who love him. No further details on the circumstances have been released, and no funeral or memorial has been announced.

Ciro Gómez Leyva, a leading Mexican television and radio news anchor, wrote on social media on 22 November that “a giant of journalism, and of life, is gone,” and that he would remember Padgett “with admiration and affection.” He closed with the words “Rest in peace, dear Humberto.”

Padgett studied journalism at FES Acatlán, a campus of Mexico’s national university, UNAM, and worked at Reforma, Radio Fórmula and Emeequis, all Mexican media outlets, according to Mexican media profiles. His books include “La monarquía de la barbarie,” on power, crime and corruption in Estado de México, the state around Mexico City.

World.title: Nigeria Boat Capsize Kills 29 Mourners
World.content:
Brief · Nigeria

A boat carrying mourners to a funeral capsized on a river in Nigeria’s Bayelsa State on Friday 20 November, and 29 people are now confirmed dead. President Bola Tinubu has approved 250 million naira (about US$181,000) for the victims’ families, Vice President Kashim Shettima announced on Sunday 22 November.

The boat was heading for the community of Ukubie in Southern Ijaw, a river district in the Niger Delta, when it went down near Oweikorogha. Governor Douye Diri says the vessel was unfit for the river and left from a boarding point the government had not approved.

Diri has set up a commission of inquiry, and Shettima urged that its recommendations be carried out. The governor also said some bodies could still be trapped inside the boat, which means the toll may rise.

In a statement on 21 November, issued by his information adviser Bayo Onanuga, President Tinubu said those who died “did not deserve to die that way.” He ordered all relevant federal disaster agencies to work together on recovery and rescue.

Shettima announced the cash on Sunday during a condolence visit to Government House, the governor’s seat in Yenagoa, saying it came on the president’s directive. He added that Tinubu has asked the Niger Delta Development Commission, a federal agency for the oil-producing region, to buy boats for riverine communities.

“Geography can determine how people travel, but it will never determine the worth of the lives involved,” Shettima said in Yenagoa on 22 November. The conversion above uses the rate from RT, a financial data provider, of 1,383 naira per US dollar on 23 November.

No. The figure is provisional because the vessel has not been raised and more bodies may be inside.

World.title: Caro Quintero’s Nephew Shot Dead in Puebla
World.content:
Mexico: Security · Brief

A man reported to be a nephew of the cartel founder Rafael Caro Quintero and his bodyguard, a retired soldier, were shot dead in the central Mexican state of Puebla on Saturday 21 November 2026. Samuel Aguilar Pala, the state’s secretary of Gobernación (its interior minister), confirmed on Sunday that a relative of Caro Quintero was among the dead.

The best-known of the dead was “a relative of Caro Quintero,” Aguilar Pala said on 22 November, adding that the bodyguard was a retired soldier, Aristegui Noticias, a Mexican news site, reported (translated from Spanish). Caro Quintero is in US custody and faces US charges over the 1985 kidnapping, torture and murder of Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena.

World.title: US Says Authorized Trade Can Use Mariel Port
World.content:
The answers calm fears among authorized traders but do not clear the sanctioned companies that ran the port’s terminal.

A cargo ship in Havana harbour, with Old Havana behind (Photo: Christian Pirkl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Brief · Cuba

Shippers and exporters afraid that touching Cuba’s main port could expose them to US sanctions got a partial answer on Friday. The US Treasury’s sanctions office said authorized trade may keep moving through the Port of Mariel, west of Havana, even though the answers leave July sanctions on the two companies that ran its container terminal untouched.

The answers came on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, from the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the Treasury unit that enforces sanctions. They are the latest step in the wider cuba news story of US sanctions policy toward Havana.

Key Facts What OFAC says authorized trade and payments may continue through Cuban ports, Mariel included.

Who OFAC, the US Treasury’s sanctions office, in two published answers, numbered 1277 and 1278.

When Released Friday, Nov. 20, 2026; the time of day was not stated.

Open Whether shipping lines and banks will return to Mariel is not yet known.

This story is part of our coverage of the cuba news. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Ex-Guard Convicted of Beating Cuban Detainee

The answers calm fears among authorized traders but do not clear the sanctioned companies that ran the port’s terminal.

The Malecón, Havana’s seafront, in 2015. File photo.

OFAC’s published answer to question 1278 opens with one word: “Yes.” US persons, meaning individuals and firms in the United States, doing business authorized under the Cuba Sanctions Regulations, the US rules on Cuba, “may continue to conduct such activity,” including making payments to and engaging with Cuban ports, “to include the Mariel Port.”

For firms outside the United States, OFAC says Washington “does not intend to target non-U.S. persons under E.O. 14404 for operating in the marine sector,” Mariel included, when they supply agricultural goods, food, medicine, medical devices, replacement parts or device software updates. Executive Order 14404, signed in May 2026, is the Cuba sanctions order, and its Nov. 5 determination is a sector-wide sanctions step covering Cuba’s manufacturing, technology, electronics and marine sectors.

Answer 1277 sets the limit: that determination “does not automatically impose sanctions on all persons who operate or have operated in the sector.” Non-US companies still “may face sanctions risk, absent an exemption or authorization,” and US persons remain barred from dealing with all Cuban nationals unless an exemption or authorization applies.
