Neither answer lifts the July sanctions the State Department placed on the two companies that ran the terminal, Terminal de Contenedores de Mariel and Coral Marítima. Shipping lines CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd suspended Cuba bookings in May over sanctions risk, and we found no word on whether they will return.

For US exporters already authorized to sell food or medicine to Cuba, the answer says using Mariel does not by itself put that trade in breach. Anyone else should check their own license, because the answers do not name every cargo.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can authorized trade still go through Mariel?

Yes, for activity already authorized under US Cuba rules, according to OFAC. The sanctions on the two terminal companies are not lifted.

Is everyone in Cuba’s marine sector now sanctioned?

No. OFAC says the sector determination does not automatically sanction everyone, though non-US firms can still face risk.

World.title: Uruguay Union Says Its Ballots Are Missing
World.content:
The union says the fairness of the vote is in question, and the electoral court had not replied when this brief was written.

File photo, December 2016. Central Montevideo and the Palacio Salvo tower seen from the Rambla Presidente Wilson on the River Plate shore. Photo: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Brief · Politics: Uruguay

Uruguay’s main union federation, the PIT-CNT, said on Sunday 22 November 2026 that voting sheets for its candidate were missing from polling places in the election of workers’ representatives to the state pension board. Its president, Marcelo Abdala, announced a formal complaint to the Corte Electoral, the country’s electoral court.

The vote fills three of the seven seats on the board of the Banco de Previsión Social (BPS), the state social security institution: one each for workers, retirees and employers. Voting was still under way in the afternoon when this brief was written.

Key Facts Who. Marcelo Abdala, president of the PIT-CNT union federation, announced the complaint on Sunday.

What. Voting sheets for List 11, headed by workers’ director Carlos Clavijo, were missing in places, the union says.

Where. At least ten polling places, including sites in Montevideo and Canelones, per reports until 11:00.

As of 15:20 in Montevideo, 18:20 GMT, Sunday 22 November 2026.

The PIT-CNT says it sent 250 voting sheets to each voting circuit, the unit of polling places, nationwide, but that voting opened without the sheets for List 11. As a result, it says, some workers could not vote for that list or ended up casting a blank ballot.

“The PIT-CNT denounces an extremely serious event that calls into question electoral equality,” Abdala said in a statement on Sunday. “This serious failing of the Corte Electoral calls into question the basic fairness of how the electoral process is organised,” the federation’s complaint says.

World.title: South Africa Party Offers Rival Council Pact
World.content:
A hung council has no party with a majority, so rivals must agree a coalition before anyone can be elected mayor.

File photo. Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city and business hub, at sunset. Photo: Frankbel, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Brief · South Africa

South Africa’s Democratic Alliance (DA), a partner of the African National Congress (ANC) in the national unity government, offered the ANC a deal on Sunday 22 November 2026 to run 137 hung local councils. Under the written proposal, the ANC would lead 93 of them, the DA 24 and the Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), a party based in KwaZulu-Natal, 20.

DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis said the party put the plan to the ANC in writing in talks on Friday 20 November and published it in full on Sunday. “We have not yet received a response,” he said.

The DA’s stated aim is five years of stable local government and an end to a “revolving door of mayors”. It also wants the ANC’s National Executive Committee, its leadership body, to authorise talks on the open terms.

By province, KwaZulu-Natal has the most hung councils on the list, 34, followed by the Northern Cape with 18 and the Free State with 15. Gauteng, the province around Johannesburg, has eight, among them the big cities of Johannesburg, Tshwane (Pretoria) and Ekurhuleni (the East Rand), where the DA says it is flexible.

The DA points to KwaZulu-Natal (KZN), the province around Durban, where it says a similar ANC, IFP and DA arrangement “has thus far saved KZN from chaos”. It warns that tying Gauteng’s recovery to unstable coalitions would mean “another five years of chaos”.

World.title: Drones Hit Khartoum and Damage a UN Building
World.content:
Early tolls differ, and the UN says a building was hit while its staff were present.

File photo. The Nile River at Khartoum. Photo: Hans Birger Nilsen, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Brief · Sudan

Drones struck Khartoum, its twin city Omdurman and Jebel Aulia, a town to the south, early on Sunday 22 November 2026, killing at least four people and damaging a United Nations building. The attacks were blamed on the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been at war with Sudan’s army since April 2023.

Witnesses heard explosions across the capital from about 02:00 to 04:30 local time (00:00 to 02:30 GMT) as air defences tried to intercept the drones. The drones were reportedly aimed at government buildings and Khartoum International Airport.

Key Facts Who. Drones blamed on the paramilitary RSF; no claim of responsibility was reported.

What. At least four dead, a UN building damaged with staff inside.

Where. Khartoum, Omdurman and Jebel Aulia, about 45 km (28 miles) south.

When. Early Sunday 22 November 2026; explosions from about 02:00 local time.

As of 22 November 2026, 18:15 GMT.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “South Africa's first woman deputy president dies at 71” Get the brief

Early tolls differ, and the UN says a building was hit while its staff were present.

Early tallies differ on how many died. One count says four, three at a home in northern Omdurman and a child south of the capital; another counts five dead, four in Omdurman’s El Thawra district and a 10-year-old in Jebel Aulia.

Injury counts also differ, at nine in one account and at least 10 in another. Omdurman lies across the Nile from Khartoum, and El Thawra is one of its districts.

Denise Brown, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator for Sudan (its top aid official there), said on Sunday that a UN building was damaged while colleagues were inside. The UN’s humanitarian office called the risk to its staff “unacceptable”.

The accounts available on Sunday evening do not say whether any UN staff were hurt. They also give no figure for the damage.

A Sudanese army source claimed the drones were launched from Bahir Dar airport in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region, a claim that could not be independently verified. Sudan’s army has made similar claims before, and Ethiopia has denied accusations that it lets the RSF attack from its territory.

No statement from the RSF or the army on these strikes was available on Sunday evening. The hit on UN premises comes as several UN agencies have reopened offices in Khartoum after being shut since the war began.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is behind the attacks?

The attacks were blamed on the RSF, but no claim of responsibility was reported on Sunday. The army source’s claim of a launch site in Ethiopia is unverified.

How badly was the UN building damaged?

Denise Brown said it was damaged while colleagues were inside. The extent of the damage and any injuries had not been stated.

World.title: Ecuador Sets Flood Plan for Voting Day
World.content:
Ecuador’s electoral council has set out who decides, who moves voters and who guards ballots if floods hit a polling site.

File photo. Voting booths marked "El voto es secreto" (the vote is secret) at the Colegio Julio María Matovelle polling station in Cuenca, Ecuador, 16 November 2025. Photo: Martín Vasco, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

ECUADOR · BRIEF

Ecuador has a plan for the moment floodwater reaches a polling station on election day, Sunday 29 November 2026. The CNE, Ecuador’s National Electoral Council, has set out an emergency protocol and tested it in a national drill on Sunday 15 November.

The CNE moved the local elections up from 14 February 2027 because of El Niño, a Pacific weather pattern that brings heavy rain. Voters will choose prefects, who govern provinces, plus mayors, councillors and the CPCCS, the citizen participation council.

Emergency protocol for evacuating flooded polling sites, with possible pauses in voting.

Where. Ecuador, in local elections for provincial prefects (governors), mayors, councillors and the citizen participation council.

When. Sunday 29 November 2026, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Ecuador time.

Open. No CNE rule found on votes already cast if a site closes for good.

As of. Sunday 22 November 2026, 18:00 GMT

Ecuador’s electoral council has set out who decides, who moves voters and who guards ballots if floods hit a polling site.

Voting runs from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on a clock that matches US Eastern Standard Time and sits five hours behind GMT. Floods could force officials to evacuate a polling site and pause the reception of votes.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B); 51 homicides per 100,000. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

File photo, 2018. Members of Ecuador’s National Electoral Council at their swearing-in in Quito, 20 November 2018. Photo: Fernando Lagla/Asamblea Nacional, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons. Not the current council.

The decision to evacuate is not automatic. First the team must decide whether the water endangers people or stops the polling boards from working.

A unified command post of three people makes that call: the coordinator of the polling site, an Armed Forces officer and a National Police representative. The post can interrupt voting and order people out.

If it orders an evacuation, the National Police direct voters out along previously set routes. Polling board members, the officials who run each voting table, secure and move the electoral material with military support.

Firefighters remove the accumulated water. Once the emergency is under control, officials inspect the site again before deciding whether voting can resume there.

Evacuation does not necessarily cancel the vote at that site. The CNE has more than 2,500 alternative venues that it can use if a site becomes unusable.

CNE president José Cabrera said in an interview on Wednesday 18 November 2026 that seven polling sites were flooded that morning, down from 21 the weekend before. He warned that the weather could force the CNE to move polling sites and even suspend or postpone voting in some areas.

“If a downpour hits us the night before and people cannot get near the polls, or if there is a landslide, we have to make decisions,” he added. We found no CNE rule on what happens to votes already cast if a site closes for good.

Related coverage: Ecuador news; what to watch in the vote; the polling sites that flooded before the vote; the flood safety guide for US travellers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who decides to stop voting at a flooded site?

A command post of three officials, one each from the site, the Armed Forces and the National Police. It decides whether the water endangers people or stops the boards from working.

Does an evacuation end voting there?

Not necessarily. Officials inspect the site once the emergency is controlled and then decide whether voting resumes.

Sources: CNE emergency protocol and national drill of 15 November 2026, as described by the CNE; CNE president José Cabrera, interview of 18 November 2026.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Finishes Runner-Up at ATP Finals in Turin
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić fell just short of the ATP Finals doubles title Sunday, losing 3-6, 7-6 (2), 10-6 to France’s Théo Arribagé and Albano Olivetti in Turin. Arévalo and Pavić took the opening set 6-3 but could not hold off the French pair, who won the second-set tiebreak 7-2 and carried that momentum into the deciding match tiebreak at Inalpi Arena, played in place of a full third set.

Arribagé and Olivetti won 10 consecutive points across the two tiebreaks to turn the match around, then closed out the decider 10-6 to claim their seventh title of the season. The defeat ended Arévalo and Pavić’s run at the season-ending tournament, which brings together eight of the year’s leading doubles teams. It was their second appearance together in the ATP Finals title match. They also finished as runners-up in 2024.

The fourth-seeded pair arrived at Sunday’s final unbeaten in Turin, including a group-stage victory over Arribagé and Olivetti. Arévalo and Pavić had reached the final with a hard-fought semifinal win over American Christian Harrison and Britain’s Neal Skupski. They came through that match 7-6 (10), 6-7 (7), 10-7.

The final also marked the end of Arévalo and Pavić’s three-year partnership. Together, they won nine tour-level titles, including the 2024 French Open and four ATP Masters 1000 tournaments. Their 2026 season included a title at Queen’s Club in London and a run to the Wimbledon final. They also reached the finals of the Masters 1000 events in Monte Carlo and Canada.

For Arribagé and Olivetti, the win capped their first appearance together at the ATP Finals. The French pair began playing together in October 2025. In the singles final, Carlos Alcaraz beat Alexander Zverev to win his first ATP Finals title.

World.title: US Helicopters Support Costa Rica Crackdown on Illegal Gold Mining
World.content:
Costa Rican police have found about 2,000 sacks of sediment and 50 processing pools on Cerro Conchuditas, a hill near the Nicaraguan border, during an air and ground operation against illegal gold mining that is being supported by helicopters from a United States government aviation program.

The Ministry of Public Security reported the findings on Saturday, two days after officers moved into the area in Cutris, a district of San Carlos in the northern part of Alajuela province. Officers remain on the hill to guard the sites, seize equipment and detain anyone found working them, the ministry said.

Alongside the sacks and pools, police reported finding 20 makeshift shelters, six tents, seven drums, 30 jerrycans, 10 hoses, an electric generator and a water pump. They also recovered rotary hammers, shovels, wheelbarrows and gasoline.

The operation brings together the Public Force, the Border Police, the Migration Police and the Intelligence and National Security Directorate (DIS). Air support comes from helicopters belonging to the US government’s Aviation Program, which works in coordination with the Air Surveillance Service (SVA), the ministry’s air wing.

The ministry did not say how many aircraft are taking part or describe the role, if any, of US personnel. The SVA received four UH-1ST helicopters from the United States in 2019 under a training and maintenance program run through the State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs.

Security Minister Gerald Campos traveled to the site on Thursday to direct the deployment, joined by the heads of the Public Force and the DIS. Much of the terrain is difficult to reach on foot, which is why the ministry combined ground patrols with flights.

Gerald Camacho, director general of the Border Police, said patrols along the border corridor run throughout the year and concentrate on the areas where illegal mining takes place. He described the current deployment as a special reinforcement operation carried out at this time of year.

Today, police said officers had moved on to nearby Cerro Fortuna, in Crucitas, where they found several extraction points in use and detained three men. The three, who police said were in the country irregularly, were referred to the San Carlos prosecutor’s office on suspicion of illegal mining. Officers seized three sacks of sediment, carpets used to wash the material and digging tools.

Ministry figures put the number of people arrested in connection with these operations at 528 so far in 2026. Of those, 239 were held over their migration status, 194 on suspicion of violating the Mining Code, 17 in drug-related cases and six under the Arms and Explosives Law.

Cerro Conchuditas lies close to the San Juan River, which marks the border with Nicaragua, and has become one of the main points for extracting and processing gold-bearing material taken from the Crucitas area. The ministry has said since 2024 that organized crime is present in the zone.

The environmental stakes are a central part of the dispute. Police have previously reported that sediment from the hill is processed with mercury or cyanide to separate the gold, and in May the Public Force said it had seized 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of cyanide and 115 kilograms (254 pounds) of activated carbon from a camp on the same hill, along with 25 active pools. Both substances can contaminate soil and the streams that drain toward the San Juan.

Campos used the visit to call on the Legislative Assembly to approve a government bill on mining in the area. He said the legal tools now available limit what police can achieve and described the work as exhausting for officers without producing lasting results.

The executive branch’s proposal, submitted in 2024, would authorize gold exploration and open-pit extraction in Cutris and remains under discussion in the legislature. The Broad Front and the National Liberation Party oppose it, arguing that reopening Crucitas to gold mining would cause environmental damage of its own.

The ministry said officers will stay on Cerro Conchuditas and in Crucitas to find further processing sites and seize materials.

World.title: Alcaraz Saves Three Set Points to Beat Zverev for First ATP Finals Title
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz defeated world No. 1 Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6 (7) on Sunday in Turin, Italy, to win his first ATP Finals title, closing the tennis season with a 14-match winning streak. The Spaniard saved three set points in the second-set tiebreak before finishing off Zverev at Inalpi Arena. The victory gave Alcaraz his third consecutive tournament title after wins in Vienna and Paris.

It also made him the fourth man to win all four Grand Slam tournaments and the season-ending championship, joining Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic. For Alcaraz, the championship was a step further than he managed a year ago, when he lost to Jannik Sinner in the ATP Finals title match. The season-ending tournament brings together the top eight players of the year.

The 23-year-old took control early against Zverev, who had reached the final without dropping a set or losing his serve. Alcaraz broke the German’s serve three times in the opening set, while Zverev struggled with errors. Zverev recovered from a break down in the second set and forced a tiebreak. He led 6-3, giving himself three chances to send the match to a deciding set, but Alcaraz fought back and eventually closed out the final 9-7 in the tiebreak.

Alcaraz had also needed a comeback to reach Sunday’s match. Playing with his left thigh strapped, he defeated American Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (1) in Saturday’s semifinals after advancing through the group stage unbeaten. Zverev reached the final by beating Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (0), 6-4. He was seeking his third ATP Finals title after winning the event in 2018 and 2021.

The defeat brought an end to a season in which Zverev won his first two Grand Slam titles, at the French Open and US Open, and rose to No. 1 in the world. Alcaraz’s late-season run followed an absence of more than four months because of a wrist injury. He returned at the US Open and went on to finish the year with titles in Vienna, Paris and Turin.

World.title: Get Paid by SINPE Móvil in Costa Rica? You Must Register the Number by Jan. 18
World.content:
If you take payments by SINPE Móvil for a rental, a tour, freelance work or any other business in Costa Rica, you now have a date. By Jan. 18, 2027, you will have to tell the tax authority which phone numbers you use to get paid. The rule was made official on Nov. 20, when the resolution was published in the official gazette, La Gaceta. Miguel Ángel Solís Sánchez, director general of the tax administration, signed it on Nov. 9. It puts into practice a decree issued in October.

This is not a new tax, and nothing is charged on your transfers. You are only reporting which numbers receive business income, so the tax authority can match the money arriving on your phone with what you declare. You have to register if you are signed up as a taxpayer, as a person or a company, and customers pay you by SINPE Móvil. You can list more than one number. That includes a number belonging to an employee or a partner if your customers send payments to it.

You do not have to register a number you use only for personal transfers, such as sending money to family or splitting a bill with friends. If you never collect business payments by SINPE Móvil, you leave the field blank. The numbers go into your file in the Single Tax Registry, known as the RUT. A new field will appear in the economic activities section of the registration and update forms. You can fill it in online through the TRIBU-CR tax platform or in person at a tax office.

If you are already registered as a taxpayer, you get 12 months to comply, and the resolution says that period cannot be extended. There is one open question. As written, the 12 months appear to run from the Nov. 20 publication date, not from Jan. 18, which would put the deadline in November 2027. The Finance Ministry has not clarified the point, so the safe reading is the earlier date.

If you sign up as a new taxpayer after the rule takes effect, you give the numbers as part of the normal registration. After that, you have to update your file whenever you add a number, replace one or stop using one for payments. Skipping it can be expensive. The penalty comes from Article 83 of the Tax Code and equals 2% of your gross income from the previous tax year. It cannot be lower than three base salaries, about 1.39 million colones ($3,108), or higher than 100 base salaries, about 46.2 million colones ($103,593).

If the tax authority does not know your income, the fine is set at 10 base salaries, about 4.62 million colones ($10,359). Those amounts use the 2026 base salary of 462,200 colones and will change if that figure does. A missing number does not trigger an automatic fine. The tax administration says each case will be weighed on its circumstances, and any penalty has to go through a formal process in which you can defend yourself. The law also allows a reduced fine if you correct the omission.

There is nothing to file yet, because the field will not be available until the rule takes effect. In the meantime, make a list of every number your customers pay, and consider moving business payments to a line you use for nothing else. A number that handles both personal and business transfers becomes part of your tax file once you register it.

It is also worth comparing your SINPE Móvil income with what you reported on your last income tax return, and talking to an accountant if the two do not match. SINPE Móvil has become the most common way to pay in Costa Rica, and the registry gives the tax authority a direct way to compare those payments with declared income.

World.title: Flights to Costa Rica Could Cost 20% More as Tourism Board Blames Fuel for Seat Cuts
World.content:
Airfares on most routes into Costa Rica are projected to rise by more than 20%, and the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) expects prices to keep climbing through 2027 as airlines reduce the number of seats they fly here. The institute attributes the reduction to swings in oil prices during the year and to operational adjustments by the airlines.

It estimates that Costa Rica could close 2026 with 15% fewer airline seats from the United States, its largest source of visitors. ICT Executive President Marcos Vargas presented a study on the possible cuts to tourism business leaders on Oct. 23. The figures first surfaced through the tourism chambers that attended.

Hans Pfister, president of the National Chamber of Ecotourism and Sustainable Tourism (Canaeco), said the reduction at Juan Santamaría International Airport near San José could reach 21% between October 2026 and August 2027. Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), put the cut at Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia at 3%.

The collapse of Spirit Airlines alone removed about 95,000 seats from the market after the carrier declared bankruptcy and shut down. American Airlines and JetBlue have also reduced some routes, according to the institute. The ICT said route changes do not necessarily point to a general decline in tourism, because airlines make those decisions based on how profitable each route is and on other commercial opportunities.

Fewer seats could lower arrivals by air, it said, but the real effect will depend on how full the remaining flights are. Since Nov. 15, the institute has been running promotion and outreach with airlines that serve the US market to offset the projected reduction. It acknowledged that its options are limited by the airlines’ own commercial decisions.

Arrival figures already show the pressure as tourist arrivals by air fell 1.9% in October compared with the same month last year, the third monthly decline in a row. Juan Santamaría, which handles nearly two of every three tourists arriving by air, has now recorded seven straight months of year-over-year declines.

The United States accounted for 51.3% of air arrivals in October. A total of 65,071 US visitors arrived that month, down 3.6% from October 2025 and the third consecutive monthly drop for that market. The cuts come as the dollar trades at record lows against the colón, which raises the cost of a stay for visitors paying in dollars. Some capacity is still being added, including JetBlue’s move to daily flights from New York to both main airports.

Fewer seats on the main US routes generally mean less choice of dates and fewer late bargains in the busiest weeks of the year. The ICT has not published route-by-route fare projections, and monthly arrival data through the high season will show how far the reductions reach.

World.title: Improved Road to Costa Rica’s Barva Volcano Opens to Drivers
World.content:
Those heading to Barva Volcano now have a newly paved road to the entrance of Braulio Carrillo National Park, following the completion of a project in the mountains of Heredia. The upgraded road through Sacramento de Barva was inaugurated on Friday. The work covered approximately 3.7 kilometers (2.3 miles) between Sacramento and the park entrance.

Crews paved the road with concrete and improved drainage along the route. The changes are intended to make the trip easier for residents and visitors, particularly during the rainy season. President Laura Fernández attended the inauguration alongside local and government officials. The project cost approximately ₡2.2 billion and was financed mainly by the Rural Development Institute, with a contribution from the Municipality of Barva.

The route also serves communities in the area, including Sacramento and San José de la Montaña. Barva Mayor Alejandra Arce said the work addressed a need for residents, especially when heavy rain affects travel. Construction disrupted access to the volcano earlier this year. For part of the work, the Barva sector opened only on weekends, and visitors had to walk from Sacramento to the park entrance.

The project has also drawn environmental concerns. Earlier this year, the citizens’ group CONCEVERDE questioned the road’s potential effects on wildlife and water resources and called for information about environmental approvals and measures to protect animals. Barva Volcano is one of two visitor sectors of Braulio Carrillo National Park. Its attractions include high-elevation forest, a crater lake and four trails: Cacho Venado, Laguna Barva, Copey and Mirador Vara Blanca.

The National System of Conservation Areas, known as SINAC, lists the park’s hours as 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. daily, including holidays. Its published entrance fee is ₡1,130 for Costa Rican citizens and residents over 13 and $13.56 for nonresidents over 13. Visitors can check current conditions and reserve through SINAC’s online services at https://serviciosenlinea.sinac.go.cr/. Because weather, access and park rules can change, travelers should confirm the latest information before setting out.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Two Most Active Volcanoes Are Quieter but Their Craters Stay Restricted
World.content:
Poás and Rincón de la Vieja produced nearly all of Costa Rica’s volcanic eruptions in the first 10 months of 2026, and both are now less active, according to the Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (Ovsicori) at the National University. Neither has returned to normal visiting conditions.

Rincón de la Vieja, in Guanacaste, was the busier of the two. Ovsicori volcanologist Geoffroy Avard said it registered hundreds of eruptions during the year. The activity began between March and April, rose sharply from July and stayed high for several months. Several of those eruptions were strong enough to produce lahars, which are flows of water and volcanic sediment that run down the slopes and into nearby river channels. The observatory raised its alert for the volcano to the level it calls Precaución for several months.

On Oct. 30, with no significant changes detected in the volcano’s deep activity, Ovsicori lowered the alert one step to Advertencia. The observatory stressed that the lower level does not mean the danger has passed. Eruptions can still occur without warning, including ones able to send lahars downslope, and it recorded 12 small eruptions between Nov. 9 and Nov. 13.

Poás, in Alajuela, was less active than in 2025. Avard said its strongest eruptions came in July and August, when some threw material almost to the crater rim, but he described them as isolated events. Activity was concentrated in the rainy season and has declined since. The crater lake at Poás rose for part of the year and has recently begun to fall. Avard said scientists have seen no drastic change linked to the drop and will keep assessing whether it could affect activity in the coming months. Ovsicori also identified two landslides inside the crater, which did not alter the overall downward trend.

Turrialba and Arenal had no eruptions in the period. Turrialba’s activity is decreasing very slowly, with landslides seen inside its crater, while Arenal remains calm after several years of gradual decline. For visitors, the restrictions introduced earlier in the year are still in place. Poás Volcano National Park is open but has admitted about half as many people since Aug. 28, with 1,064 visitors a day, mandatory helmets, two open trails and 20 minutes per group at the crater lookout.

At Rincón de la Vieja National Park, the trail to the active crater remains closed. The Las Pailas sector, with its mud pots and steam vents well below the summit, is open Tuesday through Sunday. Five areas of Upala and Liberia near the volcano have been under a yellow alert since Oct. 1.

Both parks sell entry online, and volcano parks can change their rules with little notice. The current list of closed trails and visitor limits covers the other major parks. Ovsicori keeps both volcanoes under constant monitoring.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Unfreezes Millions for Police and Courts in 2027 Budget
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Judiciary, which includes the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ), will be able to spend about 29,844 million colones ($66.9 million) in 2027 without first seeking approval from a legislative committee, after the Constitutional Chamber ordered lawmakers to strip the conditions from next year’s national budget bill.

In a second resolution the same day, the court ordered the Legislative Assembly to reverse an 8,048 million colones ($18 million) cut to public university funding. Together, the two rulings affect roughly 37,900 million colones ($85 million) in the 2027 budget.

Magistrate Ingrid Hess, who drafted the university ruling, said in remarks published last evening that the Assembly exceeded its powers when its budget committee reduced the funds by motion. She said the Constitution protects higher education through university autonomy, academic freedom and guaranteed funding, and that lawmakers may only act as arbiters when the Executive and the universities disagree.

In this case there was no disagreement, Hess said. The money covers payments to universities that the government postponed in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic and later agreed with university rectors to repay in installments. The Executive had included the installment in its draft 2027 budget before the Assembly’s budget committee approved a motion moving it to cover employer contributions to the teachers’ pension fund, Jupema.

The rulings were voted on Friday and respond to consultations filed by the Supreme Court and by a group of lawmakers. According to the court’s findings as reported on Friday, the decisions address procedural defects and do not rule on the merits of the spending choices.

The Judiciary ruling, drafted by Magistrate Anamari Garro, found substantial defects in four budget execution rules. Rule 9 tied the release of about 29,844 million colones, or 5.6% of the Judiciary’s budget, to approval by the legislature’s special committee on public income and spending. Other rules blocked ordinary transfers between budget lines and restricted the filling of vacant positions.

The court found that the Judiciary was not consulted while the bill was drafted or debated, as the Constitution requires for legislation that affects its operations, and that the rules were introduced through the budget process even though their content belongs in ordinary law. Supreme Court President Patricia Vargas said the ruling confirms warnings the Judiciary had raised publicly with the Assembly and the Executive.

She said the branch is not seeking more money but wants to use funds already approved for it, and that those resources are needed to serve the public and to fight crime and organized crime. She added that all branches had committed at a recent meeting of the heads of state powers to comply with the court’s decisions.

Michael Soto, acting director of the OIJ, said the ruling would let the agency use its funds and vacant posts in 2027, rather than giving it additional money. OIJ planning and operations chief Omar Brenes said this week that the agency had halted purchases of ballistic helmets, weapons and ammunition because of Finance Ministry cuts, leaving agents short of rounds for firearms training.

The pressure on the OIJ comes as a recent national report warned that organized crime has become Costa Rica’s third economy, and as Santa Cruz, home to Tamarindo, leads Guanacaste in homicides.

The university cut had drawn thousands of marchers into San José in October. National Rectors’ Council (Conare) President Jorge Herrera said the ruling confirms the universities’ position, and the council said in a statement that budget decisions in this area affect society beyond the campuses.

The Assembly must now remove the challenged provisions before it gives the budget final approval. The Constitution requires the national budget to be approved before Nov. 30, and ruling-party caucus chief Nogui Acosta has cited Nov. 29 as the last day for a second-debate vote. His caucus said it would wait for the full written ruling before deciding how to proceed. If lawmakers do not act, the challenged provisions are treated as excluded from the budget.

Frente Amplio lawmaker María Eugenia Román said she plans a motion to restore the university funds in the text, which would require 38 votes. The same 8,048 million colones cut also appears in this year’s second extraordinary budget, which faces a Nov. 24 vote and is not covered by the ruling.

President Laura Fernández said on Friday, before the rulings were announced, that her government would comply with any decision from the court. The rulings come amid a broader squeeze on public spending that has hit courts, police and schools, and they leave lawmakers about a week to settle how Costa Rica will fund its courts, police investigators and universities next year.

World.title: Downswell urges young Reggae Boyz to bounce back against Uzbekistan
World.content:
Wendell Downswell

Jamaica’s Under-17 head coach Wendell Downswell says his technical staff has been working on both the mental and tactical aspects of the team’s game as they seek to revive their FIFA Under-17 World Cup campaign against Uzbekistan on Monday.

The young Reggae Boyz suffered a humiliating 6-0 defeat against European champions Italy in their opening Group E encounter last week, leaving them with little room for error as they chase a place in the next round.

However, Downswell believes the heavy defeat has provided valuable lessons for his players and is confident they can respond positively in their remaining group matches.

“As a staff, we have learnt many things, a number of lessons from the encounter. We were up against one of the European giants, back-to-back champions of their confederation at this age group,” Downswell told the Jamaica Observer.

“Despite the humiliating defeat, the staff has been working assiduously from a mental and tactical standpoint with the players to gain six or four points as a means of our goal to advance to the next round,” he added.

Jamaica will need a strong response against Uzbekistan to keep their qualification hopes alive with a final group game set to be played against Ivory Coast.

Downswell, though, insists that the atmosphere within the Jamaican camp remains positive despite the setback against the Italians.

“As a Jamaican delegation, we are very optimistic and looking forward to the challenges that lie ahead. The spirit in the camp is high. One Jamaica,” he noted.

The encounter against Uzbekistan therefore represents an important opportunity for Downswell’s young charges to demonstrate their resilience and show that the opening defeat has not derailed their ambitions at the tournament.

With their hopes of progressing still alive, Jamaica will be looking for a much-improved performance as they attempt to get their World Cup campaign back on track.

World.title: IShowSpeed tests himself against Usain Bolt in new video
World.content:
The trend continued on the Jamaica leg of his Caribbean tour in April, where he participated in a relay at the National Stadium.

This meeting with Bolt, however, he describes as a lifelong dream

“This episode is so important to me. Like, my name literally has Speed in it. Obviously, I take every episode I do very seriously. But this one, I’m taking it more to the heart. I’m training so I can impress Usain Bolt, the GOAT,” he said.

He added, “My whole life I’ve been waiting for this moment. I still picture that little boy on his…on his mom’s computer, at my mom’s house, watching Usain Bolt run, watching his highlights, watching his sprints…So, I got to make that little boy happy,” he shared.

Boldon and Bolt were both present for the one-man race, in which Speed attempted to beat his training time of 10.72, passing on encouragement and guidance.

The sprinting sensation ribbed Speed even as he gave advice.

“You guys think track and field, easy,” Bolt joked, but admitted that he was genuinely impressed with the efforts from the youngster

“[He has] competitive mindset that’s why he’s pissed,” Bolt shared after one failed attempt ending in a time of 10.50.

“I think overall, he might be disappointed. But if you ask any track person, it’s impressive,” Bolt added.

When questioned on whether Speed was in Bolt’s league, the sprinter responded: “No, no, no. That’s a different story,” with a laugh.

For Speed, who eventually hit 10.35, his excitement at being guided by Bolt was immense

“This is a very exciting day for me, man. It’s like I was playing baseball with my dad, you know, like the classic,” the streamer said.

Speed expressed excitement for the journey, acknowledging Bolden’s caution that the work will be extremely difficult.

World.title: Opposition senator questions Government’s commitment to accountability
World.content:
In this video grab Opposition Senator Kisha Anderson makes her contribution to the debate on the asset tax in the legislature.

Opposition Senator Kisha Anderson has accused the Government of practicing accountability “only when it is convenient, when the questions are comfortable or when the answers are favourable”.

Anderson made the accusation Friday, during her contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Nation Debate in the Senate.

“Every Jamaican has the right to ask, ‘Weh di money deh?’, and every government has a responsibility to provide an honest answer and to account for its decisions, expenditure and performance,” said Anderson. She noted that while elections give governments the authority to govern, “what they do not give governments is the authority to operate without scrutiny”.

“The Jamaican people do not surrender their right to ask questions when they cast their ballots. Neither do they relinquish their right to know how their taxes are being spent, whether public commitments are being honoured, or whether the decisions taken in their name are improving their lives,” Anderson remarked.

She argued that accountability is not a foreign concept that Jamaica must now discover, the country having demonstrated, through experience, what can be achieved if it is taken seriously. The JMMB Director pointed to 2013 when the public debt stood at 147 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) and the steps taken, with the involvement of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and bipartisan support in the Parliament, to turn the situation around.

About the state of affairs in 2013, Anderson said, “I will not debate how we got there, as I know we all know that since independence both political parties have held state power.

“So in 2013 Jamaica had been to the IMF before, we had signed past agreements, but this time something had to be different. In May of that year when the IMF approved the 4-year Extended Fund Facility for Jamaica, it came with accountability – clear targets, strict reporting requirements and consequences for failing to meet our commitments”.

Anderson highlighted that requirements for public disclosure allowed Jamaicans to know whether their government was doing what it had promised, “And importantly, we strengthened accountability through legislation”. In this regard, she pointed to the reinforcement of the fiscal rules in 2014, establishing the framework for reducing public debt to 60 per cent of GDP by 2025/26.

Said Anderson: “The IMF programme changed the terms of accountability in effect from ‘trust us’ to ‘show us’ and accountability did not stop there. As a responsible Jamaican collective, we were mature enough under the leadership of Dr Peter Phillips at the Ministry of Finance to establish the Economic Programme Oversight Committee (EPOC)”.

Anderson told her fellow lawmakers that EPOC was part of the then Government’s commitment to transparency, led by the independent private sector. She noted that it brought together representatives from business, trade unions, civil society and the State with a straightforward mandate to monitor whether the Government was meeting its targets and report its findings to the Jamaican people, plainly and regularly.

“Every quarter, EPOC reported publicly on performance relative to target and any risks that existed. EPOC engaged with the Jamaican people and in one such engagement with residents in Swallowfield, (now) Government Senator Keith Duncan said, ‘To have oversight means that you hold the Government, any Government, to do what dem supposed to do.’

“Any Government; EPOC was not a partisan instrument. It began under one administration and continued under the next,” Anderson highlighted.

She reminded that in 2016, Prime Minister Andrew Holness re-established EPOC and told its members that it was “‘very important that the Government be kept on its toes.’”

She cited that even after the IMF arrangements ended, the Government signed a memorandum of understanding to keep EPOC in place because Jamaica had recognised the value of independent oversight.

The Opposition lawmaker also noted that EPOC’s responsibility for monitoring Jamaica’s fiscal rules passed to a permanent statutory body in 2024 with the establishment of the Independent Fiscal Commission. She said temporary oversight became part of Jamaica’s permanent institutional framework, demonstrating how accountability can turn commitments into measurable results.

Anderson also pointed to other examples of accountability, highlighting that a company listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange that raisees money from the Jamaican public must publish its unaudited results within 45 days of each quarter.

“It must file audited accounts within 60 or 90 days of its financial year-end, and a full annual report, including management’s explanation of the numbers, within 120 days.

“If a company expects to be late, it must explain why and indicate when its reports will be submitted. And if it fails to report, trading in its shares can be suspended until it complies. The Exchange exercises this power and publishes monthly regulatory reports identifying companies that are late,” said Anderson.

“Should a Government that spends hundreds of billions of the people’s dollars be held to a lower standard?” she asked.

She added that, “If these reporting standards and consequences are good enough for the shareholders of a listed company, surely they should be good enough for the shareholders of Jamaica: its citizens, the Jamaican people”.

World.title: JPL matches postponed over unpaid referee fees
World.content:
FIFA referee Daneon Parchment (right) looks on as Montego Bay United’s Demario Phillips receives treatment in a Jamaica Premier League game against Harbour View at the Montego Bay Sports Complex on September 23, 2024 during the 2024-25 season. (Photo: Paul Reid)

All Jamaica Premier League (JPL) matches scheduled for this weekend have been postponed amid an ongoing dispute over unpaid referee fees, with negotiations continuing between the league’s organisers and the referees’ association.

According to sources, the referees’ association is still owed millions of dollars.

Discussions are ongoing and the parties are hoping to reach an amicable agreement that would settle the outstanding balance, establish payment dates and allow referees to return to the pitch.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Fragile cash
World.content:
A vendor displays torn $100 and $500 bills to the Jamaica Observer.

Vendors, cab drivers, bus conductors, and other Jamaicans whose livelihoods depend heavily on cash transactions say they are taking losses as some of the country’s most frequently circulated banknotes succumb to tearing and fading, prompting concerns about their durability.

The Bank of Jamaica (BOJ), acknowledging the problem, says it is exploring ways to make the notes more resilient.

“It’s too easy to tear, man; soon as you draw them so they split… I’m not comfortable with them,” long-time Coronation Market vendor Nadine Campbell told the Jamaica Observer.

“I have [so] much in my drawer, about $5,000 [worth of] $100, $50, all of them, I just throw them down,” Campbell added.

The polymer notes now in circulation were introduced in 2023, replacing cotton-based $50, $100, $500, $1,000, and $5,000 denominations, incorporating new designs and enhanced security features. The roll-out also saw the introduction of an entirely new $2,000 denomination.

At the time, then Finance Minister Dr Nigel Clarke said the upgraded notes have the latest in material technology for greater durability, which reduces the frequency of replacement. That would have a positive impact on the BOJ’s annual spend of about $1.4 billion every year to print banknotes.

Additionally, the new notes have specific markers to facilitate ease of use by visually impaired people.

However, Jamaicans who engage in cash-heavy transactions daily are now doubtful about the notes’ longevity.

“If there’s a little tear, nobody wants it, [and] it washes out easily,” shared a vendor who identified herself as Denneshia.

“It is easy to slide out of your pocket; I don’t like them. But we have to use them because… we have to use them,” she added.

Andrew, who loads taxis plying the Price Rite/Whitehall route, had several $50 and $100 bills with microtears along the edges in his hand when the Sunday Observer spoke to him in Half-Way-Tree.

“They are quick to tear and, as you get a tear on it, it rips off completely,” he said.

In June 2026 the central bank, in an interview with the Observer, had maintained that the new notes far outlast the old cotton-based currency

— up to three years compared to 1.5 years.

When contacted for this story, the BOJ declined to comment on the complaints. However, it did admit that the lower denomination notes, including $50, $100 and $500 bills, are coming back to the bank damaged more frequently than higher denomination notes.

Almost a quarter, around 22 per cent, of the notes in these denominations that it processes are deemed unfit for recirculation.

But anecdotal evidence suggests the number could be higher, as a familiar refrain among vendors and customers with whom the Sunday Observer spoke is that they don’t return the most damaged notes.

Some, like a cab driver who identified himself as Prince, showed the newspaper their stash of damaged notes.

This is not good, look at this,” Prince said, flipping through a wad of torn bills, mostly $50 and $100 notes.

Similarly, more than half of the vendors and customers who spoke to the Sunday Observer said they have damaged bills collecting dust at home.

One vendor, who identified herself as Grace, said she had taken the torn notes to a bank to have them replaced. But that effort failed as the bank refused to take them.

“When I bring it to the bank, they told me to go and find the other piece if there’s another piece to find, but they’re not changing it,” Grace said.

That, she insisted, was opposite to her experience with the former cotton-based notes. “We always could bring them to the bank as long as they have on the serial number,” Grace explained.

She said the serial numbers are visible on the damaged $500, and $1,000 bills she had, but she has since thrown them away “because we don’t know what to do with them”.

A vegetable vendor, Gem, who said she has been selling in Half-Way-Tree for more than 15 years, told the Sunday Observer she has her own collection of damaged notes.

“As you quint [blink] they tear,” she said. “The amount that I’ve gotten I have to carry them and put down at my house, because sometimes how people ginnal you and give you, you don’t even notice. Some of them you can use a piece of tape and it’s good to go, but others…”

“Maybe one day when I am broke and don’t have any money I can draw back for them and carry them to the bank,” Gem added, laughing.

A driver who travels through Spanish Town, Frankie, maintained: “Once they have a rip, that’s it; they don’t have any value unless you take them back to the bank.”

Despite the complaints, the bills seem almost impossible to rip. Jamaica Observer reporters who tried various methods to tear a $100 bill found that it merely bent and wrinkled.

When the Sunday Observer contacted De La Rue, the British company that manufacturers the notes, an employee explained that it would be very difficult to comment without knowing the state of the notes beforehand, including how old they were and how they had been used.

However, the employee said: “If you have to work really hard to destroy the notes and then you are seeing some that are damaged, it suggests that the notes have two very different histories.”

The BOJ has blamed rough handling, including stapling and graffiti, for the state of some of the bills.

It also said in June, that while replacement rates have dropped across all denominations, it is working with the manufacturer to “identify ways to further improve durability, particularly for the lower denominations”.

The Sunday Observer then asked De La Rue whether any changes have been signed off on with BOJ regarding the notes; if so, when are they due to begin production, and whether Jamaicans could expect any tangible changes, for example, a different feel or thickness. However, the manufacturer said it was not able to comment on any conversations it had with any central bank.

In the meantime, Jamaicans who use the lower denominations the most say it’s costing them money.

“It is a loss for me, because when a passenger gives me a torn note I have to just fold it up and put it somewhere; I can’t even pass it on,” said Prince.

Another issue that several bus conductors and drivers on the Spanish Town to Kingston route pointed out was that the notes tend to stick together when they get damp or moist, leading them to give away more bills than they intend.

They explained that this regularly causes conflicts between commuters and conductors.

Similar concerns were shared by a Coronation Market vendor who identified herself as Dimples.

“It is nice, but when it is wet it can be a little tedious because it sticks together… it poses a problem because suppose a shopper comes, and they come thinking it’s one note and… pass it on to me, and I give you the change, and you go to someone else thinking you have the other money, which you don’t; it’s gonna cause a problem… there’s a little friction, and we don’t really want that,” she said.

Regular consumers had fewer issues with the currency, though they still shared complaints about it tearing.

One customer in Coronation Market was complaining about the very issue when the Sunday Observer visited.

Displaying her $500 bill with a small piece missing from the edge, she said: “I don’t have a problem with the money, but there are times when you come and you will give someone, say, $1,000 or $2,000, and they tend to give you back money that is torn. And then now when you try to spend it, nobody will take it, and that is where I have a problem,” she said.

Another customer explained that she loves the fact that the notes can stand up to water, especially with accidental washing.

“So when you check the pocket now after the clothes dry, you find the money, and it’s still all right. It’s not crushed up… So you can use it again. The only problem with it, when it tears, you have a problem, because nobody want to take it from you. But I think it was a good switch. I appreciate it,” she explained.

World.title: Safety sells Jamaica
World.content:
CHANG... my job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach

WHITEHOUSE, Westmoreland — Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang has declared that Jamaica’s continued success in tourism depends heavily on maintaining a safe environment for both visitors and residents, insisting that the country’s natural attractions mean little if people are afraid to enjoy them.

“Safety is part of the product. The most beautiful beach in the world means nothing if people are afraid to walk on it. My job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach,” Chang said to applause last Thursday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitated Sandals South Coast in Westmoreland.

The hotel, which reopened to guests on Wednesday after sustaining extensive damage during the passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, was restored over a compressed 10-month period by a combined team of Jamaican and American architects.

Chang said the Government’s investments in national security, coupled with the efforts of the security forces, were helping to create an environment in which tourists could move beyond hotel compounds and experience the wider Jamaican community without fear.

He said the ultimate goal was for visitors to feel comfortable travelling to nearby communities, visiting beaches and local attractions, and interacting with residents.

“[We want guests to] begin to feel free to go on the road and walk, take a taxi, go down to Whitehouse, go down to the beach, down to the fishing beach, buy some fried fish, and jump on any taxi and come back to the hotel without feeling fear,” he said.

“We have made significant progress, and as the ministry responded, with the support of the prime minister, we have made the investment in our security, and our police have responded,” Chang added.

He stressed, however, that safeguarding the tourism industry also means protecting the thousands of Jamaicans employed in the sector, particularly in the communities where they live.

The minister said hotel workers sometimes face criminal pressure as they return home at weekends, despite the industry’s move away from paying salaries in cash.

“Our security forces have delivered a sharp reduction in murder, and we will not ease up. We will keep strengthening policing in our resort areas and the communities where hotel workers live,” Chang assured.

He acknowledged that unemployment and other social challenges continued to contribute to criminal activity, adding that the police were also having to contend with domestic violence and less serious offences that could escalate into deadly confrontations.

Pointing to the impact of increased investment in policing, Chang highlighted an 82.14 per cent reduction in homicides in Westmoreland, which he said had previously recorded more than 100 and, at one stage, over 140 murders annually.

“Today, we have 25 for the year,” he said, while commending the work of the police leadership, including head of the Westmoreland division, Senior Superintendent Othneil Dobson.

Despite the significant decline in murders, Chang cautioned that domestic and interpersonal violence remained a troubling source of killings across the country, requiring more targeted interventions alongside conventional crime-fighting measures.

Describing the trend as “an unfortunate part of the social scene today”, he said the Government was developing a range of interventions involving communities, schools, and the police to address the problem and encourage behavioural change.

He said the police had established the Community Security and Safety Branch, while the Government intended to roll out a major anti-violence programme aimed at encouraging people to report domestic disputes before they turned fatal.

“We intend to embark on a major programme

— anti-violence

— to provide an opportunity for domestic disputes to be reported to the police early, and to avoid the fatal outcome,” Chang said.

He also disclosed that the Government had established approximately 20 domestic violence centres, with men accounting for about 30 per cent of those seeking assistance.

“Not sure what it’s saying

— men reporting threats of violence

— but we are getting responses, and we intend to expand those centres and ultimately begin to get the kind of behavioural change we want in that sector,” the minister added.

World.title: A separate Grammy category for dancehall?
World.content:
Since the nominations in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced on November 16, there has been some uproar across social media platforms by fans and some members of the entertainment fraternity alike about the non-inclusion of some notable albums by dancehall artistes.

Some of the albums include God and Time by Vybz Kartel, Eminence by Beenie Man, Heights of Fire by Capleton, Forever Reign by Masicka, NPT by Alkaline.

Some have even suggested a bias towards dancehall artistes.

The 2027 reggae Grammy nominees are Too Too Bad by Buju Banton, The Art of Acceptance by Protoje, Supernova by Runkus, Exile by Chronixx, Brightside by Ziggy Marley, and Lottery by Shaggy.

There has been a call for a separate category for dancehall artistes, while others have argued that renaming the category to Best Reggae/Dancehall Album would suffice.

A few months ago, the JUNO Awards (Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys) announced the renaming of its Reggae Recording of the Year category to Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year for the 2027 staging.

The reality, some say, is that there are not sufficient releases each year by dancehall artistes to argue for a separate dancehall category in the Grammys. The Best Reggae Album category, instituted in 1985, was allegedly on the chopping block a few years ago due to the low number of submissions. This year, the number improved to 119, compared to 73 last year.

Recording artiste, producer, and music executive Ce’Cile, who is a registered member of the Recording Academy, says the Grammys aren’t obligated to do anything to drown out the noise created each year after the nominations are announced.

“They [Grammys] are not obligated to do anything. They gave us a category, and it would be nice to have an additional dancehall category, but there are many other genres that are still not a part of the Grammys,” Ce’Cile told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

She also argued that there hasn’t been the same enthusiasm and support for local award shows.

“The Grammys can do what they want to do. How many of us within the industry are voting members? We don’t even support our local award shows.”

Well-known entertainment attorney and music business consultant Lloyd Stanbury doesn’t support renaming the Best Reggae Album category. Instead, he supports the idea for a separate category for dancehall.

“The dancehall music genre, although born out of the reggae music genre, has evolved and grown to establish itself globally as yet another distinct music genre coming out of Jamaica. Dancehall music has earned and deserves its own standalone category in the Grammys. What is needed is more membership representation in the Recording Academy of both reggae and dancehall creatives to lobby and advocate for change.

“I think we will see more qualified submissions from both reggae and dancehall when Jamaican music creatives take their activities as serious business, inform themselves, and create support teams with qualified personnel,” the respected music industry insider told the Observer.

Music producer, artiste manager, publicist and podcast host Ralston Barrett, who has more than 30 years of experience in the industry and has represented Grammy-nominated and Billboard-charting acts, concurs with Stanbury that a separate dancehall category is needed.

“I think dancehall is more vibrant than reggae right now, so I expected to see more dancehall artistes nominated. To me, it’s a slap in the face to dancehall music. Buju Banton is the only nominee I’d put squarely in the dancehall camp. Some people would include Shaggy, but his music blends dancehall, reggae, and other genres. I was hoping to see Masicka, Vybz Kartel, and Alkaline among the nominees, and I would have liked to see Capleton nominated too,” said Barrett.

Barrett continued: “I’d like to see two separate Grammy categories: Best Reggae Album and Best Dancehall Album. Right now, I don’t think we have the numbers to make a strong case for that, though. Our industry needs to get more organised and united, do more to strengthen both genres, and encourage more eligible Jamaican music professionals to join the Recording Academy as voting members. Putting dancehall by itself could encourage more submissions. A category of our own would give artistes even more reason to submit.

“We also need more dancehall artistes making strong albums. Once the album is done, you still have to market it, network, and get people to hear it. When an artiste wins, people are quick to curse the artiste or the team. Give them credit for putting in the work. And where are our own award shows in Jamaica? We should be honouring our music and the people who make it right here at home,” he charged.

Music executive, Grammy-nominated producer, and former chair of the Grammy reggae committee Cristy Barber poured cold water on the assertion that no dancehall artistes were nominated this year.

“Although some of the predictions that were spoken about were not among the six nominees this year, there are three deejays nominated — Buju, Shaggy and Runkus — this year. So there is a dancehall presence. Hard-core, crossover, however you see it, they are still dancehall. So, renaming the category probably won’t change the problem some have with the title just being reggae. But the Academy looks at the category as all-inclusive — reggae and dancehall,” Barber reasoned.

Dancehall artistes who have won the Best Reggae Album award over the years include Shabba Ranks, Beenie Man, Sean Paul, Buju Banton, and Shaggy.

World.title: ODPEM chief saw trouble long before audit
World.content:
Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management head office at Haining Road in St Andrew.Photo: Joseph Wellington

INTERNAL Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) correspondence seen by the Jamaica Observer show that Director General Commander Alvin Gayle had long held concerns about several of the issues raised by the auditor general in a report tabled in Parliament last Tuesday.

In its report the Auditor General Department said its team members who inspected warehouses holding Hurricane Melissa relief supplies found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables, and 15 unopened containers that had not been recorded in ODPEM’s inventory, exposing serious gaps in how the agency accounted for and safeguarded donated goods.

The report also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were not included in the donation schedules maintained by ODPEM.

The auditor general also raised concerns about the conditions in which relief supplies were being stored, given the presence of insects on the packaging of some consumable items.

Additionally, the inspection exposed a basic problem with the agency’s record-keeping. ODPEM did not provide auditors with store records showing the quantities of goods that should have been in Warehouse 3. This meant the auditors could not compare what they physically counted with the supplies recorded as received since November 2025 or those distributed during the period under review.

Sunday Observer sources have since pointed to repeated efforts by Gayle to address the issues before the auditor general’s report.

These include a memo dated June 22 in which Gayle wrote to the entity’s then logistics manager seeking urgent information on the agency’s readiness for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

In the memo Gayle pointed to a previous correspondence one month earlier in which he had already requested the information which had not been submitted by the logistics manager.

“Reference is made to my memorandum dated May 21, 2026, directing the completion and submission of the Hurricane Inventory Template to facilitate the consolidation and verification of the office’s operational readiness inventory for the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season.

“A review of your submission has revealed that the information provided was materially incomplete and required significant intervention by the Office of the Director General to address critical gaps. This situation is both disappointing and unacceptable,” said Gayle in the June memo.

He pointed out that the initial response from the logistics manager failed to adequately capture or provide the required information relating to all Starlink devices, including their current locations, operational status, assigned custodians, deployment details, and other relevant tracking information;

Gayle added that the logistics manager failed to provide generator inventories, including donor information, generator capacities, current locations, operational status, and additional information required under the General Stores section, including inventory balances, stock status, and other supporting details necessary for effective operational planning and reporting.

“The purpose of the exercise was to provide the Director General’s Office with a comprehensive and accurate inventory position. It is therefore unacceptable that such fundamental omissions were not identified and addressed prior to submission. The information requested falls squarely within your remit and should already have been known, maintained, and readily available through established inventory management processes and systems.

“The fact that the Office of the Director General found these significant gaps in the records that have been provided by you demonstrates a serious deficiency in the preparation, verification, and quality assurance of the submission,” added Gayle.

He directed the logistics manager to immediately review the inventory management and reporting processes within the Logistics Unit and provide a written report to include: The reasons for the incomplete submission; the measures being implemented to ensure inventory records are maintained accurately and in real time; the quality assurance mechanisms that would be instituted to prevent a recurrence of this issue and; any outstanding inventory information that remains to be verified.

“The maintenance of accurate inventory records is a fundamental operational requirement, particularly in the context of disaster preparedness, emergency response, donor accountability, and audit compliance. I expect immediate corrective action and sustained improvement in this regard. Please treat this matter with the urgency and seriousness it warrants,” said Gayle.

Days later Gayle again wrote to the logistics manager expressing concern about the receipt, storage, issue and status of the generators donated by the Government of Mexico to Jamaica following Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

The ODPEM director general demanded details on when the generators were received, amount issued and how many were still in storage.

By August an obviously frustrated Gayle wrote to the logistics manager expressing displeasure over the management of the department and his failure to maintain proper records of the supplies and donated items donated to ODPEM.

“These matters fell directly within the core responsibilities of the logistics manager, particularly the maintenance of accurate and up-to-date inventory records, the proper accounting for equipment and supplies received and distributed during disaster and relief operations, and the preparation and maintenance of records showing the final disposition of items donated by local and international partners.

“ODPEM’s mandate requires the organisation to maintain effective systems for the management, control, and accountability of resources entrusted to it in support of national disaster preparedness, emergency response and relief operations. Proper accountability for these resources is therefore fundamental to the effective discharge of that mandate and to safeguarding the wider public interest,” said Gayle to the logistics manager who resigned from ODPEM in August.

World.title: Surging left-wing Basque separatists brace for showdown with Spain’s right
World.content:
Bildu’s rise has mirrored the Basque Country’s own transformation. Over the past decade, the rugged coastal region of 2.2 million people has increasingly shed its association with ETA, the separatist militant group that waged a decades-long campaign of violence before disbanding in 2018.

As the shadow of political violence has receded, the Basque Country has consolidated its position as one of Spain’s most politically progressive and economically dynamic regions. It is now internationally recognized as an economic powerhouse — energy giant Iberdrola and banking group BBVA are both headquartered in Bilbao — and a global destination for high-end gastronomy.

“The majority of the Basque Country is socially progressive and sovereigntist,” Gorka Elejabarrieta, a Bildu lawmaker running for the Spanish parliament in Gipuzkoa, told POLITICO. “Our coalition and movement bring together those two ideas, which are hegemonic in Basque society.”

Spain’s political right has long opposed Basque separatism, but its hostility toward EH Bildu is particularly pronounced. It regards the party as “ETA’s heir” and has repeatedly questioned its legitimacy as an actor in democratic politics.

Challenging the old order

Within the Basque Country, this month’s election is also a contest to determine who will shape the region’s relationship with Madrid and its political future, with the resurgent Bildu challenging the decades-long dominance of the center-right Basque Nationalist Party (PNV).

For the past 45 years the PNV has taken a pragmatic approach to regional autonomy. Closely tied to the region’s all-important business community — the comparatively wealthy Basque Country represents about 6% of Spain’s economy — it has sought to preserve economic stability for the region in its dealings with the national government.

World.title: Far right wants to transform the EU after big national election wins
World.content:
After that, Gál said, “we have to see” how to strengthen ties between all the right-wing forces in the Parliament — the Patriots (home of Marine Le Pen’s National Rally), the European Conservatives and Reformists (of Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy) and the Europe of Sovereign Nations (of the Alternative for Germany).

The ideal would be “to grow into a huge group,” Gál said of the three factions on the right of the parliamentary chamber, but “cooperation can have different forms.”

However, they must move “step by step,” she said, adding that the Patriots must first see if “we get strengthened” in the national elections.

Sitting in her corner office in the European Parliament in Brussels, Gál, a member of Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party, said the center-right European People’s Party, the biggest in the Parliament, must take note of the surge in support for the far right.

The firewall that once existed in Brussels to keep out the far right has already been breached, with the EPP passing key legislation with the support of far-right votes. The center-right has so far avoided structured cooperation in Brussels and barred far-right parties from positions of power, although in some capitals national parties have sealed coalition deals with the far right.

Gál said she expects the EPP to scrap the firewall completely in the next few years and that the Patriots are now too big to ignore. “It cannot be that you treat millions of voters as second-class voters,” she said.

World.title: Congo warns that EU countries’ Rwanda deportation deal could fund armed militia
World.content:
“It is puzzling to see that a country that is at the heart, not just of instability, not just of conflict, but also of displacement and forced migration, is perceived to be a safe haven and … a credible partner to uphold international law,” Wagner told POLITICO.

“The issue here is that we have [EU] countries that have the means, the access, [and] the capacity to know better, making an informed choice to look the other way,” Wagner added, telling EU countries to “go back to their notes” and rethink the choice of partner.

The government of Rwanda did not respond to a request for comment.

Last week, five countries — Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands — announced they will set up a deportation hub in Rwanda. While talks are ongoing, the five countries plan to start sending people to Rwanda in 2027. It’s part of a broader push by the bloc to gain greater control over who enters the EU — and who gets to stay.

EU legislation approved earlier this year allows countries to negotiate such deals, as long as they safeguard fundamental rights. The announcement led to an outcry from rights groups, which warned that Kigali’s human rights record should disqualify it from such a partnership.

Rwanda, besides having “a well-established record of repressing dissent,” also “provides critical support to and exercises overall control over the M23 armed group in eastern Congo,” NGO Human Rights Watch said this week.

World.title: In the new world order, Europe doesn’t have a seat at the table
World.content:
At least the poor little donkey was allowed in the room.

Last week’s first-ever U.S.-Russia-China trilateral meeting in Shenzhen has been compared by some to a later meeting in Yalta, where Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt hammered out the postwar order that’s now just about clinging on for survival.

And yet, this time Europe’s diplomatic influence was nowhere to be seen.

In the run-up to his August 2025 summit with Putin in Alaska, U.S. President Donald Trump at least consulted with major European leaders. But before Shenzhen, there was no wide consultation or virtual group huddle with European allies, according to two senior European officials who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

In short, as Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese premier Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Europe was frozen out.



To be sure, Shenzhen was no Yalta. Europe wasn’t on the table to be carved up by the American buffalo, Russian bear and Chinese panda.

“At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parceled up. And we won’t allow anything like that to happen again,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a lengthy press conference in Berlin flanked by other European leaders hours after the talks. “The meeting in Shenzhen was apparently a photo opportunity,” he added.



And at first glance, maybe that’s right. When Trump was asked by Fox News what headline he wanted to come out of the summit, he lingered on the pomp and spectacle and on Xi personally receiving him at the airport, a rare move for the Chinese president. “It was a great respect and I appreciate that,” he said. “That’s a big win for us. That’s a big win for China, too. We get along.”

World.title: Lucy Powell promotes UK education in China despite risks
World.content:
Powell’s visit comes days after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting hosted his Chinese counterpart, Dong Jun, in London. Streeting praised Andy Burnham’s government for having “stepped up our interaction with China.”

Powell said ahead of the summit that education was one of Britain’s “greatest strengths” and “expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.”

She vowed to use it to “support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”

Closer cooperation on education will form part of “clear-eyed engagement with China” by the government, she said, as she promised to champion freedom of speech and academic freedom during her trip.

Her efforts to promote British education abroad come despite the security services warning about the scale of Chinese attempts to spy on the U.K.
