More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China’s espionage operations by taking funding from a Chinese spy agency, MI5, the U.K.’s domestic intelligence agency, revealed in September.

Powell specified that she would seek to “protect U.K. institutions from any collaborations that could undermine national security, or attempts to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with U.K. universities.”

U.K. officials said the trip would recognize the contribution of the 150,000 Chinese students currently studying at U.K. universities rather than actively seeking to invite more.

World.title: Costa gives Macron early Christmas present on EU budget
World.content:
The crown jewel for Macron was Costa’s plan to raise money for the EU budget from a tax on tech multinationals — a French pet project shelved in 2018 over fears of U.S. retaliation. In further concessions to the French, Costa shielded farmers’ subsidies from cuts, proposed new taxes to cap national contributions to Brussels, and deferred €10 billion in payments of EU post-Covid debt.

Underscoring the complex nature of the debate, Fabienne Keller, an MEP from Macron’s Renaissance party, said the digital tax proposal was “good news” but that the cuts overall “undermine Europe’s ambitions” and “clip its wings.”

Costa’s latest proposal for the budget ― worth roughly €1.78 trillion and due to start in 2028 ― is €44 billion smaller than the version that Ireland, in its role holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, presented last month. Governments are split between those wanting a smaller budget geared toward modern priorities like defense and competitiveness, and those demanding the EU spend more and focus on traditional areas such as farming and poorer regions.

Despite the wide disagreements, Costa and most governments are determined to get a deal by the end of the year.

“Seems like Santa Claus came early this year for the French,” said one EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this story, was granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive negotiations.

'Deeply disappointing'

Costa’s move in Macron’s direction represents a rare win in the twilight of the latter’s presidency. The beleaguered French leader steps down in May, and faces the prospect of being succeeded by far-right Eurosceptic Marine Le Pen or left-wing populist Jean Luc Mélenchon ― one of the main reasons the EU wants to get a deal on the budget this year.

World.title: Global climate talks have collapsed. Here’s what just happened.
World.content:
Missing the 1.5C target, the Paris Agreement’s most ambitious aim, loomed large in Turkey. Many nations cited the impending overshoot as justification for agreements to make deeper cuts to pollution, take stronger action to prepare for disasters and increase financial support for poorer countries.

But countries rich in oil and gas resources fought to keep any mention of fossil fuels — the main cause of global warming — out of the final text, while wealthy nations were reluctant to commit to specific funding goals.

U.N. Climate Change executive secretary Simon Stiell speaks to media after the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya on Nov. 22, 2026. | Yasin Akgul/AFP via Getty Images

The final impasse that brought down the talks revolved around the future of energy. A coalition of 130 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, demanded the COP31 text include a reference to a three-year-old commitment to phase out fossil fuels. But that was too much for some petrostates. Even recommitting to this earlier agreement was a red line for countries such as Saudi Arabia.

Another point of conflict was a paragraph in earlier drafts of the deal that appeared to put contentious carbon capture technologies on equal footing with clean power sources such as renewables. The anti-fossils coalition wanted those references deleted, arguing they catered to Riyadh’s interests to prolong the use of oil and gas.

On Sunday, Saudi Arabia pushed back. “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, and yet called carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies greenwashing,” said country negotiator Mohammad Ayoub.

In a fractious final plenary session, the EU and small islands, alongside the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland, several Latin American nations and a group of the world’s poorest countries, rejected the deal drawn up by Turkey and Australia, the conference co-hosts.

World.title: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
World.content:
The gathering drew lawmakers from the U.S. Congress and opposition leaders from Italy, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands, united in the belief that taxing the super-rich could help the left regain the political initiative.

Their pitch was that Zucman’s proposed annual minimum tax of 2% on billionaires’ wealth is a modest measure that most voters already support — and a potent answer to the far right.

“It’s the status quo which is radical,” said Zucman, who cites polls that put support for his tax in France at 86%.

“Remigration will not make your life better, but redistribution will,” said Elly Schlein, leader of Italy’s Democratic Party.

The summit ran for almost 12 hours in a hall the size of a small community theater that was packed for much of the day. Proceedings spilled into corridors and side rooms, where politicians and union leaders from the U.S., Europe and Latin America met between panels.

The event also marked the launch of the Paris Manifesto, a declaration against “international oligarchy” that pairs a minimum tax on the ultra-rich with protections for journalists and a new ownership model for AI companies. More than 100 researchers have signed it, including Nobel Prize-winning economists Joseph Stiglitz, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Daron Acemoglu.

World.title: Morocco: A surreal sculpture park turns the world upside down
World.content:
One of its most striking attractions, The House Fallen from the Sky, was created in 2010 as a tribute to the artist's grandfather. Resting on its roof at a 17-degree angle, the house contains inverted furniture, windows and bathroom fittings, creating a disorientating experience for visitors. Elsewhere, enormous chairs, tables, notebooks and wardrobes invite guests to rediscover the world from a child's perspective.

 

The park also features farmers and gardeners with oversized pumpkin and plant-shaped heads, giant ants surrounding a mud-built structure, and colourful architectural installations. Fourtou says these unusual combinations of human and botanical forms are designed to provoke curiosity and unease, while his oversized household objects recreate the sensations he experienced as a young child exploring his great-grandmother's home. The artist began transforming the site in 1999, before opening it to the public in 2024. Today, Ramakech attracts around 5,000 visitors annually. For Fourtou, the sculptures are less about nostalgia than exploring emotions, family relationships and the memories that shape our understanding of the world.

World.title: Midterms: US Democrats secure biggest House majority in decades
World.content:
The Democrats have won at least 258 seats in the 435-member House, gaining 44 from Republicans in its strongest general election performance since 1992.

 

The latest victory came in North Carolina, where Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated veteran Republican congresswoman Virginia Foxx. Four House races have yet to be decided, with contests in Minnesota and Tennessee still awaiting a result and two Louisiana races heading to runoffs in December.

The result surpasses the Democrats' gains in the 2018 midterm elections, when they picked up 40 seats during Trump's first presidency. Republicans are now set to hold no more than 177 seats, leaving them with one of their smallest House delegations in decades.

The Democratic wave extended across traditional Republican strongholds, the Midwest and the East Coast, reflecting widespread voter frustration over the cost of living, the war in Iran and allegations of corruption surrounding the Trump administration.

Democrats will also control the Senate, where they have secured 56 seats, giving the party its strongest position in Congress in more than a decade.

An ambitious agenda — and high expectations

With control of both chambers from January, Democrats are preparing an ambitious first 100 days focused on household finances, healthcare and government accountability.

Their priorities include reversing Republican cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired under Republican control. The party also intends to use congressional investigative powers to scrutinise Trump's administration, including the financial interests of the president and his family.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, is expected to become the first Black Speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on 3 January 2027.

Unlike outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, who struggled to manage a razor-thin majority, Jeffries would have considerable room to accommodate disagreements between progressive and moderate Democrats.

Nevertheless, the scale of the victory has raised expectations that the party will produce tangible results.

“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” Democratic congressman Jason Crow of Colorado told the Associated Press, pointing to Americans struggling with healthcare costs, economic insecurity and immigration enforcement.

Progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez described the election result as “a mandate for change”, while centrist Democrat Tom Suozzi argued that the party should devote most of its attention to affordability rather than investigations.

Confrontation with the White House

The Democratic takeover threatens to significantly constrain Trump during the final two years of his presidency.

Congressional committees are expected to launch investigations into the administration, potentially issuing subpoenas and demanding testimony from senior officials. Jeffries has also declined to rule out a third impeachment attempt against Trump.

The White House has responded aggressively, suggesting that some proposed investigations could amount to criminal misconduct — a claim that has intensified tensions over Congress's constitutional oversight responsibilities.

Republicans, meanwhile, face a difficult period of rebuilding. Jim Jordan of Ohio, chosen to lead the party's diminished House minority, has pledged to fight for American families and regain political ground ahead of the 2028 elections.

For Democrats, however, the immediate challenge is turning an overwhelming electoral victory into effective government. Their substantial congressional majorities offer an unusual opportunity to advance legislation, but Trump's continued control of the White House means major bills could still face a presidential veto.

Fact is: The midterm elections have fundamentally shifted the balance of power in Washington.

World.title: Finland confirms Russia is towing drone-hit cargo ship after Baltic Sea attack
World.content:
A Russian cargo ship hit by drones in the Baltic Sea is being towed out of Finnish waters by Russian rescue vessels after catching fire and drifting into Finnish territory, according to Finnish authorities.

 

Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a post on X that the Sparta II, which had posed a serious threat, had left Finnish waters. He added that "the consequences of Russia's war of aggression are also being felt in our neighbouring regions" and reaffirmed Finland's commitment to maintaining stability and security in the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian-flagged vessel, Sparta II, was reportedly struck by two drones on November 21 while sailing in the eastern Gulf of Finland, west of Gogland Island. The ship caught fire and lost its ability to manoeuvre before drifting into Finnish territorial waters. Its 16 crew members were evacuated, while Finnish and Russian rescue teams worked to contain the blaze.

The attack sparked a fire aboard the ship, forcing its 16 crew members to evacuate. One crew member reportedly sustained minor injuries.

By November 22, Russian vessels had begun towing the damaged ship away from Finnish waters following an emergency response involving maritime authorities from Finland, Estonia and Russia.

Although the immediate danger appears to have been contained, the incident raises broader questions about the security of Russian shipping, the vulnerability of Baltic maritime routes and the possibility of further military escalation near NATO territory.

A Russian military-linked vessel under attack

The Sparta II is a 121-metre cargo ship operated by Oboronlogistika, a Russian logistics company associated with the country's Ministry of Defence.

The company provides transportation and logistical support for Russian state operations, making its vessels potentially significant assets within Russia's broader military supply network.

At the time of the attack, the ship was travelling from St Petersburg toward Kaliningrad, Russia's heavily militarized exclave on the Baltic Sea, situated between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.

Kaliningrad occupies a particularly important position in Russia's military strategy. The territory hosts major naval installations and other military infrastructure, while its geographic separation from mainland Russia makes maritime transportation an important logistical connection.

The cargo carried by the Sparta II has not been publicly established. Finnish authorities indicated that military equipment could not be ruled out, although no definitive confirmation of such cargo was available.

The vessel is also subject to US sanctions, reflecting broader Western restrictions targeting Russian entities connected to military and logistical activities.

Suspected Ukrainian involvement

Finnish military officials reportedly assessed that Ukraine was likely responsible for the drone attack.

However, Ukrainian authorities had not publicly confirmed responsibility in the reporting available at the time. The identity of the attacker, the operational objectives and the precise circumstances surrounding the strike have not yet been independently established.

If Ukrainian involvement is confirmed, the incident could represent a notable development in the maritime dimension of the Russia-Ukraine war.

World.title: Germany tests Kamikaze drones and AI targeting technology in Lithuania
World.content:
Germany's armed forces have begun testing kamikaze drones and artificial intelligence-assisted targeting technology in Lithuania, marking another step in the Bundeswehr's efforts to modernize its military capabilities amid continuing security tensions between NATO and Russia.

 

The trials, conducted at the Rūdninkai military training area near the Belarusian border, involve loitering munitions developed by German defence technology companies Helsing and Stark Defence. The weapons are designed to identify and strike battlefield targets, including armoured vehicles, while potentially offering greater flexibility than conventional precision-guided weapons.

According to Reuters, the tests form part of the multinational Freedom Shield military exercise, which brings together approximately 3,800 personnel from eight NATO countries.

The exercise also provides German forces with an opportunity to evaluate how artificial intelligence can improve battlefield reconnaissance, target identification and military decision-making.

A new generation of battlefield weapons

Often referred to as kamikaze drones, loitering munitions are unmanned aircraft designed to remain airborne while searching for or waiting to engage a target. Once an attack is authorized, the drone flies into its target, destroying itself in the process.

Unlike traditional missiles, which are generally launched toward a previously designated target, loitering munitions can provide military operators with additional time to observe battlefield developments before committing to an attack.

During the Lithuanian trials, German troops tested drones against simulated armoured targets. The aircraft were equipped with inert warheads, allowing military personnel to evaluate their performance without using live explosive payloads.

The Bundeswehr is examining how such systems could complement existing artillery, reconnaissance platforms and armoured formations.

The technology has attracted increasing attention following its extensive use during the war in Ukraine, where both Ukrainian and Russian forces have employed attack drones against tanks, artillery positions, supply vehicles and other military targets.

Their widespread deployment has demonstrated how relatively inexpensive unmanned systems can threaten costly conventional equipment.

However, the conflict has also exposed significant limitations, including vulnerability to electronic interference, communication disruptions and increasingly sophisticated counter-drone defences.

Artificial intelligence enters the targeting process

Alongside the drone trials, German military personnel also evaluated Clarity, an AI-supported military intelligence and targeting platform developed by Helsing.

The software is designed to process battlefield information from multiple sources, potentially including drones, surveillance systems and other military sensors.

By analysing large volumes of information, AI-assisted systems can help identify potential targets and provide commanders with a more comprehensive picture of battlefield activity.

Traditional targeting procedures may require information to pass through several stages of analysis and communication before a military unit can respond. AI-assisted software could reduce some of these delays by identifying relevant information and presenting it to military personnel more efficiently.

Lithuania becomes a strategic testing ground

The decision to conduct the trials in Lithuania reflects the country's growing importance in NATO's eastern defence strategy.

Lithuania borders Belarus, a close ally of Russia, and Russia's heavily militarized Kaliningrad region. Its geographic position places it near one of the alliance's most strategically sensitive areas.

Germany has committed to permanently stationing a combat brigade in Lithuania, representing a significant development in its military posture.

The formation, known as Panzerbrigade 45, is expected to reach full operational capability by 2027, with approximately 5,000 military personnel and supporting civilian staff.

The brigade is intended to strengthen NATO's ability to defend Lithuania and reinforce the alliance's deterrence posture along its eastern frontier.

Testing emerging military technologies in the country allows German forces to evaluate equipment in an operational environment relevant to their future responsibilities.

The wider Freedom Shield exercise also includes conventional military activities such as manoeuvre operations, electronic warfare and cooperation between different branches of the armed forces.

Together, these activities reflect NATO's efforts to integrate traditional military formations with emerging technologies.

A changing security environment in Europe

The trials are taking place against the backdrop of continuing concern among European governments about Russia's military capabilities and the long-term security of NATO territory.

European defence officials have repeatedly emphasized the need to improve military readiness, expand ammunition production and strengthen the alliance's ability to respond to potential threats.

Russia, meanwhile, has rejected accusations that it intends to attack NATO territory and has criticized the alliance's military expansion near its borders.

The opposing positions have contributed to a security environment in which military exercises, force deployments and weapons development carry increasing strategic significance.

The future of European warfare

Germany's drone and AI trials in Lithuania illustrate a wider shift in military thinking across Europe.

Future battlefield effectiveness may depend not only on tanks, artillery and aircraft, but also on the ability to connect sensors, autonomous or remotely operated systems, artificial intelligence and human decision-makers.

The Bundeswehr's experiments represent an attempt to understand how these technologies can operate together in realistic military conditions. Whether the tested systems ultimately deliver the expected operational advantages remains to be demonstrated.

The Bundeswehr itself has acknowledged that battlefield drone success rates can be significantly lower than footage of successful strikes might suggest.

World.title: Marc Márquez wins eighth MotoGP title in Portugal, surpassing Rossi's record
World.content:
Marc Márquez clinched his eighth MotoGP world title this Sunday by being crowned world champion at the Portuguese Grand Prix, held at the Portimão circuit.

 

The Spanish Ducati rider finished in eighth place, a result that was enough to secure the championship mathematically and thus move past the seven premier-class titles of Italian rider Valentino Rossi

Márquez needed to finish at least ninth to guarantee the title without depending on other results. In the end, he took the flag in eighth after Brazilian Diogo Moreira crashed on the final lap.

The race win went to Italian Marco Bezzecchi, on an Aprilia, ahead of his teammate Jorge Martín and fellow Spaniard Raúl Fernández, who completed the podium.

The championship is the tenth motorcycle world title for the rider from Cervera, who also won one in 125cc and another in Moto2. With this total, he overtakes Rossi's nine championships, seven of them in the premier class, and draws level with Italian Giacomo Agostini in the all-time ranking of premier-class titles.

The triumph is particularly significant in view of the difficulties he has faced during the season. At the end of May, after the Italian Grand Prix at Mugello, Márquez found himself 102 points behind the then leader, Bezzecchi.

Marc Márquez, alongside former motorcycle racer Giacomo Agostini, after the end of the Portuguese Motorcycle Grand Prix on 22 November 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

A crash in the sprint race at the French Grand Prix, in Le Mans, forced him to undergo surgery, which also meant he missed the following round in Montmeló. His comeback was hampered by injuries, but from the Hungarian Grand Prix onwards he began a fightback that allowed him to claw back ground and take the lead at Misano.

After wrapping up the championship, Márquez dedicated the victory to his fans and described the title as "very special", referring to the years of work, injuries and recoveries he has had to go through to get back to the top.

World.title: French interior ministry rocked by probe into prefect's leaks to National Rally
World.content:
Five months before the French presidential election, the Interior Ministry is in turmoil. Hugues Moutouh, prefect of Centre-Val de Loire, is suspected of having passed confidential information to the National Rally.

 

On Saturday, the senior official announced that he had asked to be relieved of his duties.

In a statement, shared by the X account of the prefecture based in Orléans, Hugues Moutouh denounced a "campaign of destabilisation" that "goes far beyond" his own case and would target the institutions as well as the prefectural corps. "Through me, it is the very authority of the state that people are trying to attack", he said.

"This offensive comes at a time when some people are methodically working to weaken our institutions, to delegitimise those who embody them and to challenge the very foundations of the republican order", the prefect added.

"Calling me a mole is vile"

At the same time, in an interview with the weekly Journal du dimanche (JDD), published online on Saturday evening, Hugues Moutouh said he was "the victim of a manhunt".

"I have always served the state of one country, France, which I love deeply. Portraying me as a henchman in the pay of a party is odious, calling me a mole is vile," he said.

A former secretary general of the Interior Ministry between April 2025 and May 2026, Hugues Moutouh is suspected of having informed National Rally about investigations targeting the far-right party.

National Rally MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy, for his part, rejected these allegations on France Inter, describing them as "baseless rumours in the middle of an election campaign".

"I have the feeling that some people want to make Mr Moutouh pay for having done his job", he said, referring to the security arrangements for the National Rally congress held in Orléans at the end of October, which also prompted a counter-demonstration by opponents of the far-right party.

Le Pen denies having benefited from secret information

Marine Le Pen, National Rally candidate in the presidential election and well ahead in the opinion polls, responded to the affair on Sunday on France Inter and France 2. She said she had "never received any confidential information" from prefect Hugues Moutouh and had "never asked for any".

She added that she was "unable to say" whether anyone else in her party might have benefited from such information, as the investigation was still "ongoing".

The Paris public prosecutor's office confirmed this week, after revelations in the press, that it had opened a judicial investigation in July for suspected breaches of professional secrecy, breach of secrecy of investigations and handling the proceeds of those offences. The case has been handed to the General Inspectorate of the National Police (IGPN), nicknamed the "police of the police".

The premises of National Rally were searched at the beginning of the month, the prosecutor's office announced on Thursday. The Interior Ministry was also searched, according to a source close to the case quoted by AFP.

The investigation into the alleged leaks to National Rally stems from another search carried out as part of a separate procedure by the European Public Prosecutor's Office. According to AFP, confirming information published by Le Monde, an email from the office of prefect Hugues Moutouh was discovered at the Rome home of Frédéric Chatillon, an associate of Marine Le Pen who long handled the party's election communications.

In her interview on France Inter and France 2 on Sunday, Marine Le Pen said she did not know how this email could have been found at Frédéric Chatillon's home.

Earlier this week, AFP, citing a source close to the case, also reported that investigators had found a confidential Interior Ministry document during a search carried out as part of this European investigation. It concerns suspicions of the misappropriation of European funds by the former far-right group Identity and Democracy (ID), which included, among others, National Rally MEPs. This group was replaced in July 2024 by Patriots for Europe.

Hugues Moutouh, secretary general of the Interior Ministry alongside Anne-Marie Descôtes, secretary general of the Quai d'Orsay, on 9 January 2026. Ludovic Marin/Pool Photo via AP, File

On Friday, Hugues Moutouh was summoned by minister Laurent Nuñez. Speaking on BFMTV, the latter said that if the facts were "proven", they would be "obviously very serious", while stressing that at this stage no one had been placed under formal investigation in the case.

These suspicions of links between National Rally and a former number two at the Interior Ministry, who is still prefect of Centre-Val de Loire, come amid a particularly tense political climate, five months before the presidential election that will choose Emmanuel Macron's successor.

According to recent opinion polls, Marine Le Pen would receive more than 30 % of the vote in the first round.

World.title: Polls put Spain's PP ahead of PSOE a week before 29 November election
World.content:
The four opinion polls published this Sunday, one week before Spain's general election on 29 November, all place the Popular Party (PP) of Alberto Núñez Feijóo as the leading political force, ahead of the PSOE of Pedro Sánchez.

 

However, the surveys show differences in the distance between the two parties and in the representation that would be won by the far-right party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal.

In general, the polls in the middle of the election campaign suggest that together the PP and Vox would win between 190 and 210 seats, exceeding the 176 needed for an absolute majority in the Congress of Deputies. The PSOE would secure between 98 and 119 seats, while Frente Amplio would become the fourth-largest force in those estimates that provide specific figures for its representation.

Ipsos, in its poll published (source in Spanish) by 'La Vanguardia', puts the PP at 30.3% of the vote and 127 seats, compared with 29.8% and 119 seats for the PSOE. Vox would obtain 17.9% and 63 MPs. The two right-wing parties together would reach 190 seats.

The poll also assigns 11 seats to ERC, seven to EH Bildu and six to Frente Amplio. Junts would win five and Adelante Andalucía four.

Data10, in its tracking survey published (source in Spanish) by 'Okdiario', gives the PP 32.1% of the vote and 133 seats, and the PSOE 27% and 111 seats. Vox would reach 19% and 63 MPs. The combined total for PP and Vox would be 196 seats. Frente Amplio, together with territorial coalitions in its space, would win 6.6% of the vote and ten seats.

GAD3, in its poll published (source in Spanish) by 'ABC', estimates that the Popular Party would obtain 31.1% of the vote and 131 seats. The PSOE would be on 28.4% and 110 seats, while Vox would reach 18.1% and 63 MPs. The PP-Vox total would be 194 seats. Frente Amplio would win seven seats, with 5.8% of the vote.

Hamalgama Métrica, in its poll published (source in Spanish) by 'Vozpópuli', calculates that PP would receive 31.8% of the vote and 130 seats, while the PSOE would fall to 25.4% and 98 seats. Vox would reach 20.6% and 80 MPs, which would bring the combined total for the two parties to 210 seats. ERC and Frente Amplio would each win nine seats.

The differences between the four projections reflect different scenarios in this final stretch of the campaign. The gap between the PP and PSOE ranges from the 0.5 points calculated by Ipsos to the 6.4 points estimated by Hamalgama Métrica. The projected representation for Vox also varies, with a band of between 63 and 80 seats.

In any case, all four studies place PP and Vox above the threshold for an absolute majority and do not assign any representation to Sumar in their estimates.

World.title: Turkey prosecutors seek asset freezes on 108 high-profit traders
World.content:
Turkish prosecutors investigating a sprawling investment fund scandal have requested the freezing of securities held by 108 individuals who each allegedly earned more than $2 million in trading profits during periods of suspected market manipulation, according to a prosecutorial document cited by an opposition lawmaker.

 

The November 18 document also calls for financial institutions to closely monitor the individuals' asset movements, including large withdrawals, transfers and property transactions. However, it remains unclear whether the requested freezes have been implemented.

The development adds another dimension to a financial crisis that has engulfed investment funds worth approximately $17 billion, disrupted Turkey's stock market and raised questions about regulatory oversight and the relationship between political influence and financial markets.

According to an AFP report published on November 22, Şık, a member of the Workers' Party of Turkey (TİP), disclosed excerpts from a November 18 prosecutorial document identifying 108 individuals who each earned more than 100 million Turkish lira, equivalent to over $2 million, during periods when investigators detected suspected manipulation.

The document reportedly stated that no action had previously been taken against these individuals and that prosecutors had subsequently requested relevant institutions to freeze securities held in their accounts.

Although the document did not appear to formally identify all 108 individuals as criminal suspects, Şık said the list included people with connections to the state bureaucracy, political circles, corporate management and the financial industry.

The reported measures raise a central question in the investigation: whether the crisis was caused primarily by excessive financial risk-taking or whether some market participants benefited from coordinated trading practices while ordinary investors were exposed to potentially substantial losses.

How Turkey's investment fund crisis unfolded

The crisis erupted in September when several investment funds failed to meet investors' withdrawal requests, exposing weaknesses in portfolios that had accumulated large positions in relatively illiquid stocks.

On September 17, Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) ordered the liquidation of 131 funds managed by seven asset-management companies.

According to Reuters, the affected funds had accumulated more than $20 billion in assets during the preceding three years, attracting hundreds of thousands of investors seeking returns that could outpace inflation and the depreciation of the Turkish lira.

Allegations of manipulation and privileged access

At the center of the investigation are allegations that certain investment funds were used to inflate the prices of selected shares through concentrated or coordinated trading.

Under such a scheme, repeated purchases can push up the prices of stocks with limited freely available shares. As their market prices rise, funds holding those securities report substantial paper gains, potentially attracting additional investors.

The process can become self-reinforcing until investors attempt to withdraw their money or regulators intervene.

If large shareholders sell before prices collapse, they may realize substantial profits while remaining investors bear the consequences.

Investigators are examining whether such practices occurred and whether individuals with privileged information benefited disproportionately.

The newly reported requests for asset freezes are significant because they extend attention beyond the executives directly responsible for managing the troubled funds.

The list described by Şık reportedly includes individuals with political and bureaucratic connections, suggesting investigators are examining a potentially broader network of beneficiaries.

However, unusually large trading profits do not independently establish wrongdoing. Prosecutors would need to determine whether the gains resulted from illegal manipulation, privileged information or legitimate investment activity.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.

“This is part of a process of basically closing down all independent media that might risk reaching followers of the ruling party,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb of Human Rights Watch.

“The whole tactic of the Erdogan government has been to use court orders. The court orders are so problematic in themselves, so overreaching, so disproportionate, that this has nothing really to do with the legal process. This is all about a political crackdown.”

Turkey talks green at Cop31 while cracking down on activists

Sinclair-Webb noted that television remains the primary news source for most Turks, making both networks and individual journalists who question government policies prime targets.

Four journalist have been detained or placed under house arrest for reporting on the investment scandal.

Authorities accuse Sozcu TV of ties to followers of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for masterminding a failed 2016 coup. Four of its executives and officials have been detained. Halk TV faces separate corruption allegations.

Both broadcasters strongly deny the charges.

Investment scandal

The closing of the channels comes amid fallout from the collapse of more than 100 investment funds, which wiped out $20 billion, stranded more than 500,000 investors and triggered a stock market crash.

The scandal has implicated numerous figures linked to Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party).

According to recent polls, 80 percent of Turks are closely following the scandal, with a similar majority blaming the government.

On Thursday, protesters demonstrated outside the Capital Markets Board, the country's financial regulator, in Ankara.

Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next

Around 500 people are under investigation and more than 100 suspects have been jailed. Erdogan vowed this week that no one would escape justice and promised to expedite repayments to affected investors.

Political analyst Sezin Oney said the government is scrambling to control the public narrative as its reputation among its own voter base unravels.

“Up to now, AK Party and government circles were able to project to their base the idea that the opposition [is involved in] all sorts of corruption. So all of a sudden, that facade, that rhetoric has collapsed. Now it’s the government circles who are massively corrupt."

Debate moves online

Atilla Yesilada, a Turkey analyst at New York-based consultancy firm Global Source Partners, warned that the scandal has exposed deep flaws in financial oversight, threatening severe economic and political fallout for Erdogan.

“Turkey is heading for a recession because the institutional structure has completely collapsed,” Yesilada said. “In a free market economy, you really need regulatory boards to do their work which clearly, as we see in this instance, they don't. In fact, they enable or incentivise thieves [and make] their jobs easier."

Yesilada added that Erdogan lacks a clear path to resolve the crisis, as opposition figures release new allegations implicating AK Party associates daily.

Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy

Following the state takeover of another broadcaster last year, the loss of Sozcu TV and Halk TV marks a grim turning point for Turkish media, Oney said. However, she questioned whether the government can successfully suppress public discourse.

“It’s the end of the road for TV journalism, you don’t have any oppositional voice or oppositional debate. But people talk, people think, one way or another. Because Turkey was a thinking and talking nation before, it's very difficult to stop [that]. It is just [being done now] on social media.”

The government has accelerated efforts to police online dissent, shutting down hundreds of critical social media accounts, although new ones are emerging just as rapidly.

Meanwhile Koza TV, a previously fringe station, has seen its ratings surge after becoming a new outlet for independent reporting on the scandal – although mounting regulatory fines make its future uncertain.
