World.title: IND vs NZ first Test Day 5: New Zealand batters blunt Indian attack
World.content:
New Zealand continued to blunt India’s attack as the visitors found themselves needing five wickets to force a rare Test win in the country.

At tea on the fifth day of the first Test at Basin Reserve, the hosts were 206 for five, with 39 overs left to negotiate.

Having lost two wickets in the morning session, New Zealand tightened its approach further, adding just 87 runs in 51 overs in the first two sessions for the loss of three wickets. The only wicket of the session came three overs before the new ball was due, with Anshul Kamboj finally finding a faint edge off Tom Blundell’s willow.

Also read | IND vs NZ 1st Test Day 4: Jurel sees chance for India despite slowing Basin Reserve pitch

Kamboj, who had been consistently clocking the mid-130s, induced Blundell to play at a delivery outside off. Rishabh Pant, who caught the ball between his pads, did not hear the nick and was initially unsure. But captain Shubman Gill at covers and Dhruv Jurel at midwicket were convinced, prompting India to go upstairs. The replays confirmed the edge, ending Blundell’s stubborn resistance.

Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips, however, continued to prioritise survival over scoring, leaving India with little margin for error as the overs ticked away.

India had another opportunity to make inroads when Kamboj extracted extra bounce to surprise Mitchell. The New Zealand batter gloved the delivery, but Devdutt Padikkal, stationed at forward short-leg, could not hold on to an attempted left-handed catch.

With New Zealand still 146 runs behind and 39 overs remaining, the dropped chance could yet prove consequential.

World.title: Anthropic’s stock market debut: a record IPO, a quick fade, decabillionaires, and the risks ahead | Explained
World.content:
When Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq on November 19, investors got their first opportunity to buy shares in the company behind the Claude artificial intelligence assistant. The listing also put a public-market value of about $23 billion on the stake held by each of its seven co-founders.

But the debut raises a bigger question. Can Anthropic turn growing demand for its AI models into a profitable business when developing and running them requires enormous computing resources?

The company’s prospectus reveals the scale of its growth, the money it has raised and the financial commitments it has made to expand.

Anthropic set its IPO price at $83 a share, above the initially indicated range of $70-$78. Trading under the symbol ANT, the stock opened at $111.50 on November 19, 34.3% above the IPO price. It touched $115.10 before falling to $92.72 and closing at $97.17, up 17.1%.

The stock lost further ground on its second day of trading, November 20, closing at $88.91, down 8.5% from the previous day’s close of $97.17. It opened at $89.86 and fell as low as $83.05, just above its IPO price of $83. Trading volume stood at 400.46 million shares, less than half the 857.31 million shares traded on debut day.

World.title: Alice Huang in touch with Chinese spy agency during affair with Nvidia CEO, says NYT
World.content:
Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia’s recent scandal, kept in contact with an official ​from China’s top spy agency for more than a year during ‌her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York ​Times reported on Sunday (November 22, 2026).

Alice Huang was in ⁠touch with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the report said, ‌citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

Spokespersons for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and the Chinese Embassy ‌in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for ‌comment. ⁠Reuters has not been able to reach Alice ⁠Huang for comment.

Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an important Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions in Nvidia chip sales.

U.S. authorities have been investigating Megaspeed ​since 2024 over concerns it smuggled ‌Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China.

Sunday’s (November 22, 2026) report comes as US officials have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy, as the newspaper reported last month.

That October ‌29 article touched off a scandal that led ​to Jensen Huang’s resignation two weeks later and a steep drop in Nvidia’s stock price.

Trump administration officials have ⁠repeatedly said they have not concluded that Alice Huang spied for China.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said this month the Justice Department ‌had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was a Chinese spy.

U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton repeated that on Sunday.

“Attorney General Blanche has been very clear that this is a matter under investigation, both Ms Huang and her company, for various matters,” Mr. Clayton told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “And I’m ‌going to let that investigation play out.”

The scandal has also prompted a ​deeper look at Washington’s approach to export controls on China, with lawmakers from both parties questioning whether the ⁠Trump administration has been too lax on enforcement and regulation of the ⁠prized semiconductors.

The affair between the two itself is of less interest, Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, told NBC’s “Meet the ‌Press.”

“I hope he had a good time,” Mr. Kennedy said on Sunday (November 22, 2026). “It was the most expensive sex since Helen of ​Troy.”

World.title: 3 killed and 1 wounded in shooting at Ohio baby shower; 1 man in custody, police say
World.content:
Three people were killed and one was injured at an Ohio baby shower during an apparent domestic dispute, authorities said.

Officers responded to a shooting Saturday evening at Pandora's Magical Events Venue in Parma, about 10 miles (16 kilometres) south of Cleveland, a police news release said.

Authorities said one of the shooters, a 29-year-old man, was taken into custody, but he wasn't immediately charged. Detectives were trying to determine whether the man was the aggressor or acting in self-defence, police spokesman Scott Traxler said. A second suspected shooter, a 19-year-old man, was one of the people killed, police said.

Officials have identified two of the victims as 17-year-old Leasia England and 45-year-old Jayson Townsend. Police said Townsend was the father of the woman for whom the baby shower was being held; she was not injured.

Officials haven't released the names of the 19-year-old suspected shooter who was killed, or a 39-year-old woman who was shot in the leg.

Preliminary information indicates that the 19-year-old man was the father of the unborn baby, and witnesses told police that he was not invited to the shower, Mr. Traxler said. The man in custody appears to be a relative of the expectant mother.

Both firearms involved in the shooting were recovered by police, officials said. Detectives were reviewing surveillance video and witnesses' statements on Sunday to determine what led to the violent confrontation, Traxler said. Ballistics testing might be required to determine which gun shot each victim.

Prosecutors will eventually determine whether the man in custody should be charged with a crime, officials said.

World.title: COP31 talks fail as EU, others reject any climate deal without language on a fossil fuel phase-out
World.content:
A standoff on a fossil fuel phase-out prevented countries at COP 31, the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkiye, from achieving any consensus agreement on future climate action on Sunday (November 22, 2026), despite the conference running a record 48 hours into overtime.

The European Union led objections to COP 31 President Murat Kurum’s consensus cover text that failed to include any explicit language about moving away from fossil fuels. The EU’s stance was reportedly supported by about 130 countries.

On the other side of the divide, India is among the nations that supported the proposed cover text, as they want to keep using fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, with Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav stressing that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation.”

‘Greenwashes fossil fuel’

“We express profound disappointment with the final draft COP31 cover decision or Antalya Pact. At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short,” Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said, speaking on behalf of the EU.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach… We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” he added.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome, it needs the consensus of all parties.

‘Rollback from earlier deals’

Panama also formally objected to the text, saying that as a country battling droughts and other perilous impacts of climate change, the lack of any commitment to keep the rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees C with firm action on phasing out fossil fuels was “a setback”.

“Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it weighs too much upon technologies such as CCUS [carbon capture utilisation and storage] instead of calling for deep changes, and three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback,” said Ana Aguilar, Panama’s chief climate negotiator.

‘Equitable energy transitions needed’

On the other side, Saudi Arabia, China, and India are among the countries that are against explicit language on fossil fuel and expressed comfort with the way the cover text language was framed, while also expressing misgivings about the lack of clarity on adaptation finance. The countries are part of the Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) coalition, who are insistent on the use of fossil fuel in the foreseeable future to further their economies, but have also significantly deployed renewable energy.

Indian Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said that India’s voice had shaped the draft COP 31 outcome, especially on food security, livelihoods, and cultural practices recognised in action on methane. However, in a post on X, he emphasised that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation. Energy transitions must be nationally determined, just and equitable, backed by finance, technology and capacity-building for developing countries.”

Amandeep Garg, who was leading India’s delegation but speaking in his capacity as a spokesperson on behalf of the LMDC, said on the floor: “Everyone has worked tirelessly, and despite our discomfort with some elements of the text, we are willing to move forward, and continue to engage.” The LMDC expressed “concern” about the principles of equity and common but differentiated responsibility not being adequately reflected, adding that there was a “dilution” of the principle of developed countries taking historical responsibility and meeting their obligations.

“At the threshold of crossing 1.5 deg. C, we have raised a fundamental point – we need to reflect why we are here. Whose emissions, both past and continuing, have exhausted the global carbon budget? The cover decision does not reflect this, and only repeats agreed paragraphs from previous decisions to reflect responsibility and does not connect this with the imminent prospect of exceeding 1.5 deg. C,” he said.

‘Climate action must be anchored in science’

The inability of a COP presidency to pass a consensus text is perceived as a sign of failure but the consensus driven nature of the agreement is such that no country or bloc has veto power and every clause must be unanimously agreed to by all 190+ country representatives.

“Antalya will go down as the first COP held in a 1.5°C overshoot reality, and it has exposed a difficult truth: multilateral climate action cannot move at the pace of the lowest common denominator when parties remain unwilling to compromise on the fundamental challenge of transitioning away from fossil fuels,” said Nakul Sharma, senior policy advisor on India at the E3G climate think tank, said in a statement, “Rejecting the cover decision was not a failure of diplomacy; it reflected the need to protect the credibility of the Paris Agreement and keep global climate action anchored in science.”

World.title: West Bengal BJP president Samik Bhattacharya calls for protest over attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh
World.content:
West Bengal Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) president Samik Bhattacharya on Sunday (November 22, 2026) called for a protest against the alleged persecution of Hindus in Bangladesh.

“Blood is being shed in Bangladesh, and it is our brothers who are suffering. As a Bengali Hindu, I believe we must take to the streets,” the BJP leader told media persons.

Noting that India had played a crucial role in the creation of Bangladesh, the BJP Rajya Sabha MP expressed his opinion that Bangladesh was created on the basis of religion, not on the basis of the Bengali language.

“Bangladesh was not created for the sake of language. If it had been, Bengali-speaking Hindus in Bangladesh would not be dying like this today,” he said. Mr. Bhattacharya said that the fundamental question at that time should have been the protection of people and the creation of a democratic environment. Instead, the leadership surrendered to religious fundamentalism, he said.

Wounds of Partition

Claiming that the wounds of Partition continued to haunt the subcontinent, the BJP leader said that it was religious minorities, particularly Hindus in Bangladesh, who were bearing the consequences. Blaming Partition on Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi, Mr. Bhattacharya claimed that had Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose become independent India’s first Prime Minister, he would never have accepted the two-nation theory or allowed the subcontinent to be divided into India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.

The remarks by the West Bengal BJP leader come at a time when fresh political tensions have erupted in Bangladesh. Attempts at normalising the India-Bangladesh relationship in recent months have been hindered by former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s presence in India, where she took refuge on August 5, 2024. Ms. Hasina has announced that she is keen to return to Bangladesh.

World.title: FSSAI orders prosecution against Bisleri International for unsafe packaged drinking water
World.content:
Food regulator FSSAI on Sunday (November 22, 2026) said it has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International, as it found its sample of packaged drinking water "unsafe".

In a social media post, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said it has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd regarding "unsafe packaged drinking water".

A regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" was collected from the premises of Bisleri International for analysis.

"The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006," the regulator said.

Upon appeal by the company, the sample was sent to the referral food laboratory, which also declared it "unsafe" due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the regulator added.

The findings of the lab established violations relating to unsafe food under the law. Hence, the FSSAI said it has granted sanction to launch prosecution under the FSS Act, 2006, against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd.

Through a social media post, FSSAI said it has sanctioned prosecution against a few other companies, including Vasant Masala Pvt Ltd, Tit-Bit Foods India Pvt Ltd, Mimansa Industries and Asha Confectionery.

The regulator has suspended the licence of Urmi Lifesciences LLP and Gaur Ayurvedic Store for non-compliance of rules and regulations.

FSSAI has also issued a product recall order against Asha Confectionery. The company has been asked to withdraw pre-pack chocolate filled cookies as they were found unsafe.

During this calendar year, the FSSAI has stepped up enforcement actions against food business operators (FBOs) and also e-commerce companies.

The regulator has also cracked down against energy drink and alcoholic beverage makers.

World.title: Days after Akvan, Rs 212 cr imminent relief to 5.73 lakh Bengal farmers hit by cyclone
World.content:
Even as the West Bengal government has prepared a list of the farmers affected due to the rain triggered by Cyclone Akvan, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday announced a Rs 212.3-crore preliminary compensation package for over 5.73 lakh farmers whose crops and horticultural produce were damaged.

Cyclone Akvan made landfall near the Gopalpur coast in neighbouring Odisha on Friday morning, bringing rain across southern West Bengal.

“Our government is a farmer-friendly government,” the CM reassured the farmers, while sharing that secretaries have been instructed to investigate the matter further.



Adhikari said around Rs 205 crore was released from the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) for immediate relief, taking the total allocation, including assistance for seeds and other components, to Rs 212.3 crore, PTI reported.

World.title: Delhi Confidential: Parliament session suspense, BSP’s AI push, ex-SC judge memoir row
World.content:
Session suspense

Hours after BJP president Nitin Nabin declared at a meeting in Chandigarh that women’s reservation in legislatures will be implemented “soon”, BJP circles in the Capital were abuzz with the possibility of a special session of Parliament in the coming week. According to party insiders, several prominent leaders were already on their way to the Capital despite no clarity on whether the announcement meant the ‘delimitation package’ would be taken up during a special session or the scheduled Winter Session.

BSP’s AI push

Mayawati-led Bahujan Samaj Party has finally joined the AI bandwagon ahead of the Assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh. While most other parties are already using advanced technologies to boost their campaign, the BSP on Sunday launched AI-generated videos to take its message to the masses. BSP leaders are sharing these videos to invite people to the December 6 public meeting of Mayawati at Ambedkar Memorial in Lucknow. Party leaders claim young BSP workers have developed these videos as a tribute to Dr B R Ambedkar. Technology has not been the strong point of the BSP when it comes to public outreach. The party started using social media platforms years after other parties did.

World.title: ‘You are being scammed’: How a small Delhi Police team is rescuing digital arrest victims
World.content:
On October 1, Bhim Singh was about to liquidate his mutual funds, the last of his savings and the only cushion between a 73-year-old retiree and financial ruin. He had already broken his fixed deposit and sent Rs 25 lakh to men he believed were officers of the law.

Now they were scaring him into selling the rest, and he was planning to part with some of his wife’s jewellery. For 11 days, he and his 65-year-old wife had been under “digital arrest” in their modest house in Roshan Pura, a middle-class locality near the Delhi-Gurugram border, confined by people who were never in the room.

Then his phone rang again.



“Hello, this is Inspector Parveen Kumar, from Delhi Police. Have you transferred the money into this account? Aapke saath scam ho raha hai. Woh police nahi hai (You are being scammed. Those men are not the police),” said the voice on the other end.

Singh was in a bind. For days he had been shown an Enforcement Directorate notice, an FIR copy bearing the Supreme Court’s name, and a courtroom where a judge in a black robe presided. Now a stranger was telling him that all of it was false, and that the stranger was the real police. Who was real and who was not had moved beyond his mental grasp.

“I initially doubted him,” Singh says. The caller sent him videos of other digital-arrest victims, so that he could see what was happening to him. “I called him and asked if he also wanted to put me under digital arrest. But when he said he did not need money, I was inclined to listen. It was the first time in nearly 15 days that I had not been asked to pay money.”



Delhi has become one of the country’s most vulnerable cities for digital arrests, and its elderly are the favoured targets. Delhi has become one of the country’s most vulnerable cities for digital arrests, and its elderly are the favoured targets.

Singh was saved. He did not send another Rs 3.44 lakh he was about to.

His rescue was the work of a unit that did not exist in March: the Proactive Victim Identification & Protection Team of the Delhi Police. It is tiny — one inspector and two head constables — and does something Indian policing has rarely tried.

“It looks for people in the middle of a digital arrest, while the scam is still running, and tries to talk them out of it,” a senior police official said.

Delhi has become one of the country’s most vulnerable cities for digital arrests, and its elderly are the favoured targets. Many live alone while their children work punishing jobs or live abroad.

“In digital arrest cases, policing has so far prioritised recovering the money and tracing the accused. But in most cases, once the money moves, it’s gone. It hops across accounts and leaves the formal banking system, through crypto and hawala channels, often before the victim has finished explaining what happened,” says a senior police officer. “Hence, we decided that we should trace the victims and not let the money leave. That’s how the unit was formed in March this year”

The special unit

If you dial 1930, the national cyber-fraud helpline, from Delhi, the person most likely to pick up is Inspector Kumar. He oversees the helpline’s control room at the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit of the Delhi Police.

“As I was handling the 1930 helpline, I was the first point of contact for the victims,” he says. “They usually called with such distress, with no idea of what had befallen them. So I had the practice of being extremely patient and sensitive to each caller.”

When the police set up the new team in March, they gave it to Kumar to handle. Senior officers say the choice came down to that patience, and to the fact that he already coordinated regularly with both IFSO and the Ministry of Home Affairs’ Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, or I4C.

Kumar works from IFSO’s Rohini branch. His two deputies, the head constables, operate from the cyber agency’s offices at Connaught Place.

The mandate, Kumar says, went beyond answering complaints. The team was asked to reach people while they were still being duped, in real time. “We have to save the victim, and anyhow keep them engaged,” he says. “No matter what they say to us, or how difficult they are to convince.”

The team’s main operation is to track suspected money transactions, and to find the next victim before the money moves again.

“Whenever we get a cyber fraud complaint, we first get the details of the account the victim transferred the money to,” Kumar says. “The head constables at Connaught Place get in touch with the bank, and also get details of the victim. We then check if that (suspect’s) account is still receiving money. If yes, then someone somewhere is still being scammed.”

The head constables then try to reach that second victim.

But it is not as simple as picking up a phone, says Kumar. Convincing is the hard part, because the police are competing with a well-produced show.

The challenge, he says, is that victims believe the scammers are the real police, and the scammers have gone to great lengths to make that belief hold. Victims, he adds, are shown genuine-looking FIRs and official notices, and some sit through live court proceedings.

When the head constables cannot get through, Kumar takes over.

“It’s difficult to beat that,” says a police officer. “In most of our cases of digital arrest, we call them and tell them that we are the real police. We try to take them into confidence by telling them that we are not going to ask for any money. We send them videos related to cases of digital arrest, so that they can look at it and then realise that the same thing is happening to them.”

Once the unit gets through, officers insist that a relative or a friend sits beside the victim for as long as the scammers keep calling.

The rescue

Similar was the chain of events on September 29, when Bhola Thakur, a 78-year-old retired Army captain from Sagarpur, called 1930. He was emerging from a 15-day “digital arrest” during which he had sent about Rs 4 crore to cyber criminals, in six transactions.

“They claimed that SIM cards and credit cards had been issued on his Aadhaar and misused in Canada,” says a police officer. “He was then put on a video call with a person impersonating an IPS officer of PS Daryaganj, who threatened him with arrest in a money laundering case.

Out of fear, he transferred a large sum of money in multiple transactions from his BOB, ICICI and SBI accounts.”

The police traced where the money went. It had landed in a first-layer mule account at Axis Bank in Hyderabad, Telangana, and the account was still filling.

Between September 21 and September 29, another Rs 1.45 crore had poured in from five different accounts. They belonged to a retired Indian Railways employee, 70; a cloth trader, 80, from Rajasthan; a businessman, 50, from Gujarat; a hospital assistant, 65, from Maharashtra; and

Bhim Singh.

When Inspector Kumar called Singh he was getting ready to send another Rs 3.44 lakh to the men who had kept him under “digital arrest”, and was planning to sell some of his wife’s jewellery.

Like Singh, the other four — three of them elderly and each at a different stage of “digital arrest” — were stopped from sending more money. In all, the Delhi Police says, they kept more than Rs 75 lakh out of the fraudsters’ hands.

But what had already been sent could not be saved. “The money that had been transferred had already moved to other accounts,” says a police officer. “It is now not in the formal banking system. So, it’s difficult to say how it will be recovered.”

The challenges

The team now handles two to three digital arrest cases every day. However, multiple officers say that at present, saving a victim of digital arrest is still an exception.

One senior officer says that of every 10 calls made to victims, perhaps only one or two end as Singh’s did. Another senior officer said the rate of saving a victim from further loss is closer to one in 15.

According to the I4C, at least 21,900 complaints of digital-arrest fraud came in between January and August this year, and more than Rs 647 crore was lost. How much was recovered is not known.

At an open-house discussion on safeguarding human rights against digital arrest scams, Justice V Ramasubramanian, chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission, said that recovering even a part of the money was a hassle for victims.

The legal and procedural processes, he said, proved lengthy, costly and distressing. “At times, the process of recovery becomes more painful than the process of losing money.”

Trust a hurdle

Trust is the next hurdle. “Lonely senior citizens are also very sceptical,” says another officer who has worked with IFSO. “After paying that much to fake cops, it’s difficult for them to trust again when they are called by the real ones.”

Kumar remembers a case from June, when he found that an account in Gujarat’s Jamnagar had transferred more than Rs 25 lakh to a mule account.

“He was a senior citizen and refused to believe me. Even after I asked him to call 1930,” Kumar says. “I then called the local SHO in the area, who visited his house with a team. But the man didn’t open the door. He had told the fraudsters that people dressed in khaki were standing outside. The scammer convinced him that the SHO was a fraud, and the team ended up waiting hours outside his house.”

Why scam can’t be stopped at the start?

There is also a limit built into the method. The unit can identify a victim only after that person has sent money to the fraudster at least once, so it cannot stop a scam at the start.

For middle-class and lower-middle-class families, the first few transactions often take most of their savings. Singh handed over Rs 25 lakh in one go and had only Rs 3-4 lakh left to transfer.

Finally, there is the question of scale. The obvious answer would be to spread the work across district cyber police stations, but senior officers say that could cost them the “golden hour.”

“It sounds like a good idea. But you have to understand that the first call will always come to us, as we handle the 1930 control room,” says Additional Commissioner of Police (IFSO) Sanjay Bhatia. “The time we will spend alerting the PS, and getting them in touch with the victim, can be used to stop the transaction. Also, the process of finding the victim requires us getting details from the banks. As every major bank’s nodal officer is connected to IFSO, it’s easier for us to access them,” Bhatia adds.

World.title: PM Modi, Nepal PM to flag off Ayodhya–Janakpur direct train today, operations begin Nov 28
World.content:
In a major push to religious tourism and cross-border connectivity, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah will virtually flag off the Saryu-Kamala Express connecting Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh to Janakpur in Nepal, from Delhi on Monday.

Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath will also participate in the inauguration ceremony at Ayodhya Dham railway station, officials said.

Ayodhya is the birthplace of Lord Ram, while Janakpur in Nepal is revered as the place of birth of Goddess Sita.



Regular operations of the train will begin on November 28, providing pilgrims and passengers a direct rail connection between the two important centres associated with the Ramayana tradition. Officials said the 604-km journey will take approximately 19 hours, eliminating the need for passengers to change trains en route.

World.title: ‘Every single person knew’: AB de Villiers claims Australia also tampered ball in 2018 Durban Test
World.content:
South Africa batting great AB de Villiers has reacted to the growing furore of the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal, claiming that every Australia player knew about the ball-tampering tactic during the infamous series.

De Villiers, who featured in the Cape Town Test and scored 64 in the first innings and 63 in the second, said he believed the ball-tampering had also taken place during the opening Test in Durban, rejecting the focus on whether players knew that sandpaper was being used.

The focus on the controversy from eight years ago resurfaced after Usman Khawaja’s explosive revelations in his recent memoir, ‘Sabr’, which has led to disagreements with former teammates, including current Test captain Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood.

World.title: Dulquer Salmaan’s poor acting, abysmal Kochi accent make this rom-com a hate-watch classic
World.content:
There’s something spectacularly alluring about Dulquer Salmaan’s on-screen romance. It makes us fall in love not only with him but with the film as a whole, and even with romance itself. But all this happens only if the film is good: well-written and well-made. If the film is bad, Dulquer’s on-screen romance can have the opposite effect and make us cringe. The experience becomes far worse if the film has disastrous comedy too. Director BC Noufal’s Oru Yamandan Premakadha is the best example to understand how annoying a poorly made Dulquer Salmaan romantic comedy can be.

Lallu (Dulquer Salmaan) is the son of John Kombanaayil (Renji Panicker), a renowned lawyer, and Nancy (Viji Ratheesh). Although he belongs to an affluent family, Lallu leads a “modest life” — while still staying in his massive bungalow — and works as a daily-wage house painter. He finds happiness in the little things in life with his friends, Vicky (Soubin Shahir), Paanchikuttan (Salim Kumar), and Teni (Vishnu Unnikrishnan). Although Lallu has scores of female fans, he remains single, as he hasn’t found “the one” who gives his heart that “spark.” One day, he comes across Diya (Nikhila Vimal), who gives him the “spark,” but fate starts playing cruel jokes on them exactly at that moment.

Don’t Miss | Bachelor Party D’eux movie review: A ghost of the OG film that needs to be exorcised ASAP



Forced nostalgia and recycled humour

Oru Yamandan Premakadha (A Humongous Love Story) is one of the cringiest Malayalam films of the century. It isn’t bad-bad, but not a scene goes by without making us shudder. And every time we cringe, we can see what writers Bibin George and Vishnu Unnikrishnan — both also play key roles in the film — thought of while writing those lines, jokes, and scenes. They assumed these would make the audience LOL or hit them square in the chest, just like they did in Amar Akbar Anthony (2015) and Kattappanayile Rithwik Roshan (2016). But literally everything they thought would work backfires, turning the film into a massive joke with no actual laughs.

Dulquer Salmaan in Oru Yamandan Premakadha. (Credit: Facebook/@OruYamadanPremakadha) Dulquer Salmaan in Oru Yamandan Premakadha. (Credit: Facebook/@OruYamadanPremakadha)

Throughout the movie, Bibin and Vishnu lean heavily on nostalgic elements. However, they aren’t shady about it; they acknowledge it upfront, portraying Lallu as a person who thrives on nostalgia. We hear him say things like, “Rain, tea, Johnson master (legendary music composer) — Just wow!” showing how obsessed he is with elements and combinations that evoke nostalgia. He even has photos of characters from children’s weekly comic magazines on his wall. But the issue is that none of these elements seems naturally woven into the script.

Also Read | Aakasamlo Oka Tara movie review: Dulquer Salmaan shines in a moving tale of love and dreams

Instead, it feels as though the writer duo took note of everything that worked in their earlier films and simply rehashed it. For example, the wordplay in Kattappanayile Rithwik Roshan — especially the use of unconventional words in certain situations and the redefining of terms for comedic effect — evoked laughter then. Throughout Oru Yamandan Premakadha, we see desperate attempts at the same, with a few examples being Anthass for awesome/wow, Omanakutty for okay, Chitraguptan for Parippu Vada, and Thikkurissy for cheers. But nothing works.



Dulquer Salmaan’s worst styling and an intolerable Kochi accent

Since childhood, girls around him have been going gaga over Lallu, and he gets proposals often. However, he rejects them all because they don’t give him the “spark.” I understand this must be a fantasy of men to have women go after them, like how they show in ads for Axe perfume. But Oru Yamandan Premakadha, in my opinion, features Dulquer’s worst look in a film. Even his styling is so atrocious that the women pursuing him, as shown here, end up reflecting poorly on Malayali women.

Dulquer Salmaan with Salim Kumar, Soubin Shahir, and Vishnu Unnikrishnan in Oru Yamandan Premakadha. (Credit: Facebook/@OruYamadanPremakadha) Dulquer Salmaan with Salim Kumar, Soubin Shahir, and Vishnu Unnikrishnan in Oru Yamandan Premakadha. (Credit: Facebook/@OruYamadanPremakadha)

In one scene, Teni says that Lallu has no haters. But honestly, this dialogue alone must have earned Dulquer at least 10 haters in real life, and the movie as a whole must have earned him thousands.

If we tell Oru Yamandan Premakadha’s Dulquer, “Your Kochi accent is so sexy; say it again,” and he actually says it, we might puke. His accent is that bad, and its inconsistency is a blessing. I usually hate it when actors are inconsistent with their accents due to their carelessness. But in Oru Yamandan Premakadha, I was rooting for moments when Dulquer accidentally dropped his thick Kochi accent because it was intolerable.

By the way, I am surprised that house painters didn’t call for a ban on this film for portraying them as loafers who fleece clients without doing proper work.



Lazy coincidences, casual casteism and tone-deaf tropes

Oru Yamandan Premakadha is marred by unfunny one-liners and so-called comedic moments that don’t make one laugh. There’s a scene where a man who works as a butcher accidentally cuts his birthday cake the way he chops meat. Although people around him on screen laugh, we might yawn. The one-liners are essentially cringeworthy nonsense masquerading as observational comedy.

ICYMI | Welcome to Central Jail: ‘There’s rock bottom, 50 feet of cr*p’, and then this Dileep film

Not just the dialogues; the script is shoddy overall. Coincidences are fine when one or two are slipped in, but when the whole movie is packed with them, that’s just lazy writing. For instance, the opening act shows Lallu’s birth, and Diya’s mother (Lena) is also there, pregnant with her. It was initially believed that Lallu was stillborn, but then he starts crying, prompting the doctor to label him “special.” Seeing Lallu return to life, Diya’s mother begins having contractions, suggesting that Lallu’s voice somehow triggered her birth. The desperation in this scene to forge a connection between them beyond the conventional is just sad.

Aside from the objectification of women and misogyny, which are prevalent in the film, there is also casteism. Lallu’s father is presented as a dignified gentleman whom the entire locality respects because he is a renowned lawyer, or so one person says in the opening scene. Sure, some lawyers do receive a measure of respect. However, Oru Yamandan Premakadha never provides any evidence beyond that line to show he is a good lawyer. Instead, early on, we see that he is supremely casteist as he warns a young Lallu against playing with kids from the nearby 3-cent colony (a derogatory term used to describe settlements of SC/ST communities). The worst part is that it’s delivered as a casual dialogue, in/directly revealing just how casteist the makers could be.



Oru Yamandan Premakadha is one of the best films to hate-watch whenever we are feeling down. Dulquer Salmaan’s abysmal performance is a testament to the fact that an actor is only as good as the director, and BC Noufal’s contributions as director to this film remain a mystery because we never feel like it had a helmer. Both Nadirshah’s songs and Bijibal’s background score are equally disastrous, adding to the film’s woes.

Nevertheless, I am glad Oru Yamandan Premakadha is no Saleem (2009).

Memories of Blunder is a column in which we dissect some of the worst South Indian movies and performances of all time. No offence to anyone whose name surfaces here. They may all have potential, but they blew it that one time. However, don’t play the song if you can’t face the music, right?

World.title: Rajiv Kuumar on Ramayana’s success, struggles: ‘After this film, I hope to get that respect’
World.content:
Television actor Rajiv Kuumar has been earning praise for his portrayal of Sita’s father King Janaka in Ramayana Part 1. Rajiv now hopes the Nitesh Tiwari directorial will open more doors for him in the film and OTT space. In an exclusive interview with SCREEN, the actor opens up about his experience of working on Ramayana. He also shares his views on the controversies surrounding the film.

During the interview, Rajiv Kuumar spoke about how he bagged the role of Sita’s father King Janaka in Ramayana. He said, “Mukesh Chhabra’s casting agency had shown Niteshji an old audition of mine, and I was cast based on that. So, technically, I didn’t even audition for this film. It was like a gift from God. When I was cast, I didn’t know it was going to be such a big film. Usually, when you see a huge star cast, you expect the film to be mounted on a grand scale. But you associate that level of grandeur with Sanjay Leela Bhansali’s films. I wasn’t expecting such lavish sets and a production of this scale. Most of the scenes I shot involved minimal VFX and were filmed on actual sets. I didn’t know this was India’s biggest-budget film.”



Also Read: ‘Sita is not weak, not dependent only on Ram’: Indira Krishnan defends Sai Pallavi’s Ramayana portrayal

View this post on Instagram A post shared by rajivkuumar (@rajivkuumaractor)

Talking about the reactions to his role in Ramayana, Rajiv shared, “I had only two scenes in the film. It’s a very small part, but a very important one. I was not expecting that people would call me, but I have been getting messages on social media. People are calling me, sending pictures, and congratulating me. Everyone’s response is good. I personally believe that our industry needs a lot of successful films. Only then does the producer have faith that he can make a better film. If he makes a good film, then thousands of people will get jobs. If the film flops, the producer will give up, and that’s very bad for our industry. I always believe that the producer should make money.”

“Professionally, the level at which I move in the industry, I always have the struggle to survive. But after this, I might get a certain quality of work, including more OTT and more films. I don’t want my financial conditions to push me towards TV again. After this film, I hope I get that respect; it has already started. I am from NSD, batch of 1997. Rajpal Yadav was my batchmate. As soon as he came into the industry, he got such a great role in Jungle. He clicked with audiences and became a star. Nawazuddin was my senior; he got his due in 2008. So maybe I am yet to get my due,” he added.

Rajiv Kuumar on working with Sai Pallavi and Ranbir Kapoor in Ramayana

Sharing screen space with Sai Pallavi and Ranbir Kapoor was quite an experience for Rajiv Kuumar. “It was a wonderful experience. Sai came over to introduce herself. While we were shooting the wedding sequence, she approached me and asked if I was playing her father. She said she had seen me earlier and thought I would be playing her on-screen father. I also had scenes with Ranbir. He is very good-natured and shared a great rapport with the actors playing his brothers. Ranbir, Addinath and Ravie would talk to each other as though they had known each other for years. Even Arun and Indiraji shared a close bond with the rest of the cast, making them look like a close-knit family. It didn’t feel like Ranbir was such a big star.”



Rajiv Kuumar on Ramayana controversies

While Ramayana Part 1 has emerged as a success, it has also drawn criticism for allegedly glorifying Ravana and portraying Sita as a warrior. Sharing his views on the same, Rajiv Kummar said, “Valmiki has written Ramayana in Sanskrit, and then there have been different versions of it. I met a friend recently who is from Mithila. She said that they strongly believed that if Sita’s father told her about the Shiv Dhanush and how it can be lifted, then they must have even taught her about weapons and the art of war. It is like making a controversy out of nothing. They must have done a lot of research and paid a lot of attention to these things. They must have gotten a reference from somewhere that Mata Sita used to use weapons.”



Talking about Ravana’s glorification, Rajiv added, “I think it’s very unfair to criticise a film by just seeing one part. The bigger you make the villain, the bigger your hero will look. And this was shown in the movie. Many people used to say that Ravana was very intelligent and learned. Now, when his learning is glorified, it’s very important. If we look at it character-wise, Ram’s character has a lot of grandeur. And when the second part starts, and he faces that great villain, he looks very beautiful.”

World.title: After Jaipur Polo Grounds takeover, Delhi’s Polo final finds a new home
World.content:
Just below the Delhi Cantonment Metro station, a signboard points towards the Delhi War Cemetery. Take that road, cross the railway line, and it leads to the Army Polo

and Riding Centre (APRC) at Parade Square, near Naraina and Todapur. On Sunday afternoon, the approach was thick with cars and spectators arriving for the Cavalry Gold Cup final.

Parking was plentiful, visitors kept coming, and the grounds had the air of a festival about to begin. Yet for many of those walking in, the day carried a quieter feeling too, one of looking back.

For years, the final was played at the Jaipur Polo Grounds in Lutyens’ Delhi, a venue that had become inseparable from the tournament itself. This year, with the grounds taken over by the Central government, the match moved here. “We all grew up with the Jaipur ground, so there is a deep attachment to it,” a club member said. “But there is also relief that the tournament carries on at all.”

World.title: Govt moves to overhaul ‘weak’ audit system
World.content:
• FBR task force flags weaknesses in existing review framework

• Cabinet approves SECP Amendment Bill 2026 after consultation

• Proposed legislation aims to strengthen independent audit oversight

ISLAMABAD: The government has decided to overhaul the country’s ent­ire audit system after the Prime Min­ister’s Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) Task Force described the existing framework as weak, saying it discourages local and foreign investm­ent and limits access to capital markets.

Documents seen by Dawn suggest the government plans to introduce legislative amendments in parliament to reform the existing audit system.

The proposed amendments will be introduced in the light of recommendations made by the Prime Minister’s FBR Task Force, which has already raised serious concerns over weaknesses in the existing audit framework, according to the document.

In this regard, the government will introduce legislation, including the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) (Amendment) Bill, 2026. A similar bill was passed by the National Assembly in 2021 after scrutiny and recommendations by the NA Standing Committee on Finance. However, it was withdrawn from the Senate in 2022 for resubmission. The federal cabinet has now approved the proposed bill again after extensive consultations and reviews by three ministerial-level committees.

The task force has also recommended amendments to the Audit Oversight Board (AOB) law to improve tax collection.

The process of reforming the AOB was already underway, but market-related concerns continued to highlight weaknesses in audits. Pakistan’s existing AOB law did not comply with international standards, an official briefing document said.

“Investors and lenders rely on audited accounts, but weak audits discourage local and foreign investment and access to capital markets.

“The International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the securities market standard-setter, declared Pakistan non-compliant with independent audit oversight. The European Union (EU) also withdrew Pakistan’s equivalence status for independent audit oversight,” it added.

The report cited Unity Foods and SE Foods as examples of companies affected by weak audits and prospectus disclosures. It also highlighted concerns over Hascol’s audited accounts.

The report said developed and developing countries had amended their laws and shifted from self-regulatory oversight by accountancy bodies to independent audit oversight. Even smaller jurisdictions, including Sri Lanka, Mauritius and Botswana, are compliant members of the International Forum of Independent Audit Regulators (IFIAR), it added.

It has been learnt that the proposed system will end the dominance of private auditors.

The document said the federal cabinet had approved the draft legislation following a comprehensive review by the FBR Task Force, IFIAR, SECP and AOB, along with extensive consultations with stakeholders. The proposed legislation is expected to strengthen Pakistan’s international recognition and establish an effective audit oversight system.

The salient features of the SECP Amendment Bill, 2026, are as follows:

The independence of the nominating committee responsible for appointing AOB board members will be strengthened by including the FBR chairman in place of the president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Pakistan (ICAP).

AOB board members will not be permitted to have any association with audit firms.

The AOB board will be responsible for policy matters, while management, operations and adjudication will be handled in line with governance principles and the board’s regulatory functions.

The AOB will conduct regular, risk-based inspections of auditors of Public Interest Companies (PICs) to assess compliance with professional auditing standards.

Accountancy bodies will continue to conduct regular inspections and Quality Control Reviews (QCRs) of non-PIC audits under the oversight of the AOB.

The AOB will directly investigate complaints and references from the SECP, State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and FBR after approval by its board or a designated committee.

Standard action will be taken against individuals who refuse to provide required information, while the AOB will also be empowered to file complaints concerning criminal offences involving falsification.

World.title: PM to attend ECO moot in Iran after Russia trip
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will undertake his first official three-day visit to Rus­sia from Nov 30, aiming to strengthen bilateral ties and secure energy and inve­stment agreements bef­ore travelling to Iran for the 18th Economic Coo­peration Organisation (ECO) Summit on Dec 3 and 4.

During his meeting with Russian President Vladi­mir Putin, discussions are expected to focus on ene­rgy cooperation, defence, trade, regional security and investment, a source in the Prime Minister’s Office told Dawn.

The revival of Pakistan Steel Mills, established with Russian assistance, is also likely to feature prominently, alongside potential Russian investment in Pakistan’s oil and gas sectors.

The two countries are likely to examine possibilities for Russian cooperation in restoring the industrial facility, alongside broader initiatives aimed at supporting Pakistan’s industrial development.

Following the Russia visit, Prime Minister Shehbaz will represent Pakistan at the ECO summit in Tehran, where leaders of 10 member states will discuss regional trade, connectivity, energy, tran-sportation, investment and industrial cooperation.

The summit comes ahead of Pakistan assuming the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27.

World.title: Rice exports up by 0.35m tonnes in four months
World.content:
LAHORE: Pakistan’s total rice exports surged by 353,000 tonnes to reach 1,351,000 tonnes during the first four months (July-October) of the current fiscal year 2026-27.

The exports were propelled by a massive 62pc jump in Basmati shipments that defied severe maritime disruptions across the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, and the broader Middle East.

According to trade figures for the July-Oct 2026 period, Basmati exports climbed by 116,000 tonnes compared to the corresponding period last year to stand at 301,000 tonnes. Meanwhile, non-Basmati shipments expanded by 140,000 tonnes year-on-year to reach 1,049,000 tonnes.

The remarkable expansion in Basmati export volume came despite heightened geopolitical tensions involving Iran, shipping route diversions, skyrocketing ocean freight charges, and elevated marine insurance premiums.

Market analysts attribute the resilience of the premium grain segment to a combination of domestic policy support and strong agricultural fundamentals. Specifically, the extension of the Drawback of Local Taxes and Levies (DLTL) scheme through September, substantial carryover stocks, an expanded cultivation area, double-cropping in select regions, higher per-acre yields, and favourable weather conditions combined and culminated in a bumper Basmati harvest.

In the coarse grain segment, Pakistani exporters managed to post a 16pc increase in non-Basmati shipments despite fierce price competition from heavily subsidised Indian rice as well as aggressive offers from Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Myanmar.

The country-wise trade data for October 2026 shows that the Philippines emerged as the single largest buyer of Pakistani rice during the month with imports of 87,478 tonnes, followed by Tanzania at 43,747 tonnes and Kenya at 33,078 tonnes. Other major destinations during October included the United Arab Emirates with 25,305 tonnes, the European Union with 21,200 tonnes, Central Asia with 16,400 tonnes, China with 11,949 tonnes, and Saudi Arabia with 7,655 tonnes.

World.title: Any talks with India on terrorism must be 'evidence-based', says Musadik Malik
World.content:
Federal minister Musadik Malik said on Sunday that any dialogue between Pakistan and India on terrorism must be “based on evidence”.

Malik is in New Delhi on a three-day trip to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, making him the first Pakistani minister to visit the neighbour since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended an SCO meeting in May 2023.

Pakistan has repeatedly offered to hold talks with India to resolve outstanding disputes, including the water issue.

In video clips shared by India’s ANI news agency on Sunday, Malik responded to queries from Indian media and stressed that he had repeatedly presented Pakistan’s stance before the reporters.

“I am giving you a stable response that whenever discussions take place, they will be based on evidence, and they will certainly happen,” he affirmed, saying if New Delhi wanted a “lasting solution”.

“You must also have some issues, [though] our issues are much greater than yours, and we also need a lot of evidence […] Whenever dialogue takes place, it will be based on evidence,” the climate change minister reiterated.

Malik said Pakistan had repeatedly stated that evidence relating to terrorism could be presented through both bilateral and multilateral forums. “You may bring evidence; we also have evidence that we want to present,” he added.

India’s foreign minister had said in June 2024 that his country wanted to “find a solution to the issue of years-old cross-border terrorism” with Pakistan. However, a military conflict between the neighbours last year has intensified tensions and escalatory rhetoric from India.

In May 2025, a four-day confrontation between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan.

Islamabad had strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation .

In another clip, Malik noted that India had invited a representative from Pakistan to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a multilateral event.

“I am your guest. You invited me to a specific forum; I am present before you. I answered all those questions you asked about this forum,” the minister said, remarking that he had conveyed the “voice of my heart” to the people across the region through the forum.

Malik stated, “You are today asking me questions for which you did not invite me. When you invite me for that question, I will appear. However, you first ought to invite me and say ‘we want to speak bilaterally with you’.”

‘Will speak on IWT when invited to do so’

The minister was also asked about his remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), but said he would comment on the matter when invited to do so.

“You have currently invited me to speak on topics about which I have already spoken, that when temperatures rise, climate is destroyed, Glofs happen. Glofs and glaciers are blind, they do not know whether to fall on the right or the left,” he said, highlighting the shared threat climate change poses to both neighbours.

He further said, “You have called me for culture and civilisation [discussions]. I am your guest, you are my host […] You have asked me the same question a 100 times and I have responded to it a 100 times.”

In his remarks at the SCO forum on Saturday, Malik had termed climate change an “enemy” of civilisations and pointed out its impact on South Asian countries that bore the brunt of climate destruction.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between Pakistan and India, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year after the Pahalgam attack, which was followed by the four-day military conflict between the two sides.

Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that New Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

Backing Islamabad’s stance, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) on Aug 31 ordered New Delhi to uphold the IWT, declaring that the treaty remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

The IWT, brokered by the World Bank in 1960, allocates the three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — largely to Pakistan, and the three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India.

The treaty has survived wars, crises, and political tensions for more than six decades and is considered a rare example of durable water-sharing cooperation between the two neighbours.

World.title: Varma century in vain as Pakistan Shaheens down India A in Asia Cup Rising Stars clash
World.content:
Pakistan Shaheens overcame a late challenge from Tilak Varma to beat India A by 48 runs in their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha on Sunday, defending a total of 313 after bowling out their opponents with five balls to spare.

Skipper Varma struck a century before becoming the last man dismissed for 100 off 149 balls, while Shahbaz Ahmed made 56 in a seventh-wicket stand that briefly revived India’s hopes.

But Pakistan’s bowlers held their nerve in the closing overs, with Hasan Nawaz claiming three wickets and Ali Raza taking three for 56.

India’s chase had begun to unravel after an explosive start from Abhishek Sharma. The left-hander made 70 off just 42 balls, hitting six fours and six sixes, but his dismissal at 93-3 in the 16th over left the visitors with considerable ground to make up.

Pakistan’s spinners then tightened their grip. Sufyan Moqim bowled Kumar Kushagra for two before Hasan removed Rinku Singh and Suryansh Shedge, leaving India struggling at 129-6 in the 26th over.

Varma, who had struggled to find the boundary during the middle overs, found support in Shahbaz.

The pair added 112 runs for the seventh wicket, taking the score to 241 before Raza broke the stand by having Shahbaz caught by Hasan for 56 off 49 balls.

Raza then bowled Vipraj Nigam for a duck, while Imran Randhawa dismissed Harshit Rana to leave India nine down.

Varma reached his second century of the tournament, but the milestone offered little consolation as Ahmed Daniyal had him caught by wicket-keeper Rohail Nazir in the 50th over to seal Pakistan’s victory.

Controversial toss

Earlier, Pakistan had posted 313 after winning a dramatic toss and electing to bat on a slightly dry surface.

The toss decision was initially called incorrectly by the match referee, who announced tails after Varma flipped the coin on Pakistan skipper Abdul Samad’s call of heads.

Samad pointed out the error and the officials corrected the decision in Pakistan’s favour. The captains did not shake hands, continuing the protocol observed in recent encounters between the sides.

Pakistan’s openers Shamyl Hussain and Maaz Sadaqat gave their side a flying start, putting on 66 for the first wicket. Shamyl made 33 off 23 balls before Ayush Badoni had him caught by Harshit Rana at short third. Rana then trapped Rohail leg-before for a duck, with Pakistan on 67-2.

The exchanges between Rana and the Pakistan batters had added an edge to the powerplay, with the Indian fast bowler involved in heated verbal exchanges and giving Shamyl an animated send-off.

Maaz and Hasan rebuilt the innings, with the former scoring 59 off 63 balls for his second successive half-century.

Hasan went on to make 79 off 82 deliveries, while Farhan Yousaf’s 56 off 48 balls and Imran’s quickfire 23 helped Pakistan push past 300, which was proven enough for the side at the end.

World.title: Independent media not as 'independent' as it could be: Mehdi Hasan
World.content:
• US journalist says news gatekeeping has been outsourced to Silicon Valley

• Says every journalist ‘needs to be’ a content creator now

DOHA: Journalism has undergone a major transformation since the advent of social media and independent news platforms, bringing both opportunities and challenges. These changes were the focus of a talk titled The New Gatekeepers by British-American journalist Mehdi Hasan at the Doha Film Festival.

Drawing on his experience at mainstream outlets including the BBC, CNN, Al Jazeera, Sky News and MSNBC, Hasan discussed the changing media landscape and his move towards independent journalism through his own media company, Zeteo, after his MSNBC show was cancelled.

Speaking about news gatekeepers, he said that historically only a handful of people could communicate with mass audiences because billionaires, corporations and governments controlled the technology and resources needed to spread information. That has now changed.

“It’s good that we have democratised access to the news. Today anyone in this room can go out with a microphone, camera and a WiFi connection and potentially reach more people than a BBC, CNN or an Al Jazeera journalist,” he said.

However, Mr Hasan stressed he was not opposed to gatekeeping itself, arguing that journalism still needed fact-checking and professional standards. “I am still a journalist, not a YouTuber or content creator. I am still on YouTube, but I do fact-check. The problem with the old gatekeepers was not the gates. It was that they were opening the gates to the powerful and shutting them to the powerless.”

Citing a Reuters Institute survey, he noted that, for the first time, more people were getting their news from social media than from news websites and apps. “We are already in a brave new world,” he remarked.

But the democratisation of information had not eliminated gatekeeping; instead, it had transferred much of that power to Silicon Valley, where technology executives such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg exercise considerable influence.

Hasan described it as “insane” that platforms controlled by Zuckerberg, including WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook and Threads, were used by a substantial proportion of the world’s population, with many relying on them for news.

He warned that algorithms could undermine the news business, as had already happened to numerous publishers.

Asked whether independent media was truly independent, Hasan acknowledged that it was not as independent as it could be. Although such outlets were often free from corporate, government or billionaire ownership and relied on subscribers rather than advertising, they faced another pressure: “audience capture”.

“If you are fully funded by your subscribers, then you would tell them what they want to hear,” he said.

He cited his own experience at Zeteo, where subscribers cancelled their subscriptions during the 2024 US election for diametrically opposed reasons, illustrating the difficulties of maintaining an independent editorial space.

On whether every journalist now had to become a content creator, Mr Hasan said the two roles had increasingly overlapped. “I think every journalist does have to be a content creator now, which is a double-edged sword. But I don’t think every content creator or YouTuber is a journalist.”

Addressing the crisis of trust in information, he argued that journalism itself was not responsible for the decline in public confidence. “I don’t think journalism is inherently bad, evil or has lost trust. I think institutions, people and journalistic practices have lost trust. People are craving journalism, facts, evidence, information and news about the world,” he said.

Mr Hasan also rejected the idea that corporate media was dead, arguing that established organisations remained essential because independent outlets lacked the resources and expertise for large-scale news gathering, foreign coverage and extensive investigative reporting.

He said he could not undertake the kind of investigative journalism produced by The New York Times due to lack of resources. However, he said, mainstream media had failed audiences in several areas, creating demand for alternative sources of information.

Agenda, objectivity

On editorial agendas and objectivity, Mr Hasan admitted that he had his own agenda, arguing that no media organisation was entirely neutral. “I don’t believe that there is any neutral media outlet, but my position is that journalists are allowed to have opinions as long as they are based on facts. I believe in objectivity. Neutrality and objectivity are not the same. I don’t believe you should be neutral between good and evil.”

He identified another major challenge for independent journalism: audiences’ reluctance to pay for news. Without subscriptions or paywalls, he argued, it was difficult to fund the reporting and information gathering needed to sustain quality journalism.

World.title: ‘Global food import bill up 1.9pc in 2026’
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Global expenditure on food imports is expected to increase moderately in 2026, with the global food import bill projected to reach $2,267 billion, up 1.9 per cent from the revised estimate of $2,224.8 billion, according to a new United Nations report.

According to the Food Outlook published by the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), import bills are expected to rise for most food groups in 2026, led by animal products and the oil seed complex, while cereals are also projected to record an increase.

Prospects for the remainder of 2026 and 2027 remain subject to several unce­rtainties, including firming prices of some food commodities, higher energy costs, weather conditions and financing constraints faced by some importing cou­ntries. Since mid-year, international prices of cereals and sugar have risen after remaining lower earlier in the year, while vegetable oil prices remained firm.

FAO warns energy costs and supply disruptions may raise bills in 2027

Higher energy prices have raised freight costs, while renewed disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could restrict fertiliser supplies, affecting crop yields in 2027, despite fertiliser prices easing from their April peak.

The El Nino phenomenon, which is now established and strengthening, has added to the uncertainty, with its effects likely to vary across regions and crops.

FAO has urged timely financial support and expanded funding for food and fertiliser imports, warning that rising commodity prices and delays in assistance could increase pressure on vulnerable importing countries in 2027.

In most years of rising import bills over the past decade, high-income countries (HICs) accounted for between half and nearly all of the increase, including 79pc in 2025. However, their share of the increase in 2026 is projected at just 13pc, while upper-middle-income countries (UMICs) are expected to account for about two-thirds, the report says.

Import bills for cereals, the main staple foods, and oil seeds are rising for the first time in four years, while expenditure on vegetable oil imports continues to increase. The cereal import bill is expected to rise by 3pc, or $8.9bn, mainly reflecting a partial recovery in purchases by some UMICs following steep cuts in 2025.

In the oil seed complex, strong demand from processors and firm international prices are pushing import bills higher across both product groups.

The import bill for oil seeds and oleaginous fruits is projected to increase by 9.9pc, or $12.7bn, with most of the rise concentrated in middle-income economies. UMICs are expected to account for about 70pc of the increase, while lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) will contribute much of the remainder. Ani­mal products and other food items are also making substantial contributions to the increase in the global import bill.

In contrast, the import baskets of low- and middle-income countries are more heavily weighted towards staple foods. Their combined food import bill is projected to increase by 4.9pc, or $36.5bn, in 2026, led by oil seeds and cereals.

Most of this increase is expected to be concentrated in UMICs, whose import bill is projected to rise by 5.1pc, or $28.3bn, largely driven by the same food groups.

The food import bill of LMICs is expected to increase by 3.1pc, or $5.3bn, mainly due to higher spending on vegetable oils and oilseeds, while their import bills for cereals and sugar are projected to decline.
