World.title: When Indigenous peoples survive, the rest of us do too
World.content:
We cannot control when El Niño arrives, but we can control how much of our natural defense — forests, watersheds, water, rivers — we destroy before it does

“Neighbors” is Rappler People section’s space for community and human interest stories told in a personal way.

As the Philippines showcased its cultural heritage on the ASEAN stage, we celebrated Indigenous traditions before the world, even as the communities keeping them alive continue to struggle to defend their ancestral lands at home.

Across the country, Indigenous Peoples have been sounding a warning we have been slow to hear.

“Ang proyektong iyan ay isang dambuhalang linta na sisipsipin lahat ng yaman ng bundok. Hindi naman po pansarili ang aming ipinaglalaban.” (That project is a giant leech that will suck the mountain dry of its riches. What we are fighting for is not for ourselves alone.)

These were the words of an Aeta elder opposing the proposed Pax Silica development in Tarlac.

In General Nakar, Quezon, a Dumagat mother who marched 150 kilometers against the Kaliwa Dam described her burden:

“Tuwing naglalakad po kami, tuwing naiisip ko ang gagawin sa amin at mangyayari sa amin at sa susunod na henerasyon, halos ako po ay naiiyak sa daan dahil pakiramdam ko pasan ko ang Sierra Madre.” (Every time we walk, when I think about what will happen to us and to the generations after us, I almost cry because I feel as though I am carrying the Sierra Madre on my shoulders.)

Communities and environmental groups warn that the dam threatens the biodiversity of the Sierra Madre.

A giant leech draining a mountain. A Dumagat mother carrying the Sierra Madre on her shoulders. Different communities, different threats, but the same warning: what is being lost in the name of progress does not belong to them alone.

Ancestral lands in development’s path

For generations, Indigenous communities have practiced a resilience that reminds us survival depends not only on what we take from the Earth, but on what we leave behind.

I have never forgotten a fisherman I met in an Indigenous community. He carried a pouch barely larger than a clutch bag. When I asked why he didn’t bring something bigger, he answered: “That is enough for one day. Tomorrow is another day. The river provides what is needed. To take more is to take from someone else.”

In that tiny pouch lived a philosophy deeper than many policy papers: enough is enough.

Even as we are urged to conserve water and prepare for climate extremes, we continue to sacrifice the forests and watersheds that sustain our rivers and shield us from drought and floods. We cannot control when El Niño arrives, but we can control how much of our natural defense we destroy before it does. Preparedness begins long before reservoirs fall and crops wither. It begins with what we choose to protect.

In Capas, Tarlac, a proposed technology hub associated with Pax Silica promises investment and jobs, while Aeta communities fear displacement and threats to their ancestral lands and water sources.

The contrast is striking: a people rooted in the land for generations confronting an industry promising the technological future. Beneath it lies an older question: What is land worth?

To most of us, land is property, measured in titles and market values. Yet across Indigenous communities I’ve encountered, I hear the same truth: Ang lupa ay buhay.

The land is life. It is where ancestors are buried and children are born. Rivers hold stories. Mountains mark histories. Forests are pharmacies, kitchens, classrooms, and places of worship.

Protecting forests is protecting waters

I have witnessed this through my work with Bantay Gubat rangers, many of whom are Dumagat. They risk their lives patrolling the Ipo Watershed against illegal logging, fires, and other threats, protecting a vital water source for millions in Metro Manila.

There, the connection between their survival and ours becomes tangible: in protecting their ancestral forests, they are also protecting the water that flows into our homes.

And they are hardly alone. On Sibuyan Island, the Sibuyan Mangyan Tagabukid and fellow residents have resisted nickel mining. In 2023, residents formed a human barricade against trucks carrying nickel ore to protect the island’s ecosystems.

In Boracay, behind the powdery white sand and postcard-perfect resorts lies another story: the Ati have faced displacement and the loss of traditional livelihoods as tourism and development transformed their ancestral lands.

In Bugsuk, Palawan, Molbog and Pala’wan communities have fought for ancestral lands and fishing waters threatened by private commercial interests, including pearl farming — a struggle Indigenous advocates call “blood pearls.”

In Kalinga, the historic resistance of the Kalinga and Bontok peoples to the Chico River Dam lives on, as members of the Balatoc community resist mining and communities along the Chico River raise concerns over hydropower projects threatening their ancestral lands and livelihoods.

The project changes — a technology hub, a dam, a mine, a resort. The generation changes. The landscape changes. But the question remains: Who gets to decide what Indigenous land and water are worth?

Economies that restore, not exhaust

Progress need not come at the expense of preservation. We can build economies that restore rather than exhaust, and livelihoods that sustain rather than displace. True progress is measured not only by what we gain, but by what we preserve.

The answer matters far beyond these communities. An estimated 85% of the Philippines’ Key Biodiversity Areas lie within ancestral domains, yet these lands remain threatened by mining, logging, infrastructure, and other development projects.

Too often, we reduce the living world to what it can produce: a forest becomes timber, a mountain becomes minerals, a river becomes cubic meters of water, a coastline becomes real estate. But not everything of value can be priced. In safeguarding the land, we safeguard ourselves.

Indigenous Peoples’ rights need no justification beyond the fact that they are rights. Yet their survival is bound to our own. Their struggles may unfold far from our homes, but what they protect sustains us. What they lose, we eventually lose too.

If we wish to honor Indigenous cultures before the world, perhaps we should begin by listening to their voices at home — to both the cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor, as Laudato Si’ urges us.

Ang lupa ay buhay. The land is life. And without it, none of us survives. – Rappler.com

Sarah Bautista-Abaño is an environmental and human rights advocate who has worked closely with Indigenous communities on ancestral land rights, environmental protection, and community empowerment. A trained wildlife ranger, she has served alongside Indigenous forest guardians protecting critical watersheds and forests. She is also a wife, mother of three daughters, and avid mountaineer.

World.title: [Newspoint] Drifting away
World.content:
It does manage to put live, talking people on the stand. But have they got something, anything, to disprove, or at least cast a doubt on, the impeachment charge that Vice President Sara Duterte has unexplained wealth?

The defense has a fundamental problem: it has no witnesses. And that possibly is the reason it is drifting away.

It does manage to put live, talking people on the stand. But have they got something, anything, to disprove, or at least cast a doubt on, the impeachment charge that Vice President Sara Duterte has unexplained wealth?

Not even those among them who keep, or have access to, documents and records that may be of help to Duterte admit, on cross examination, that they have not so much as laid eyes on any such exculpatory evidence. No wonder their testimonies go around and around. But trust pro-Duterte senator-judges to exploit the situation by way of an “intervention” — that’s the privilege senator-judges have of inserting themselves at just about any time during the hearings to put questions to the witness on the stand or parties to the trial or simply to speak their minds as they please.

The last hearing before the impeachment court took a break last week for the ASEAN meeting had provided an occasion for one of the more obvious and strained of those interventions. On the stand was a friend of Manases Carpio’s. Carpio figures at the trial being Sara Duterte’s husband, as co-owner with her of whatever wealth credited to her, explained or unexplained, and vice versa.

I’m still trying to explain to myself how a one-time, quarter-of-a-million-peso personal expense by Carpio on sneakers to give away could be fair subject of testimony. Well, I can only guess that it is to do with the singular nature of the trial, one conducted not by professional judges but by senators, making it as much a political as a judicial process.

In any case, the defense promoted Carpio’s gesture as a virtue. The prosecution, on the other hand, attacked it from the perspective of the constitutional provision admonishing public officials and their families to live simple lifestyles, an admonishment that ought to vibrate with singular resonance in a lopsided society like ours.

Senator-judge Pia Cayetano herself sounded incredulous and expressed herself with the passion she is known to bring to any public role she takes on, although this time, sans tears. Actually, her impassioned yet dry performance rather suited the preachy point she was making: How could anyone — like me — have missed Manases Carpio’s great benefaction!

The problem was this: Not only was the size of the largesse scandalous, the bestowal seemed misplaced — it didn’t really benefit the truly needy, let alone the desperate poor, thus constituting such precise ostentatious display of wealth as the Constitution disallows and also making Carpio’s friend Chadrin Parian witness to patronage, in fact a beneficiary of it, by his own admission.

If anything, Pia Cayetano has been consistent through the trial — consistent, that is, in her support for the impeached. To be sure, she has her counterparts on the court, not surprising, really, in proceedings where politicking cannot be avoided, as precisely the case with an impeachment trial.

Cayetano’s politicking can be a trifle too tawdry, though. In defense of Carpio, she did not stop at extolling his patronage; she even gave two popular and current examples for good measure. But then, again, the problem was that one was a false example, and the other even tended to show precisely how patronage could trump a potentially fair and virtuous arrangement.

Our own Alex Eala, the world-tennis phenomenon, owed no patron, hadn’t needed one. She got to where she is much on her own — her own talent, her own determination, her own initiative, her own hard work, her own sweat and tears. On the other hand, pole-vaulter EJ Obiena seems to me just the type to find use for a patron like Carpio.

Obiena was a state-accredited athlete. That assured him the money and other things he needed to fulfill his promise. Just as he began to rise to world class, the Philippine Sports Commission, the agency in charge of him, suspected him of fund misuse and suspended his entitlements. But before he could clear himself, the Philippine Olympic Committee, a nongovernmental organization running on private sponsorships and subsidies, took over as his patron — not unlike an institutional Manases Carpio.

In a further attempt to show that nothing was wrong with Carpio’s quarter-of-a-million-peso gesture, Cayetano cited her own family’s generosity toward athletes. While I’m prepared to give her and her family the benefit of the doubt, I find the circumstances in Carpio’s case simply too scandalous for him to deserve any excuses.

All that said, I realize that the trial has been going off-course and that I, for one, have allowed myself to be carried along. My own excuse is that I just cannot leave alone anything thrown in the air for all to hear that needs straightening out. It’s a professional compulsion. – Rappler.com

World.title: ABS-CBN saw the future, GMA made the money, now both must change
World.content:
Former arch-rivals are now business partners. Open their latest financial report cards for the first nine months of 2026, you will see why.

If you turned on your television on a Sunday night in September 2026 and flipped to GMA-7, you would have seen something once unthinkable: Vice Ganda’s irreverent talk show, Gandang Gabi Vice, was airing on GMA’s main channel.

For decades, ABS-CBN (Kapamilya) and GMA Network (Kapuso) fought a bitter war over ratings and stars. Yet by late 2026, Gandang Gabi Vice shared GMA’s airwaves with It’s Showtime and a joint season of Pinoy Big Brother, while Coco Martin’s action series Sigabo and Face to Face with Ate Koring anchored rival TV5.

Former arch-rivals are now business partners. Open their latest financial report cards for the first nine months of 2026, you will see why.

Even with its nationwide congressional franchise and top TV ratings, GMA Network lost P77.37 million in the third quarter (July to September) alone. That rare loss wiped out almost everything it earned earlier in the year, dragging its nine-month profit down by 98% to P32.85 million, down from P2.07 billion in 2025. Meanwhile, franchise-less ABS-CBN saw its nine-month loss widen to P2.96 billion, pushing its overall net worth into down to negative P2.01 billion.

How did we get here? Neither company was blind to the internet. Both saw smartphones and streaming coming long before Congress shut down ABS-CBN’s Channel 2 in 2020. But neither boardroom had a crystal ball. Each made bets that looked smart at the time, only to find out in 2026 that winning the audience is no longer the same as winning the business.

ABS-CBN built the kitchen early, then lost the dining room

To understand how ABS-CBN survived losing its broadcast license in 2020, picture a Michelin-star chef who spent years building a modern kitchen, only to have the main restaurant torn down halfway through renovations.

Long before Congress shut down Channel 2, ABS-CBN’s executives saw people changing how they watched TV. Something along the same line as a chef noticing diners changing how they ate. Instead of waiting for dinner to be served at a fixed hour in a single living-room dining hall, Filipinos were starting to order takeout on their phones, and watching shows on smartphones and streaming apps anytime and anywhere. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

Between 2015 and 2019, ABS-CBN poured money into building a world-class kitchen. In Bulacan, it secured government approval from the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) in 2016 and 2018 to develop Horizon IT Park. These were soundproof, climate-controlled, Hollywood-style indoor soundstages designed to cook up shows that met international streaming standards long before Netflix became a daily habit in Manila. In its 2018 annual report, management declared that that viewers wanted content “anytime, anywhere, on any device, in any medium.” They launched its own delivery app, iWant—essentially a local Netflix where fans could stream shows directly over the internet without needing a TV antenna—alongside overseas service TFC.tv. Behind the scenes, a unit called The Big Dipper worked around the clock digitizing 60 years of classic recipes—old movies and teleseryes—while data-analytics arm Probabilistic Insights studied what online customers liked to order.

At the same time, ABS-CBN built a fleet of delivery vans through Sky Cable. It sold cable TV, SkyDirect satellite dishes, and Sky Fiber home internet. The logic was simple: walk-in traffic at a free restaurant rises and falls with the economy, so monthly internet and cable subscriptions from households would give the chef a steady safety net. By 2019, that cable and broadband segment was bringing in P9.79 billion a year and turning a modest profit.

ABS-CBN planned to transition slowly over 10 years, using the P20 billion or more it earned each year from commercials in its massive free TV dining room to pay off the bank loans used to build its new kitchen.

Then came May 5 and July 10, 2020. Regulators ordered Channel 2 off the air and Congress killed its franchise. The chef didn’t just lose a permit, the entire main restaurant building was boarded up overnight. Millions of walk-in diners vanished instantly, along with the TV ads they brought in. Annual revenue crashed in half, from P42.84 billion in 2019 down to P21.42 billion in 2020, and P15.85 billion by 2025.

As ABS-CBN president Carlo Katigbak told stockholders during their August 2026 annual meeting: “These are not normal times for your company. We have been through one crisis after another, most of them existential in nature… It is a chance to decide whether ‘In the Service of the Filipino’ was just a compelling slogan that served us well in good times, or if it is the genuine reason for our existence, proven because we embraced it in impossible times.”

With no restaurant building of its own, the chef did the only thing possible: shut down side businesses like the KidZania Manila theme park, slashed annual spending on physical equipment by 90%. It kept cooking in the kitchen, and started renting stalls inside other people’s food courts. ABS-CBN supplied signature dishes to former rivals like GMA, TV5, and A2Z, streaming daily on YouTube (Kapamilya Online Live, which grew to 54.8 million subscribers and 58.7 billion views by early 2026), licensing dramas to Netflix, Prime Video, and Viu, and touring global acts like P-pop group BINI.

Play Video

On an operating level, that early bet on the kitchen worked. In the first nine months of 2026, ABS-CBN’s content business brought in P8.96 billion. That’s over 85% of the entire company’s revenue. Without one-time 2025 election ads, and core content sales actually grew 6%, while recurring operating cash earnings rose 17%.

Why the chef is still underwater

If its shows are still selling, why is ABS-CBN still losing billions? Because while the kitchen is busy, the chef is still paying off old mortgages on closed buildings and a bleeding delivery arm. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

First is Sky Cable. Once meant to be ABS-CBN’s safety net, Sky Cable suffered when regulators shut down SkyDirect in June 2020. Families also ditched cable TV for pure fiber internet from PLDT, Globe, and Converge. After a planned P6.75-billion sale of Sky Cable to PLDT fell apart in February 2024, ABS-CBN was stuck with a shrinking unit that forced billions of pesos in paper write-downs on old cables and equipment. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, Sky Cable’s revenue fell another 41% to P1.55 billion. it lost P923 million, plus P190 million to dismantle old copper lines as it migrated subscribers onto Converge ICT’s fiber network.

Second is old debt. Before 2020, ABS-CBN and Sky Cable borrowed billions to build studios, broadcast towers, and cable lines. Losing its broadcast license broke the safety rules attached to ABS-CBN’s bank loans with BPI and UnionBank, turning roughly P8.5 billion in parent debt into bills due right away. Across the whole group, ABS-CBN carries almost P12 billion in loans. Paying interest alone drained P751 million in the first nine months of 2026, eating up the cash its shows earned.

Third is the tough math of online video. On its own TV channel, a network sells ads and keeps all the money. On YouTube, ad money gets split with the platform, while paying stars and filming daily dramas remains expensive. High production costs left the segment with a net loss of P2.03 billion over nine months.

That financial strain is why ABS-CBN announced an urgent P6-billion rescue deal in August 2026. Private investment firm I&C Holdings Corp. put in P3.5 billion, alongside P2.2 billion from three Lopez family holding companies, and P300 million from Lopez, Inc. to pay down overdue bills and bank loans. As ABS-CBN chairman Mark Lopez put it when announcing the deal: “It tells us there are people who continue to believe in the Company and in our mission of being In the Service of the Filipino.”

GMA stayed focused and hit a goldmine

GMA Network’s story is very different. GMA was not blind to the internet either. It launched GMA New Media Inc. (NMI) back in July 2000 as its “innovation center and future-proofing agent.” Over the years, NMI built GMA’s major news websites (GMANetwork.com and GMA News Online), pioneered text-to-TV polling, built apps for corporate clients like SM and Ayala, and even created generative AI sportscasters (Marco and Maia) in 2023.

Yet for video, GMA followed a very different playbook from ABS-CBN. Instead of spending hundreds of millions on its own app like ABS-CBN’s iWant, GMA acted like a smart bakery that chose not to build its own delivery app and put its videos onto free websites viewers already used, like YouTube (joining YouTube’s Player for Publishers program in 2017), Hooq, and iFlix. That strategy required very little upfront software spending and gave GMA massive online crowd —surpassing 99 million combined subscribers across 20 YouTube channels by end-2025—without adding debt. The trade off was simple: GMA had to share ad revenue with YouTube and never owned direct monthly subscription.

When ABS-CBN was forced off Channel 2 in 2020, advertisers rushed to GMA. Between 2020 and 2022, GMA hit a historic goldmine. It had its best three years ever, making roughly P19 billion in combined net profits. GMA ruled free TV and hit a record P7.57 billion profit in 2021. ((READ: Fewer viewers, ad options: How ABS-CBN shutdown alters PH media landscape)

What GMA bought and the billions it paid out

With cash pouring in and almost no debt, GMA made two major choices during those boom years.

First, GMA doubled down on upgrading old-school free TV. As government moved to retire fuzzy analog TV signals, GMA poured money into Digital Terrestrial Television (DTT), building new transmitters and selling GMA Affordabox set-top boxes and GMA Now phone receivers.

Old antennas often catch grainy pictures, so DTT upgrades airwave signals into crisp digital TV with extra free channels, all without needing Wi-Fi or mobile data. Because older TVs cannot read digital signals alone, GMA launched the Affordabox in 2020, a small converter box that plugs into an older TV so families can watch clear digital channels for free. In 2021, GMA also launched GMA Now, a tiny pocket-sized antenna that plugs into an Android phone and turns it into a portable TV without burning mobile data.

Second, GMA paid out massive cash dividends. Between 2021 and 2025, GMA declared P24.32 billion in cash to its stockholders, including P6.56 billion in 2021, P7.05 billion in 2022, and P5.35 billion in 2023. By traditional corporate standards, this made total sense. GMA has a formal dividend policy to return at least half of prior year profits to stockholders, and for a profitable, virtually debt-free market leader, handing surplus cash back to owners is standard practice.

The catch is what GMA missed by giving away almost every peso of its windfall instead of reinvesting it: it did not build a global streaming platform where it owns the subscriber, it did not buy up external film or animation studios to grow its creative library, and it kept a thinner cash buffer right before TV ad money hit a wall. (READ: TV ads decline, influencer marketing rises: Why it’s harder now for TV shows to make money)

The warning signs in GMA’s numbers

Looking back without a crystal ball, GMA’s choices made sense in 2020. The problem is that Filipino viewers skipped right past TV converter boxes and went straight to TikTok, YouTube, and Netflix on their phones. By May 2025, GMA had to slash the price of Affordabox from P799 to P699 as hardware sales slid.

Even before 2026, GMA’s financial reports showed profits cooling down from that 2021 peak, sliding from P7.57 billion (2021) to P5.46 billion (2022), P3.16 billion (2023), and P2.06 billion (2024), before edging up slightly to P2.20 billion in 2025 only because of midterm election ads.

In 2026, the slide became a cliff. In its September 2026 financial report, GMA admitted that the 33% drop in ad revenue wasn’t just because 2025 election ads were gone. Regular corporate ad sales fell, too, which management blamed on cautious business spending and a “structural shift in media consumption from traditional broadcasting to internet-based platforms.”

In the first nine months of 2026, 89% of GMA’s revenue (P8.64 billion out of P9.67 billion) still came from ads, with traditional TV and radio making up the largest slice. Even though GMA’s YouTube ads are growing and it licenses hit shows like Maria Clara at Ibarra and Pulang Araw to Netflix and Viu, nearly 9 out of every 10 pesos it earns still tied to an aging broadcast engine. Digital ads and streaming deals are growing, just not fast enough to replace the big-ticket TV commercials that are shrinking.

Why owning the towers became a trap

Think of GMA as a mall owner and ABS-CBN as a Michelin-Star chef.

GMA owns the 25-year congressional franchise and 115 physical TV stations across the country. It owns the building and controls the foot traffic. But when shoppers stay home, a mall owner cannot simply unplug 115 broadcast towers, turn off the electricity, or lay off thousands of regular reporters, engineers, and crew overnight. That is why, when GMA’s revenue fell 31% in the first nine months of 2026, its operating costs could only drop 13%, pushing GMA into its rare P77.37-million third-quarter loss.

ABS-CBN is the chef whose main restaurant dining room was torn down in 2020. Today, it cooks in the modern kitchen it built years ago and rents stalls inside other people’s malls. It airs It’s Showtime on GMA-7, co-producing Pinoy Big Brother, and bringing Gandang Gabi Vice onto Channel 7. The signature recipes sell, but the chef is still paying off old mortgages on closed buildings and a bleeding delivery arm (Sky Cable) that eats every peso the kitchen makes.

For about 30 years, Philippine television was a fight to the death over who owned the tallest broadcast tower. By late 2026, the ratings war is over, replaced by a survival pact.

ABS-CBN was forced to change before it could afford it. GMA had the time and cash to prepare, yet now faces the exact same squeeze.

In an age when Filipinos watch whatever they want on their phones, the mall owner needs the chef’s star power to keep shoppers walking through the doors, and the chef needs the mall owner’s towers to reach every corner of the country. Neither side is celebrating yet, because in 2026, sharing the stage is the only way to keep the lights on. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: ‘Living in Water’ is an exercise in empathy
World.content:
'We don't experience the climate crisis the same way,' says journalist Ana P. Santos

MANILA, Philippines – What is it like to live with floodwater? The people in Isla Tibaguin, Bulacan tell their story in the 360 virtual reality documentary ‘Living in Water.’

Flooding is a regular occurrence in a country beset by an average of 20 storms a year, but some places experience harsher conditions. Investigative journalist Ana P. Santos wanted the format to create an empathy exercise for viewers who do not have quite the same relationship with water as the people in Isla Tibaguin.

“Hindi lahat tayo pare-pareho ng nararanasan ng climate crisis,” Santos said on Saturday, November 21, during a talkback in Rappler’s Social Good Summit 2026. (We don’t experience the climate crisis the same way.)

The documentary takes the viewer, who wears a headset wrapped around their head, in an immersive 360 experience of the flooded island.

Viewers can look around and inspect their surroundings, adopting the perspective of a person standing in the middle of the flooded area. The only thing missing is the wet sensation of water around the legs.

“‘Yung experience ko o ‘yung gusto sana nating ipahiwatig sa paggawa ng isang virtual reality and 360 immersive experience ay ‘yung pag bridge ng understanding, at ‘yung pag bridge ng empathy gap,” Santos said.

(My experience, or what we wanted to convey using the virtual reality and 360 immersive experience, is to bridge understanding and the empathy gap.)

The film was shown in sessions with limited audience during Rappler’s summit. Furnitures inside houses are partly submerged, a mother cooks a meal for their family standing on floodwaters, and children wade outside to play.

The documentary followed island residents Riri Sacdalan and Angie Atieza. They joined Santos in the talkback. Atieza shared that she was happy they got to share their story.

“Kasi tanong nga po namin, paano kaya nila mararamdaman ‘yung nararamdaman namin?” Atieza said on Saturday. “Kung sila ang nasa sitwasyon namin, kaya kaya nila tulad namin?” (That was our question, how will they feel what we feel? If they were in our position, will they endure like us?)

The film showed Atieza cooking for her children, talking with the barangay chairperson, and visiting the flooded village hall. The documentary also showed Sacdalan waking up to floodwaters, his grandmother sitting idly on a bed immersed in water.

Rising seas are driven by climate change and a warming world. In the Philippines, this is exacerbated by flood control infrastructure that turned out to be ghost projects or substandard ones.

Between living with regular floods and leaving the place they call home, many residents chose to stay. An immediate solution that residents can resort to, if they have the money to do so, is to raise their houses from the ground.

“Para sa akin sa totoo lang, hindi ko po magawang umalis sa isla,” Sacdalan shared with the audience. (For me, in truth, I can never leave the island.)

“Kaya ko nasabi po na dito ako pinanganak, dito ako lalaki, dito ako tatanda, dito ako mamamatay. Kasi po nandodoon po ang buhay namin.”

(I have said that this was where I was born, this is where I will grow up, grow old, and die. This is where our life is.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Can climate diplomacy build on the collapse of COP31?
World.content:
Delegates from around the globe attend the COP31 opening in Turkiye on November 9, 2026.

Despite the lack of a major deal, there is a shift toward smaller coalitions and initiatives among like-minded countries to drive faster emissions cuts and climate action

ANTALYA, Turkey – The collapse of COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday, November 22, without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change.

For the small, vulnerable countries most exposed to rising sea levels and the increasingly extreme weather scientists link to rising carbon emissions, annual UN conferences are their chance to draw the world’s attention to their plight and seek financial help.

But the failure of the Turkish talks, which follows on from weak outcomes at other COPs in recent years, lays bare the need for change.

Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, director of environment in Peru’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said “the credibility of the process” was at stake.

“This system needs in-depth reforms,” he said.

Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief representing the UN convention that underpins international climate talks, said the consensus-based system can still function, but work was needed.

“I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here,” he said as the talks ended on Sunday.

3 decades of seeking a global solution

Two stand-out victories for UN climate diplomacy were the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, when the world for the first time agreed on legally binding targets to curb climate emissions and the 2015 Paris agreement, which established an aspiration to limit global warming to no more than 1.5 degrees Celsius.

A major difference in Paris compared with Antalya was that the US was still engaged in the climate process in 2015.

The Antalya talks, the first since a UN report saying the world was set to breach the 1.5 C threshold that can prevent the worst consequences of warming, marked the second climate conference since US President Donald Trump withdrew from the UN climate process.

China, the world’s biggest carbon emitter, but also a major part of the solution as a provider of low-carbon technology, has attended the talks but sought to be low profile.

James Fletcher, who led the CARICOM group of Caribbean nations in Antalya, cited the lack of a major power backing a positive outcome as a big issue.

“There isn’t that one party that has sufficient gravitas that can get parties that may be far apart to come together,” he said.

Delegates said, however, the need for a multilateral deal to direct the shift toward renewable energy has become less necessary as renewable energy becomes economically compelling.

China’s clean energy exports last year alone, for example, will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year once deployed — an amount equal to the emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The business world as a result is less dependent on COPs to guide investment decisions.

“It used to be that you’d worry about how these (COP) decisions might affect the investment signal,” said Chris Dodwell, co-head of the sustainability centre at Impax Asset Management.

“I don’t think they really have that impact anymore …. the economics have taken over and are driving the transition.”

And bad as the absence of a deal was, some saw a hint of the positive in the wider refusal to accept a weak deal.

The determination of big oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia, to block language on fossil fuel, arguably reflected the scale of progress that has been achieved.

“The fact that they are blocking so much is also an expression of the fact that we are accelerating the transition,” Mattias Frumerie, Sweden’s chief negotiator, said.

“They’re seeing the direction of travel and this is the forum where they can express their frustration.”

Smaller groups find common cause

Like-minded governments, meanwhile, have focused on smaller groups to get things done. They have formed alliances to push together for faster emissions cuts and to rally finance, forestry initiatives, and efficiency programs.

Such forums include the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, or TAFF, the Green Grids Initiative, the Global Methane Pledge and the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance.

“There is growing interest in how can we work together to move, not through consensus, but through a coalition of people that are willing to work together,” said Maina Talia, climate minister of Tuvalu, which will next year host TAFF. As one of the low-lying Pacific island nations, Tuvalu is particularly keen for rapid action to address climate change.

He said he expected roughly 90 countries to send representatives including Britain, Mexico and Nigeria.

Fiji, another Pacific island, voiced its exasperation with COP.

“It is exhausting and frustrating and disappointing when you come year in, year out and there is no movement,” Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s climate minister, said.

The country’s chief negotiator, Sivendra Michael, however, said the consensus-driven process of COPs remained vital to ensuring the progress achieved by previous conferences was maintained.

“I do not know how else we are going to bring together all the parties that have committed legally to a legally binding agreement, hold up to their commitments, and discuss how they implement these commitments,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Miley Cyrus weds drummer Maxx Morando in California
World.content:
COUPLE. Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando attend the world premiere for the television show "Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special" in Los Angeles, California, US, March 23, 2026.

The 33-year-old singer announces the marriage on Instagram on Sunday, with the wedding photographs captioned simply 'M + M' and '11.21.26'

Grammy-winning pop star Miley Cyrus married her longtime partner, drummer Maxx Morando, in a private ceremony in California, with black-and-white pictures of the event posted on social media.

The 33-year-old singer announced the marriage on Instagram on Sunday, with the wedding photographs captioned simply “M + M” and “11.21.26.”

Cyrus wore a backless white silk gown, while Morando, 28, appeared in a classic black suit and white shirt at Saturday’s event.

People magazine and Entertainment Tonight were among the first to report the news. Representatives of the couple did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Cyrus and Morando reportedly married in Palm Springs, a month after performing “Let’s Get Married” together at the Hollywood Bowl, a song that features in Cyrus’ latest studio album, Bass Persuades.

Cyrus and Morando have been together for about five years. They met on blind date in 2021, Cyrus told British Vogue in an interview.

“Well, it was blind for me and not really for him,” the singer said in 2023. “I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’”

In December, Cyrus spoke of her engagement to the drummer during an appearance on ABC’s “Good Morning America”.

Morando is the drummer for Liily, a Los Angeles-based alternative rock band affiliated with Atlantic Records, the band says on its website.

The “Flowers” singer was previously married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth, who filed for divorce in Los Angeles in 2019. – Rappler.com

World.title: Piattos Snow Cheese? Just another hit for URC as sales top P130B
World.content:
NEW. URC president and CEO Irwin Lee shows reporters the company's latest snack, Piattos Snow Cheese on Friday, November 20.

URC's Irwin Lee has had quite a year, with the limited edition Snow Cheese Piattos selling out, C2 climbing in Vietnam, and Munchy's making its mark in Malaysia

You can’t have lunch with the head of the country’s biggest snack company without sampling some of those goodies at the table.

And no less than Universal Robina Corporation (URC) president and CEO Irwin Lee was ready to show off his latest product, Piattos Specials Snow Cheese, a limited-edition flavor packaged in a white and blue bag.

Sweet, creamy, and lightly cheesy, the new chips take inspiration from the Korean snack trends that have become popular among younger consumers.

“It’s flying off the shelves,” Lee told reporters on Friday, November 20. “We’re out of stock in a lot of places. We have to make more of it. We’re catching up on supply.”

“‘Pag pumatok ‘yan (If it’s a hit), and if there’s a clamor for it, we’ll make it permanent,” he added.

By then, the bag was empty. After all, it’s not every day you get to share chips with the man in charge of making them.

Biscuits, beverages, billions

Of course, there’s much more to URC’s business than this bag of Piattos might betray.

The Gokongwei-led food manufacturer is on track to surpass P175 billion in revenue this year, having already raked in P130.7 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 5% year-on-year.

One particularly bright spot has been URC’s international business, which now accounts for roughly 20% to 25% of sales.

Take C2, for example. The ready-to-drink tea beloved by Filipinos has apparently won over hearts in Vietnam too, jockeying for the top position against a local brand for the past six months.

“It’s number one in urban Vietnam. And we’re number two in rural,” Lee said, adding that it was the Philippine flavors — lemon and apple in particular — that were topping the charts.

Over in Malaysia, URC’s P24.6-billion acquisition of Munchy’s in 2021 has been “very, very, strong,” according to Lee, solidifying its position as the country’s leading biscuit player.

“We’re running very tight on our biscuit line capacities, so we have to really expand in Malaysia,” he said.

URC expects to maintain its annual capital expenditures of around P6 billion to P8 billion in 2027, with about 15% to 20% allocated to its overseas operations and the biggest chunk of that going to Malaysia.

Back home, however, Filipino consumers have been more cautious.

Lee said inflation has bifurcated growth across categories. Chip sales have slowed down to a low 2% to 3% increase.

Meanwhile, biscuits and bakery products are still enjoying double-digit growth, as are premium drinks like Vitasoy and Blu. And even though chips in general are having a slow year, premium snacks like Calbee potato chips are still selling briskly, with growth in the strong double-digits.

A fan of Vico

Speaking of treats, URC also has a hand in making Christmas a little sweeter for residents of a certain slice of the metro. And it turns out Lee is quite fond of the man running the place too.

It’s Pasig Mayor Vico Sotto, whose reputation for good governance has earned him admirers well beyond the city.

URC has longstanding ties to Pasig, where founder John Gokongwei Jr. established the company’s predecessor. It still operates flour milling and animal feed facilities there.

Among the goodies that have found their way into Pasig’s annual Christmas giveaway packs are sachets of Swiss Miss hot chocolate, distributed locally by URC. A warm cup of that rich, milky drink with marshmallows is the highlight of many a holiday get-together.

Lee said he had given the Pasig local government a good price for its purchases. But it turns out that the real treat — at least for URC employees — is the job of delivering the goods to city hall. After all, that delivery run might just come with a chance to meet the mayor himself. – Rappler.com

World.title: [New Rx] Why Philippine cities should issue their own bonds
World.content:
On November 13, the Bureau of the Treasury announced a three-year retail dollar bond targeting at least US$200 million, with a minimum investment of US$200. Metrobank pointed to relative calm in oil prices and bond yields as key timing factors. If the national government can ask ordinary savers to lend dollars, similar debt instruments could help local government units (LGUs) finance hospitals, water systems, and infrastructure closer to home.

Asian Development Bank (ADB) president Masato Kanda estimated ASEAN’s infrastructure needs through 2040 at US$7.1 trillion, including US$227 billion for healthcare facilities. Government budgets cover only 45% of these costs. Furthermore, PAGASA’s warning of a strong El Niño persisting into 2027 highlights the need for LGUs to finance water infrastructure. Localities should evaluate leak repairs and water storage projects that can repay loans or municipal bonds through utility fees.

Why state-bank loans dominate

Local bond authority dates back to 1975 for provinces and cities, and the 1991 Local Government Code extended it to municipalities. While cities like Urdaneta and Puerto Princesa have issued bonds, state-bank borrowing still dominates. For instance, Urdaneta pursued a ₱500 million LandBank loan in 2026 rather than issuing new bonds.

ADB studies show state banks offer rates close to the national government’s borrowing cost. Because bonds involve legal, underwriting, and disclosure expenses, they must offer distinct advantages — such as longer fixed-rate terms or broader investor reach. The World Bank notes that weak project preparation remains a primary bottleneck for LGU borrowing. Regional peers offer useful models: Vietnam has piloted municipal green bonds for water projects, while Jakarta has prepared revenue bond offerings.

Approved Official Development Assistance (ODA) projects often stall due to missing or delayed national budget counterpart funds. DEPDev’s 2024 portfolio review highlighted a ₱13.98 billion gap between counterpart needs and available allocations. Where agreements assign a share to creditworthy LGUs, municipal revenue bonds could fund those local contributions for income-generating utilities, as permitted under Section 299 of the Local Government Code.

Start with LGUs that can repay

To succeed, local issuance should start with credit-worthy LGUs and revenue-generating projects like water systems or public markets. Requirements must include audited accounts, independent credit ratings, and robust debt-service coverage. Investors could range from domestic commercial banks and institutional funds to retail savers.

Prior to issuance, LGUs must secure land titles, complete engineering designs, and enforce strict procurement rules. Cities maintain financial discipline through national oversight and the statutory 20%-of-regular-income debt-service limit.

Zero-coupon bonds secured by sinking funds or patrimonial land offer another viable structure, as demonstrated by Victorias, Negros Occidental, which successfully issued and repaid housing bonds. Looking ahead, Congress could authorize broader general obligation bonds for creditworthy LGUs to finance essential non-revenue infrastructure like flood control.

Healthcare bond options

Two options exist for financing healthcare expansion. First, Congress could authorize PhilHealth to issue short-term general obligation bonds backed by general revenues to manage emergency cash-flow needs or launch new health benefits. Second, public specialty hospital corporations could issue revenue bonds backed by receipts from premium private amenities.

Following models from Singapore’s National University Hospital and Bangkok’s Siriraj Piyamaharajkarun Hospital, surplus proceeds from paying patients could cross-subsidize public wards while preserving the Universal Health Care Act’s mandated basic bed quotas (90% in government hospitals and 70% in specialty centers).

The treasury knows how to reach savers. Let credit-worthy LGUs do the same for projects ready to build and able to repay. Their delivery record should determine how far the market grows. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is a physician, healthcare investor, and adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines Manila College of Public Health. His New Rx column examines Philippine healthcare and public policy through a Korean and regional Asian lens.

World.title: Manibela begins two-day transport strike
World.content:
Manibela began its two-day strike on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, to protest the supposed leadership change at the Land Transportation Office. Photo from Manibela

MANILA, Philippines — Transport group Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkaisang Terminal ng Transportasyon (Manibela) began its two-day strike on Monday to protest the supposed leadership change at the Land Transportation Office (LTO).

READ: WALANG PASOK: In-person classes, court operation suspensions on Nov. 23

Manibela members, led by president Mar Valbuena, marched and staged a demonstration in front of the Land Transportation Office’s (LTO) central office in Quezon City.

Article continues after this 

The group launched the strike to protest the supposed removal of LTO Chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao.

According to Valbuena, Manibela was among those who witnessed the reforms Lacanilao implemented at the agency.

“Is this how it is, dear president? Even though we know that the current leader is doing good and right, he will simply be removed?” Valbuena said in Filipino.

“At a time when the transport sector is dying?” he added.

Valbuena attributed several of the LTO’s accomplishments directly to Lacanilao, including the agency’s improved service delivery and the apprehension of erring drivers and public utility vehicle operators.

Article continues after this 

The group’s strike is expected to last until Tuesday, Nov. 24.

Several schools have already suspended in-person classes in Metro Manila due to the demonstration.

Article continues after this 

READ: DOTr to offer free rides in parts of NCR during 2-day transport strike

Meanwhile, the Department of Transportation is offering free rides along select routes for commuters affected by the transport strike on both days, from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.

World.title: Engine overheating eyed in fire-hit passenger vessel off Cebu
World.content:
Coast Guard personnel assist passengers of MV OceanJet 168 after the vessel caught fire while en route to Ormoc City, Leyte, from Cebu City on Sunday, November 22, 2026. (Photo courtesy of PCG)

CEBU CITY — Engine overheating may have caused the fire that hit a fast craft traveling from Cebu City to Ormoc City in Leyte on Sunday, authorities said.

Regulators from the Marine Industry Authority (MARINA) have already suspended MV Oceanjet 168’s safety certificate while investigations are ongoing.

The vessel reportedly caught fire while navigating waters off Compostela in northern Cebu past 10 a.m. on Sunday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.

Article continues after this 

READ: MARINA suspends fast craft’s safety certificate after fire on Sunday

It departed Cebu City at 9:30 a.m. and was carrying 311 passengers.

Capt. Jerome Lozada, commander of Coast Guard Station Central Cebu, said the vessel’s master reported the incident to the Coast Guard Sub-Station Aduana at around 10:40 a.m.

Initial information indicated that the fire was caused by engine overheating and was extinguished a minute after it started, at 10:22 a.m.

No casualties were reported, and all passengers have been accounted for.

Article continues after this 

The PCG immediately coordinated with the shipping company to transfer passengers to the vessel’s sister ship, MV OceanJet 88, amid rough sea conditions.

The transfer operation started at 1:35 p.m. in waters off Tayud, Consolacion, Cebu, and was completed by 2 p.m.

Article continues after this 

Upon arrival at Pier 1 of Aduana Wharf in Cebu City, PCG personnel and the Philippine Red Cross provided medical assessments and assistance to the passengers before they disembarked.

MV OceanJet 168 was subsequently brought to Labogon Shipyard in Mandaue City for repairs.

Meanwhile, the fast craft’s suspension would remain in effect until the vessel complied with applicable safety requirements and satisfactorily passed the necessary survey or inspection, MARINA said.

READ: Fast craft from Cebu City catches fire; all passengers safe

The agency also said it would investigate the cause of the fire and determine if there were any administrative violations of maritime safety regulations.

World.title: Visayas Grid on red, yellow alert anew
World.content:
.

MANILA, Philippines — The Visayas Grid will be placed under red and yellow alerts on Monday, Nov. 23, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said.

In an advisory, the NGCP said the Visayas Grid would first be placed under a yellow alert from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m., before transitioning to a red alert from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m.

Another yellow alert would be implemented immediately afterward and would last until 8 p.m.

Article continues after this 

According to the NGCP, a red alert is issued when power supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the grid’s regulating requirement. A yellow alert means the operating margin is insufficient to meet the grid’s contingency requirement.

READ: NGCP: Mindanao reserves may run out by 2028

The NGCP said the Visayas Grid’s current available capacity is only 2,473 megawatts (MW), while its peak demand exceeds this at 2,527 MW.

Among the factors cited by the NGCP that contributed to the alert declaration were the unavailability of Visayas’ large coal plant TVI 2 due to an unplanned outage, the derated capacity of TV1, and the unavailability of PCPC and KSPC Unit 2 due to planned outages.

The NGCP also cited limited power imports from Mindanao due to the planned outages of GNPK Unit 3, STEAG Unit 2, and FDC Unit 3.

Article continues after this 

The NGCP also noted that eight plants had been on forced outage since November, one since October, two since September, two since August, one since June, three since 2025, one since 2024, two since 2023, and one since 2021.

Meanwhile, 21 plants were also operating at derated capacities, leaving a total of 612.5 MW unavailable to the grid. /mcm

World.title: Better sugar prices lift spirits of Bukidnon planters
World.content:
Sugarcane planters in Bukidnon smile as they claim their first quedan certificates at their local planters’ association on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, buoyed by a strong opening millgate price of P2,600 per bag of raw sugar. Photo by Mark Neo Lim.

MARAMAG, Bukidnon — Sugarcane planters across Bukidnon welcomed the opening of quedan trading last Friday, with millgate prices reaching a favorable P2,600 per bag of raw sugar despite threats of red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI) infestation and rising labor and hauling costs.

Quedan trading involves negotiable warehouse receipts that prove ownership of a specific volume of sugar stored in a mill or bonded warehouse.

Almeric Batoy, president of the San Roque Backyard Raiser and Sugarcane Farmers Association (SRBRSFA), said the better millgate price was a welcome relief to many farmers as they began harvesting and selling their produce.

Article continues after this 

“The first quedan trading price is good. (We are) hoping the (P2,600) price will continue,” he added.

SRBRSFA, a 22-member block farming group in Maramag whose members cultivate two to five hectares each, delivers freshly harvested sugarcane to Crystal Sugar Co. Inc. in North Poblacion, Maramag, because of its proximity to their farms.

The group urged the government to address the RSSI infestation and high production costs to provide further relief to sugarcane farmers.

Batoy said local sugarcane planters remain wary that the government may allow sugar imports once the current moratorium expires.

The Department of Agriculture (DA) earlier clarified that the ban on sugar imports remains in effect until December 2026 to protect domestic producers following the close of the crop year in September.

Article continues after this 

READ: Pests, El Niño, rising costs threaten sugar production

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said the policy prioritizes locally produced sugar to stabilize domestic market prices amid strong raw sugar output.

Article continues after this 

As quedan trading begins, milling operations across the so-called Bukidnon Sugar Milling District are operating at near-full capacity.

Based on the district’s daily milling summary on Nov. 19, BUSCO Sugar Milling Co. Inc. in Barangay Butong, Quezon, operated at 86 percent capacity utilization, processing 15,539.49 metric tons (MT) against its daily capacity of 18,000 MT. Its average sugar recovery reached 1.76 Lkg per ton cane (Lkg/TC), with a 1.99 percent trash rate.

Meanwhile, Crystal Sugar Co. Inc. exceeded its rated daily capacity of 12,000 MT, operating at 102 percent utilization and milling 12,202.37 MT. Its average recovery was 1.75 Lkg/TC, with a 2.39 percent trash rate.

Combined, the two mills processed 27,741.86 MT against the district’s daily capacity of 30,000 MT, reflecting an overall utilization rate of 92.47 percent.

READ: Sugar sector opposes tax hike amid El Niño, pest threats

Albert Tutor, planters coordinator and data analyst at Crystal Sugar Co. Inc., said the plant has experienced minimal mechanical issues and maintained a steady cane supply, particularly from southern Bukidnon farms, allowing it to consistently maximize its daily milling capacity of 12,000 MT.

Despite the strong start to the milling season, some growers remain anxious about looming weather threats.

Your subscription could not be saved. Please try again. Your subscription has been successful. Subscribe to our daily newsletter SIGN ME UP

Mercy Inda, 58, a sugarcane farmer from Barangay Dagat-Kidavao, Valencia City, expressed concern over her five-hectare farm, which is scheduled for harvest in March 2027. She cited state weather bureau forecasts of an impending El Niño phenomenon next year that could threaten her yield and capital. /mcm

BALANGA CITY, Bataan — A 60-year-old woman riding a tricycle was reportedly killed when a speeding pickup truck rammed into the vehicle at 9 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 22, police said.

The passenger died on the spot.

World.title: 1 hurt as rido erupts in Lanao del Sur
World.content:
Police secure the national highway leading to the town proper of Balabagan, Lanao del Sur, as warring families exchange gunfire over a family feud. One person was injured in the skirmishes that erupted around noon on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Photo by PRO-BAR.

COTABATO CITY — A firefight erupted in Balabagan, Lanao del Sur, around noon on Sunday, Nov. 22, involving two warring Moro clans and leaving one person injured, police said.

Capt. Steffi Salanguit, spokesperson for the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR), said the rido, or clan feud, involved the Sampiano and Karim families, both from Balabagan.

She identified the wounded as Adnan Maute, 26, a resident of Barangay Poblacion and a member of the Sampiano family.

Article continues after this 

READ: DOJ forms multiagency group to resolve ‘ridos’

Responding police officers rushed him to Dr. Serapio Montaner Jr. Al-Haj Memorial Hospital in Malabang, Lanao del Sur, for medical treatment.

Citing a report from the Malabang municipal police, Salanguit said members of the Karim family allegedly initiated the skirmishes by firing at members of the Sampiano family in Barangay Calilangan, Balabagan, at around 1 p.m.

She said the fighting lasted until about 5 p.m. No close-contact firefight was reported, but the parties exchanged gunfire from a distance.

The warring families are locked in a long-standing clan feud triggered by personal grudges.

Article continues after this 

No civilian evacuations were reported, Salanguit said.

Personnel from the Balabagan municipal police, backed by elements of the 2nd Provincial Mobile Force Company under the Lanao del Sur Provincial Police Office, have been deployed in the conflict area to prevent further skirmishes. /mcm

World.title: Rain, cloudy skies expected in parts of PH on Nov. 23
World.content:
GRAPHICS BY INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — Rain and cloudy skies are expected to affect several areas in the country on Monday, the state weather bureau said.

In its latest weather forecast, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the northeast monsoon, or amihan, will bring rain over Batanes and the Babuyan Islands, while the shear line is expected to affect Cagayan Valley.

READ: PH Weather Updates Today: Storm News and PAGASA Forecasts

Article continues after this 

“There will be cloudy skies and scattered rains due to the intertropical convergence zone in Eastern Visayas, Davao Region, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Soccsksargen, Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur,” Pagasa weather specialist Aldczar Aurelio said.

World.title: Rights Groups Demand Action Against Myanmar Junta After Historic Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
Rights groups are urging governments to step up diplomatic pressure, impose fresh sanctions and isolate the military regime following Thursday’s landmark International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017.

It was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Rights advocates say the historic ruling must now translate into concrete measures to hold the regime accountable, rather than remain a symbolic legal victory.

“This is a big blow for [regime leader] Min Aung Hlaing at a time when he is trying to persuade the world to normalize relations,” Tun Khin, president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), told The Irrawaddy.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, as well as ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine State.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, although the court has no independent enforcement mechanism.

If Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling’s orders, the UN Security Council can act to enforce them, according to Article 94.2 of the UN Charter.

Tun Khin said his organization had called on the UK to organize a meeting of the UN Security Council. Though regime allies Russia and China would likely veto any resolution, they would be forced to explain such a move. London has called for a meeting.

“We hope it will result in new sanctions,” Tun Khin said.

Tun Khin expressed concern that the return of the Rohingya is still impossible due to the policies of both the Myanmar military regime and the ethnic Arakan Army (AA), an anti-regime armed group that controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships.

Lucky Karim, executive director of the group Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, said that as an initial step following the ICJ ruling, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member countries should stop engaging with the Myanmar regime.

She noted that this year nine countries have hosted self-appointed president Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw the 2017 atrocities as military chief. She urged all countries to stop welcoming him. Despite the bilateral engagements, Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from ASEAN’s top-level summits.

“I think the regional states should apply the same rule [as ASEAN] and take a pause for now. Stop hosting him and rolling out the red carpet and engaging him,” Lucky Karim said.

The ICJ decision was welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (HRW), along with foreign ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Turkey, as well as Myanmar’s civilian National Unity Government (NUG).

As immediate actions, London ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché from the UK and issued an urgent call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

More than 190 local rights groups welcomed the ICJ ruling.

The regime rejected the verdict. Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for the military-appointed government, said on Friday: “The truth is we were wrongly accused.”

Emphasizing the fact that the verdict was not unanimous, she said, “Not all the judges voted for it, so it’s not a fair judgment.”

The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Meanwhile, the AA said it would act in the best interests of the state following the landmark ruling.

“We need to wait for the regime’s report to the Court. For example, will the regime deny it, or will they say they can’t pay compensation?” Rakhine politician Pe Than told The Irrawaddy.

Backed by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Gambia brought the case in 2019, alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the Genocide Convention. It took seven years to reach a final verdict in the case.

The Myanmar regime has continued to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across the country since the 2021 coup.

Since seizing power, the regime has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners. The group said the regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, while millions of young people have fled abroad amid forced conscription, security fears, inflation, widespread crime, job scarcity and escalating conflict.

The NUG reaffirmed its commitment to justice, citizenship, and human rights norms for the Rohingya in a statement Thursday.

It said communities across Myanmar continue to face airstrikes, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and forced displacement, while hospitals, schools, monasteries and churches have also come under attack.

“The pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by action to end the military junta’s continuing violence against civilians throughout Myanmar,” it said.

Tun Khin said the ICJ judgment is good news for everyone in Myanmar. “Now they [the regime] are officially responsible for genocide and facing renewed international pressure instead,” he said.

World.title: U.S. Sanctions Two More Myanmar Regime-Allied Scam Warlords
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two more top leaders of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) on Thursday, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

Commander-in-chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One join four other senior leaders of the regime-allied militia on the U.S. sanctions list.

Saw Steel, Saw Sein Win, San Aung and Sai Kyaw Hla were added last November as part of Washington’s crackdown on the multibillion-dollar border scam industry targeting Americans.

Also sanctioned Thursday was Cambodian national Zhao Hui and two of his scam-linked firms.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.”

Thursday’s order was the U.S. latest action targeting Myanmar individuals in a crackdown on online scam compounds in Southeast Asia that defrauded an estimated $7.2 billion from Americans in 2025 alone.

The sanctions freeze any U.S.-based assets held by targets and make it illegal for Americans to do business or financial transactions with them.

Saw Shwe Wah took over protection of scam operations in DKBA-held Sone See Myaing, Kyauk Khet, Waw Lay, and Phaya Thonezu in December 2025 after replacing the blacklisted Saw Steel as DKBA’s commander-in-chief.

At least seven scam major compounds were under DKBA protection in 2025. However, staged regime raids on KK Park, Shwe Kokko, and Myawaddy in October and November last year forced a mass relocation to the DKBA’s Sone See Myaing headquarters, while others reportedly dispersed inland to villages under the group’s control.

“Shwe Wah has full oversight. The online scams are operating under his protection since he holds the highest position of the group,” a source familiar with DKBA administration told The Irrawaddy.

“Smaller scam sites are now scattered across DKBA territory. Despite their size they still have concrete buildings.”

He confirmed that DKBA-protected scam operations are concentrated in its Sone See Myaing stronghold, though others have relocated to villages in the Mulayit mountain range, roughly 20 km inside the border.

Following last year’s Myawaddy crackdown — widely dismissed as a publicity stunt — scammers reportedly flocked south to the Thai-Myanmar border town of Phaya Thonezu (Three Pagodas Pass) under the command of Colonel Saw A One.

Washington added him to its sanctions list Thursday, claiming he oversaw an expansion of scam operations and buildings.

“Tens of thousands of fraudsters flooded in here during the crackdown over there [in Myawaddy], turning this place into a large scam hub,” a resident of Phaya Thonezu told The Irrawaddy. “Since then, the scam buildings have expanded.”

He added that restrictions on movement make it difficult to determine the exact number of scam compounds and workers, though he confirmed the presence of two major compounds in the town and many more hidden nearby in restricted forest

The U.S. escalated its border scam crackdown in 2025, sanctioning leaders of the regime-allied Karen National Army (formerly the Karen Border Guard Force) including Saw Chit Thu and his two sons.

Washington has since formed the Scam Center Strike Force with Thailand to seize evidence, intercept fleeing scam bosses, and cut off cross-border supplies to compounds.

Jeanine Pirro, who oversees the Strike Force, met with Thai officials in Bangkok this week to discuss strengthening bilateral intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border crackdowns against the scam syndicates.

The Irrawaddy could not reach DKBA headquarters for comment.

World.title: ‘Ungrateful and Two-Faced’: Why a Chinese Analyst Slammed Myanmar’s Junta Chief
World.content:
Following Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, a Chinese commentator responded that the junta was attempting to dodge its own political failures by simply attributing its opponent’s combat effectiveness to external assistance.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that resulted in the seizure of the Myanmar military’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and eventually left the regime stripped of control over most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State. The offensive brought about one of the most humiliating defeats in the Myanmar military’s modern history.

The regime chief insisted the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), one of the alliance members, did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” Min Aung Hlaing said, his voice filled with rage.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

On Friday, the Chinese commentator, who claims to “specialize in Myanmar and Southeast Asia”, made the comments on Chinese social media platform WeChat under the title “The Myanmar Military’s Misunderstanding of China: An Analysis of Min Aung Hlaing’s Unspoken Accusations”.

The commentator, whom The Irrawaddy has learned is knowledgeable about Myanmar affairs and familiar with Naypyitaw, argued that Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks went beyond an assessment of the military’s battlefield defeats.

“He was not explaining his assessment of the enemy; he was assigning blame. He attributed the EAOs’ victory in Operation 1027 to ‘covert support from China,’” the author says.

The commentator also said the Myanmar military has never been on the pro-China end of the country’s political spectrum. From General Aung San, the founder of the Myanmar military, to successive generations of leaders like Than Shwe, Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing, all have been full of misunderstandings and suspicions toward China, the author said.

Regarding the junta’s loss in Operation 1027, the author said the Myanmar military failed to look inward for the cause of the collapse of its combat capability after 2021. “The real collapse occurred internally: troops were replenished through forced conscription, military officers’ families enjoyed special privileges, running businesses within the military was rampant, and grassroots morale was shattered. The Myanmar military has failed to rectify these long-accumulated bad habits,” the author pointed out.

“Shoving all the blame onto ‘external assistance’ is the easiest explanation, but also the one that solves absolutely nothing,” the author added.

China mediated a ceasefire between the alliance and the military in January 2024. In April 2025, under Chinese pressure, the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio, allowing the Myanmar military to re-enter the city.

The author says these developments should have encouraged the Myanmar military to rely more on China’s mediation efforts to facilitate negotiations and de-escalation. Instead, the junta leadership interpreted them differently.

“Instead, not only were they ungrateful, but they stubbornly believed: ‘Since the EAOs listen to China and stop fighting when told to, they must also be taking orders from them to attack the Myanmar military; therefore, any military action by the EAOs must be masterminded by China behind the scenes.’”

“If China were truly covertly supporting the EAOs, Lashio would never have been returned. This is the hardest evidence to refute the ‘covert support’ theory, but unfortunately, it is never mentioned in the Myanmar military’s narrative,” the author argues.

The commentator also pointed out that whenever the Myanmar military wants China to pressure ethnic armed groups, it invokes the concept of pauk-phaw, or fraternal, ties. When it needs China to support its economy, open border ports, or buy agricultural products, it repeats the slogan “China-Myanmar Community With a Shared Future.” Yet, the moment domestic governance goes wrong, it immediately shifts the blame to China, the author says.

“This two-faced mentality of simultaneous dependence and suspicion is currently the deepest rift in China-Myanmar relations.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Rejects ‘Unfair’ Rohingya Genocide Ruling at ICJ
World.content:
NAYPYITAW—A historic ruling by the top UN court that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority was “not fair,” the regime’s presidential spokeswoman said Friday.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, the court’s president said.

Asked about the ICJ decision at a press conference in the capital Naypyitaw, spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe called it unfair.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she said, noting the 9-6 vote.

“So this was not a unanimous decision,” she added. “I would say it is not fair.”

Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

But the ICJ ruling dismissed Myanmar’s argument that it was carrying out counter-insurgency operations.

“There is no evidence before the court that, in the conduct of the clearance operations, Myanmar distinguished between civilians and alleged (Rohingya) fighters,” the judgment said.

It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges have determined that a state committed genocide.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh during the crackdown, the court said.

Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, it said, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

No enforcement

The court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation, with specific sums to be determined later.

While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling may heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy.

China, an enduring partner after the coup, raised concerns of judicial overreach after the ICJ ruling.

One of the ICJ’s judges is from China and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.

The U.S. reacted with caution, stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the international court.

Despite determining in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Washington has more recently pushed back on another case before the court, involving accusations by South Africa that U.S. ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Lashes Out at Beijing, Scammer Whac-a-Mole Continues in Shan, and More
World.content:
Min Aung Hlaing hints at Chinese hand in resistance’s Operation 1027

Putschist president Min Aung Hlaing is still groping for an explanation for Operation 1027, the humiliating Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that stripped his regime of most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on the offensive.

He insisted the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

Then came the interesting part: “There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he added.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country, few observers were left in doubt that it was a swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance.

The comments echoed Min Aung Hlaing’s complaints at the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

They come after Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun delivered a body blow to Naypyitaw by urging “high-level autonomy” for ethnic minorities, a suggestion that flies in the face of the military regime’s centralization doctrine.

Regime chief fingers neighbors for sustaining ‘insurgents’

In the same outburst, Min Aung Hlaing also accused the two neighbors that have made the biggest effort to accommodate his regime—China and Thailand—of sustaining “insurgents” by encouraging trade through border crossings they control.

He started with Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and MNDAA, which now control much of Myanmar’s border with China. “In Kachin, the KIA runs border gates at the Chinese border. In northeastern Myanmar, the MNDAA runs Chinshwehaw gate,” he said.

“Taxation from illegal trade has sustained and financed insurgents,” he complained.

In Kachin, the regime has also lost control over the lucrative rare earth mines, which are now a major source of revenues for the KIA. The situation is not much different in northern Shan, where the regime has lost key border crossings with Yunnan as well as rare earth and other mineral resources.

On the surface, he was only accusing Thailand of directly facilitating trade through resistance-held territory at the Thaw Le Hta crossing in Hpapun, avoiding direct accusations against China except by inference and association.
