World.title: LNP authorises Instagram account promoting itself as Queensland news source
World.content:
A social media account promoting itself as a Queensland news source only disclosed it was authorised by the Liberal National Party following questions from the ABC.

This month Queensland Breaking News started sharing Instagram reels from government press conferences spruiking announcements made by ministers.

Its posts on transport and infrastructure projects have been re-posted by Premier David Crisafulli and Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, with its best performing content reaching almost 10,000 views.

The account's maroon and white logo featuring a map of Queensland is in stark contrast to LNP's trademark blue.

Following questions to the government from the ABC an authorisation statement was added to the account's bio to appear alongside its tagline "latest updates from across QLD".

An LNP spokesperson said: "Queensland Breaking News is one of many pages used by the LNP to share information about what the LNP Government is delivering for Queensland."

An authorisation was added to the bio for the Queensland Breaking News Instagram account after questions from the ABC. (Supplied: Instagram)

While an authorisation was added, it is not a legal requirement. In Queensland, authorisation of election material, including social media accounts, is only required 12 months before a state election.

For the next state election in 2028, this will apply from October next year.

The Electoral Commission of Queensland does not regulate authorisation of election matter outside of the authorisation period.

It is among a string of politically linked accounts promoting themselves as news sources at both a state and federal level.

Queensland Politics Newsfeed, which is authorised by Queensland's Labor opposition, has been active since 2024 when the party was in office.

It posts reels from press conferences, with Opposition Leader Steven Miles prominently featured and uses the hashtag #qldupdates.

Across the border, an Instagram account with the handle @nswnewsroom states that it is authorised by the Labor Party. According to the Sydney Morning Herald, this detail was added after the government was approached for comment.

NSW Labor's 'newsroom' social media account raises a political eyebrow From a "breaking" news-style post about the gun buyback scheme to a video of jacarandas blooming, the scribes behind the social media account have been busy.

Australian National University marketing lecturer Dr Andrew Hughes said the accounts "purport" to be reporting on the news but only tell one side of the story.

"They are growing in popularity in use because they fall outside a hard definition of being election material which would then have to be authorised," he said.

"It is attractive to a party because it might take some time for someone, like a normal person, to deduct that is being done by a party."

The Instagram page posts press conferences from LNP politicians in Queensland. (Instagram: @qldbreakingnews)

Dr Hughes said political advertising laws should be changed to capture such accounts to reflect the changing media landscape and strategies used to reach voters.

"In the age of digital and social media, it is ongoing, it does not stop," he said.

Dr Hughes said including an authorisation on an account allows a political party to say they are not hiding who they are and where the information is coming from.

"In the modern age of social media, you don't want to go for paid; you want to get the viral effect, which is it is shared by people among their networks," he said.

World.title: Cricket NSW slams door on Bears' North Sydney NRL homecoming
World.content:
Cricket NSW has slammed the door on a Bears NRL pre-season homecoming, ruling out making North Sydney Oval available for Perth to play at in February.

Cricket officials informed the Bears today that they would not accept any financial compensation for use of the venue, given it would remove cricket for at least five weeks.

It comes after NRL executive chair Peter V'landys last week said it would be "beyond comprehension" for cricket to deny the expansion club a romantic homecoming.

V'landys also claimed a $200,000 compensation fee would be "silly", after Cricket NSW indicated that would be the cost to take the pitch out and put it back in.

The Bears will play in the NRL in 2027. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But Cricket NSW chief executive Lee Germon said ultimately, money was not a factor, and instead his sport had to look after the North Sydney Cricket Club and stop them being moved for four games.

"It became very evident the impact to cricket was too great to agree to this request," Germon said.

"North Sydney have been playing at North Sydney Oval since 1895, so it is very much a key home and a spiritual home for them as well.

"We want them to play as much cricket as we can there.

"But because it is such a great cricket ground we have WBBL and international women's matches there as well, which also restricts accessibility for the club."

Bears unlikely to be able to play at oval in future

Germon warned it was unlikely cricket would be moved out of North Sydney in the future for the Bears due to the annual schedule.

That would leave Perth never able to play at the Bears' spiritual home, given North Sydney is unlikely to be considered fit for a regular-season NRL match.

"It's a key cricket ground," Germon said.

"We are faced with this every year. We would love to host a Sheffield Shield final at the SCG, but we can't because of the AFL.

Can the Bears live between North Sydney Oval and Perth? North Sydney Oval kept the spirit of the Bears alive during their darkest hours. But what role can the famous old ground play in the foundation club's resurrection in Perth?

"It's the world we live in. Cricket has the rights to North Sydney Oval in cricket season, and cricket is a summer sport.

"So it's very unlikely we would be able to accommodate any request of this nature, moving forward."

Germon said he had some sympathy for the Bears, who are scheduled to play their first pre-season match at the little-known western Sydney ground, Eric Tweedale Stadium.

But asked how he thought V'landys may feel about the situation, Germon said he was not fussed.

"I don't know, I don't know him. And I don't really care," he quipped.

"It's a decision we have made and it is a decision in the best interest of our sport."

AAP

World.title: Police find body of man who jumped into Melbourne's Yarra River
World.content:
Police believe they have found the body of a man who disappeared after jumping into the Yarra River in Melbourne's CBD yesterday.

Witnesses say the 26-year-old began struggling in the water after he and another man, 30, jumped from Princes Bridge beside Flinders Street Station around 11:45am on Sunday.

The second man made his own way out of the water.

The area was crowded with locals and tourists, including shoppers at a weekly Southgate riverside market.

A bystander jumped into the river to try to help the man but he disappeared under the water and did not resurface.

A large crowd who were on Princes Bridge at the time tried to direct first responders to where the man had disappeared.

A large number of people saw the man disappear under the water in the Yarra River on Sunday. (ABC News: Georgia Lenton-Williams)

Police and the SES searched the river for the rest of the day and into the evening, covering a large section of the river beside the popular Southbank restaurant precinct, Crown Casino, Federation Square and Birrarung Marr parkland.

The search resumed this morning.

Just after 1pm, Victoria Police announced a body had been found on the north-east side of the river near Federation Square.

"The deceased is yet to be formally identified but believed to be the man who jumped into the water from Princes Bridge yesterday morning," a spokesperson said.

The death is not being treated as suspicious.

Police will prepare a report for the coroner.

World.title: Sydney Opera House disabled access changes unsafe, some patrons say
World.content:
Sydney Opera House patrons and some staff have slammed changes to the building's disabled access, which they claim are unsafe and were made without proper consultation.

Accessible drop-off at the Opera House has been moved from the underground loading dock to the main arrival area at the Macquarie Street Gatehouse.

Patrons requiring assistance are now picked up from the gatehouse by golf buggies and driven to the door.

Barbara Hutchinson said the new arrangements were difficult to navigate for her and her friend, Jane Stone, who uses two walking sticks and has difficulty walking long distances.

"[Before] we were able to access the loading dock, and they allowed taxis to go down and unload people and they were beautifully helpful," Ms Hutchinson told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings.

"They had wheelchairs and walkers, all sorts of things. But we went on Tuesday night and we were told that's no longer available.

"It does make it very difficult for people who are very disabled and in a wheelchair."

Ms Stone said she was able to safely navigate the new buggy system but that some disabled people would struggle.

"The distance between the front of the [buggy] seat and the back of the seat in front is very small," she said.

The Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA) sent an open letter on October 29 on behalf of staff to Sydney Opera House management which detailed safety concerns with the new buggy system.

The union said it was yet to receive a formal response.

MEAA acting chief executive Adam Portelli said there had been two incidents in which staff and a patron were injured while travelling in the buggies.

"Patrons who previously were able to enter or leave from the venue directly now need to get dropped off and picked up 150 metres away, brave the elements, and then get a buggy into the Opera House," Mr Portelli said.

"The buggy itself … presents a real OHS risk."

In a statement, a Sydney Opera House spokesperson said the change removed the need for visitors to use back-of-house pathways, mitigating the safety risks of moving through a working loading dock while consolidating all visitor arrivals in one location.

It said there were three enclosed buggies for transporting visitors between the arrival area and the building, two of which were fitted with ramps for wheelchair users.

"The Opera House is committed to delivering the highest standard of customer service, inclusivity and patron safety," they said.

David, an Elizabeth Bay resident, said he had been visiting the Opera House since it opened in 1973.

He said the change was made without any warning.

"It's just appalling," he said.

"[Visitors] were essentially told to get out of the car and to get into a buggy. And when you're an older person without the ability to put any weight, any strength, one step is one step too far," he said.

World.title: Premier vows to criminalise coercive control at 16 Days in WA event
World.content:
The WA government says it will introduce legislation to make coercive control a standalone criminal offence next year, as the niece of a woman who was murdered by her estranged husband warned domestic violence deaths don't happen in isolation.

WARNING: This story contains the name and image of a First Nations person who has died.

Premier Roger Cook made the announcement in his speech at a 16 Days in WA event today, an annual statewide campaign to stop violence against women, and family and domestic violence.

Coercive control refers to patterns of abusive and manipulative behaviours used by one person to dominate another, and can involve threats, surveillance, insults and withholding money.

Sixteen Days in WA is an annual campaign against domestic violence. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

In 2023 the state government said it would take a phased approach to criminalising coercive control, by first reforming the Restraining Orders Act and implementing reforms like more training for police officers and education.

This approach was recommended by the WA Office of the Commissioner for Victims of Crime.

Refusing to look away

Former AFLW player Kirby Bentley told the 16 Days in WA event the story of her aunt Andrea Louise Pickett, who was murdered in January 2009 by her estranged husband.

Kirby Bentley says her aunt's death followed years of coercion. (ABC News)

"Her death didn't happen in isolation," she told those gathered.

"It followed years of abuse, intimidation, threats, coercion and repeated attempts to seek help.

"Despite everything she did, she was not protected.

Murder victim's family sues The family of murdered Indigenous woman Andrea Pickett sues the WA government and the state's police service, in what lawyers call a landmark case for Australia.

"The coronial [inquest] findings documented that he'd been killing family animals and making statements that killing animals would make it easier for him to kill a human."

Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence Minister Jessica Stojkovski said everyone needed to play their part.

"While governments have an important role to play, lasting change happens when communities refuse to look away," she said.

"When enough people decide that silence is no longer neutrality.

'When enough people choose to act, when enough people have the confidence to ask: 'Are you safe?'"

Jessica Stojkovski says the proposed changes involve recognising abuse in all its forms. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Mr Cook said family and domestic violence should have no place in society.

"Coercive control legislation is an important milestone in strengthening support for family and domestic violence victim-survivors and expanding reform to hold perpetrators to account across the state," he said in a statement.

Announcement follows inquest

Data from the 2021–22 Personal Safety Survey compiled by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) measured rates of physical and sexual assault, family and domestic violence, economic and emotional abuse, stalking, sexual harassment, and childhood abuse.

It found 23 per cent, or 2.3 million women and 14 per cent, or 1.3 million men had experienced emotional abuse by a current or previous partner.

According to the ABS, 16 per cent of women and 7.8 per cent of men had experienced economic abuse from a current or previous partner.

Last year, as part of a wider funding package to address family and domestic violence (FDV) across the state, coercive-control training was due to be rolled out to first responders.

The government said criminalising coercive control was part of broader $121 million package of changes to strengthen prevention, improve support for victim-survivors and increase accountability for people who use violence.

Fix failings that led to Floreat murders, DV advocates say Two women's murders at the hands of Mark Bombara must not go in vain, advocates for domestic violence victims and survivors say.

Earlier this month, a week-long coronial inquest investigated the murder of Jennifer Petelczyc and her daughter, Gretl, by Mark Bombara, who then fatally shot himself.

He had gone to their house in Floreat looking for his estranged wife, Rowena, who was a friend of Jennifer Petelczyc.

During the inquest, Kathryn Kraus, the lawyer representing Rowena Bombara and her daughter, Ariel said the double murder was preceded by years of domestic violence, including coercive and financial control.

World.title: Sam Wood's new lawyer says he wants to propose justice mediation
World.content:
Former Bachelor Sam Wood has proposed mediation as he faces serious domestic violence charges, allegedly committed against his wife.

Mr Wood, who normally resides in Melbourne, was holidaying at a Noosa apartment complex with his family last month when he was arrested.

The 46-year-old was charged with assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation.

Bradford Hill, from BJH Law, appeared before Maroochydore Magistrates Court for his new client Mr Wood.

Mr Hill told the court he had picked up the brief of evidence this morning and told the court they wanted to "propose justice mediation" to the prosecution.

Mr Hill told the court he was applying to have MPO Legal withdrawn as Mr Wood’s legal representation.

The charges were adjourned for two weeks.

Sam Wood's legal team leaves Maroochydore Magistrates Court after his matter was mentioned on Monday. (ABC News: Madeline Grace)

In Queensland, justice mediation provides an alleged offender the chance to discuss the matter with the victim, but only if the victim consents.

It is designed to bring together a person harmed by a crime and the person who caused the harm.

Mr Wood will remain remanded in custody after already spending nearly two months behind bars.

Bail decision adjourned

Mr Wood was refused bail at Maroochydore Magistrates Court last month and then again in the Supreme Court of Brisbane.

An appeal for the second bail refusal was heard in Queensland's Court of Appeal last week.

The prosecution maintained their arguments during the bail application that Mr Wood was at risk of reoffending and opposed the grounds of appeal.

Defence barrister Paula Morreau represented Sam Wood at the Court of Appeal. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Crown prosecutor Jessica Guy told the court a prison call, between Mr Wood and his father which was played in court last week, demonstrated he was at risk of interfering with witnesses and contacting them.

In the call Mr Wood said he needed to speak with his wife, and asked whether the domestic violence charges could be dropped if she changed her police statement.

Defence lawyer Paula Morreau KC said what Mr Wood said was "ill-judged", but argued he was "stating a desire, not requesting it".

She said it did not establish he would breach any bail conditions.

The decision was adjourned.

World.title: Drone strikes kill four in Khartoum and damage UN building
World.content:
Drone attacks on Sudan's capital, Khartoum, have killed at least four civilians and injured at least nine others, according to local reports, in the latest strikes that underscore how drones are reshaping the country's war.

The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group fighting the Sudanese army, was blamed for the attacks, which also damaged a United Nations building, the UN said in a statement.

Explosions were heard in the early hours as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and the city's airport.

Satellite imagery shows horrors of El-Fasher Satellite imagery has shown pools of blood in Sudan's El-Fasher, after the RSF militia took control. For relatives — finding out who has survived has turned into a torturous task.

Video shows a home reduced to rubble, with locals reporting residents trying to rescue family members trapped under the rubble.

The Sudanese military said the drones were launched from Ethiopia. The government has repeatedly accused its neighbour of allowing attacks to be staged from its territory. Addis Ababa denies the claim.

In a statement responding to Sunday's attack, the UN's coordinator for Sudan, Denise Brown, said drone strikes were causing "untold suffering".

Drone warfare has surged in recent months, accounting for 80 per cent of civilian deaths in the first half of the year.

Experts say both sides are being supplied with drones by countries in the Middle East and beyond, weaponry capable of striking targets at a distance without risking fighters.

Drone warfare on the rise

A report released by the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR) found drone attacks killed more than 1,630 civilians in Sudan between January and the end of October 2026.

The report said the use of drones had evolved this year, but the "unbearable toll of the war on the Sudanese people has remained as consistent as ever, amid flagrant disregard for the protection of civilians".

Reports of mass killings, rapes and starvation in Sudan Reports from the Sudanese city of El-Fasher of mass killings, rapes and other violence "may constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity", the International Criminal Court has warned.

Last month, 80 people were killed near a market in al-Dibab, in West Kordofan, in southern Sudan. It was one of at least 39 drone strikes on markets this year.

More than three years of fighting in Sudan has produced one of the world's most dire humanitarian situations and forced more than 14 million people from their homes.

Almost 34 million people need humanitarian assistance.

Human rights organisations have continuously warned of mass killings, indiscriminate attacks and reprisals against civilians.

The UN, rights organisations and journalists have documented widespread use of sexual violence as a weapon of war across conflict zones.

Aid organisations say the war has killed more than 200,000 people and pushed parts of the country into famine. It is likely the death toll is much higher.

The war began in April 2023 when a confrontation between two military leaders, army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, fractured into a complex conflict.

The Sudanese army secured Khartoum from the RSF in May 2025. Since then, an international presence has gradually returned to the capital along with 2.5 million returnees, according to the UN Refugee Agency as of October 2026.

The army now controls much of the east of the country, while the RSF dominates large parts of the west, including Darfur. Fighting continues, concentrated mostly in Darfur and Kordofan and now Blue Nile state, as the army advances across central Sudan.

World.title: Wet season warning of deadly mosquito virus in remote WA
World.content:
Health authorities are warning that Aboriginal children in Western Australia's north are the most vulnerable to contracting the potentially deadly Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV).

From November to March, the Kimberley wet season brings torrential rain and high humidity, creating ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes and cutting off road access for medical support.

Authorities are concerned about the potential for JEV, along with Murray Valley encephalitis and Ross River fever.

JEV is a mosquito-borne virus that can cause inflammation of the brain. However, humans are "dead-end hosts," meaning they cannot pass the disease on to other people.

While the immune systems of 99 per cent of those infected will clear the virus without symptoms, in 1 per cent of cases the virus crosses into the central nervous system.

This causes severe encephalitis, which carries a fatality rate of up to 30 per cent, according to Australia's Department of Health.

Health authorities are urging people in Western Australia's Kimberley region to avoid mosquito bites where possible. (Supplied: Stephen Doggett)

Despite there being no reported human infections of JEV in Western Australia, Department of Health medical entomologist Abbey Potter said Aboriginal children in remote Kimberley communities were the most likely to experience JEV symptoms.

"Based on the over-representation of Aboriginal children presenting with Murray Valley encephalitis, we would consider them to be the highest risk cohort for JEV," she said.

The disease spread to mainland Australia in 2022 following a five-year drought in the eastern states.

Abbey Potter says Aboriginal children living in remote Kimberley communities are among the most vulnerable to developing mosquito-borne symptoms. (Supplied)

The subsequent heavy rainfall and widespread flooding attracted nomadic native waterbirds, where the virus was transmitted from the birds to local mosquito populations and commercial piggeries.

There have been 11 recorded deaths across New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, and South Australia since the 2022 outbreak.

Mosquito-borne virus numbers

Over the past two years, two cases of Murray Valley encephalitis have been confirmed in the Kimberley region.

In February last year, the WA Department of Health confirmed a child was receiving medical treatment after acquiring "the infection in the east Kimberley region".

In June, a woman died from Murray Valley encephalitis after being infected while travelling in the West Kimberley.

Meanwhile, from January to June this year, there were 27 recorded infections of Ross River fever throughout the region.

Torrential rain and high humidity from November to March create ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes. (Supplied: Wayne Bishop)

Dr Potter said increased mosquito breeding in the wet season and communities becoming cut off were a concern.

"For those reasons, we are currently working with the Aboriginal environmental health sector to undertake surveillance in regional and remote WA, which is going to provide much more real-time data about virus activity in communities," she said.

She also highlighted the Department of Health's Fight the Bite campaign, which provides tips on avoiding mosquito bites and has rolled out free mosquito repellent to remote Kimberley communities.

The WA government is offering free insect repellent kits to community groups across the state. (ABC News: Charlie Mclean)

Community taking action

Djarindjin Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Nathan McIvor said the community, 200 kilometres north of Broome, took precautions to protect children.

"We educate our community, we go around to households and tell them to tip out any stagnant water, and to keep children inside during the early morning and early evening," he said.

"I've got a lot of mosquito repellent in my office that I hand out to people when they say they need some."

Nathan McIvor says messaging is in place to prompt people to avoid mosquito bites. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

He also encouraged residents to get vaccinated at Djarindjin's medical clinic against mosquito-borne diseases, following recent cases of viruses like Ross River in the community.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Defence barrister tells court ‘love makes fools of us all’ during closing address
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial.

The evidence in the trial has concluded and Justice Natalie Adams has predicted the jury will retire for their deliberations this week.

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were allegedly murdered by former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon.

Today, defence barrister John Stratton, SC, is delivering his closing address to the jury after the final hour of the Crown’s closing. The judge will deliver a summing up after Stratton concludes his address.

Lamarre-Condon, a former NSW police officer, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024.

Both men died of gunshot wounds from the accused’s police-issued Glock pistol.

Hatfield started his closing address last week by alleging that Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird and Davies were “in cold blood” after developing obsessive and jealous infatuation with Baird.

The court has heard that Baird ended his non-exclusive relationship with Lamarre-Condon in November 2023 after becoming aware of the accused’s attempts to ward off rivals for Baird’s romantic attention.

During his closing address, Hatfield alleged that Lamarre-Condon’s testimony about the men’s deaths was “a story put together afterwards to explain away two deliberate killings”.

The prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took steps to conceal his crimes before handing himself in to police on February 23, fours days after the alleged murders, as investigators closed in.

The accused disclosed the location of the men’s bodies after being told by police about the “no body, no parole” laws, Hatfield said, and the jury might think there was “self-interest in it for him”.

“The fact is, the bodies were left rotting for a further four days after he was arrested ... evidence all the while being destroyed on their bodies,” Hatfield said. “You can imagine the grief … that the families were going through.” The prosecutor submitted that to the extent Lamarre-Condon was attempting to rely on his disclosure of the bodies’ location as assisting him in relation to liability for murder, “it does nothing at all for him”.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Rainbow Sexual, Domestic and Family Violence Hotline (1800 497 212) and Lifeline (13 11 14).

World.title: Auric Mining gears up for December WA gold plant delivery
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Auric Mining gears up for December WA gold plant delivery Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor November 23, 2026 — 2:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Close Share A A A

Auric Mining has kicked its plan to become a standalone gold producer into high gear, revealing the relocation of a recently acquired processing plant to its Burbanks hub in Western Australia’s Goldfields is running ahead of schedule. The company says dismantling work on the infrastructure package, currently in Queensland, is now in its final phase, with transport to the Burbanks site, 9km south of Coolgardie, scheduled to begin in the first week of December. The move is a critical step in Auric’s plan to establish its own integrated mining and processing operation, centred on its flagship Munda gold mine. Auric Mining’s acquired mill deck structure being dismantled ahead of relocation to its Burbanks gold processing hub near Coolgardie in Western Australia. Specialist contractor Interquip has removed most conveyors and is dismantling the screening deck, which sorts crushed rock by size, while removal of the mill’s elevated steelwork nears completion. Machinery and structural components are being staged, packaged and preserved for transport. In the coming week, Auric says the contractor will finish dismantling the jaw crusher, which breaks large rocks into smaller pieces, together with its hopper and feeder, before tackling the remaining crushing shed and associated steelwork. Load-out preparations are running in parallel ahead of the first scheduled truck movements in December.



‘This project is a key component of our broader growth strategy and a cornerstone to establishing our own processing capability at Burbanks.’ Auric Mining managing director Mark English Auric snapped up the package just two months ago, securing a three-stage crushing circuit, mill deck structures, dust extraction system, critical spares, store inventory and supporting steelwork for a mere $1.2M. The buy followed its $4.4M acquisition of the historic Burbanks processing site in late 2024, giving Auric an established brownfields location for its proposed gold processing hub with existing power and water. Management expects the bargain-basement acquisition to deliver substantial capital savings, having previously estimated equivalent new equipment would cost $15M to $25M. That leaves serious daylight between the purchase price and replacement cost, even after allowing for refurbishment, relocation and installation expenses. Crucially, the machinery operated successfully for four years before dismantling. The company believes this will streamline reinstallation and reduce commissioning risks, while digital scans of the original concrete footing layouts should help engineers position the equipment accurately and fast-track reconstruction. Auric Mining managing director Mark English said: “This purchase and relocation of near-new infrastructure will deliver a substantial cost benefit relative to a new-build alternative while significantly reducing development lead times. This project is a key component of our broader growth strategy and a cornerstone to establishing our own processing capability at Burbanks.”



The historic facility previously handled 180,000 tonnes annually, and Auric’s July scoping study outlines a 600,000-tonne-per-annum carbon-in-leach operation using cyanide to extract gold. Management has flagged potential expansion to double capacity to 1.2 million tonnes, targeting first processing in April 2028, subject to approvals and funding. Auric has already demonstrated a knack for turning modest investments into serious returns. Its Jeffreys Find joint venture near Norseman turned a $1.2M investment into $16.5M in cash distributions, while Munda’s starter pit delivered 8886 ounces, a whopping 46 per cent above budget. Munda’s 192,000-ounce resource, 87km from Burbanks by road, is earmarked as cornerstone feed for the new-look Burbanks plant. Most recently, the company boosted its inventory, picking up the 102,000-ounce Union Jack resource just 15km away and acquiring Iron Maiden’s historical 68,500-ounce estimate near Norseman, pending due diligence. Auric finished September sitting on a healthy $33.05 million cash pile and no corporate debt, before securing commitments for a further $17 million through a two-tranche placement, partly subject to shareholder approval. A proposed $3 million share purchase plan could swell its war chest to about $53 million, giving the company plenty of financial firepower to push ahead with its Burbanks gold processing ambitions and exploration across its expanding Goldfields portfolio. Australia’s booming gold sector has put a premium on processing capacity and Auric believes owning its own mill could be an ace up its sleeve. It would give the company greater control of its destiny, freeing it from third-party processing bottlenecks, boosting potential margins and opening the door to additional regional ore sources.



With the plant components packed and ready to roll and a hefty pile of cash built from previous mining successes, Auric is putting together the pieces of its production puzzle. The arrival of the trucks at Burbanks in December will mark more than just a logistical milestone; it will represent the physical construction of a new Goldfields producer. World.title: Molly Meldrum dies aged 83
World.content:
Tributes to Australian music legend Ian “Molly” Meldrum have come from politicians, actors, sports clubs and pop stars following his death at the age of 83. The former Countdown host and Hey Hey It’s Saturday stalwart had long been in ill health and died at 5.30am on Monday at the Epworth Hospital in Richmond, in inner Melbourne. He will be granted a state funeral. Molly Meldrum has died aged 83. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Australian music legend, journalist, producer and cultural icon Ian Alexander ‘Molly’ Meldrum AM … He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him,” his family said via a statement shared with this masthead. “Affectionately dubbed ‘The Guru’, Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music. He shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them … He lived and breathed music, believing in its power to unite, to inspire and to lift up young musicians.”



Loading Born in Orbost in eastern Victoria in 1943, Meldrum became one of Australia’s most notable champions of music. Throughout his career, he worked as a music journalist, critic, record producer, television presenter and musical entrepreneur. Meldrum’s love of music began at an early age, when he would listen to musical soundtracks and opera pieces on his family’s gramophone. This passion continued to blossom when he picked up a job as a pop reporter at Go-Set magazine while studying law at the University of Melbourne. It was there that he adopted his nickname “Molly”, given to him by fellow Go-Set contributor Stan Rofe. Known as the “Peter Pan of Pop”, Meldrum went on to champion local and global artists alike, helping to boost major acts like AC/DC and Russell Morris, and also bringing international icons including Elton John and Madonna to Australian television.



Related Article Obituaries Rod Stewart persuaded Molly Meldrum to miss his flight and stay for dinner. It saved his life In 1974, he helped develop Countdown, working as a talent co-ordinator, interviewer and presenter on the show. Wearing his trademark Stetson hat, his catchphrase “do yourself a favour” went on to become a touchpoint in Australian pop-cultural history. Shortly after Countdown ended, Meldrum joined Hey Hey It’s Saturday, hosting the popular music and entertainment segment Molly’s Melodrama. He also hosted the Australian leg of Live Aid (Oz for Africa ) in 1985. Gavin Wood, who worked with Meldrum on Countdown, described his friend and former colleague as “one of the craziest, most colourful, funniest and most beautiful people you could ever have the pleasure of meeting”. There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him. Gavin Wood



“He was absolutely one of a kind, and it was a privilege to know him,” Wood wrote on Facebook. “What he has done for the Australian music industry is simply phenomenal. His contribution, passion, enthusiasm and unwavering commitment to Australian artists helped shape an entire generation of music and entertainment. “There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him. He was an original, a trailblazer and a true institution of Australian entertainment. Fly high my friend.” Meldrum was inducted to the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014. Getty In a tribute posted to X, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Meldrum “loved music almost as much as we loved him”. “He gave new artists a leg up and established artists a welcoming embrace. And over the years... he became a central part of the Australian soundtrack. We were lucky to have him,” Albanese wrote.



One of his most memorable TV moments was in 1977 during a Countdown interview with His Majesty King Charles III, then the Prince of Wales. Visibly nervous, Meldrum was seen stumbling through takes. The moment became so iconic that the Prince later joked about it during Countdown’s 40th anniversary special. Singer Marcia Hines thanked Meldrum for “everything that he did for us all in the Australian music industry and worldwide”. “Can’t believe that he has gone,” she wrote in a tribute on Facebook. “Rest in peace, my friend. You’ll be missed.” Loading Posting on Instagram, singer Kate Ceberano recalled “travelling across town by tram and bus to stand in a queue outside ABC studios to watch this man on Countdown, our mighty guru of all things music, our gateway to the stars, our ringleader, our bumbling stumbling FAN of artists of all shapes and colour”. “He simply wanted the world to hear what he could hear, wanted you to see what he was looking at and then blow it up to 11... He was the fan all artists wish to have. They don’t make ’em like that any more. My heart is aching today at the loss.”



Federal Arts Minister Tony Burke, meanwhile, said the country had lost an icon. “For generations of Australians, Molly was more than a familiar face on our television screens. He was an advocate of Australian music, talent scout, journalist, producer and broadcaster who helped shape the soundtrack of our nation,” he said. “One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music. A true champion of Australian talent, you will be missed, but never forgotten.” Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said in a post that Meldrum’s family had asked for a state funeral and that he would honour that wish. “On Sunday nights, you’d switch on Countdown and there was Molly in his hat, telling you about a band he reckoned you’d love. By Monday morning, people were lining up at the record shop asking for the song he’d played. Imagine what it meant if that was your song… A giant of the Australian music industry and a true character.” Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson paid her respects in a statement, saying “Australia has lost a legend, and Victoria has lost one of its favourite sons”. “Molly brought music, laughter and joy into the living rooms of millions of Australians, while championing generations of Australian musicians… Above all, he will be remembered for his generosity, his warmth and the enormous affection Australians held for him.”



Related Article 'Supposedly I'm an icon … I don't like that': Molly Meldrum Though largely known for his time on the screen, Meldrum also produced Russell Morris’ hit The Real Thing, which climbed to No. 1 on the Australian charts in 1969. Entertainment reporter Richard Wilkins, speaking on Nine’s Today show, said Australian music would not be what it is without Meldrum’s “incredible contribution over the years”. “On a personal note, I shared so many overseas trips with Molly, which was a joy and a curse – he lost 13 passports, that was the tally I got to.” Promoter Paul Dainty said in a statement that Meldrum’s contribution to music was immeasurable. “He championed artists, broke new ground, brought music into people’s homes and lives, and gave generations of musicians a platform and an audience. His influence reached far beyond Australia, and his legacy will live on through the artists he supported and the millions of people he inspired.” The St Kilda Saints, the AFL team Meldrum famously supported, paid tribute saying he “changed and brightened the lives of so many across a storied career.”



Meldrum in 1978. Meldrum also supported rugby league in its formative years in Victoria. Melbourne Storm chief executive Justin Rodski said Meldrum was a long term No.1 ticket holder, saying he “embraced Melbourne Storm with genuine passion, pride and enthusiasm”. American band Blondie shared their sadness at the news, saying “Molly was instrumental in Blondie’s success in Australia, championing our music and introducing us to a whole new audience. We will always be grateful for his belief in us and the doors he helped open.” Iva Davies, frontman of Icehouse, said on X that Meldrum “was such a bright, larger than life figure in our Australian music scene for so many years with positive influence on so many careers via his work on Countdown, as a journalist, producer, advocate and friend”. Australian pop group Human Nature also honoured Meldrum, who championed them during their rise in the ’90s. “He was such a huge presence in the Australian music industry and was a great friend and supporter of so many up-and-coming bands and artists – ourselves included. Thanks for everything Molly. Rest easy,” the group wrote on Facebook.



Actor Jason Donovan also paid tribute, reflecting the experience of many Australians, saying Countdown was a big part of his childhood. “A truly unique character… there will never be another quite like him. I have some wonderful memories of Molly over the years. I particularly remember him appearing on Neighbours alongside Kylie, Guy and myself ... Always spirited, full of fun, with a wonderful sense of humour and an infectious enthusiasm for life.” Meldrum had lived with an acquired brain injury, the result of a fall from the roof of a pool house at his home in 2011 that left him in an induced coma for weeks. He was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 1986, and was the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014. World.title: Suspended Swans return for pre-season training as Hawks welcome Merrett, King and Hodge
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2027 Suspended Swans return for pre-season training as Hawks welcome Merrett, King and Hodge Jonathan Drennan and Jon Pierik Updated November 23, 2026 — 1:24pm ,first published 11:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. In today’s AFL briefing: Swans stars Heeney and Warner return from banishment

Hawks recruits hit the track as focus turns to body language Pullman quartet return to track alongside Papley Jonathan Drennan Sydney Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon trained officially with the club for the first time on Monday since being cleared, along with North Melbourne recruit Nick Blakey, of criminal conduct by Victoria Police after a night of partying at the Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Isaac Heeney arrives at Bat and Ball Oval with teammates for first day of pre-season. Janie Barrett



Tom Papley also trained with the squad for the first time since the AFL suspended him for the first three games of the 2027 season after police caught him driving with cocaine and MDMA in his system earlier this month. Papley has been summoned to appear before Waverley Local Court this Thursday. Papley’s suspension is the strongest penalty imposed on a player caught on a public drugs matter. Chad Warner at training on Monday morning. Janie Barrett The Swans banned the “Pullman Five” for the remainder of the season in August for breaching the club’s behavioural standards, and were also barred from All-Australian honours. Speaking to this masthead, Warner said he was looking forward to repaying the faith of his teammates during his suspension.



“We’ve been training with everyone probably for a couple of months now over at Centennial [Park],” Warner said. “Everyone’s getting back in the groove, gelling, and I can’t wait [for pre-season], to be honest. “The boys have been great, and I think from the start they’ve all just wanted to do what they can, really. Tom Papley at the Swans firs pre-season training session on Monday. Janie Barrett “There’s obviously a lot of things people can’t do as well, so everyone’s in a tough position, but I think that’s the best thing about mates and teammates like this – they’re always going to have your back.” Bice, Jordon, Heeney and Warner are all free to play in the round one clash against Geelong at the SCG on March 17.



Warner arrived early to training to complete running drills on the oval that is commonly used for community football, while Papley arrived with a heavily strapped right knee and left the session early. Blakey began training with North Melbourne on November 9, joining the club’s first- to fourth-year players who started pre-season earlier than the Swans because they did not qualify for the finals. Loading Warner and Heeney trained with senior teammates in an unofficial session at Centennial Park last week. Monday was the first day of official pre-season for first- to fourth-year players. The rest of the Swans senior players including Errol Gulden, James Rowbottom and Brodie Grundy will return to training next Monday.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The AFL has an equalisation problem. This is what it has to do next Michael Gleeson Sports columnist Asked last week about the reintegration of Heeney, Warner and Jordon into the club, Swans AFLW star Chloe Molloy said her primary concern was ensuring the culture of her squad was protected. “I have no idea [how reintegrating Heeney, Warner, Jordon will go],” Molloy said. “All I know is there is a culture within the [AFL]W program that I want to nurture and be a part of.” More to come



Recruits on track as Hawks focus on body language Jon Pierik Hawthorn hope they can respond in the manner of their 2012 brethren, as fitness staff demanded strong body language after a gruelling running drill to finish the opening morning of official pre-season training. Back to business: Star forward Nick Watson was among the first-to-four-year players who officially returned to training on Monday. Getty Images While Monday technically was the return date for first-to-fourth-year players at the Hawks’ Dingley training base, there were several blue-chip stars who also took part in the intense two-hour session under a beating sun, complete with annoying flies.



The Hawks have redemption on their mind in 2027 after successive preliminary final defeats, the pain of which was similar to those who experienced the 2012 grand final loss to the Swans, this spurring a hat-trick of flags. David Hale, now the Hawks strategy and opposition coach, but a member of that ’12 team and of the ensuing three premiership sides, said he could sense the added drive this squad led by coach Sam Mitchell has. View post on X “Any time you get that close to what you want to do and succeed in, that motivation grows stronger. I was a part of a group in 2012 that was the same. You know, the next three years panned out well for us then,” Hale said. “This group, as well, wants to taste success. So, hopefully, setting a good foundation now will put them in a good position come that time of year [finals] again.”



High-profile recruits Ben King and Zach Merrett were among the big names who impressed, King working well inside 50m alongside Nick Watson. Fellow forwards Jack Gunston and Mabior Chol were not on the field, while Jack Ginnivan, Blake Hardwick and Tom Barrass are also not required to return to training until next week. Related Article Draft Luke Hodge’s son officially a Hawk; Drums and ‘duxes’ on frenetic AFL draft night An injury-free James Sicily moved well, while his co-captain Jai Newcombe ran laps for nearly an hour. Frankston defender Jackson Voss has been invited to train with the club in a bid to win a supplementary selection period list spot, while the small smattering of fans were delighted to watch Conor Nash after the Irishman’s season ended in August because of a neck injury, which required surgery. He recently returned home to be married, but has been working diligently over the off-season. “Yeah, he [Nash] has always been a very important player for the role that he plays, that big-bodied defensive mid who can put pressure on around the ball,” Hale said.



“Obviously, the [Cam] McKenzie and [Josh] Ward types we saw flourish in the back end of last year in his absence, but he’s a quality player, and we know what he can bring when he’s up and going.” Draftees Cooper Hodge, the son of four-time premiership great Luke, and ruckman Benji van Rooyen, the younger brother of Melbourne star Jacob, also took to the track and showed glimpses of why they were highly-rated selections last week. Conor Nash trained well upon his return from neck surgery on Monday. Getty Images The Hawks worked through a series of drills on all aspects of their game, Hale expecting the league-wide trend towards greater scoring, including through more forward handballs or greater numbers at the contest, to continue next season. What is already clear is that the Hawks are a gifted running team, and will again look to use this to their advantage.



While general fitness and football fitness are crucial, coaches also want strong body language after completing gut-wrenching runs, the Hawks breaking into groups at the end of their session to complete a series of interval “aerobic power” lap running. Related Article AFL 2026 Your AFL club’s list is taking shape, but there could be some late plot twists yet “I’m not sure it’s better [Hawks’ fitness compared to rivals], but our running profile has always been something we’ve spoken about as a group. It can be an advantage, whether that’s at the end of the first quarter, the end of the last quarter,” Hale said. “So, against the best, you know, it might come down to, as you said, in the prelim finals in the last 30 seconds. So, that’s why they [players] run around ovals, and that’s why they have to keep a smile on their face at this time of year.” When players were allowed to briefly regain their breath after completing bursts of running, for instance, over four minutes, then three minutes, fitness coaches loudly reminded them about “body language” and to “stay up”, with few players collapsing to their haunches or bent over with hands on knees.



Hale said projecting an unrelenting image to opponents was important. “Yeah, it’s a battle within your own head, but it’s a battle within the group as well to make sure we keep pushing ourselves to get better,” Hale said. Former Hawthorn star Tom Mitchell sparked a furore this month when he criticised the West Coast Eagles for their poor body language after exhausted players crashed to the turf, having completed a gruelling series of sprints. World.title: What to stream this week: Amy Poehler’s five-star comedy, plus five more picks
World.content:
What to stream this week (clockwise from top left): Primetime Preacher$; Sweetpea; Dead Man’s Wire; The Slightest Touch; Dig; and Oobah - Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This week’s picks include Amy Poehler’s best work since Parks and Recreation, a series by gonzo British filmmaker Oobah Butler, a stylish true-crime thriller by Gus Van Sant, the second season of the black comedy Sweetpea and a moving documentary featuring Colin Farrell. Dig ★★★★★ (Binge) Amy Poehler is back. Yes, she’s been everywhere in the 2020s, busy launching the world’s biggest podcast (Good Hang), directing films, lending her voice to a $US1.6 billion ($2.38 billion) box office hit (Inside Out 2) and, among other things, hosting two reality competitions I had no idea existed (Making It and Baking It). But none of those has matched the comedy magic of Parks and Recreation – the beloved mockumentary running from 2009 to 2015 following a handful of Indiana public servants, led by Poehler as the ever-optimistic Leslie Knope. Until now. Amy Poehler plays archeologist Elise, who is overseeing a dig in Greece, using a series of American undergraduates as free labour. Created by Poehler with Parks’ co-creator Michael Schur, Dig is a rare, special show: an instantly at-ease comedy with a unique premise, relentless jokes, a warm, gooey centre and terrific cast chemistry. Poehler plays Elise, an archeologist helping her boss Neville – a delightfully pompous Hugh Laurie – oversee their annual dig in Greece, using a series of useless American undergraduates as free labour in the brutal, sweltering heat.



Despite the advances of hunky, romantic mayor Stavros (Kayvan Novak), Elise is single-minded. “You know my motto! Work hard and never have fun,” she says, with much more acidity than Leslie Knope ever mustered. Related Article ★★★

Review A Netflix drama about jailed crypto billionaires is an easy sell, but The Altruists offers something more complex If only something were to shake her up: if the shock of the Papyrus title credits weren’t enough, perhaps Dig’s flash-forward opening, seemingly involving a dead body, will be? Don’t mind that too much: it’s mostly poking fun at the overused TV trope. Dig doesn’t really need mystery to propel itself anyway once it glides back to the camp’s first day, where Elise is surprised to see Dylan, a 29-year-old chaos magnet who ghosted the dig five years ago. Played by Australia’s Geraldine Viswanathan (Miracle Workers), Dylan is all energy with no direction or patience: “Let’s press double-speed on the podcast,” she says while someone’s speaking. Meanwhile, Dylan’s ex-fiance (Jon Pointing) is now engaged to her antithesis, Claire – an uptight preservationist played by Antonia Thomas, who between this and Two Weeks in August has found a niche as a posh British woman in Greece. Then there’s Patty (Fina Strazza), a baby-voiced undergraduate whose only friends back home are her cows and who is completely overwhelmed by any task given to her. Hugh Laurie plays Neville, the pompous boss of Elise (Amy Poehler), in Dig. Before long, the four become unlikely allies, working on a secret dig together. It’s this core dynamic that feels most like the Parks and Recreation magic, as these ridiculous characters develop very genuine, heartfelt friendships while sneaking around.



Dig’s 10 episodes feel like the show’s natural end, but it’s difficult to not hope Elise and co return for one more archaeological hunt. Parks and Recreation helped catapult Chris Pratt, Aubrey Plaza, Aziz Ansari and Adam Scott into leading roles. With such a dynamic cast and sharp, confident comedy, a season or two more of Dig would do the same for Viswanathan, Thomas and Strazza. Gonzo documentarian Oobah Butler’s new series is his funniest, most outrageous work yet. Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow ★★★★ (HBO Max) Gonzo British filmmaker Oobah Butler has made a career from elaborate hoaxes, first generating headlines in 2017 with a prank for Vice Magazine in which he gamed TripAdvisor’s reviews to turn the shed in his shabby backyard into The Shed at Dulwich, briefly London’s top-rated restaurant on the site. Related Article ★★★

Review The villain in this show will make your blood boil. But it’s not a person Butler’s since moved beyond YouTube with outrageous Channel 4 specials (How I Made £1 Million in 90 Days), but his first TV series – produced by A24, with a noticeably bigger budget – might be his funniest, most outrageous work yet. A cross between The Chaser’s most outlandish pranks and Nathan For You (Nathan Fielder’s surreal reality series helping struggling businesses), Scams For a Better Tomorrow’s five episodes each focus on a new money-making scheme.



Most are inspired by decidedly 2026 scams, such as an “AI-powered” dating app wholly reliant on overworked humans, or manufacturing hype around Butler’s rap project inspired by the music industry’s use of bot farms. Some are timeless, such as Butler pretending to be a Cambodian prince, revealing a world of questionable royal titles used for royal treatment. Just don’t be turned off by the pilot, focused on skincare and wellness. The slightly condescending revelations (did you know clinical trials can be fudged?) and mean-spirited jabs at influencers give way to more focused, wittier pranks that punch up, depending on your view of wine critics. Dacre Montgomery (left) and Bill Skarsgaard in Dead Man’s Wire. Dead Man’s Wire ★★★★ (Netflix) An enigmatic cast – including Bill Skarsgaard, Colman Domingo, Industry star Myha’la and Australia’s Dacre Montgomery – leads Gus Van Sant’s latest film, a stylish true-crime thriller inspired by a 1977 hostage situation that unfolded live on US airwaves for three days. (Sound familiar? Jon Hamm recently led American Hostage, a sluggish TV take on the same event.) Darkly funny with an eat-the-rich bent, Dead Man’s Wire doubles as Van Sant’s ode to a ’70s crime drama, full of claustrophobic close-ups, freeze-frames and a cameo from Dog Day Afternoon’s lead Al Pacino. Tammy Faye Bakker and her then-husband, television evangelist Jim Bakker, in 1986. AP



Primetime Preacher$ ★★★ (Netflix) A true-crime pioneer, filmmaker Joe Berlinger has been in Netflix’s content mines since 2019, producing glossy explainers on Jeffrey Epstein, Ted Bundy and more notorious figures. His latest turns towards scandals surrounding American televangelists in the ’80s. Despite a wider framing, it’s focused on Jim Bakker, a prosperity gospel preacher who defrauded believers of hundreds of millions. It’s a fascinating story, albeit one told many times before, including in the recent Oscar-winner The Eyes of Tammy Faye, focused on Bakker’s eccentric wife. Best suited for the unfamiliar, though interviews with Bakker’s ex-security and son are illuminating. Ella Purnell in Sweetpea. Sweetpea ★★ (Binge) Starring Ella Purnell (Yellowjackets, Fallout) as a British wallflower-turned-serial killer, Sweetpea is a vantablack comedy: Darkness so intense it could be mistaken for depth, though it’s hard to discern what meaning it contains. Season two picks up where we left Rhiannon in 2024, standing bloodied over a body as her sister enters their family home. Despite Purnell’s talents, Rhiannon remains the show’s main issue: a feminist-ish Dexter who isn’t particularly cunning or controlled, with little perverse thrill in watching her evade detection, or, in this season, confront a copycat killer. Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell in the documentary The Slightest Touch.

World.title: Body found after two men jumped off Princes Bridge into the Yarra
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaVictoria Police Body found after two men jumped off Princes Bridge into the Yarra Shelby Brooks and James Costa November 23, 2026 — 1:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The body of a 26-year-old man is believed to have been recovered from the Yarra River at Southbank, the day after two men were seen jumping from Princes Bridge on Sunday morning. While the body is yet to be formally identified, police said it was believed to be a man who jumped into the river with his 30-year-old friend on Sunday. Loading The death is not being treated as suspicious and a report would be prepared for the coroner, police said. Witnesses reported seeing two men jump into the river from Princes Bridge on St Kilda Road in the CBD at about 11.45am on Sunday. Only one of the men emerged from the water.



A bystander on Southbank said she saw a third man jump into the river to help, and was able to pull the surviving man from the water. Police divers and search and rescue squads searched the water for the missing man on Sunday and again on Monday morning, before the body was recovered. A witness said they saw a bystander jump in and help one man out of the water. Shelby Brooks One passerby, Brooke Humphrey, told The Age that two men she believed to be drunk had approached her husband on Princes Bridge around 10.50am on Sunday. “[They] asked my partner if he wanted to jump off the bridge with them into the water. My partner said, ‘No thanks, it doesn’t sound like a great idea’,” Humphrey said.



“I thought they were joking, and it was just drunken rambling.” Related Article Victoria Police Police scouring Yarra after two men spotted jumping off Princes Bridge Melbourne’s Lord Mayor Nick Reece told ABC 774 on Monday that he had spoken to police over the weekend and that the family were “quite traumatised by this”. “An investigation is still underway, so I’m constrained in what I can say,” Reece said. One onlooker told the ABC he saw two men jump from the bridge, and said one looked as though he tumbled into the water and began to struggle moments after he broke to the surface.



“His mate tried to help him but unsuccessfully and after a little while he just didn’t come back up,” he told the ABC. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Former reality TV star Sam Wood is seeking mediation as he fights serious domestic violence charges for allegedly strangling his wife. The Melbourne-based fitness influencer has made the request days after his distressed prison call, where he asked to speak to his wife, was heard in court. Sam Wood (right) rose to fame on the third season of The Bachelor in 2015, where he and Snezana Wood (left) met. Getty Images Wood, 46, has spent seven weeks in custody since being arrested during a family holiday in Noosa. He is accused of strangling his wife Snezana, whom he met on Network Ten’s hit reality show The Bachelor in 2015.



Wood did not appear at Maroochydore Magistrates Court on Monday when his lawyer Brad Hill sought a two-week adjournment, proposing justice mediation to the prosecution. Related Article Queensland courts ‘Need to be able to talk to my wife’: Wood’s desperate plea from behind bars played in court Justice mediation in Queensland provides a chance for the alleged offender and victim to discuss the matter, but can only occur if the latter consents. Wood’s matter was adjourned until December 7 and he remains in custody. It came after a court heard a phone call Wood made from jail to his father saying: “I need to be able to talk to my wife”.



The call was played when his request for release reached Queensland’s Court of Appeal on November 17 after two lower courts had denied him bail. “There is no way she would want this,” Wood told his father Andrew in the October 30 call. “We had a bad fight but if she thought I was going to jail, there would be no way.” Snezana and Sam Wood in 2016. Hausmann Communications A highly distressed Wood discussed in the call activities that could breach his proposed bail conditions, including a ban on contacting Snezana.



“If she changes her statement, the police would not have a leg to stand on,” he said, at times sobbing. Justice David Boddice said at the latest bail application Wood could be heard discussing his wife making a statutory declaration that the alleged choking did not happen. “That is classic interfering with witnesses,” he said. A decision on bail has been reserved. An earlier hearing was told Wood allegedly shut a door between himself and Snezana, and her daughter Eve Markoski-Wood while they were on holiday in Noosa on October 3.



He then allegedly grabbed his wife by the throat and pushed her against the wall. “She felt his grip become tighter. It’s alleged the complainant couldn’t breathe anymore and couldn’t yell out for help,” Justice Patrick McCafferty said in his October 30 decision to deny Wood bail. Former Bachelor star Sam Wood has been wiped from his former fitness program following domestic violence charges. It was alleged Wood told Snezana and her daughter they could both die. Wood earned a national profile as a star of The Bachelor’s third season in 2015, launching a successful home fitness business, 28 by Sam Wood.



He reportedly sold it in 2022 for more than $70m but remained the face of the online platform. The platform was rebranded in late October, removing all references to Wood. Snezana also built her own large profile, gaining more than 330,000 followers on Instagram. She has not posted since the alleged assault. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2027 Perth finally land their marquee man as PNG’s next target plays golf with PM Dan Walsh and Christian Nicolussi Updated November 23, 2026 — 1:06pm ,first published 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Perth Bears have landed their first marquee signing, with Matt Burton to join the club from 2028, as Hudson Young officially signed a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs after his management asked the Canberra Raiders over the weekend to waive the ten-day cooling-off period. After several weeks of negotiations, Burton has told Canterbury he will link with the incoming Bears on a three-year deal worth at least $1.2 million per year, sources not authorised to comment publicly have confirmed to this masthead. Matt Burton is off to the Bears in 2028. NRL Photos Burton is yet to officially sign his new contract, but has committed his future to the fledgling franchise in an agreement which will take advantage of the 20 per cent marquee salary cap allowance granted to the Bears by the NRL after their initial struggles in the player market. The 26-year-old was wooed by coach Mal Meninga and former Bulldogs teammates Toby Sexton and Josh Curran on a recent tour of the WA capital and the deal, which will have an additional two-year option in his favour, has proved too lucrative to turn down.



Perth have the ability to accommodate Burton immediately for their inaugural 2027 season. But as it stands, Canterbury plan to keep the centre/five-eighth on their books next year. Young, meanwhile, visited Port Moresby more than a fortnight ago, and told this masthead upon returning to Sydney, “It is in the back of my mind I can do two or three years up there and come home and be mortgage free”. Hudson Young is set to ink a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs. The 28-year-old will see out 2027 in Canberra before moving to the NRL newcomers on a tax-free deal worth $1 million a season. PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters said he was looking forward to working with Young again after their time together with the Australian Test side in 2025.



“I really enjoyed working with Hudson during my time in Kangaroos camp last year and can’t wait to see him continue his career in a PNG Chiefs jersey,” Peters said. “Hudson plays with an aggressive style which I have no doubt the people of Papua New Guinea will love to see. He will be an important leader in our group, and I look forward to working with him in season 2028 and beyond.” Chiefs target AJ Brimson. Getty Images Young’s signature comes on the same day another Chiefs target, AJ Brimson, spent the day enjoying a round of golf with Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape. Brimson is expected to sign a three-year deal worth about $2.1 million after being granted permission by the Gold Coast Titans to explore a move to the Chiefs. The Queensland Origin and England international is determined to be the Chiefs’ first-choice No.1.



Brimson’s move to PNG will free up funds for the Titans to pursue Storm skipper Harry Grant. The game’s best hooker comes off-contract at the end of 2027, met with Gold Coast powerbrokers last Friday and could make a call as early as this week on whether he takes up a lucrative extension at Melbourne or a three-year Titans offer worth more than $3 million. It has been a busy few days for the Chiefs after Broncos pair Deine Mariner and Xavier Willison, along with North Queensland’s representative back-rower Jeremiah Nanai, all inspected the club’s facilities. The club also met Sam Walker for the first time last Tuesday in Brisbane before the halfback boarded a flight to the US to celebrate the Sydney Roosters’ premiership success. Walker is also weighing up interest from the Roosters’ bitter rivals, South Sydney. Roosters halfback Sam Walker has met with the Chiefs and has fielded interest from South Sydney Getty Images Raiders officials confirmed Young’s management asked for the cooling-off period to be waived, which means the Chiefs can announce their biggest forward signing to date.



Canberra had tabled Young a club-record $4.4 million four-year deal – and were prepared to go to a fifth year. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Cricket NSW says North Sydney Oval will always be off limit for the Bears The club is happy to extend Simi Sasagi, Noah Martin, Zac Hosking and Matt Nicholson. There were reports the Raiders were keen on Brisbane’s Jordan Riki and Cronulla’s Briton Nikora on 2028, but there is little interest from the club. Canberra coach Ricky Stuart is expected to meet Penrith’s four-time premiership winner Liam Martin in the coming weeks about potentially replacing Young in the back row. Martin has made it known he wants to re-commit to the Panthers, but is open to having a conversation with Stuart and moving closer to his hometown of Temora.



Canberra are in the market for middle forwards, with Wests Tigers prop Bunty Afoa put in their shop window by the Kiwi’s management team. Meanwhile, the Tigers and Manly are close to agreeing a deal for Jamal Fogarty, with the Sea Eagles prepared to pay part of the halfback’s wage the next two seasons. The Tigers have since granted Latu Fainu permission to seek a deal for 2027 only before returning to the joint venture. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Defence barrister tells court ‘love makes fools of us all’ during closing address
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial.

The evidence in the trial has concluded and Justice Natalie Adams has predicted the jury will retire for their deliberations this week.

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies were allegedly murdered by former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon.

Today, defence barrister John Stratton, SC, is delivering his closing address to the jury after the final hour of the Crown’s closing. The judge will deliver a summing up after Stratton concludes his address.

Lamarre-Condon, a former NSW police officer, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the shooting deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024.

Both men died of gunshot wounds from the accused’s police-issued Glock pistol.

Hatfield started his closing address last week by alleging that Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird and Davies were “in cold blood” after developing obsessive and jealous infatuation with Baird.

The court has heard that Baird ended his non-exclusive relationship with Lamarre-Condon in November 2023 after becoming aware of the accused’s attempts to ward off rivals for Baird’s romantic attention.

During his closing address, Hatfield alleged that Lamarre-Condon’s testimony about the men’s deaths was “a story put together afterwards to explain away two deliberate killings”.

The prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took steps to conceal his crimes before handing himself in to police on February 23, fours days after the alleged murders, as investigators closed in.

The accused disclosed the location of the men’s bodies after being told by police about the “no body, no parole” laws, Hatfield said, and the jury might think there was “self-interest in it for him”.

“The fact is, the bodies were left rotting for a further four days after he was arrested ... evidence all the while being destroyed on their bodies,” Hatfield said. “You can imagine the grief … that the families were going through.” The prosecutor submitted that to the extent Lamarre-Condon was attempting to rely on his disclosure of the bodies’ location as assisting him in relation to liability for murder, “it does nothing at all for him”.

World.title: Auric Mining gears up for December WA gold plant delivery
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Auric Mining gears up for December WA gold plant delivery Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor November 23, 2026 — 2:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Auric Mining has kicked its plan to become a standalone gold producer into high gear, revealing the relocation of a recently acquired processing plant to its Burbanks hub in Western Australia’s Goldfields is running ahead of schedule. The company says dismantling work on the infrastructure package, currently in Queensland, is now in its final phase, with transport to the Burbanks site, 9km south of Coolgardie, scheduled to begin in the first week of December. The move is a critical step in Auric’s plan to establish its own integrated mining and processing operation, centred on its flagship Munda gold mine. Auric Mining’s acquired mill deck structure being dismantled ahead of relocation to its Burbanks gold processing hub near Coolgardie in Western Australia. Specialist contractor Interquip has removed most conveyors and is dismantling the screening deck, which sorts crushed rock by size, while removal of the mill’s elevated steelwork nears completion. Machinery and structural components are being staged, packaged and preserved for transport. In the coming week, Auric says the contractor will finish dismantling the jaw crusher, which breaks large rocks into smaller pieces, together with its hopper and feeder, before tackling the remaining crushing shed and associated steelwork. Load-out preparations are running in parallel ahead of the first scheduled truck movements in December.



‘This project is a key component of our broader growth strategy and a cornerstone to establishing our own processing capability at Burbanks.’ Auric Mining managing director Mark English Auric snapped up the package just two months ago, securing a three-stage crushing circuit, mill deck structures, dust extraction system, critical spares, store inventory and supporting steelwork for a mere $1.2M. The buy followed its $4.4M acquisition of the historic Burbanks processing site in late 2024, giving Auric an established brownfields location for its proposed gold processing hub with existing power and water. Management expects the bargain-basement acquisition to deliver substantial capital savings, having previously estimated equivalent new equipment would cost $15M to $25M. That leaves serious daylight between the purchase price and replacement cost, even after allowing for refurbishment, relocation and installation expenses. Crucially, the machinery operated successfully for four years before dismantling. The company believes this will streamline reinstallation and reduce commissioning risks, while digital scans of the original concrete footing layouts should help engineers position the equipment accurately and fast-track reconstruction. Auric Mining managing director Mark English said: “This purchase and relocation of near-new infrastructure will deliver a substantial cost benefit relative to a new-build alternative while significantly reducing development lead times. This project is a key component of our broader growth strategy and a cornerstone to establishing our own processing capability at Burbanks.”



The historic facility previously handled 180,000 tonnes annually, and Auric’s July scoping study outlines a 600,000-tonne-per-annum carbon-in-leach operation using cyanide to extract gold. Management has flagged potential expansion to double capacity to 1.2 million tonnes, targeting first processing in April 2028, subject to approvals and funding. Auric has already demonstrated a knack for turning modest investments into serious returns. Its Jeffreys Find joint venture near Norseman turned a $1.2M investment into $16.5M in cash distributions, while Munda’s starter pit delivered 8886 ounces, a whopping 46 per cent above budget. Munda’s 192,000-ounce resource, 87km from Burbanks by road, is earmarked as cornerstone feed for the new-look Burbanks plant. Most recently, the company boosted its inventory, picking up the 102,000-ounce Union Jack resource just 15km away and acquiring Iron Maiden’s historical 68,500-ounce estimate near Norseman, pending due diligence. Auric finished September sitting on a healthy $33.05 million cash pile and no corporate debt, before securing commitments for a further $17 million through a two-tranche placement, partly subject to shareholder approval. A proposed $3 million share purchase plan could swell its war chest to about $53 million, giving the company plenty of financial firepower to push ahead with its Burbanks gold processing ambitions and exploration across its expanding Goldfields portfolio. Australia’s booming gold sector has put a premium on processing capacity and Auric believes owning its own mill could be an ace up its sleeve. It would give the company greater control of its destiny, freeing it from third-party processing bottlenecks, boosting potential margins and opening the door to additional regional ore sources.



With the plant components packed and ready to roll and a hefty pile of cash built from previous mining successes, Auric is putting together the pieces of its production puzzle. The arrival of the trucks at Burbanks in December will mark more than just a logistical milestone; it will represent the physical construction of a new Goldfields producer.
