Perth Bears have landed their first marquee signing, with Matt Burton to join the club from 2028, as Hudson Young officially signed a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs after his management asked the Canberra Raiders over the weekend to waive the ten-day cooling-off period. After several weeks of negotiations, Burton has told Canterbury he will link with the incoming Bears on a three-year deal worth at least $1.2 million per year, sources not authorised to comment publicly have confirmed to this masthead. Matt Burton is off to the Bears in 2028. NRL Photos Burton is yet to officially sign his new contract, but has committed his future to the fledgling franchise in an agreement which will take advantage of the 20 per cent marquee salary cap allowance granted to the Bears by the NRL after their initial struggles in the player market. The 26-year-old was wooed by coach Mal Meninga and former Bulldogs teammates Toby Sexton and Josh Curran on a recent tour of the WA capital and the deal, which will have an additional two-year option in his favour, has proved too lucrative to turn down.



Perth have the ability to accommodate Burton immediately for their inaugural 2027 season. But as it stands, Canterbury plan to keep the centre/five-eighth on their books next year. Young, meanwhile, visited Port Moresby more than a fortnight ago, and told this masthead upon returning to Sydney, “It is in the back of my mind I can do two or three years up there and come home and be mortgage free”. Hudson Young is set to ink a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs. The 28-year-old will see out 2027 in Canberra before moving to the NRL newcomers on a tax-free deal worth $1 million a season. PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters said he was looking forward to working with Young again after their time together with the Australian Test side in 2025.



“I really enjoyed working with Hudson during my time in Kangaroos camp last year and can’t wait to see him continue his career in a PNG Chiefs jersey,” Peters said. “Hudson plays with an aggressive style which I have no doubt the people of Papua New Guinea will love to see. He will be an important leader in our group, and I look forward to working with him in season 2028 and beyond.” Chiefs target AJ Brimson. Getty Images Young’s signature comes on the same day another Chiefs target, AJ Brimson, spent the day enjoying a round of golf with Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape. Brimson is expected to sign a three-year deal worth about $2.1 million after being granted permission by the Gold Coast Titans to explore a move to the Chiefs. The Queensland Origin and England international is determined to be the Chiefs’ first-choice No.1.



Brimson’s move to PNG will free up funds for the Titans to pursue Storm skipper Harry Grant. The game’s best hooker comes off-contract at the end of 2027, met with Gold Coast powerbrokers last Friday and could make a call as early as this week on whether he takes up a lucrative extension at Melbourne or a three-year Titans offer worth more than $3 million. It has been a busy few days for the Chiefs after Broncos pair Deine Mariner and Xavier Willison, along with North Queensland’s representative back-rower Jeremiah Nanai, all inspected the club’s facilities. The club also met Sam Walker for the first time last Tuesday in Brisbane before the halfback boarded a flight to the US to celebrate the Sydney Roosters’ premiership success. Walker is also weighing up interest from the Roosters’ bitter rivals, South Sydney. Roosters halfback Sam Walker has met with the Chiefs and has fielded interest from South Sydney Getty Images Raiders officials confirmed Young’s management asked for the cooling-off period to be waived, which means the Chiefs can announce their biggest forward signing to date.



Canberra had tabled Young a club-record $4.4 million four-year deal – and were prepared to go to a fifth year. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Cricket NSW says North Sydney Oval will always be off limit for the Bears The club is happy to extend Simi Sasagi, Noah Martin, Zac Hosking and Matt Nicholson. There were reports the Raiders were keen on Brisbane’s Jordan Riki and Cronulla’s Briton Nikora on 2028, but there is little interest from the club. Canberra coach Ricky Stuart is expected to meet Penrith’s four-time premiership winner Liam Martin in the coming weeks about potentially replacing Young in the back row. Martin has made it known he wants to re-commit to the Panthers, but is open to having a conversation with Stuart and moving closer to his hometown of Temora.



Canberra are in the market for middle forwards, with Wests Tigers prop Bunty Afoa put in their shop window by the Kiwi’s management team. Meanwhile, the Tigers and Manly are close to agreeing a deal for Jamal Fogarty, with the Sea Eagles prepared to pay part of the halfback’s wage the next two seasons. The Tigers have since granted Latu Fainu permission to seek a deal for 2027 only before returning to the joint venture. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Mercury cuts ribbon on Northland's $287m Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm
World.content:
Northland's first wind farm has been officially opened today as the region continues its transformation from energy importer to significant producer of renewable power.

Mercury's Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm, with 12 towers producing 77 megawatts (MW) of electricity in a good breeze, is not the biggest in the country by any means - but its turbines are by far the tallest.

Each measures 206m from ground to rotor tip, making them taller than any structure in New Zealand bar Auckland's Sky Tower.

The project, at Omamari, on the wild west coast north of Dargaville, cost $287 million.

The expected annual output of 220 gigawatt-hours (GWh) is roughly equivalent to the power used by 31,000 homes.

Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton opened the wind farm this afternoon with Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambert and Northland MP Grant McCallum.

Hamilton said the first turbines started generating power in July, with final commissioning, testing and site rehabilitation expected to continue until early 2027.

The project was on track to be completed on time and on budget.

Hamilton thanked mana whenua Te Roroa, landowner Pāmu and the Kaipara community for their support.

Getting the 80-metre-long turbine blades from Northport, on the east coast, to Dargaville and then up the west coast to Omamari was a major transportation feat. Supplied / Viv Trounson

About 180 people worked on site each day at the peak of construction. More than 250,000 hours of work had been clocked up without any serious accidents.

Kaiwaikawe boosted Mercury's generation diversity with wind farms in Northland, central North Island, Otago and Southland complementing the company's hydro and geothermal generation, Hamilton said.

"The wind blows differently across the country. Having wind farms spread across multiple regions reduces reliance on the weather in any one place, contributing to a more resilient and secure electricity system for New Zealand."

One of the objections raised when the wind farm was first mooted was its proximity to wetlands frequented by the endangered bittern or matuku-hūrepo.

The company had set up a $640,000 Bittern Management Fund to support DOC and iwi programmes protecting the birds, and made a $360,000 commitment to GPS tracking, Hamilton said.

The company was also contributing $30,000 a year to the Kaiwaikawe Community Fund.

The first two funding rounds had paid for, among other things, bikes for tamariki at Kaihu Valley School, science equipment for Dargaville Primary School and operating costs for Dargaville Menz Shed.

Just last month, Mercury opened the South Island's largest wind farm, the 46-turbine Kaiwera Downs near Gore. It cost just over $600 million, produced enough power for 96,000 homes, and was built in two stages.

Earlier this month the company broke ground on the $506m, 40-turbine Puke Kapo Hau Wind Farm in Otago.

Getting the enormous Kaiwaikawe turbine blades from Northport, on the opposite coast, to Omamari was a major transportation feat, with only one known mishap when a truck veered off a metal road into a drain.

Each blade is 80m long, making a rotor diameter of 162m.

Ngāwhā geothermal power station remains Northland's biggest producer of renewable energy. Peter de Graaf

The rise of an energy exporter

The opening of Kaiwaikawe continues Northland's evolution from a power-importing region - reliant on electricity transported large distances over vulnerable transmission lines, as seen in the 2024 pylon collapse - to a significant producer of renewable energy.

The Far North is already a net exporter of energy, thanks to Top Energy's geothermal power plant at Ngāwhā, near Kaikohe, and Lodestone Energy's Kohirā Solar Farm just outside Kaitāia.

Ngāwhā produces 57MW and operates 24 hours a day, unlike wind or solar plants.

Top Energy plans to boost its output to 89MW in coming years. Its current annual generation is around 450GWh.

Kohirā, which produces about 55GWh a year, was New Zealand's first utility-scale solar farm when it started operating in 2023.

The ability to export much more power from the Far North to Auckland, where it is most needed, is limited by a lack of capacity in the transmission lines between Kaikohe substation and Marsden Point.

There are no such issues in the Whangārei district thanks to spare capacity in the lines from Marsden Point to Auckland, built to accommodate oil-fired power stations that have long since been dismantled.

World.title: Young soldier admits giving cannabis to 'all the boys' at Burnham Military Camp
World.content:
A soldier will be dismissed from the New Zealand Defence Force after admitting to supplying cannabis to other soldiers at Canterbury's Burnham Military camp.

Private Raniera Vercoe, 21, pleaded guilty to a total of six charges in connection with selling, supplying and using cannabis between September 2024 and June last year, at a court martial on Monday.

Vercoe was ordered to serve three months in detention at the Services Correctional Establishment at Burnham and will then be dismissed.

He was charged with selling and supplying cannabis to a soldier in November and December 2024, smoking cannabis at Burnham Military Camp and in Rotorua between September 2024 and June 2025, supplying cannabis to soldiers over the same period and possessing cannabis and a cannabis grinder in June 2025.

Vercoe also admitted consuming the class B drug MDMA at an unknown location in February 2025.

The court martial heard that cannabis was smelt coming from Vercoe's room in June last year.

During a search of his room by military police, cannabis, ziplock bags and a set of scales were found and his phone was seized.

The solider was charged with smoking cannabis at Burnham Military Camp. RNZ / Anna Sargent

Cellphone analysis showed a series of message referring to supplying and using cannabis.

The summary of facts said text messages showed that Vercoe supplied at least one ounce, or 28 grams, of cannabis between September 2024 and June 2025.

The messages outlined selling small amounts of cannabis on three occasions and discussed smoking cannabis.

In a statement to military police, Vercoe admitted that various slang terms referred to cannabis.

He said he did not sell cannabis but "would give it to all the boys" and people would put money in his bank account without his knowledge.

Vercoe said a person would at times offer to buy him dinner in exchange for cannabis or "cones" he had shared with him.

In a December 2024 text message a solider inquired about getting cannabis on "tick", or asked if he was sold out.

In another text message in April 2025, Vercoe offered to supply cannabis to a solider and said he was going to "wake and bake", suggesting he was planning to smoke cannabis.

Defence lawyer Josh Lucas said that Vercoe's sentence should reflect his youth at the time of the offending.

He said Vercoe was also now a father of two and the main breadwinner for his family.

Lucas said that Vercoe had counselling relating to the offending and was drug-free.

In sentencing, Judge Jonathan Moses said using and dealing drugs within a military environment was dangerous and an extremely serious breach of standards.

World.title: WorkSafe notified after fire alarm fails during major Auckland blaze
World.content:
WorkSafe has now been notified after evacuation alarms failed to go off during a major office building blaze in downtown Auckland.

The fire took hold on Friday in the basement of seven-story ClearPoint House on Fanshawe Street with multiple explosions being witnessed and thick black smoke billowing out to street level.

Fire and Emergency told RNZ at the time it was concerning that the building's fire alarms did not sound.

Crews instead had to evacuate workers floor by floor.

WorkSafe said it was notified on Monday, but that this did not yet constitute a formal investigation.

"We are making initial enquiries to determine the circumstances," it told RNZ.

The safety regulator said it makes enquiries after each notification to find out if it fits under WorkSafe or if another agency like FENZ or a local council would be best to respond.

The alarms failing to sound was just one problem faced by first responders on Friday.

RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

The other was a fire hydrant, needed for water, having been earlier covered by roading crews.

Watercare said on Friday it would be making sure the hydrant was "fully exposed" as soon as possible.

It said it appeared the hydrant was covered during construction work and that it was looking into how and why.

Fire crews were seen digging up the roading during the fire to access the hydrant.

Fire and Emergency said on Friday crews found an 11,000 volt cable ablaze as well as two vehicles.

Lines company Vector told RNZ on Monday that FENZ was still investigating the fire's cause.

World.title: Pay equity law changes exert a 'dystopian' effect over low-paid women, says union for teacher aides
World.content:
The union for teacher aides say it is "shocking" the Government has barred pay equity reviews for 10 years, claiming last year's law changes exert a "dystopian" effect over low-paid women.

But Ministry of Education lawyers say the amended law is explicit in setting a 10-year bar to review claims, and the union cannot circumvent it.

NZEI Te Riu Roa brought a case to the Employment Court in Wellington on Monday, arguing the Ministry of Education had an obligation to ensure pay equity, including recurring reviews of previous settlements, despite the 2025 changes.

Teacher aides had a 2020 pay equity settlement - which included a three-yearly review - and union members rallied outside court on Monday, saying their pay rates in real terms had dropped in the six years' since the settlement.

Megan Vant, the lawyer for the Secretary of Education, said a specific section of the 2025 amendment limits new pay equity claims for the same group to every 10 years, apart from exceptional circumstances.

Parliament's intention was clear, she said.

Vant referred to Minister Brooke van Velden's statements in the House that short review periods made it difficult to decide whether pay differences were due to pay equity issues re-emerging, or short-term labour market issues.

"She described the ability to raise a claim again after 10 years as having a 10-year review date, and as more robust."

She also said claims required a lot of data gathering, analysis and resources for both parties, and the 10-year limit sought to address that.

While employers still had an obligation for pay equity, it was not an ongoing responsibility to update pay equity pay rates during those 10 years, Vant said.

Susan Hornsby-Geluk, co-lawyer for the Secretary of Education, said she wanted to address the "elephant in the room" of last week's High Court judgement, which found the Government breached women's rights when it scrapped dozens of pay equity claims last year.

Despite the ruling, the Employment Court still needed to apply the current law and the intention behind it, she said.

She said Justice Paul Radich's judgement confirmed no reviews could occur in a 10-year period.

"Rightly or wrongly, what the act does is for a period of 10 years is removes protections against re-emerging discrimination."

Ally Kingi at the teacher aide pay equity rally outside the Wellington District Court. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Lawyer for NZEI Peter Cranney said he felt uncomfortable arguing this case with a caretaker Government in charge.

"Here we have the Government coming into the court a few days after finding that Parliament unlawfully breached the Bill of Rights Act, and urging the Court, despite the caretaker nature of the arrangements currently in place, to take the most chilling and narrow view to this issue."

Employers still had an obligation to ensure pay equity due to another section in the Act setting out employer responsibilities, he said.

"The language of that section says [the Secretary of Education] does have [an obligation]."

The law applied to tens or hundreds of thousands of low-paid women, and in a "shocking result", prevented workers from bargaining about pay equity issues for at least 10 years, he said.

"This is not an academic issue... this is people covered by these claims that cannot live on the money they are getting.

"It removes rights, it's dystopian in its effect."

Cranney said the law changes had been a "very serious human rights issue", and sections had to be read in line with the Government's obligations under international human rights laws.

World.title: The Remarkables ski-field puts fast-track application for expansion on hold
World.content:
Queenstown ski resort The Remarkables has put its fast-track application to expand into neighbouring Doolans Basin on hold.

Owner NZSki is proposing to build the country's biggest gondola, unlocking an extra 262 hectares of south-facing ski terrain and almost doubling the resort's daily number of visitors.

In a minute published on Friday, an expert fast-track panel agreed to suspend the application for up to five months while NZSki, councils, the Department of Conservation (DOC) and Kā Rūnaka worked through unresolved legal and technical disputes.

In correspondence published on the fast-track website, DOC described Doolans Basin as an "ecologically unique basin of exceptionally high ecological importance" with an "unreplicated variety of vegetation".

"The extent of the required earthworks alone is massive and will traverse, and have irreversible effects on the ecology of some extraordinary and extreme natural landforms," it said.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6397505343112

DOC said NZSki's plans to turn a tarn into a snow-making reservoir would destroy what it regarded as a high-value wetland, while NZSki argued it was merely a rock and gravel depression.

DOC also questioned NZSki's plans to use progressive vegetation trimming to discourage native McCann's skinks from the construction zone, saying they should be salvaged by hand.

Otago Regional Council said it wanted more information on the project's impact on freshwater ecosystems, including downstream fish habitats.

Kā Rūnaka listed 12 key concerns, including potential breaches of the Ngāi Tahu Treaty settlement, inadequate assessment of cultural effects and the impact on taonga wildlife.

Doolans Basin has long been a popular destination for backcountry skiers and other alpine recreationists. RNZ / Katie Todd

'Indisputable' recreational and economic benefits

NZSki chief executive Paul Anderson said the company wanted to work with DOC and Kā Rūnaka to make sure they trusted its expertise.

"We've been operating on the Remarkables now for four decades so we've got a lot of experience doing development in ecologically sensitive areas and rehabilitating those areas for any impacts," he said.

"A study done in 2020 on the 40-year impact of the ski area on the Remarkables found that there's been no known loss of a rare or threatened plant or animal."

NZSki CEO Paul Anderson at The Remarkables. Supplied/Nick Gibbard

Anderson said the company was willing to consider alternative methods for skink relocation but it felt using the tarn as a water reservoir was the "least impactful way to do snow-making".

In response to Otago Regional Council's comments, Anderson said the effects on waterways were expected to be "extremely minimal, if any impact at all".

The company respected iwi concerns and wanted to have a "really strong partnership that lasts for decades" with Kā Rūnaka, he said.

Anderson said NZSki planned to extend its existing conservation programmes to the basin, including predator and weed control.

He said the Remarkables Conservation Area covered 33,000 hectares and NZSki was seeking permission to use 262 hectares.

"It's a very, very tiny part of the entire estate," he said.

In its application, NZSki said the expansion would almost double the resort's capacity to 6000 visitors at a time, with flow-on effects for the local economy.

The company said the expansion would increase local visitor spending by at least $112 million per year within 10 years of completion.

"The economic benefits and the benefits to our community's recreation opportunities are indisputable," Anderson said.

Doolans Basin, where NZSki is proposing to expand The Remarkables ski area. RNZ / Katie Todd

Fears over backcountry ski access

Companies that have long used Doolans Basin for backcountry ski touring have also pushed back on NZSki's plans.

Queenstown Mountain Guides wrote to the expert panel urging it to decline the application.

The company said there were few other places nearby that offered high-quality beginner and intermediate ski touring without requiring long approaches or a helicopter.

It said NZSki's own recreation assessment had rated the effect on backcountry ski sports as "very high or high", yet NZSki had not quantified the potential losses to local guides with existing DOC permits.

Anderson said the gondola would improve backcountry access, enabling tourers to venture further into the basin.

"We've got a really strong relationship with Queenstown Mountain Guides. They actually access The Remarkables using our access road and crossing our private land at the bottom of the mountain and we will continue to enable that access," he said.

NZSki was asked to submit a progress report to the expert panel by 29 January, detailing which technical and legal disputes had been resolved.

It would then need to file a memorandum to resume processing its application within 100 working days of the 20 November start date - by 20 April 2027.

Anderson said NZSki was aiming for closer to 60 days, or mid-February.

World.title: Former Silver Fern captain Julie Carter dies, aged 60
World.content:
Netball New Zealand says it's deeply saddened by the death of former Silver Ferns captain Julie Carter, aged 60.

A crafty goal attack, who could also slot in at wing attack, Carter played 50 Tests for New Zealand between 1986 and 1993.

She became the Silver Ferns' 16th captain when she took up the role in late 1992.

Carter first rose to prominence through the schoolgirl ranks in Waikato, where she was earmarked early as a future Silver Fern.

In 1986 she made her debut for the national side. After missing selection in 1987, she bounced straight back and became a regular in the black dress from 1988 to 1993.

As captain she led the Silver Ferns to 10 wins from 11 Tests, a record that reflected both her leadership and her competitive drive.

Carter is the second former Silver Fern captain to have died this year. In August, former Silver Fern captain Ana Noovao died aged 58, after a long illness.

Noovao, a midcourter, played for New Zealand between 1989 and 1992 and was named the 15th captain of the Silver Ferns, who she led for six Tests in 1992.

Julie Carter, Southern Sting, Coca Cola Cup netball in 1999. Scott Barbour / www.photosport.nz

Carter's career spanned a period of change for the Silver Ferns, and she played a key part in building the foundations of a new era for the team.

Her career highlights included representing New Zealand in the demonstration match at the 1990 Commonwealth Games in Auckland, being a member of the Silver Ferns team that won silver at the 1991 World Championships in Sydney and winning a gold medal at the 1989 World Games in Germany.

Silver Fern #80 was known as one of the great thinkers of the game and was tough and uncompromising under the goal, while setting high standards for herself and those around her.

Carter played her domestic netball for Waikato before moving to Wellington in 1990. She later made the move further south and in 1998 and 1999 played for the Southern Sting in the Coca Cola Cup. Her side won the title in 1999 against the defending champion Otago Rebels.

After retiring, she remained involved in netball as a coach and inspiring the next generation of players.

World.title: Lead detected in fish caught near Saipan lagoon
World.content:
Northern Mariannas authorities are investigating after lead was detected in a sample of fish caught near Tanapag in Saipan's lagoon.

The Bureau of Environmental and Coastal Quality says the metal was found in a sample of triggerfish, locally known as pulonon.

This occurred during testing conducted for a wider study of marine contamination around Saipan.

It has prompted health and environmental authorities in the Northern Mariana Islands to investigate possible risks to people who regularly eat locally caught seafood.

The findings were released last week, following the collection of 186 fish from 40 locations around the island in August and September last year.

No advisory yet against eating local fish

The study covered 19 species commonly caught or eaten by residents and was partly prompted by longstanding concerns over pollutants left behind by World War II and subsequent activities.

Chromium was also detected in 20 of the 40 samples tested, although authorities said the laboratory could not determine whether it was the more harmful form of the metal.

Copper and zinc were detected at levels considered low, while cadmium was not found in any sample.

Further laboratory results for other metals and chemicals are still pending.

Authorities say additional testing near Tanapag may be needed but have stressed that no advisory against eating local fish has been issued.

The Bureau said the findings remain preliminary and do not mean locally caught fish are unsafe to eat.

However, authorities are paying particular attention to possible lead exposure, especially among young children and pregnant women.

World.title: 'Fundamentally broken': CEO says tax rules favour multinationals over locals
World.content:
Audio player for " DeliverEasy is calling on Uber Eats to pay their fare share " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2750054%2Ffundamentally-broken-ceo-says-tax-rules-favour-multinationals-over-locals

DeliverEasy is calling on Uber Eats to pay their fare share Midday Report Download MP3 6m

The boss of a locally owned food delivery company says the tax system is "fundamentally broken" after finding out it is paying four times as much tax as Uber Eats, on a fraction of the revenue.

Documents filed by Portier New Zealand Limited, which operates Uber Eats, show it generated more than $1.16 billion in revenue over the past four years, but recorded only $945,000 in net income tax expenses.

Over that same period, Delivereasy generated $118 million - one-tenth what Uber Eats managed - but paid more than $4m in tax, more than four times as much.

"The way that Uber - and a lot of multinational tech companies as well, I guess - orchestrate this is through something called an intercompany service fee," Delivereasy chief executive Tim Robinson told Midday Report.

"So when companies like Uber or Google or Amazon operate in New Zealand... they can pay back basically a service fee for the use of the technology or the use of the brand."

In 2025, Portier's accounts show a gross profit of $143.7m in New Zealand, but it paid $140.2m of that in intercompany service fees, leaving an on-paper profit before tax of just $2.6m.

Robinson said the company effectively decides what its fees are, and sends that "to other countries where the tax rate is lower than New Zealand".

While legal, Robinson said it created an unfair situation where multinationals like Uber could avoid income tax local providers could not, and use that advantage to undercut rivals on pricing.

The previous Labour government was looking to level the playing field with a digital services tax, which would target companies on revenue, not profit. It was projected to bring in up to $146m a year, but was dropped by the coalition government.

Delivereasy started the year before Uber Eats arrived in New Zealand. Supplied / Delivereasy

Robinson said while it was a valid solution, there were already rules around intercompany transfer fees that could be beefed up or better enforced.

"We probably need to look at strengthening the rules we've got in place at the moment and being really explicit about what can be charged back and what can't be and how these companies are calculating these fees, because at the moment it's very coincidental... Almost all of their profits is the same number."

Delivereasy started in 2016, a year before Uber Eats launched in New Zealand.

Uber has in the past repeatedly said it complies with its tax obligations. It has been approached for comment.

In cancelling the digital services tax, Revenue Minister Simon Watts at the time said the previous Labour government had introduced the bill in 2023 because of a perceived lack of progress from other countries in developing a similar measure - but the situation had since changed.

"A global solution has always been our preferred option, and we have been encouraged by the recent commitment of countries to the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development] work in this area," he said.

World.title: Joeys come back to Earth with frustrating World Cup result
World.content:
The Joeys have been left facing a slightly nervy final group match before guaranteeing their spot in the knockout stages at the Under-17 World Cup following a frustrating goalless draw against Denmark.

Australia's bright soccer teenagers, who had begun so sparkly with Akol Akon inspiring them to a 2-0 victory over Argentina in Doha, were brought down to Earth somewhat as they dominated possession and chances against the Danes only to draw a blank.

The Joeys could not quite find the killer blow against the Danes. (Getty Images: Lewis Storey )

With Argentina bouncing back to beat Mozambique 2-1 later on Sunday, local time, the outcome of group C is not cut and dried going into the final round of pool games on Wednesday.

Australia still leads the way on four points, with Argentina and Mozambique both on three and Denmark on one.

Just a draw against Mozambique would guarantee a top-two place in the group and give Carl Veart's players a place in the last 32, while even defeat to the African side might not be calamitous because the 48-team format awards places to the eight best third-place finishers.

Young Aussies stun Argentina Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon inspires the Joeys to a shock 2–0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style in Qatar.

But Australia will still want to deliver a better display than the one it produced against Denmark, which was hammered 4-0 by Mozambique in its opening outing.

Brisbane's 17-year-old box-to-box midfielder Emmett Shaw was named the player-of-the match but he will rue missing the best chance of the match when he should have sunk a free header in the 74th minute while unmarked.

While Australia enjoyed 66 per cent of possession, it took it 55 minutes to get a shot on target, with Shaw's long-range free-kick proving far too hopeful, although Akon did come closer with a curling free kick in the 69th minute.

Impressive young Brighton keeper Charlie Wilson-Papps did not have a great deal to do but, when really called on in the 83rd minute, he got down sharply to make a key stop to thwart a low shot, Denmark's best chance of the match.

AAP

World.title: In F1's 'most chaotic race ever', Piastri finally able to find his mojo
World.content:
With a beaming grin from ear to ear, covered in champagne and looking like a man who had a weight lifted off his shoulders, Oscar Piastri summed up his stunning Las Vegas Grand Prix in six words: "It was a lot of fun."

2026 has not been Piastri's year, and of the top drivers in F1, he has had the most disappointing season.

But on the Las Vegas Strip, in a grand prix that teammate Lando Norris called the "most chaotic race ever", Piastri found his mojo, and has allowed himself the chance to finish 2026 with a bang.

Piastri third, snaps at McLaren team, in Vegas GP with 352 overtakes Oscar Piastri produces his finest performance of the 2026 season, claiming a sensational podium in Las Vegas after starting 17th on the grid.

Following on from the bitter disappointment of losing out in last year's thrilling world championship fight to Norris, Piastri's 2026 season started horribly, and never really got any better.

The soaring highs of leading the championship in 2025 felt like a distant memory when he failed to start the opening two races this season.

But a second-place finish in Japan and third in Miami — rounds three and four of the season — gave a false hope that Piastri could be in contention again in 2026.

It wasn't to be.

Piastri would not be on the podium in the next 16 grands prix, the longest streak of his F1 career.

Meanwhile, Norris claimed three brilliant race wins and is fighting to finish third in the championship, while Piastri languishes in seventh.

The Las Vegas Grand Prix, on paper, should have been like the rest of Piastri's 2026 — a struggle.

He qualified seventh, took a penalty for adding a new internal combustion engine to his power unit, and started a lowly 17th on the grid.

What followed was tremendous racecraft, as Piastri sliced his way through the field.

Oscar Piastri's third place finish in Las Vegas was his first podium since Miami, 17 rounds ago. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Alastair Staley)

In a race where the field was pretty much bunched up for all 50 laps, and with a ridiculous 352 overtakes across the grand prix, Piastri made sure he was going forward more than he was going backwards.

He didn't have it all his own way. He was behind his teammate when the safety car was called and dropped from ninth to 13th while he had to wait for Norris to pit first.

That still didn't matter.

Piastri just went back to work, picking off his rivals one by one, until the most unlikely of podiums was in sight.

He had a bit of luck to get there. George Russell hitting the wall, and Kimi Antonelli losing battery power late in the race cleared the path for Piastri's podium finish — but the Victorian had made his own luck.

And luck is something he has had little of in 2026.

Asked post-race if he had turned a corner, and could eye off bigger and better things in 2027, Piastri, as usual, remained grounded.

"It's hard to say. I think the pace in general was pretty strong, so I was happy," her said.

"But that was such a particular race — the next two weeks are not going to look like that."

He's right. The next two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will not look like the frantic, action-packed, drama-filled grand prix in Las Vegas.

But history suggests there could be at least one similarity — Piastri on the podium.

Piastri's first win in F1 was the Qatar sprint race in 2024, and he went on to finish third in the grand prix.

Last year he again won the sprint race, and should have won the grand prix had it not been for a disastrous pit strategy by McLaren, which practically handed the race win to Max Verstappen. Piastri still finished second that day.

Now he goes into a track that, statistically, he is exceptional at, and has confidence following one of the best drives from anyone this season.

Piastri also has success at Abu Dhabi, with a best finish of second, which he achieved last year. He started on the front row there as well in 2024, but was taken out by Verstappen on the first lap.

He is heading to tracks he enjoys, and where he has enjoyed great results.

His Las Vegas podium does not mean he has turned the corner, and Piastri is the first to acknowledge that.

But the terrific performance could not have come at a better time, and could be the first step in his rise back to the top.

World.title: How Prespakis and Rowbottom are leading new era of AFLW stars
World.content:
Since the AFLW was made an 18-team competition, much speculation heading into the league's night of nights has been whether star Roo Jasmine Garner will earn the recognition she deserves.

Where in the past it has been players who have been around from the competition's inception who were the top vote-getters in the AFLW Best and Fairest Award — eight of the 10 winners to date were listed in the first two seasons — this year it is the top two draftees from the 2021 draft who are shaping up as the best chance at winning on Monday evening.

Garner is still a genuine chance at the medal, as is Sydney dynamo Chloe Molloy, but it is Charlie Rowbottom and Georgie Prespakis who are deemed the genuine frontrunners.

Ahead of that draft night in 2021, Rowbottom made waves by nominating the Queensland draft pool — obviously, before there was a truly national draft — and as a result, was taken with the first pick by Gold Coast. That left the other top pick contender, Prespakis, to fall to Geelong at number two.

Both have been vital cogs of their respective midfields across their seven seasons, and although some raw numbers do look very similar, the way they play their footy could not be more different.

What looks similar

As pure ball winners, both Prespakis and Rowbottom have been right at the top of the league throughout the home-and-away season.

They have each attended the most average centre stoppages for their respective sides, and therefore their average contested possession and clearance numbers also sit first and second across the league.

Georgie Prespakis (AFLW rank) Charlie Rowbottom (AFLW rank) Avg. Disposals 30.6 (sixth) 32.6 (second) Avg. Handballs 17.3 (second) 16.8 (third) Avg. Contested Possessions 17.6 (first) 17.3 (second) Avg. Clearances 8.1 (first) 7.9 (second) Avg. Hard Ball Gets 5.2 (first) 4.9 (second)

Each strong at the source, they are key starting points for their respective teams' attack. They have both played every game this season — for teams that reached finals for the first time since 2023, no less — and regularly starred along the way.

What is different

After that first phase of play, however, each player prioritises differently. Rowbottom tends to remain a tough, defensive option, bringing her physicality, while Prespakis is that sleek runner taking the ball forward.

Charlie Rowbottom has been a leader in the Gold Coast midfield this season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

The Gold Coast star is staunch in tight, choosing to release her running teammates like Niamh McLaughin, Ava Usher, and Lucy Single.

Her capacity to be the big body drawing attention that ultimately creates space for those on the outside was critical to the Suns' game plan this year, which averaged nearly four more goals per game in 2026 than it did in 2025.

So, for Rowbottom, the numbers that stand out in addition to those above are her average tackles (6.2) and marks (3.6), while she also pressed forward to kick a career-best five goals.

She is not a player who repeatedly gets involved in a transitional passage of play; rather, she is often the starting point and has developed the capacity to become the end point more reliably.

She finished with five or more tackles in seven of her games, and 10 or more clearances in four of those.

Prespakis is more of that player who remains involved in running handball chains to set up those inside her team's attacking 50. She was the number one score involvement player across the AFLW in the season, sits first for average loose ball gets (7.6) and sixth for average metres gained (428.2).

No-one playing in the AFLW has more score involvements than Georgie Prespakis this season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Adam Trafford)

Her clearance game is more about her agility to evade danger and run the ball out, with her handball numbers more indicative of those back-and-forths as she and teammates dash up the field.

This resulted in six home and away games with eight or more score involvements, and seven recording 400 or more metres gained.

This style of play was emblematic of how the Cats played their footy this year. Fast, predictable to one another, and with every intention to take the game forward.

Georgie Prespakis Charlie Rowbottom Avg. Tackles 5.1 6.2 Avg. Marks 2.5 3.6 Avg. Intercepts 5.2 3.9 Avg. Metres Gained 428.2 328.3

For an effective midfield to operate, each style of midfielder is necessary: the big-bodied contested beast, and the dashing metres-gained player. It is fair to say that — maybe except Garner herself — each of Prespakis and Rowbottom has been the best of their respective style of midfielder this year.

Should one of the pair claim the medal on Monday night, it would be a key signifier of this fresh era of the AFLW, leaning on those players who have enjoyed greater junior pathway opportunities, and greater support in their talent development at the elite level.

World.title: CA says Cummins backing not a sign it is taking sides in sandpaper spat
World.content:
Todd Greenberg insists Cricket Australia has not taken Pat Cummins's side in the ball-tampering saga, adamant that keeping the quick as Test captain should not deter others from contributing to the upcoming truth forum.

Cummins is expected to train again at the SCG early this week, as he and the fellow pacemen press on with their preparations for the first Test against New Zealand starting on December 9.

The 33-year-old confirmed on Saturday he would contribute to CA's independent forum, and make his own submissions over the events of the 2018 South Africa tour.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

It is expected the quick will deny any prior knowledge of the use of sandpaper on the ball on that tour until Cameron Bancroft was caught in Cape Town, a position the bowlers have maintained since that day.

Officials will lay out the parameters for the forum in the coming days, but have already made clear there will be no further sanctions, regardless of the findings.

There had initially been a fear that only those with an axe to grind may contribute, following claims by Usman Khawaja and Bancroft that the entire team knew of the ball-tampering plot.

David Warner and Chadd Sayers have also backed the claims raised in Khawaja's book, which kicked off the renewed furore a month ago.

But Cricket Australia CEO Greenberg has now had to deny that the CA board publicly standing by Cummins to remain captain on Saturday had swung it back in the other direction, and dissuaded those with opposing views.

Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg says the organisation is not picking sides amid the reignited Sandpapergate furore. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )

"I don't see it that way, because I support their version of events and their ability to share what they think happened at that period of time," Greenberg told the BBC.

"That's their version. Equally, that's Pat's version as well.

"I am not putting someone's version of events over somebody else's. That's the one thing we're not doing.

"Pat has been the captain for five years, we haven't made any changes.

"If we were to, that would believe someone's events over the others."

Then-Australian coach Darren Lehmann has repeatedly denied prior knowledge of the plot to use sandpaper in Cape Town. (Jason McCawley - CA/Cricket Australia via Getty Images)

Beyond Cummins, then-coach Darren Lehmann has also indicated he will contribute, after denying Bancroft's assertions that he was aware of the plot on Saturday night.

Greenberg also maintained that the board's unanimous support of Cummins did not mean they thought Khawaja or Bancroft were lying.

Asked what would happen if the majority of the 2018 touring party — including staff and players — claimed everyone knew, Greenberg suggested nothing would change.

"Then so be it," Greenberg said.

"We're going in with an open mind and without providing sanctions."

Steve Smith received a heroes welcome at the SCG when he lined up for New South Wales in the Sheffield Shield on Sunday. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Former CA board member Michael Kasprowicz reiterated on Monday that the 2018 bans handed down to Steve Smith, Warner and Bancroft were not solely related to tampering.

Kasprowicz was a director in 2018 when CA's investigation found the trio were the only three to know of the plot.

"I am not sure it is actually about sandpaper, because the umpires didn't even change the ball," Kasprowicz told AAP.

"I know from a board point of view at the time, it wasn't about damaging the ball. It was about damaging the brand.

"That's why steps had to be made in those circumstances."

Usman Khawaja (left) will link up with Darren Lehmann (right) during an exhibition T20 clash in Cairns on Sunday night. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Kasprowicz is due to link up with both Khawaja and Lehmann in the celebrity cricket Gold Clash in Cairns on Sunday night.

Asked if he believed the sanctions may have been different had Khawaja or Bancroft given their most recent accounts then, Kasprowicz was uncertain.

"I don't know, eight years ago is eight years ago," the 38-Test seamer said.

"Your receipts and tax records only last for seven and you have to chuck them.

"That's why I am thinking what is going on right now is even more extraordinary."

Cricket on Sunday attempted to move on from the Sandpapergate saga, with Steve Smith returning from his neck injury to the Sheffield Shield alongside Nathan Lyon.

Smith spent most of the day fielding at slip for NSW, taking a catch to remove Test hopeful Jack Clayton on 10 in the middle session at the SCG.

He also bowled two overs of leg spin in the final session, to strong applause from a crowd of just under 2,000 at the SCG.

AAP

World.title: Horne-Francis planning to recruit Nasiah during AFL Origin camp
World.content:
Jason Horne-Francis is open to throwing his weight around in South Australia's AFL Origin camp to recruit St Kilda superstar and friend Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera.

South Australia and Western Australia today named their first five representatives for next year's Origin match, to be played at Perth Stadium on February 27.

Wanganeen-Milera and Port Adelaide's Horne-Francis were picked by SA coach Craig McRae, along with Saints co-captain Callum Wilkie, Adelaide skipper Jordan Dawson and Collingwood boom recruit Lachie Neale.

Players committed to 2027 AFL Origin SOUTH AUSTRALIA: Jason Horne-Francis, Callum Wilkie, Lachie Neale, Jordan Dawson, Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera WESTERN AUSTRALIA: Patrick Cripps, Charlie Cameron, Kysaiah Pickett, Luke Jackson, Tom Barrass

Wanganeen-Milera rejected massive interest from his native South Australia in 2025 to re-sign on a two-season, $4 million deal with the Saints.

Locking away the silky 23-year-old playmaker on an extension is top of St Kilda's agenda.

This year's Origin revival match between WA and Victoria allowed Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli to build a connection with Zak Butters, who crossed from Port Adelaide in the off-season.

While already mates with Wanganeen-Milera, Horne-Francis is mindful of the recruitment opportunity Origin camp presents.

"That worked, didn't it," he told reporters, referring to the Butters-Bontempelli connection developed through Victoria's Origin team.

Marcus Bontempelli (background) successfully recruited Victorian teammate Zak Butters (foreground) to the Western Bulldogs. (Daniel Carson/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

"So maybe I've got to try to do the same thing. Not that we need any more bonding time — we see each other bloody all the time anyway.

"We ran out together in the [Indigenous] All-Stars as well, so it will be good to run out with him again and see what he's got for us."

The 23-year-old admitted he might have to battle with Crows rivals to wrap an arm around Wanganeen-Milera, who finished fourth in St Kilda's best-and-fairest this season.

"There might be a bit of push and shove there," the Port ball-winner said.

St KIlda star Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera is once again in high demand as he comes out of contract. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Horne-Francis and other Adelaide-based SA representatives may have to go through Wilkie to get some alone time with Wanganeen-Milera.

"I won't let him talk to Dawson or anyone from Port," Wilkie joked.

"He'll stay right under my wing.

"Nas is amazing at putting that [contract speculation] to bed and focusing on us and what he brings to the club on field and off field."

Wilkie said he and Wanganeen-Milera had been speaking about the possibility of donning the SA jumper all year.

Collingwood coach Craig McRae will lead Wanganeen-Milera and South Australia in the Origin clash. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"That's what's so special about it," he said.

"You think when you're getting drafted you're never going to be able to pull the colours on again."

WA coach Dean Cox's first selections are Hawthorn defender Tom Barrass, Brisbane forward Charlie Cameron, Carlton skipper Patrick Cripps, Fremantle ruck Luke Jackson and Melbourne livewire Kysaiah Pickett.

Cripps, who captained WA against Victoria this year, is also due to come off contract at the end of next season.

Carlton captain Patrick Cripps has no plans to finish his AFL career in WA. (Getty images/AFL Photos: Matt King)

But the dual Brownlow Medal winner hosed down the possibility of finishing his illustrious career in his home state after the Blues made the finals under now-permanent coach Josh Fraser, despite starting last season 1-8.

"I've been here that long, you sort of become ingrained in the club," Cripps said.

"I sort of feel like a Carlton supporter these days … this is my 14th season.

"I've always loved playing footy at Carlton and been driven to try and build the club from the ground up, and I'm really excited about where we are right now."

AAP

World.title: India breaks New Zealand Test record with monster innings in Wellington
World.content:
India has broken the record for the highest Test score in a match played in New Zealand as it put itself in a commanding position to win the first Test in Wellington.

New Zealand reached 2-119 at the close of play on day four as it fought to save the first Test after India declared on a mammoth 9-720 with an imposing first-innings lead of 352.

India's assault was led by Rishabh Pant (128), whose six sixes took his career tally to 108 in just 53 Tests, now second behind all-time best Ben Stokes (138). Pant surpassed former NZ captain Brendon McCullum (107) during the innings.

New Zealand's hopes of a result rest on batting for much of the remainder of the match and forcing a draw, despite losing Tom Latham for a duck and first-innings centurion Henry Nicholls for 31.

Opener Devon Conway, who scored his 22nd Test half-century on his way to an unbeaten 59, and Rachin Ravindra (27 not out) will resume on day five with the Black Caps still 233 runs from forcing India to bat again.

India's pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah (1-33) again made an early breakthrough, sending Latham back on the second ball of the innings, the New Zealand skipper edging behind to take a pair.

Nicholls, whose 175 was the backbone of New Zealand's first-innings 368, got an edge and a bit of thigh pad on a Prasidh Krishna delivery, and Dhruv Jurel showed stunning reflexes to take the catch at short leg.

Jurel had earlier become the sixth batter to score a half-century in India's innings before being caught in the deep for 78, triggering the declaration an hour before tea.

India had resumed on 4-486 on another sunny morning at the Basin Reserve with the clear intent of pushing their 118-run lead out to the sort of tally that would take the possibility of a New Zealand victory out of the equation.

There are few better batters for such a task than Pant, and the swashbuckling wicketkeeper showed the full range of his shots as he approached his ninth Test hundred.

Pant was finally caught on the boundary for 128 off the bowling of Ravindra to bring up lunch, but the punishment for New Zealand continued into the second session.

Jacob Duffy finished with 1-201 off 33 overs. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

India's final score was well clear of its previous best innings tally in New Zealand of 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009 — a match they won by 10 wickets.

All-rounder Glenn Phillips (3-154) picked a couple of wickets as the Indian batters went for their shots ahead of the declaration to make his figures a bit more respectable.

Seamer Jacob Duffy, though, finished with unenviable figures of 1-201 from his 33 overs, only 28 runs shy of New Zealand's most expensive ever bowling display, which spinner Stephen Boock tallied against Pakistan in 1989.

Reuters

World.title: Wallabies still have a pulse despite nervous moments in win over Wales
World.content:
In Les Kiss's words, the Wallabies "earned their corn" with their gritty 29-26 Nations Championship win over Wales in Cardiff.

After ending a four-match losing streak, the Wallabies coach struck a relieved but proud figure when he and captain Harry Wilson fronted the post-match media conference.

It couldn't be described as a polished display on the field, nor was there a moment during the match where it seemed the Wallabies were dominating their opposition.

Each time they opened up an encouraging lead on the scoreboard, it never felt as though Wales was too far away from clawing its way back into the contest.

Wallabies defeat Wales The Wallabies hold on to defeat Wales 29-26 following a thrilling finish to their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

But winning breeds confidence, which had been in short supply for the Wallabies following losses to New Zealand (twice), England and Scotland.

"They had to work hard for it and I think tonight was a true Test match [and] they earned their corn and got what they deserved," Kiss said.

An improved defensive effort was among the positives in the Wallabies' performance.

While three of the four tries they conceded came from driving mauls off line-outs, they denied Wales more than once with their scramble defence deep inside the 22.

"When we do it [defence] well, it's a real point of difference for us," Wilson said.

"I thought our D-zone [inside 22] defence tonight was unbelievable."

The Wallabies' aerial game in attack also showed glimpses of its potential, with Max Jorgensen's second-half try an example of the pressure they can apply to opposition teams.

The line-out was strong (they enjoyed a clean sheet on their throw), highlighted by Josh Canham's clutch steal when Wales was camped inside the Wallabies' 22 during the first half.

Wallabies lock Josh Canham (right) enjoyed an excellent all-round performance. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

But the Wallabies let themselves down with poor discipline, especially inside their territory.

They conceded nine penalties in the opening 40 minutes, seven of which were on their side of the halfway line.

By full-time, the Wallabies had given 11 penalties away inside their half, with Wilson shown a yellow card in the 77th minute for one of those indiscretions.

If the Wallabies do the same against Ireland at Twickenham next weekend, they won't be shown any leniency.

Kiss admits the Wallabies' penalty count gave him "the shits".

"Discipline was a little bit disappointing, I must say … it kept them [Wales] in the game with field position and a few things like that," he said.

"So we're going to have to look at that as well."

Ikitau to the fore

Among individual performances, Carter Gordon looked assured at fly half.

The Wallabies were still pedestrian at times with ball in hand, however Gordon did enough to indicate he's the most suitable candidate to wear the number 10 jersey.

Wallabies fly half Carter Gordon looked solid against Wales. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Len Ikitau was deservedly named player of the match, again proving he's a world-class operator.

But the question remains whether he's better suited to inside or outside centre.

When the Wallabies pulled off their upset 42-38 win over the world champion Springboks in Perth in September, his performance at outside was superb until he left the field injured.

On that occasion, he was partnered in the centres by Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable for the Wallabies' Nations Championship campaign in Great Britain.

Ikitau played inside centre against Wales, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii admirably slotting in at 13.

Len Ikitau was outstanding in the Wallabies' win. (Getty Images/CameraSport: Ian Cook)

A permanent Ikitau-Paisami midfield combination may be the Wallabies' best option at next year's Rugby World Cup, although Suaalii's stocks at outside centre rose in Cardiff, even though he appears more comfortable on the wing.

For now, the Wallabies will turn their focus to the Ireland Test, which pits the two third-ranked teams from the respective Nations Championship groups against each other.

Their spirits will be buoyed by halting their losing streak, but Kiss knows the pressure of Test rugby never lets up.

"Test match footy doesn't hand you things easy," Kiss said.

World.title: Bellamy to end Storm coaching stint after 2027 NRL season
World.content:
Melbourne can officially begin planning for life after Craig Bellamy, after the veteran coach confirmed the longest tenure in NRL premiership history would end in 2027.

After years of speculation about his future, Bellamy will officially finish with the Storm next year at the end of his 25th season in charge of the club.

The 67-year-old's call to walk away comes after he was diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder this year.

Craig Bellamy's coaching CV NRL - Brisbane Broncos (2002): Two matches, one win, one loss

NRL - Melbourne Storm (2003-current): 630 matches, 433 wins, 195 losses, two draws

NRL premierships: 2012, 2017, 2020 (all with Storm)

State of Origin - New South Wales (2008-10): Nine matches, two wins, seven losses

But he still hopes to play some role around the club after 2027, with the five-time premiership-winning coach the most powerful figure in the Storm's history.

"I love this club and everything it represents, the people, our history and our fans," Bellamy said.

"I still have huge passion for the job, and I'm excited about what we can achieve together in 2027.

"While 2027 will be my final season as senior coach, I'm determined to make the most of the opportunity and give everything I can to our club and our players.

"I've always said I'll continue coaching while I believe I can make a positive contribution, and I feel I can still do that.

"I also feel the time is right to make 2027 my final year."

Cameron Munster is one of several big-name Storm stars who are off-contract at the end of the 2027 season. (Getty Images: Pete Dovgan/Speed Media/Icon Sportswire)

Bellamy's decision to officially call stumps comes after chief executive Justin Rodksi admitted on Friday the uncertain future had complicated contract talks with the club's biggest names.

Harry Grant, Cameron Munster and Stefano Utoikamanu are all off-contract at the end of 2027, with the Storm facing an uphill fight to retain all three.

Melbourne hasn't been able to provide clarity on who will coach the club in 2028, unable to officially move on appointing a successor until Bellamy had decided his future.

Billy Slater remains the biggest name linked with Melbourne after he walked away from the Queensland State of Origin job in August.

Billy Slater is the highest-profile name tipped to be Bellamy's successor for the Storm. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Slater does sit on Melbourne's part-time staff, but has so far suggested he does not want to coach in the NRL.

Bellamy also declared in August that Melbourne's next coach should come from within, with Marc Brentnall, Ryan Hinchliffe and Bellamy's son Aaron his full-time assistants.

Brad Arthur, Michael Maguire, Anthony Seibold and Jason Ryles are among coaches to have come out of Bellamy's system in Melbourne.

Arthur is currently coaching Leeds in the Super League, but has signalled a desire to return to the NRL, while Maguire is under pressure at the Broncos.

Ryles is on the verge of signing an extension at Parramatta, while Seibold is a free agent after being sacked by Manly last season.

"Craig is one of the greatest coaches in the history of rugby league, and we're proud of everything he has achieved in the game," Storm chairman Matthew Tripp said.

"We're also delighted he'll have one final season in charge in 2027.

"While we would obviously love to have Craig coaching our team forever, we understand how significant this decision is and are incredibly grateful that we will have another season with him leading our club."

AAP

Tech.title: Kodak’s next collectible is a tiny digital photo frame that doubles as a tracker
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After expanding its Charmera collection with a Millennium Edition featuring Y2K-inspired designs earlier this year, Reto’s follow-up to its tiny Kodak camera is an equally small digital photo frame you can use to display your shots. But while the Charmera’s usefulness stopped at snapping grainy photos and terrible videos, the Kodak SlideTag goes one step further. It also functions as a Bluetooth tracker that’s compatible with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks.

The Kodak SlideTag will be available for $34.99 each and, like the Charmera, will feature a series of retro designs distributed in mystery boxes so you don’t know which one you’re going to get. Kodak also sells a complete set of all eight vintage designs for $279.92 if you don’t like mysteries; however, there’s a ninth “secret edition” only available in the individual boxes with a sleek metallic finish.

The SlideTag is a bit smaller than a classic Kodak film slide, but far more functional and versatile. Image: Reto

For those who grew up in an era where projectors are small enough to integrate into phones, the SlideTag is designed to look like a modernized version of the film slides that were used to project photos decades ago. Instead of film, the SlideTag features a 1.54-inch color E Ink screen that mixes six colored inks to display photos at a resolution of 240 x 240.

Illustrations with bold, defined colors will translate best to the SlideTag’s color E Ink screen. Image: Reto

The color reproduction won’t be as accurate as an LCD or OLED screen, but the SlideTag can hold and cycle up to 12 photos transferred to the device over Bluetooth from Kodak’s Memory Link app running on a mobile device. You can also use it to display a short to-do list, contact details, a countdown timer, or a QR code linking to wherever you want.

As a tracker it’s not quite as functional as an Apple AirTag or Google’s Pixel Tag, which use features like ultra wideband (UWB) and Channel Sounding to make them easier to find. The SlideTag sticks to basic Bluetooth with a range of up to 30 meters out in the open and a 75-decibel buzzer to help locate it when you’re close. Battery life will vary depending on how frequently you use tracking features or refresh the displayed image, but the SlideTag uses a common CR2032 coin cell battery that’s easy to replace.

Tech.title: We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN:

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”

Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages on CBS News’ Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, but sounded a much more ominous tone.

“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”

While the outages over the last week were not believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.

The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets.

Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

Update November 22nd: Added clarification that Smith was speaking on Face the Nation, not to CBS generally. Due to a typo, this article originally stated that the outages were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, the missing word has been corrected.

Tech.title: Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage
Tech.content:
The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.

“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

Tech.title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.

Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.

Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

Tech.title: Some of our favorite Switch 2 games are cheaper through Black Friday
Tech.content: Black Friday is a great time to expand your game library because it’s a chance to catch deals that aren’t normally happening throughout the year. That’s true for Nintendo Switch 2 games, as well. In addition to a $50 off sale on one of its console bundles, Nintendo is also knocking $20 off some of the Switch 2’s best titles.
